# Mote rules

<!-- Generated by `mote rules --all --format markdown`; do not edit by hand. -->

552 rules, 485 enabled by default. Severity: **HIGH** — almost certainly a bug or a serious reliability hazard; **MEDIUM** — a likely problem or a significant maintainability cost; **LOW** — minor or stylistic. The default quality gate fails a pull request on new HIGH findings only. Change severities, parameters and enablement in `.mote.yaml` (`mote config explain <file>` shows the effective settings).

- [Java](#java) — 326 rules
- [JavaScript / TypeScript](#javascript--typescript) — 221 rules
- [Engine (meta rules)](#engine-meta-rules) — 5 rules

### java/abs-of-hash-or-random

**Math.abs of a hash code or random integer**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: numbers, overflow

Detects `Math.abs(..)` applied directly to a hash code (`x.hashCode()`,
`Objects.hash(..)`, `Objects.hashCode(..)`, `Arrays.hashCode(..)`) or to an unbounded random
integer (`random.nextInt()`, `random.nextLong()`), and the same done by hand: `h < 0 ? -h : h` or
`if (h < 0) h = -h;` on such a call or on a local variable initialized with one.

**Why it matters.** These values range over every `int` (or `long`), including
`Integer.MIN_VALUE`, whose absolute value does not fit: `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` is
`Integer.MIN_VALUE`, still negative. Code that uses the result as an array index, a bucket or
a shard number (`Math.abs(key.hashCode()) % n`) then fails with a negative index — rarely, for
one unlucky key, which makes the bug hard to reproduce.

**How to fix.** Reduce first, or clear the sign bit.

```java
// Noncompliant
int bucket = Math.abs(key.hashCode()) % buckets;

// Compliant
int bucket = Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), buckets);
int other = (key.hashCode() & 0x7fffffff) % buckets;
```

`Math.abs(h % n)` (already reduced) and bounded random calls (`nextInt(bound)`) are not
reported. Random receivers must provably be a `java.util.Random`.

### java/abstract-class-without-methods

**Abstract class without methods**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: design

Detects `abstract` classes that declare no methods and no constructors, and
(with `interface_candidates`, on by default) abstract classes that are an interface in
disguise: no fields, constructors, initializers or concrete methods, only `public abstract`
methods.

**Why it matters.** `abstract` promises behaviour that subclasses complete. A class without
any method has nothing to complete: the keyword is only used to prevent instantiation, which
misleads readers looking for the abstract part.

**How to fix.** If the class just holds data, make it a concrete class (with a private or
protected constructor if instances should not be created directly). If it only groups
constants or nested types, make it a `final` class with a private constructor.

```java
// Noncompliant
public abstract class Defaults {
    public static final int TIMEOUT = 30;
}

// Compliant
public final class Defaults {
    public static final int TIMEOUT = 30;

    private Defaults() { }
}

// Noncompliant: nothing but a contract
public abstract class Shape {
    public abstract double area();
}

// Compliant
public interface Shape {
    double area();
}
```

A `private` constructor does not count as a method: an abstract class whose only constructor is
private can neither be instantiated nor extended outside its own body.

Not reported: classes that extend a class or implement an interface (they may leave
inherited abstract methods to subclasses), generic classes (the "type token" idiom relies on
anonymous subclasses), `sealed` classes, annotated classes, and classes with a private
constructor that are extended inside their own body (`extends Shape` or `new Shape() { … }`).
An abstract class with a `protected` or package-private abstract method, a field, a
constructor, or a concrete method is not an interface candidate: an interface could not keep
it.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `interface_candidates` | `true` | Also report abstract classes that only declare public abstract methods (no state, constructors, concrete or non-public methods): an interface says the same and leaves implementors free to extend another class. |

### java/accessor-uses-wrong-field

**Accessor uses a different field than its name** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: copy-paste, suspicious

Detects one-statement getters and setters that read or write a different field
than the one their name refers to, while that field exists in the same class with the same
type: `getWidth() { return height; }`, `setFirst(T v) { this.last = v; }`.

**Why it matters.** Accessors are written in batches by copying the previous one, and a
forgotten rename compiles fine when both fields have the same type. Callers then read the
wrong value, or their updates land in another field and the intended one keeps its old value.
Nothing fails until the data is visibly wrong.

**How to fix.** Use the field the accessor is named after.

```java
// Noncompliant
public int getHeight() { return width; }
public void setHeight(int h) { this.width = h; }

// Compliant
public int getHeight() { return height; }
public void setHeight(int h) { this.height = h; }
```

Only accessors whose body is a single `return field;` or `field = parameter;` are checked, and
only when the class declares a field with exactly the accessor's property name and the same
declared type as the field actually used, and the used field has a twin: its own accessor of
the same kind, itself a one-statement accessor that either uses the same field too (`getWidth`
next to the faulty `getHeight`, both returning `width`) or uses the field the faulty one is
named after (the two swapped their fields). Two accessors on one field, or a swapped pair, is
the copy-paste signature, while a getter deliberately exposing another field (a proxy, a
default) has no twin. An accessor whose body carries a comment is taken as deliberate, and so
is the getter of an alias property whose setter writes both fields (a misspelled or renamed
property kept for compatibility: `setColour(c) { color = c; colour = c; }` with
`getColour() { return color; }`).

### java/ambiguous-varargs-argument

**Ambiguous argument to a varargs parameter** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: varargs, null

Detects a single argument in a variable-arity (`...`) position that does not
become the one element it looks like:

* a bare `null` passed as the only variable argument of a method declared in the same class
  (`log("x", null)` for `log(String msg, Object... args)`) or of `Arrays.asList`: Java passes
  it as the array itself, so the method receives a `null` array, not an array holding `null`;
* a primitive array (`int[]`, `byte[]`, …) passed alone to `Arrays.asList`, `List.of`,
  `Set.of` or `Stream.of` whose result is then searched or counted (`.contains(..)`,
  `.indexOf(..)`, `.size()`, `.count()`) or looped over with a non-array variable:
  primitives cannot be the elements of a generic list, so the result has exactly one
  element — the array.

**Why it matters.** The callee then throws a `NullPointerException` when it reads the array's
length or loops over it (`Arrays.asList(null)` always does), and a one-element list of an
array makes `contains` always false and `size` always 1.

**How to fix.** Cast `null` to state the intent — `(Object) null` for an array with one
`null`, `(Object[]) null` for no array — or pass an empty array; for primitive arrays use
`Arrays.stream(values).boxed()` or `IntStream.of(values)`.

```java
// Noncompliant
boolean known = Arrays.asList(ids).contains(id);   // ids is an int[]
format("value: %s", null);

// Compliant
boolean known = Arrays.stream(ids).anyMatch(i -> i == id);
format("value: %s", (Object) null);
```

Not reported: a primitive array whose one-element list is stored, returned or passed on
(`List<int[]> rows = List.of(row)` can be intended); methods of other classes (their
overloads are unknown), classes with a superclass or interfaces (an inherited overload or
default method could take the call), overloaded methods, callees that check the array for
`null` themselves, and `Method.invoke(target, null)`, where a `null` array means "no
arguments" by design.

### java/anonymous-class-could-be-lambda

**Anonymous class could be a lambda**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: idiom, readability, java8

Detects an anonymous class that implements a functional interface — a JDK one
such as `Runnable`, `Callable`, `Comparator`, the `java.util.function` types, `ThreadFactory`
or `ActionListener`, or an interface of the same file with a single abstract method — by
defining just that method, with no fields, no other members and no use of `this`.

**Why it matters.** Since Java 8 a lambda states the same behavior without the class
declaration, the repeated method signature and the extra indentation: the reader sees the
code that runs instead of the boilerplate around it. An anonymous class also always creates a
new object and, in an instance context, keeps a reference to the enclosing object even when
it doesn't use it; a lambda that captures nothing is a shared constant and one that doesn't
use `this` holds no reference to the enclosing object.

**How to fix.** Replace the anonymous class with a lambda (or a method reference).

```java
// Noncompliant
executor.execute(new Runnable() {
    @Override
    public void run() {
        refresh(cache);
    }
});
names.sort(new Comparator<String>() {
    @Override
    public int compare(String a, String b) {
        return a.length() - b.length();
    }
});

// Compliant
executor.execute(() -> refresh(cache));
names.sort((a, b) -> a.length() - b.length());
```

Only reported for files compiled for Java 8 or later. Not reported: anonymous classes with
fields, initializers or several methods; bodies that use `this` or `super`, call the method
itself recursively, or call methods the object inherits (`toString()`, `hashCode()`, the
interface's default methods), which a lambda would resolve differently; generic methods;
parameters or local variables named like variables of the enclosing method (a lambda cannot
redeclare them); objects whose target type a lambda would not get (a `var` or `Object`
variable, a receiver of a call, an argument of generic methods such as `List.of`,
`Arrays.asList` or collection `add` / `put`); and `PrivilegedAction`, whose lambdas make
`doPrivileged` calls ambiguous.

### java/application-error-subclass

**Application class extending java.lang.Error** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: error-handling, exceptions

Detects classes declared with `extends Error` (`java.lang.Error`).

**Why it matters.** `Error` is the branch of the throwable hierarchy for failures of the
virtual machine itself — out of memory, stack overflow, a class that fails to link — which an
application is not expected to handle. Handlers are written accordingly: `catch (Exception e)`
and most frameworks' error boundaries let an `Error` pass, logging and cleanup code often
skips it, and some runtimes stop the thread or the process on one. An application failure
thrown as an `Error` therefore escapes the handling written for application failures.

**How to fix.** Extend `RuntimeException` for failures callers are not expected to handle,
or `Exception` for ones they must declare or handle.

```java
// Noncompliant
public class ConfigurationError extends Error {
    public ConfigurationError(String message) { super(message); }
}

// Compliant
public class ConfigurationException extends RuntimeException {
    public ConfigurationException(String message) { super(message); }
}
```

Only direct subclasses of `java.lang.Error` are reported: subclasses of `AssertionError`
(custom assertion failures of test libraries) and of the JDK's other `Error` types, and
classes extending an `Error` class declared in this file or imported from elsewhere, are left
alone.

### java/arithmetic-no-op

**Arithmetic operation without effect**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: arithmetic, redundant, suspicious

Detects operations that cannot change the value of an `int` or `long` operand:
adding, subtracting, or-ing or xor-ing `0`, multiplying or dividing by `1`, and-ing with `-1`
(`0xFFFFFFFF`), the same as compound assignments (`x += 0`, `x *= 1`), multiplying or dividing
a `float` or `double` by `1`, and `Math.round`, `ceil`, `floor` or `rint` of an integer value.

**Why it matters.** Such an operation is at best noise that makes the reader look for a
meaning that is not there, and often the trace of a mistake: a constant that was meant to be
something else, an offset that was never filled in, a mask that was meant to be `long`
(`value & 0xFFFFFFFF` keeps all 64 bits of a `long`, because the `int` literal is `-1`), or a
rounding applied after an integer division has already truncated the result
(`Math.ceil(total / pageSize)` never rounds up).

**How to fix.** Remove the operation, or write what was meant: `0xFFFFFFFFL` for a 32-bit
mask, a floating-point division before rounding (`Math.ceil((double) total / pageSize)`).

```java
// Noncompliant
int pages = (int) Math.ceil(total / pageSize);
long low = value & 0xFFFFFFFF;

// Compliant
int pages = (int) Math.ceil((double) total / pageSize);
long low = value & 0xFFFFFFFFL;
```

Not reported: `char`, `byte` and `short` operands (`c + 0` is the usual way to get a
character's code as an `int`), operations whose literal changes the type (`x + 0L`,
`x * 1.0`), adding `0.0` to a floating-point value (it turns `-0.0` into `0.0`), shifts,
expressions made only of literals (`1 * 60 * 1000`), and aligned series where the same
expression is combined with other literals nearby (`buf[off + 0] = a; buf[off + 1] = b;`).

### java/array-brackets-on-name

**Array brackets after the name instead of on the type**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions, arrays

Detects array brackets placed after a variable, parameter or field name
(`String args[]`) or after a method's parameter list (`int values()[]`) instead of on the type.

**Why it matters.** The brackets are part of the type. Written after the name, they split the
type in two: a reader scanning the left column sees `String` where the variable is a
`String[]`, and `int[] grid[]` is a two-dimensional array whose dimensions sit on both sides of
the name. The trailing form exists for compatibility with C; Java code reads more easily when
the whole type is written in one place.

**How to fix.** Move the brackets to the type.

```java
// Noncompliant
public static void main(String args[]) { … }
private int counts[];
int values()[] { … }

// Compliant
public static void main(String[] args) { … }
private int[] counts;
int[] values() { … }
```

Covered: fields, local variables, parameters (record components included), methods and
annotation elements. The rule is off by default: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

### java/array-hash-code

**hashCode() of an array**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: arrays, equality

Detects `hashCode()` called on an array, and `Objects.hashCode(array)`.

**Why it matters.** Arrays don't override `hashCode()`: the value is derived from the
array's identity, not its contents. Two arrays with the same elements hash differently, so a
`hashCode()` implementation built this way breaks the `equals`/`hashCode` contract, and
cache keys or checksums computed from it are meaningless.

**How to fix.** Use `Arrays.hashCode(array)` (or `Arrays.deepHashCode` for nested arrays).
Note that `Objects.hash(a, b)` with several arguments is fine for non-array values but also
uses identity for any array argument.

```java
// Noncompliant
public int hashCode() { return 31 * id + tags.hashCode(); }

// Compliant
public int hashCode() { return 31 * id + Arrays.hashCode(tags); }
```

Only expressions whose type the resolver proves to be an array are reported.

### java/array-to-string

**Array converted to a string**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: arrays, strings

Detects an array converted to a string with `toString()`, `String.valueOf(..)`,
or string concatenation (`"ids: " + ids`, `s += ids`).

**Why it matters.** Arrays don't override `toString()`: the result is the type code and
identity hash, e.g. `[I@1b6d3586`, never the contents. Log messages, error texts, and keys built
this way are useless or, worse, silently wrong.

**How to fix.** Use `Arrays.toString(arr)` (or `Arrays.deepToString(arr)` for nested arrays);
for a `char[]` that holds text, `new String(chars)` or `String.valueOf(chars)`.

```java
// Noncompliant
log.info("ids: " + ids);
String key = bytes.toString();

// Compliant
log.info("ids: " + Arrays.toString(ids));
String key = Arrays.toString(bytes);
```

`String.valueOf(char[])` is not reported: that overload returns the characters. Only operands
whose type the resolver proves to be an array are reported.

### java/arrays-as-list-stream

**Arrays.asList(..).stream() instead of Arrays.stream or Stream.of**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: streams, idiom

Detects `Arrays.asList(..).stream()`: a list is built only to be streamed.

**Why it matters.** `Arrays.stream(array)` and `Stream.of(a, b, c)` state the intent in one
call and skip the list wrapper. With a primitive array the long form is also wrong:
`Arrays.asList(intArray)` does not box the elements but makes a one-element `List<int[]>`,
so the stream holds the array itself, not its numbers. `Arrays.stream(intArray)` gives an
`IntStream` of the values.

**How to fix.** Stream the array with `Arrays.stream(array)`; stream separate values with
`Stream.of(..)`.

```java
// Noncompliant
long n = Arrays.asList(names).stream().filter(String::isBlank).count();
Stream<String> s = Arrays.asList("a", "b").stream();

// Compliant
long n = Arrays.stream(names).filter(String::isBlank).count();
Stream<String> s = Stream.of("a", "b");
```

Only `java.util.Arrays.asList` (qualified or statically imported) is considered. Not reported:
a single argument whose type the resolver does not know (it may be an array or a value),
`asList()` without arguments, and `parallelStream()`.

### java/assert-argument-order

**Expected and actual values swapped in an assertion**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: tests, junit

Detects JUnit equality assertions (`assertEquals`, `assertNotEquals`,
`assertSame`, `assertNotSame`, `assertArrayEquals`) whose *actual* slot holds a constant — a
literal, a class literal, an enum constant, or a `static final` field — while the *expected*
slot holds a computed value.

**Why it matters.** JUnit's parameters are `(expected, actual)`. The assertion still passes or
fails the same way when they are swapped, but the failure message becomes misleading:
`expected:<[computed value]> but was:<[the constant]>` sends the reader looking for the bug in
the wrong place.

**How to fix.** Put the constant first.

```java
// Noncompliant
assertEquals(order.getStatus(), Status.SHIPPED);
assertEquals(items.size(), 3);

// Compliant
assertEquals(Status.SHIPPED, order.getStatus());
assertEquals(3, items.size());
```

Only test files are checked, and only calls that provably go to JUnit 3/4 (`org.junit.Assert`,
message first) or JUnit 5 (`org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions`, message last) — TestNG uses the
opposite order and is left alone. Not reported: both arguments constant, boolean or `null`
literals (other assertions fit better), a first argument named `expected…`, files that
declare their own assertion helper of the same name, and values of unrelated types
(`assertNotEquals(point, "42")` with `point` declared as a class of the project): such an
assertion tests the `equals` of the object in the first slot against a value of another type,
and swapping the arguments would test the constant's `equals` instead.

### java/assert-boolean-literal

**assertEquals with a boolean literal**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: tests, clarity

Detects `assertEquals` calls where one of the compared values is the literal
`true` or `false`.

**Why it matters.** `assertTrue(x)` / `assertFalse(x)` say the same thing more directly, and
avoid the common mix-up of expected and actual arguments. The dedicated assertion also reads
better in failure messages.

**How to fix.** Replace the call with `assertTrue(…)` or `assertFalse(…)` (keeping the message
argument, if any).

```java
// Noncompliant
assertEquals(true, cache.isEmpty());
assertEquals("must be closed", false, conn.isOpen());

// Compliant
assertTrue(cache.isEmpty());
assertFalse("must be closed", conn.isOpen());
```

Covers JUnit 4 (message first), JUnit 5 (message last), and TestNG argument orders. Not
reported when the file declares its own `assertEquals` helper.

### java/assert-public-argument

**assert used to check a public method's argument**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: assertions, api

Detects an `assert` at the start of a `public` method of a `public` class that
checks the method's parameters (`assert count >= 0;`, `assert name != null : "name";`).

**Why it matters.** Assertions are disabled unless the JVM runs with `-ea`, which production
deployments rarely do. The check therefore exists only in tests: in production a caller
passing an invalid argument is not stopped at the boundary, and the bad value travels on
until it fails somewhere unrelated, or corrupts state silently. Arguments of a public API are
exactly the values the class does not control.

**How to fix.** Validate public arguments with a check that always runs:
`Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name")`, `if (count < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(…)`.
Keep `assert` for internal invariants of private code.

```java
// Noncompliant
public void resize(int capacity) {
    assert capacity > 0 : "capacity must be positive";
    …
}

// Compliant
public void resize(int capacity) {
    if (capacity <= 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be positive: " + capacity);
    }
    …
}
```

Only the leading statements of the method body are considered, and only assertions whose
condition mentions a parameter and nothing but parameters, literals and `null`. Test code is
not checked.

### java/assert-throws-multiple-calls

**Several calls inside an assertThrows lambda**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: tests, junit

Detects `assertThrows`, `assertThrowsExactly`, and `assertDoesNotThrow` calls
whose lambda does more than the one call under test: it holds several statements, or it
passes the result of another call as an argument (`() -> parser.parse(load(file))`).

**Why it matters.** The assertion passes as soon as *any* code in the lambda throws the
expected exception. When setup code shares the lambda with the call under test, a failure in
the setup makes the test pass for the wrong reason, and readers can't tell which call is
expected to fail.

**How to fix.** Prepare everything before the assertion and keep a single call inside the
lambda.

```java
// Noncompliant
assertThrows(ParseException.class, () -> {
    Parser parser = new Parser(config);
    parser.parse("{");
});
assertThrows(ParseException.class, () -> parser.parse(readFixture("broken.json")));

// Compliant
Parser parser = new Parser(config);
assertThrows(ParseException.class, () -> parser.parse("{"));
String broken = readFixture("broken.json");
assertThrows(ParseException.class, () -> parser.parse(broken));
```

Only test files are checked. Arguments that cannot reasonably throw are ignored: calls
without arguments (getters), calls on JDK types and values (`List.of`, `Arrays.asList`,
`text.getBytes(UTF_8)`, also statically imported: `asList(..)`), `new` of JDK classes (`java.*`
and Swing values such as `new SortKey(0, ASCENDING)`), constructors without arguments, and the
arguments of assertions (`assertNotNull(new Parser(input))`). JDK calls that declare checked
exceptions do count, since they can fail: file and reflection APIs such as
`File.createTempFile(..)`, `Files.readString(..)`, `Class.forName(..)`, `Thread.sleep(..)`, and
`new FileInputStream(..)`, `new URL(..)`, `new URI(..)`.

### java/assert-with-side-effect

**Side effect inside an assert** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: assertions, side-effects

Detects `assert` statements whose condition changes state: an assignment, an
increment or decrement, or a call to a well-known mutating method of a JDK collection,
iterator, atomic variable, lock or file (`list.remove(x)`, `it.next()`,
`counter.incrementAndGet()`, `file.delete()`, …).

**Why it matters.** Assertions are disabled by default at run time (they need `-ea`). With
assertions off, the whole condition is skipped — including its side effect. The program then
behaves differently in production than in tests: the element is never removed, the counter
never incremented, the file never deleted.

**How to fix.** Perform the action unconditionally and assert on its result.

```java
// Noncompliant
assert pending.remove(job) : "job was not pending";

// Compliant
boolean removed = pending.remove(job);
assert removed : "job was not pending";
```

The message part of the `assert` (evaluated only on failure) is not checked. Method calls
count only when the receiver's type is provably one of those JDK types; lambdas in the
condition are skipped.

### java/assertion-description-after-check

**Assertion description after the check**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: tests, assertj

Detects AssertJ assertions that end with a description or failure-message call
placed after the check: `assertThat(total).isEqualTo(10).as("order total")`.

**Why it matters.** AssertJ runs each check as soon as it is called. A description set
afterwards is attached to an assertion that has already passed or failed: when the check
fails, the error is thrown before `as(..)` runs and the report lacks the description the
author wrote for exactly that case.

**How to fix.** Put `as(..)`, `describedAs(..)`, `withFailMessage(..)` or
`overridingErrorMessage(..)` before the check.

```java
// Noncompliant
assertThat(order.total()).isEqualTo(expected).as("order total");

// Compliant
assertThat(order.total()).as("order total").isEqualTo(expected);
```

Only statements whose chain starts with an AssertJ `assertThat` (statically imported from
`org.assertj`, qualified with `Assertions`, or called on a soft-assertions object) and ends
with a description right after a check (`is…`, `has…`, `contains…`, `doesNot…`, …) are
reported.

### java/assertion-in-thread

**Assertion inside a thread body**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: tests, concurrency

Detects test assertions (JUnit, AssertJ, Hamcrest, TestNG, Truth) inside a
lambda or anonymous class that runs on another thread whose failure is never collected: the
body of a `new Thread(..)`, a task given to `Executor.execute(..)`, and a task given to
`ExecutorService.submit(..)` or `CompletableFuture.runAsync/supplyAsync(..)` whose returned
future is thrown away.

**Why it matters.** A failed assertion throws an `AssertionError` in the thread that runs it.
In a plain thread or an `execute`d task, that error goes to the thread's uncaught-exception
handler (a stack trace on the console); in a discarded future it is stored and never looked
at. Either way the test method itself carries on and passes: the assertion looks like
protection but cannot fail the test.

**How to fix.** Bring the outcome back to the test thread: keep the `Future` and call `get()`
(which rethrows the failure), collect errors in a thread-safe list and assert on it after
`join()`, or compute the value in the task and assert on it in the test.

```java
// Noncompliant
executor.submit(() -> assertEquals(200, client.call().status()));

// Compliant
Future<?> f = executor.submit(() -> assertEquals(200, client.call().status()));
f.get();
```

Only test files are checked. Not reported: assertions guarded by a `catch` of `Throwable`,
`Error` or `AssertionError` inside the task, assertions in a `catch` block that also hands the
caught error to a collector (`errors.add(e)`, `failure.set(e)`: the recommended fix, the test
checks the collection after `join()`), tasks that do more work after the assertion (a latch
count-down or flag after it makes a failure visible to the test as a timeout), and files that
install an uncaught-exception handler.

### java/assignment-in-condition

**Assignment used as a condition**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, confusing

Detects an `if`, `while`, or `do … while` whose whole condition is an
assignment, such as `if (found = true)`.

**Why it matters.** For `boolean` variables the compiler accepts `=` where `==` was almost
certainly meant, and the condition then always takes the assigned value. Even when the
assignment is deliberate, readers can't tell it apart from that typo.

**How to fix.** Use `==` if a comparison was meant; otherwise assign first and test the variable
on its own.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (ready = isReady()) { start(); }

// Compliant
ready = isReady();
if (ready) { start(); }
```

An assignment that is only part of the condition — the reading-loop idiom
`while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null)` — is not reported, and neither is an assignment
wrapped in an extra pair of parentheses (`if ((ok = retry()))`), which marks it as
intentional.

### java/assignment-in-operand

**Assignment or increment inside an expression**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: side-effects, readability

Detects increments, decrements, and assignments buried inside a larger
expression — a method argument, an operand of another operator, an array index, a ternary
branch — instead of standing as statements of their own.

**Why it matters.** An expression that both computes a value and changes a variable makes
the reader track two things at once, and the order of those effects is easy to misread
(`items.get(i++)` vs `items.get(++i)`). Such code is also fragile to edit: moving or
duplicating the expression duplicates the side effect.

**How to fix.** Perform the update in its own statement, before or after the expression.

```java
// Noncompliant
process(items.get(index++));
total = base + (delta = compute());

// Compliant
process(items.get(index));
index++;
delta = compute();
total = base + delta;
```

Not reported: statements (`i++;`, `a = b = 0;`), `for` loop headers, expression lambdas
(`() -> count++`), the value of a `return`, a variable initializer, or an assignment's right
side (`int n = count++`), assignments inside the condition of an `if`, `while`, `do`, or
`for` (the `while ((line = r.readLine()) != null)` idiom; see
`java/assignment-in-condition`), and increments or decrements in a loop condition
(`while (n-- > 0)`). An increment or decrement inside an `if` condition
(`if (++attempts > MAX)`, `if (count++ > 0)`) is reported: whether the test sees the old or
the new value is exactly what readers get wrong. By default `++`/`--` used directly as an array index
(`buf[pos++] = b`) are accepted as idiomatic; set `report_array_index` to report them too.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `report_array_index` | `false` | Also report `++`/`--` used directly as an array index (`buf[pos++]`). |

### java/atomic-equals

**equals() on an atomic number or boolean**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: equality, concurrency

Detects `equals(..)` called on an `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicLong`, or
`AtomicBoolean`.

**Why it matters.** The atomic wrappers are mutable holders and do not override `equals`
(or `hashCode`): `new AtomicInteger(1).equals(new AtomicInteger(1))` is `false`, and
`counter.equals(5)` is always `false`. Code that looks like a value comparison is really an
identity check.

**How to fix.** Compare the current values: `a.get() == b.get()`, or
`counter.get() == 5`.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (retries.equals(maxRetries)) { giveUp(); }

// Compliant
if (retries.get() == maxRetries.get()) { giveUp(); }
```

Only receivers whose type the resolver proves to be one of the three classes are
reported.

### java/bigdecimal-from-double

**BigDecimal constructed from a double**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: numbers, precision

Detects `new BigDecimal(x)` (and `new BigDecimal(x, mathContext)`) where `x`
is a floating-point literal or an expression of type `double`/`float`.

**Why it matters.** Most decimal fractions have no exact binary representation, and this
constructor preserves the binary value exactly: `new BigDecimal(0.1)` is
`0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625`. The error then leaks into
amounts, comparisons (`compareTo`, `equals`), and rounding — the very things `BigDecimal` is
used to get right.

**How to fix.** Build the value from its decimal text: `new BigDecimal("0.1")`, or from a
`double` with `BigDecimal.valueOf(d)`, which goes through `Double.toString` and yields `0.1`.

```java
// Noncompliant
BigDecimal rate = new BigDecimal(0.07);
BigDecimal total = new BigDecimal(price * quantity);

// Compliant
BigDecimal rate = new BigDecimal("0.07");
BigDecimal total = BigDecimal.valueOf(price * quantity);
```

Literals whose value is exactly representable (`new BigDecimal(1.0)`, `new BigDecimal(0.5)`)
are not reported, and neither are arguments whose type is unknown or a `BigDecimal` converted
to `float`/`double` on the spot (`new BigDecimal(amount.floatValue())`): the code already holds
the exact decimal value and asks on purpose what the binary type makes of it.

### java/boolean-literal-comparison

**Comparison with a boolean literal**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: clutter, readability

Detects comparisons with a boolean literal (`x == true`, `x != false`,
`false == x`), conditional expressions that just produce a boolean literal
(`c ? true : false`, `c ? false : true`), boolean literals that a logical operator ignores
(`x && true`, `x || false`), and negated literals (`!false`).

**Why it matters.** The literal adds nothing: the expression is already a boolean. The extra
words make conditions longer and invite mistakes such as `if (x = true)`.

**How to fix.** Use the value directly, negating it where needed.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (isValid() == true) { ... }
if (enabled != false) { ... }
return count > 0 ? true : false;
if (ready && true) { ... }

// Compliant
if (isValid()) { ... }
if (enabled) { ... }
return count > 0;
if (ready) { ... }
```

`x && false` and `x || true` are not reported here: the literal decides the whole condition,
which is a constant condition rather than clutter.

Note that for a `Boolean` object both forms throw on `null`; if `null` must be treated as
`false`, write `Boolean.TRUE.equals(x)`.

### java/boxed-boolean-condition

**Boxed Boolean used as a condition**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: null-safety, boxing

Detects an expression of type `java.lang.Boolean` (the wrapper, not the
primitive) used directly as the condition of an `if`, `while`, `do`, `for`, or `?:`, or as
the operand of `!`.

**Why it matters.** The condition auto-unboxes the wrapper with `booleanValue()`. A
`Boolean` can be `null` — a missing map entry, an unset field, a nullable database
column — and then the condition throws `NullPointerException` instead of taking a branch.

**How to fix.** Decide what `null` means and say so explicitly: `Boolean.TRUE.equals(flag)`
(null counts as false), `!Boolean.FALSE.equals(flag)` (null counts as true), or use a
primitive `boolean` where `null` is not a valid value.

```java
// Noncompliant
Boolean enabled = settings.get("enabled");
if (enabled) { start(); }

// Compliant
if (Boolean.TRUE.equals(enabled)) { start(); }
```

Not reported: `Boolean.TRUE`, `Boolean.FALSE`, `Boolean.valueOf(..)`, and values unwrapped
with a non-null fallback (`opt.orElse(false)`, `defaultIfNull(x, Boolean.FALSE)`,
`requireNonNullElse(x, false)`), which are never null; local variables initialized with a
non-null value, or declared without one and only ever assigned non-null values; pattern variables (`o instanceof Boolean
b`), and variables that the same method compares with `null`. Only expressions whose type
the resolver proves to be `Boolean` are reported, and only when the variable, field, or
method involved is declared in this file with a type mentioning `Boolean`.

### java/boxed-primitive-constructor

**Deprecated wrapper-class constructor**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: performance, deprecated

Detects `new Integer(..)`, `new Long(..)`, `new Short(..)`, `new Byte(..)`,
`new Double(..)`, `new Float(..)`, `new Boolean(..)`, and `new Character(..)`; also other
constructors that only rebuild a value the JDK already offers: `new String("text")` and
`new String()` (the literal is already a `String`), and `BigInteger` / `BigDecimal` built from
a value the class has a constant for (`new BigDecimal(1)`, `new BigInteger("10")`: use
`ONE`, `TEN`, `ZERO`, and `TWO` where it exists — `BigInteger.TWO` from Java 9,
`BigDecimal.TWO` from Java 19), which gives the same value without parsing or allocating.

**Why it matters.** These constructors are deprecated for removal. Each call allocates a new
object, bypassing the caches that `valueOf` uses, and invites identity bugs: two boxes built
this way are never `==` even when their values are equal.

**How to fix.** Use the static factory (`Integer.valueOf(..)`, `Boolean.valueOf(..)`,
`Character.valueOf(..)`), the parser (`Integer.parseInt(..)`) when a primitive is enough, or
plain autoboxing.

```java
// Noncompliant
Integer count = new Integer(0);
Boolean flag = new Boolean(text);

// Compliant
Integer count = Integer.valueOf(0);
boolean flag = Boolean.parseBoolean(text);
```

Classes of your own that happen to be called `Integer`, `Long`, … are not reported. Neither
are `new String(..)` in test code (tests build distinct instances on purpose) or one assigned
to a variable that the file compares with `==` or `!=` (an identity sentinel), nor
`BigDecimal` values with a fraction or exponent (`new BigDecimal("1.0")` has another scale
than `ONE`), nor other whole numbers (`new BigDecimal("19")` reads well and `valueOf` would
gain little).

### java/boxing-roundtrip

**Throwaway boxing or temporary object**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: performance, boxing

Detects a wrapper created with `Integer.valueOf(..)` (or `Long`, `Double`,
`Float`, `Short`, `Byte`, `Boolean`, `Character`) whose primitive value is taken right back:

* explicitly, `Integer.valueOf(text).intValue()`;
* implicitly, by assigning or returning it where the matching primitive is expected
  (`int n = Integer.valueOf(text);`, `return Long.valueOf(s);` in a method returning `long`).

It also detects other temporary objects that exist only for one call a static method or a
literal makes without them:

* a primitive boxed only to call `toString()`, `hashCode()` or `compareTo(..)` on the wrapper
  (`Integer.valueOf(n).toString()`), which `Integer.toString(n)`, `Integer.hashCode(n)` and
  `Integer.compare(a, b)` do directly;
* `String.valueOf(x)` as an operand of a string concatenation, which converts `x` itself;
* `new Foo().getClass()`, which `Foo.class` names without creating an object.

**Why it matters.** Parsing or converting through the wrapper allocates (outside the small
value cache) and reads as if an object were needed. `Integer.parseInt(..)` and its siblings
say what is meant and return the primitive directly; for a primitive argument the round trip
is simply the argument itself. The other temporary objects are the same waste: an allocation
and a detour the reader has to see through.

**How to fix.** Call the parse method (`Integer.parseInt(s)`, `Double.parseDouble(s)`,
`Boolean.parseBoolean(s)`), or use the primitive value as is; call the static helper; drop
the `String.valueOf`; use the class literal.

```java
// Noncompliant
int port = Integer.valueOf(text).intValue();
long id = Long.valueOf(raw);
String label = Integer.valueOf(count).toString();
String line = "total: " + String.valueOf(total);

// Compliant
int port = Integer.parseInt(text);
long id = Long.parseLong(raw);
String label = Integer.toString(count);
String line = "total: " + total;
```

Not reported: unboxing to a different primitive (`Integer.valueOf(s).longValue()`, which
widens), `new Integer(..)` (see `java/boxed-primitive-constructor`), wrappers whose class is
not the JDK's, wrappers built from a string before `toString()` (the round trip normalizes
the text), `String.valueOf` of an array (`char[]` prints its characters, concatenation would
print the array), next to a non-string operand (removing it would turn the `+` into an
addition) or around an expression with operators (removing it needs parentheses), `getClass()` on objects built with constructor arguments (the constructor may do
work) or anonymous classes, and boxed functional-interface types in signatures (an API
choice).

### java/broad-expected-exception

**Exception expectation covers several calls**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: tests, junit

Detects exception expectations that cover more than the one call meant to
throw: a JUnit 4 `@Test(expected = X.class)` (or TestNG `expectedExceptions`) on a test whose
body makes calls in more than one statement, and an `ExpectedException` rule (`thrown.expect(..)`)
followed by more than one statement that makes calls.

**Why it matters.** The expectation is met as soon as *any* of the covered code throws the
exception. When the setup or a second call can throw it too, the test passes for the wrong
reason and keeps passing when the code under test stops throwing. Statements after the call
that throws never run, so checks placed there (`verify(..)`, assertions) are silently skipped.

**How to fix.** Keep the setup outside the expectation: use `assertThrows` around the single
call expected to throw (JUnit 4.13+, JUnit 5), and put further checks after it.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Test(expected = IllegalStateException.class)
public void rejectsSecondStart() {
    Engine engine = new Engine(config);
    engine.start();
    engine.start();
}

// Compliant
@Test
public void rejectsSecondStart() {
    Engine engine = new Engine(config);
    engine.start();
    assertThrows(IllegalStateException.class, engine::start);
}
```

Only test files are checked. A statement counts when it calls a method or creates an object;
declarations with literal values, constructions without arguments (`new Parser()`), a final `fail(..)` (it throws an `AssertionError`, not the
expected exception), and calls inside lambdas or anonymous classes do not count.

### java/byte-sign-extension

**Byte sign-extended into a wider value** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: numbers, bitwise, io

Detects two ways a signed `byte` corrupts a wider value:

* a `byte` OR-ed or added, unmasked, into a value assembled from shifted parts:
  `(b[0] << 8) | b[1]`, `(hi << 16) + lo` with `lo` a `byte`;
* an `int read()` method (the `InputStream` contract) returning a `byte` expression directly:
  `return buffer[pos++];`.

**Why it matters.** Bytes are signed. Before `|` or `+`, a byte is widened to `int` with
sign extension, so `0x80`–`0xFF` become `0xFFFFFF80`–`0xFFFFFFFF`, and OR-ing that sets every
higher bit of the result: `(0x12 << 8) | (byte) 0x80` is `-128`, not `0x1280`. An
`InputStream.read()` must return `0`–`255` or `-1` for end of stream; returning a raw byte
reports `-1` (end of data) for the byte `0xFF` and negative values for all bytes above `0x7F`.

**How to fix.** Mask the byte: `b & 0xFF`.

```java
// Noncompliant
int length = (header[0] << 8) | header[1];
public int read() { return data[pos++]; }

// Compliant
int length = ((header[0] & 0xFF) << 8) | (header[1] & 0xFF);
public int read() { return data[pos++] & 0xFF; }
```

Only operands whose type the resolver proves to be `byte` are reported, and only in an
expression that also contains a left shift by 8 or more (a value being assembled from bytes).
The high byte of such an expression (the shifted one) is not reported: its sign often
intentionally makes the result negative.

### java/case-conversion-without-locale

**Case conversion without a Locale**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: i18n, locale

Detects `String.toUpperCase()` and `String.toLowerCase()` called without a
`Locale`.

**Why it matters.** Without an argument the conversion uses the JVM's default locale, so the
result depends on where the program runs. The classic surprise is Turkish: `"TITLE".toLowerCase()`
gives `"tıtle"` (dotless ı), which then fails to match keys, file names, SQL keywords, or
protocol tokens. Such bugs only show up on machines configured with that locale.

**How to fix.** Pass `Locale.ROOT` (or `Locale.ENGLISH`) for machine-readable text; pass the
user's locale explicitly when the text is meant for display.

```java
// Noncompliant
String key = name.toLowerCase();

// Compliant
String key = name.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
String title = heading.toUpperCase(userLocale);
```

Only receivers known to be a `String` are checked: a value whose type the resolver knows, the
result of any `toString()`, an enum's own `name()`, and the parameter of a lambda passed to a
stream operation over strings (`names.stream().filter(n -> n.toLowerCase()…)`), and the file
name a `FilenameFilter` lambda receives (`dir.list((d, name) -> name.toLowerCase()…)`, also
for `File.listFiles` and `FileDialog.setFilenameFilter`). For
comparisons, `equalsIgnoreCase` avoids the conversion altogether.

### java/case-insensitive-equals

**Case-converted strings compared with equals**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: strings, performance

Detects two strings compared after converting both to the same case in the
default locale — `a.toLowerCase().equals(b.toLowerCase())`, the same with `toUpperCase`, or
`a.toLowerCase().compareTo(b.toLowerCase())` — and a string converted to lower (upper) case
compared with a literal that is already all lower (upper) case:
`s.toLowerCase().equals("yes")`.

**Why it matters.** `equalsIgnoreCase` and `compareToIgnoreCase` say what is meant and compare
character by character without building two new strings for every comparison. The
conversions also depend on the default locale when no `Locale` is given: in a Turkish locale
`"TITLE".toLowerCase()` contains a dotless `ı`, so the comparison fails where
`equalsIgnoreCase` succeeds.

**How to fix.** Compare the original strings with the ignore-case method.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (header.toLowerCase().equals(expected.toLowerCase())) { … }
if (answer.toLowerCase().equals("yes")) { … }

// Compliant
if (header.equalsIgnoreCase(expected)) { … }
if ("yes".equalsIgnoreCase(answer)) { … }
```

Only receivers the resolver proves to be `String` are considered. Not reported: one side
converted and the other not (the other may legitimately be mixed case), conversions to
different cases, conversions with an explicit `Locale` (other than `Locale.getDefault()`), on both
sides or on one side compared
with a literal (`s.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT).equals("yes")`: whole-string case mapping, which
differs from the character-wise ignore-case methods for a few letters such as `ſ` or `ı`, is
then a deliberate choice), `toUpperCase` before `compareTo` (it orders `_` and the other characters between
`Z` and `a` differently from `compareToIgnoreCase`), literals that contain letters of both cases or non-ASCII letters (whose case
mapping differs between the two approaches), `Objects.equals` (null-safe, unlike
`equalsIgnoreCase` on a `null` receiver), and other comparisons such as `startsWith` or
`contains`.

### java/catch-generic-exception

**Catching a generic exception**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: error-handling

Detects `catch` clauses for `java.lang.Exception` or
`java.lang.RuntimeException`.

**Why it matters.** A catch-all handler written for one expected failure also swallows every
other one: a `NullPointerException`, an `IllegalStateException` from a bug, an exception added
to a callee later. They all get the same treatment, usually a log line, and programming errors
turn into silently wrong behaviour.

**How to fix.** Catch the specific exception types the code in the `try` block is expected to
throw (use a multi-catch for several), and let unexpected ones propagate.

```java
// Noncompliant
try {
    config = parser.parse(file);
} catch (Exception e) {
    config = Config.defaults();
}

// Compliant
try {
    config = parser.parse(file);
} catch (IOException | ParseException e) {
    config = Config.defaults();
}
```

Not reported: handlers whose last statement is a `throw` (the exception keeps propagating,
usually wrapped because the callee declares `throws Exception`), empty handlers (with or without
a comment; left to `java/empty-catch-block`), `try` blocks calling JDK methods declared
`throws Exception`
(`AutoCloseable.close()`, `Callable.call()`), and test code.

### java/catch-programming-error

**Programming error caught instead of fixed**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: error-handling, suspicious

Detects catch clauses for `NullPointerException` or
`IllegalMonitorStateException` in production code.

**Why it matters.** Both exceptions are thrown when the program itself is wrong: a reference
that should have been checked was `null`, or `wait`/`notify`/`unlock` was called without
holding the lock. Catching them treats the symptom: the bug stays, the handler also swallows
every *other* occurrence of the same exception in the protected code (including ones nobody
anticipated), and the state the code was manipulating may be left half updated. A null check
or the correct lock says what the code expects; a handler hides it.

**How to fix.** Find out which reference can be `null` and test it (or make sure it can't be),
or call the monitor methods while holding the lock; then remove the handler.

```java
// Noncompliant
try {
    return customer.getAddress().getCity();
} catch (NullPointerException e) {
    return "";
}

// Compliant
Address address = customer.getAddress();
return address == null ? "" : address.getCity();
```

Not reported: test code (tests catch these on purpose to check that they are thrown), a catch
parameter named `expected`, handlers with a comment in their block (a documented workaround,
typically for a failure inside a library the author cannot fix), handlers that throw the caught exception on (always, to keep a
later `catch (Exception e)` from wrapping it, or when it is not the one they expect), and
throwing these exceptions — `Objects.requireNonNull` and
explicit `throw new NullPointerException(…)` for a null argument are the JDK's own
convention. Wrapping the caught exception as the cause of another one
(`throw new IllegalStateException("…", e)`) does not count as throwing it on: the handler
still turns the bug into a different failure that callers may catch and handle, so it is
reported.

### java/catch-throwable-or-error

**Catching Throwable or Error**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: error-handling

Detects `catch` clauses for `java.lang.Throwable` or `java.lang.Error`
(also as one alternative of a multi-catch).

**Why it matters.** `Error`s signal conditions an application usually cannot recover from:
`OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`, `LinkageError`, a failed assertion. Catching them
(directly or through `Throwable`) and carrying on leaves the JVM in a doubtful state and hides
the real problem behind whatever the handler does next.

**How to fix.** Catch the exceptions the protected code can actually throw, typically
`Exception` subclasses. If a last-resort handler is really needed (the top of a worker thread),
log and rethrow, or let the default uncaught-exception handler do its job.

```java
// Noncompliant
try {
    process(batch);
} catch (Throwable t) {
    log.warn("batch failed", t);
}

// Compliant
try {
    process(batch);
} catch (IOException | ParseException e) {
    log.warn("batch failed", e);
}
```

Handlers that always end by throwing (rethrowing or wrapping the error, so it keeps
propagating) are not reported: a final `throw`, or a final `if`/`else` whose branches all
end that way. Neither is a `Throwable` clause that follows a `catch (Error e)` clause of the
same `try`, which has already taken every `Error`.

### java/chained-assignment

**Chained assignment**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions, readability

Detects statements and declarations that assign one value to several
variables through a chain of assignments: `a = b = 0;`, `int x = y = size();`.

**Why it matters.** A chain reads like one assignment and hides the others: the eye stops at
the first `=`. It also binds the variables together in a way that is easy to break: whoever
later needs a different value for one of them has to untangle the chain, and with variables of
different types the outer one receives the inner one's converted value (with a `float f`,
`double d = f = 0.1;` stores 0.10000000149…). One assignment per statement keeps each
variable's value visible.

**How to fix.** Write one assignment per statement.

```java
// Noncompliant
first = last = null;
int width = height = 0;

// Compliant
first = null;
last = null;
height = 0;
int width = 0;
```

Not reported: assignments nested inside other expressions (`while ((line = in.readLine()) !=
null)`), which `java/assignment-in-operand` and `java/assignment-in-condition` cover. The rule
is off by default: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

### java/class-literal-is-instance

**Class literal isInstance instead of instanceof**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: idiom, clarity

Detects `isInstance` called on a class literal: `Foo.class.isInstance(x)`.

**Why it matters.** With a class literal the type is known when the code is written, and
`x instanceof Foo` is the language's own test for it: shorter, checked by the compiler (it
rejects a test that can never succeed, such as a `String` against `Integer`), and able to bind
a pattern variable (`x instanceof Foo foo`) that removes the cast which usually follows.
`Class.isInstance` exists for types only known at run time, held in a `Class` variable.

**How to fix.** Write `x instanceof Foo`.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (Number.class.isInstance(value)) {
    total += ((Number) value).doubleValue();
}

// Compliant
if (value instanceof Number number) {
    total += number.doubleValue();
}
```

Not reported: `isInstance` on a `Class` held in a variable, field or parameter, the method
reference `Foo.class::isInstance` (a ready-made predicate for streams), and primitive class
literals (`int.class.isInstance(x)` is always false: another problem).

### java/class-name-string-comparison

**Class compared by name**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: types, refactoring

Detects a runtime class name compared with a string literal through `equals`:
`x.getClass().getSimpleName().equals("Foo")`, and `x.getClass().getName()` (or
`getCanonicalName()` / `getTypeName()`) compared with a name that has no package.

**Why it matters.** The compiler cannot check a class name hidden in a string: renaming the
class silently breaks the comparison, simple names collide across packages, and subclasses
or proxies (`Foo$$EnhancerByCGLIB`) never match. Worse, `getName()` returns the *fully
qualified* name, so comparing it with `"SQLTimeoutException"` is always `false`.

**How to fix.** Compare `Class` objects or use `instanceof`.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (event.getClass().getSimpleName().equals("OrderCreated")) { … }
if (ex.getClass().getName().equals("SQLTimeoutException")) { … }   // always false

// Compliant
if (event instanceof OrderCreated created) { … }
if (ex instanceof SQLTimeoutException) { … }
```

Not reported: `getName()` compared with a fully qualified literal (a common way to test for
an optional class without depending on it), prefix tests such as `startsWith("java.")`, and
non-literal values.

### java/class-naming

**Type naming convention**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: naming, convention

Detects classes, interfaces, enums, records, and annotation types whose name
does not follow the configured convention (by default PascalCase: an uppercase letter followed
by letters and digits, no underscores).

**Why it matters.** Java code is read far more often than written; a consistent naming scheme
lets readers tell types, variables and constants apart at a glance, and it is what every Java
tool, framework, and developer expects.

**How to fix.** Rename the type (and its file, for top-level public types).

```java
// Noncompliant
class order_line { }
interface httpHandler { }

// Compliant
class OrderLine { }
interface HttpHandler { }
```

Letters are classified by Unicode case (`Äpfel` is fine), and an underscore between two digits
(a version number such as `Api2_0`) is accepted. Not reported: files that bind native code
through JNA, whose structure and callback types mirror native names (`SERVICE_STATUS`). The
`format` parameter takes a preset name (`PascalCase`, `camelCase`, `UPPER_SNAKE`,
`snake_case`); regular expressions are not supported.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `format` | `"PascalCase"` | Naming preset for type names: `PascalCase` (`^[A-Z][a-zA-Z0-9]*$`), `camelCase`, `UPPER_SNAKE`, or `snake_case`. Arbitrary regular expressions are not supported; the regular expression of a preset is accepted as an alias. With an unknown v… |

### java/clone-override

**clone() implemented**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: design

Detects implementations of `clone()`, and classes that implement `Cloneable`
without declaring `clone()`.

**Why it matters.** The `Cloneable`/`Object.clone()` mechanism is fragile: it creates objects
without calling a constructor, copies fields shallowly (mutable state ends up shared between
copies), doesn't work with `final` fields that need a fresh value, forces casts and the checked
`CloneNotSupportedException`, and every subclass must remember to override it correctly.

A class that implements `Cloneable` but declares no `clone()` is a half-done version of the
same thing: `Object.clone()` stays `protected`, so no other class can copy it, and the marker
only suggests a copy facility that does not exist.

**How to fix.** Provide a copy constructor or a static copy factory that builds the new object
explicitly (and drop `Cloneable`).

```java
// Noncompliant
@Override
public Order clone() {
    try {
        return (Order) super.clone();
    } catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) {
        throw new AssertionError(e);
    }
}

// Compliant
public Order(Order other) {
    this.id = other.id;
    this.lines = new ArrayList<>(other.lines);
}
```

Not reported: abstract/interface declarations without a body, and `clone()` methods whose
only statement throws (the idiom that forbids cloning). A class implementing `Cloneable`
without `clone()` is not reported when it extends another class (which may provide the
`clone()` that `Cloneable` enables), when it calls `clone()` itself (`(Order) this.clone()` in a
copy method of its own), or in test code (fixtures that exercise `Cloneable` handling).

### java/cognitive-complexity

**Cognitive complexity of functions should not be too high**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: brain-overload, complexity

Flags functions whose **cognitive complexity** is above a threshold (default 15).

Cognitive complexity estimates how hard a function is to *read*: every break in linear flow (`if`, loops, `catch`, `switch`, jumps, chains of mixed boolean operators) adds a point, and nesting makes each of those cost more. Functions that score high take longer to understand, are harder to test exhaustively and attract bugs when changed.

**How to fix:** extract well-named helper functions, return early instead of nesting, and replace flag-driven branching with separate functions or polymorphism.

```text
// Noncompliant: nested branches inside loops inside conditions
process(items) {
  if (enabled) {
    for (item of items) {
      if (item.ok) { if (item.big) { ... } else { ... } }
    }
  }
}

// Compliant: guard clause plus a helper
process(items) {
  if (!enabled) return;
  for (item of items) handle(item);
}
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `threshold` | `15` | Highest cognitive complexity allowed for one function |

### java/collapsible-if

**Collapsible if statements**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: readability, nesting

Detects an `if` statement without `else` whose only content is another `if`
statement without `else`.

**Why it matters.** Two nested conditions with nothing in between are one condition written
in two places. The extra nesting level costs indentation and attention without adding
meaning.

**How to fix.** Merge the conditions with `&&` (parenthesize them if they contain `||`).

```java
// Noncompliant
if (file != null) {
    if (file.exists()) {
        load(file);
    }
}

// Compliant
if (file != null && file.exists()) {
    load(file);
}
```

Not reported when the outer block contains a comment, which may document one of the
conditions.

### java/collection-passed-to-itself

**Collection passed to its own bulk method** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: collections, suspicious, copy-paste

Detects a collection or map passed as the argument of one of its own bulk
methods: `c.addAll(c)`, `c.removeAll(c)`, `c.retainAll(c)`, `c.containsAll(c)`,
`m.putAll(m)`.

**Why it matters.** The result is fixed and rarely what was meant: `containsAll(self)` is
always `true`, `retainAll(self)` and `putAll(self)` change nothing, `removeAll(self)` empties
the collection (a slow `clear()`), and `addAll(self)` duplicates every element of a list (a
set is left unchanged; some implementations throw `ConcurrentModificationException`). It is
almost always a copy-paste slip for another variable (`merged.addAll(other)`).

**How to fix.** Pass the collection that was meant, or call `clear()` if that was the intent.

```java
// Noncompliant
allowed.retainAll(allowed);

// Compliant
allowed.retainAll(granted);
```

Receivers must be plain names or field references (no calls), and the resolver must prove
they are a `Collection` or a `Map`.

### java/collection-return-null

**Null returned instead of an empty collection or array**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: null, collections

Detects `return null;` in a method declared to return a collection
(`Collection`, `List`, `Set`, `Queue`, … or any implementation), a `Map`, or an array.

**Why it matters.** Callers of such methods naturally loop over the result or ask for its
size. A `null` breaks that expectation: every caller must remember a special check, and the
one that forgets fails with a `NullPointerException` far from the cause. An empty result says
"nothing" just as clearly and needs no special handling.

**How to fix.** Return an empty collection or array.

```java
// Noncompliant
List<Order> findOrders(Customer c) {
    if (c == null) {
        return null;
    }
    return repository.ordersOf(c);
}

// Compliant
List<Order> findOrders(Customer c) {
    if (c == null) {
        return List.of();          // or Collections.emptyList(), new Order[0], …
    }
    return repository.ordersOf(c);
}
```

Only the literal `null` is reported — returned directly or as one arm of a conditional
expression (`return found ? list : null;`) — only in methods (not lambdas), and only when the
declared return type is known to be an array, a `java.util.Collection`, or a `java.util.Map`
(also JDK classes that are maps by inheritance, such as `java.util.jar.Attributes`; a
`java.security.Provider`, a map of service properties, is not reported).
Methods annotated `@Nullable` (or `@CheckForNull`) document the `null` deliberately and are
not reported, and so are methods whose Javadoc `@return` mentions `null` (`@return the
matched groups, or null if there is no match`): there `null` is a documented result of its
own, often distinct from an empty one. Neither are `byte[]` and `char[]` results, which
usually carry data where `null` means "no value" (a SQL `NULL`, as in `ResultSet.getBytes`), nor test code, where
stubs and mocks return `null` on purpose.

### java/collection-size-comparison

**Emptiness checked by comparing the size**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: collections, readability

Detects emptiness checks written as size comparisons: `x.size() == 0`,
`x.size() != 0`, `x.size() > 0`, `x.size() < 1`, `x.size() >= 1`, `x.size() <= 0` (and the
mirrored forms) on collections and maps, and the same comparisons of `length()` on strings.

**Why it matters.** `isEmpty()` states the intent directly and is never slower; for some
collections (for example concurrent ones) computing the size is expensive while checking
emptiness is constant time.

**How to fix.** Use `isEmpty()` or `!isEmpty()`.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (orders.size() == 0) { return; }
if (name.length() > 0) { greet(name); }

// Compliant
if (orders.isEmpty()) { return; }
if (!name.isEmpty()) { greet(name); }
```

Only receivers whose type is known to be a `Collection`, a `Map`, or a `String` are reported.

### java/colon-switch-expression

**Switch expression with colon labels** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, switch

Detects `switch` expressions (a `switch` that produces a value) whose cases
use the old colon form, `case X:` followed by statements and `yield`, instead of arrow labels.

**Why it matters.** The colon form keeps the fall-through semantics of the classic switch
statement: a group without `yield` or `throw` runs into the next one, which is exactly the
mistake switch expressions were designed to rule out. Arrow labels never fall through, need no
`yield` for a single expression, and make each case visibly self-contained.

**How to fix.** Rewrite each group as `case X -> value;` (or `case X -> { …; yield value; }`
when it needs statements).

```java
// Noncompliant
int days = switch (month) {
    case FEBRUARY:
        yield 28;
    case APRIL, JUNE, SEPTEMBER, NOVEMBER:
        yield 30;
    default:
        yield 31;
};

// Compliant
int days = switch (month) {
    case FEBRUARY -> 28;
    case APRIL, JUNE, SEPTEMBER, NOVEMBER -> 30;
    default -> 31;
};
```

Not reported: `switch` statements, which may use either form. The rule is off by default: it
is part of the `conventions` profile.

### java/commented-out-code

**Commented-out code should be removed**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: unused, clutter

Flags runs of comments that contain source code rather than prose.

Commented-out code distracts readers, rots as the surrounding code changes and is never compiled or tested. Version control already keeps old code.

**How to fix:** delete it. If it documents an alternative, describe the alternative in prose.

```text
// Noncompliant
// int retries = 3;
// connect(host, retries);
connect(host);
```

Documentation comments, license headers and tool directives are ignored.

### java/compare-to-min-value

**Comparison method returns Integer.MIN_VALUE**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: comparison

Detects a `compareTo(..)` or `compare(..)` implementation that returns
`Integer.MIN_VALUE`.

**Why it matters.** Callers commonly reverse an order by negating the result
(`-a.compareTo(b)`, `Comparator.reversed()` in hand-written code). In two's complement
`-Integer.MIN_VALUE` is still `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, so the "reversed" comparison still says
"less than" and sorting, binary search, and tree maps quietly misbehave.

**How to fix.** Return `-1`, `0`, or `1` (or delegate to `Integer.compare`).

```java
// Noncompliant
public int compareTo(Version other) {
    if (other == null) return Integer.MIN_VALUE;
    return Integer.compare(number, other.number);
}

// Compliant
public int compareTo(Version other) {
    if (other == null) return -1;
    return Integer.compare(number, other.number);
}
```

Only `return` statements of methods named `compareTo` (one parameter) or `compare` (two
parameters) are checked, including both branches of a returned conditional expression.
Returns inside lambdas are not considered.

### java/compare-to-specific-value

**compareTo() result compared with a specific value**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: comparison

Detects the result of `compareTo(..)` or `compare(..)` being tested for equality
with `1` or `-1` (`== 1`, `== -1`, `!= 1`, `!= -1`).

**Why it matters.** The comparison contract only promises a negative number, zero, or a
positive number. Many implementations return other values — `String.compareTo` returns the
difference between the first differing characters, and hand-written comparators often return
`a - b` — so `compareTo(..) == 1` is `false` for many "greater" results.

**How to fix.** Test the sign: `> 0`, `< 0`, `>= 0`, `<= 0`.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (version.compareTo(required) == -1) { upgrade(); }

// Compliant
if (version.compareTo(required) < 0) { upgrade(); }
```

Only calls named `compareTo` with one argument or `compare` with two arguments are
considered.

### java/compare-to-without-comparable

**compareTo() in a class that is not Comparable** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: api-misuse, comparison

Detects a method `int compareTo(Foo other)` declared in class `Foo` when the class
does not implement `Comparable` (it has no superclass and no interfaces).

**Why it matters.** The method looks like the natural ordering of the class, but nothing in
the JDK knows about it: `Collections.sort(list)` does not compile, and a `TreeSet<Foo>`, a
`TreeMap<Foo, …>` or `Arrays.sort(array)` compile fine and then throw `ClassCastException` at
run time, because they cast the elements to `Comparable`. Usually `implements Comparable<Foo>`
was simply forgotten.

**How to fix.** Declare `implements Comparable<Foo>` and mark the method `@Override`; or, if the
ordering is only one of several, turn it into a `Comparator<Foo>` constant.

```java
// Noncompliant
final class Version {
    public int compareTo(Version other) { … }
}

// Compliant
final class Version implements Comparable<Version> {
    @Override
    public int compareTo(Version other) { … }
}
```

Only classes and records without `extends` and `implements` clauses are checked (a supertype
declared elsewhere might be `Comparable`), and only when the parameter is the class itself.
Static methods and classes whose `compareTo` is used as a method reference in the same file
(`list.sort(Foo::compareTo)`, a deliberate comparator) are not reported.

### java/compare-to-without-equals

**compareTo() without equals()**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: equality, collections

Detects classes that implement `Comparable` with their own `compareTo` but do
not override `equals` (and `hashCode`), so they inherit the identity comparison of `Object`.

**Why it matters.** The JDK collections do not agree on how such objects are compared:
`TreeSet`, `TreeMap` and `Collections.binarySearch` use `compareTo`, while `HashSet`,
`HashMap`, `List.contains` and `List.remove` use `equals`. Two distinct objects that compare
as `0` are one element in a `TreeSet` and two in a `HashSet`; `list.remove(x)` does not
remove an element that sorts exactly like `x`. The `Comparable` contract strongly recommends
that `compareTo` be consistent with `equals` for this reason.

**How to fix.** Override `equals` (and `hashCode`) using the same fields that `compareTo`
compares, or document why the natural ordering is deliberately inconsistent with equality.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Version implements Comparable<Version> {
    int major, minor;
    public int compareTo(Version o) { … }
}

// Compliant
class Version implements Comparable<Version> {
    int major, minor;
    public int compareTo(Version o) { … }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { … }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(major, minor); }
}
```

Only classes that implement `Comparable` directly are checked, and only when every superclass
is known not to define `equals`: no `extends`, a class of this file (checked the same way),
or `Object`, `Number`, `Thread` or an exception class. Abstract classes, records, enums and
classes with Lombok annotations are skipped.

### java/concrete-collection-type

**Concrete collection type in a declaration**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: design, collections

Detects fields, method parameters, and method return types declared with a
concrete collection class — `ArrayList`, `LinkedList`, `Vector`, `HashMap`, `LinkedHashMap`,
`TreeMap`, `Hashtable`, `HashSet`, `LinkedHashSet`, `TreeSet`, and from
`java.util.concurrent` / `java.util` also `ConcurrentHashMap`, `CopyOnWriteArrayList`,
`CopyOnWriteArraySet`, `ArrayDeque`, `PriorityQueue`, `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`,
`ConcurrentLinkedDeque`, `LinkedBlockingQueue`, `ArrayBlockingQueue`, `LinkedBlockingDeque` and
`PriorityBlockingQueue` — rather than an interface such as `List`, `Map`, `Set`,
`ConcurrentMap`, `Queue`, `Deque`, or `BlockingQueue`.

**Why it matters.** A concrete type in a signature ties every caller to one implementation:
switching to another list or map, returning an unmodifiable view, or passing a
`List.of(..)` now needs changes elsewhere. Declaring the interface keeps the choice of
implementation a local detail.

**How to fix.** Declare the interface (`List`, `Map`, `Set`, or `SortedMap` / `NavigableMap` /
`Deque` when that behaviour is needed) and keep the concrete class only in the `new`
expression.

```java
// Noncompliant
private ArrayList<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();
public HashMap<String, Integer> totals(ArrayList<Order> input) { ... }

// Compliant
private List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();
public Map<String, Integer> totals(List<Order> input) { ... }
```

Local variables are not reported. Also not reported: variables on which a method specific to
the implementation is called (`ensureCapacity`, `addFirst` on a list, `firstKey`,
`elementAt`, `mappingCount`, `addIfAbsent`, …; queue and deque methods are fine when the
suggested interface is a `Queue` or a `Deque`); classes whose concrete type is the point
(`IdentityHashMap`, `EnumSet`, `Stack`, `DelayQueue`);
`@Override` methods and methods of anonymous classes, whose signatures are dictated by a
supertype; annotated declarations; and fields of `Serializable` classes, where a concrete
serializable type is sometimes chosen on purpose.

### java/conditional-mixed-boxed-numbers

**Conditional mixes different boxed number types** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: boxing, suspicious

Detects conditional expressions (`c ? a : b`) whose two results are numbers of
different types where at least one is a wrapper object, and the code treats the result as an
object: both operands are wrappers (`Integer` and `Long`), or one is a wrapper and the
result is stored in an `Object`, `Number`, `Comparable` or `Serializable` variable.

**Why it matters.** When the operands of `?:` are different numeric types, Java applies
numeric promotion: it unboxes the wrappers and widens the value to the larger type. The
result is a primitive `long` or `double`, boxed again as a `Long` or `Double` if an object is
needed. Two surprises follow: an operand that is `null` throws a `NullPointerException`
although neither side is primitive, and the chosen `Integer` comes out as a `Long` (or `1`
becomes `1.0`), which breaks later `equals` checks, `instanceof` tests and map lookups.

**How to fix.** Give both operands the same type (convert one explicitly), or use an
`if`/`else` that assigns each object as it is.

```java
// Noncompliant
Number n = useLimit ? limit : total;     // Integer limit, Long total: limit becomes a Long

// Compliant
Number n;
if (useLimit) {
    n = limit;
} else {
    n = total;
}
```

Both operand types must be proven by the resolver, and at least one must show in its syntax
