(a literal, or a variable with a declared type). Conditionals whose operands are both
primitives, or whose result goes to a primitive variable (where the conversion is expected),
are not reported.

### java/confusing-member-name

**Confusing member name** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: naming, confusing

Detects member names that are easy to misread:

* a method with the same name as its class (`public void Invoice() { … }`): it looks like a
  constructor but is an ordinary method — usually a constructor that got a return type by
  mistake, so it never runs when an object is created;
* two methods of one class whose names differ only in letter case (`getUrl` and `getURL`);
* two fields of one class whose names differ only in letter case (`count` and `Count`).

**Why it matters.** Readers (and code completion) treat such names as the same word. Calling
or assigning the wrong one compiles and fails silently, and a "constructor" with a return type
leaves every field it was meant to initialize at its default value.

**How to fix.** Remove the return type if a constructor was meant; otherwise rename one of the
members so the names differ in more than case.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Invoice {
    private String Number;
    private String number;
    public void Invoice() { number = "0"; }
}

// Compliant
class Invoice {
    private String externalNumber;
    private String number;
    public Invoice() { number = "0"; }
}
```

Not reported: a `static` method named like its class (it can't be a mistyped constructor, e.g.
the `main` entry point of a class named `main`), a field and a method sharing a name (a
record-style accessor), overloads, a
constant (`static final`, or a `static` field named in capitals) paired with a field (`NAME`
and `name` is a common convention for the name of a property), pairs where one method is
`@Deprecated` (a renamed method kept for compatibility) or `@Override` (its name is imposed by
a supertype), and test code (tests of case-sensitive property handling need such names).

### java/constant-if-condition

**if condition is a boolean literal**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious, dead-code

Detects `if` statements whose condition is the literal `true` or `false`.

**Why it matters.** The branch is decided at compile time: with `if (true)` the `else` part is
dead and the test is noise; with `if (false)` the body never runs. Such conditions are usually
leftovers of debugging or of switching code off by hand, and they hide real logic: a reader
has to notice the literal to know that half of the statement is dead.

**How to fix.** Keep only the branch that runs, delete the dead one, or restore the real
condition. To switch behavior on and off, use a named configuration flag.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (false) {
    audit(order);
}
if (true) {
    ship(order);
} else {
    hold(order);
}

// Compliant
ship(order);
```

Not reported: conditions that merely *contain* a literal (`if (DEBUG && ready)`), named
constants such as `if (DEBUG)` (a deliberate compile-time switch), and loops (`while (true)`
is the usual way to write a loop that exits from inside). Also not reported:

* `if (false)` whose body only throws, with no `else`. That is a known way to make `javac`
  accept a `catch` of a checked exception that the `try` block throws without declaring it
  (a call into Kotlin code, a sneaky throw):
  `try { kotlinApi(); if (false) { throw new IOException(); } } catch (IOException e) { … }`.
* A constant condition explained by a comment: an own-line comment directly above the `if`
  (no blank line between), or an own-line comment inside one of its blocks. A comment at the
  end of the `if` line itself does not count.

### java/constant-naming

**Constant naming convention**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: naming, convention

Detects constants whose name does not follow the configured convention (by
default UPPER_SNAKE: uppercase letters and digits, words separated by single underscores).
A constant here is a `static final` field — or an interface field, which is implicitly
`static final` — of a primitive type or `String`.

**Why it matters.** Upper-case constant names tell readers that a value is fixed for the
lifetime of the program, which is useful when reasoning about the code; mixed conventions blur
that distinction.

**How to fix.** Rename the constant.

```java
// Noncompliant
static final int maxRetries = 3;
static final String defaultName = "n/a";

// Compliant
static final int MAX_RETRIES = 3;
static final String DEFAULT_NAME = "n/a";
```

Not reported: `serialVersionUID`, logger fields, arrays, and `static final` fields of other
types (collections, loggers, mutable objects), whose naming conventions vary between teams,
and files that bind native code through JNA (names mirror native constants). The `format`
parameter takes a preset name; regular expressions are not supported.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `format` | `"UPPER_SNAKE"` | Naming preset for constants: `UPPER_SNAKE` (`^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*(_[A-Z0-9]+)*$`), `camelCase`, `PascalCase`, or `snake_case`. Arbitrary regular expressions are not supported; the regular expression of a preset is accepted as an alias. With an … |

### java/constants-only-interface

**Interface holding only constants**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: design

Detects interfaces that declare nothing but constants.

**Why it matters.** An interface defines a type. Using one as a namespace for constants
invites classes to "implement" it just to use the names unqualified, which leaks the
constants into the public API of those classes and all their subclasses — forever, since
removing an interface is a breaking change.

**How to fix.** Move the constants to a `final` class with a private constructor (or to an
`enum` when they form a closed set), and use `import static` where short names are wanted.

```java
// Noncompliant
public interface Limits {
    int MAX_USERS = 100;
    int MAX_ROLES = 10;
}

// Compliant
public final class Limits {
    public static final int MAX_USERS = 100;
    public static final int MAX_ROLES = 10;

    private Limits() { }
}
```

Interfaces that extend other interfaces, or that declare methods or nested types, are not
reported.

### java/constructor-calls-overridable

**Constructor calls an overridable method**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: inheritance, initialization

Detects constructors of non-final classes that call a method of the same class
which a subclass can override (not `private`, `static` or `final`).

**Why it matters.** Java runs the superclass constructor before the subclass's field
initializers and constructor body. If the superclass constructor calls an overridable
method and a subclass overrides it, the override runs on a half-built object: its fields
still hold `null`, `0` or `false`, so it can throw a `NullPointerException` or quietly
compute with defaults, and anything it stores may be overwritten by the subclass's own
initializers right afterwards.

**How to fix.** Make the called method `private`, `static` or `final`, make the class
`final`, or move the call out of the constructor (a factory method that constructs and then
initializes).

```java
// Noncompliant
class Widget {
    Widget() {
        layout();              // Button.layout() runs before Button's fields are set
    }
    protected void layout() { … }
}

// Compliant
class Widget {
    Widget() {
        layoutBase();
    }
    private void layoutBase() { … }
    protected void layout() { layoutBase(); }
}
```

Off by default: whether it matters depends on whether subclasses exist, which a single file
cannot tell. Only calls made by the constructor's own statements (a call statement, the right side
of an assignment, a local's initializer; not calls in nested blocks or lambdas), without a
receiver or on `this`, to methods declared in the same
class are considered; constructors (or classes) marked `@SuppressWarnings("this-escape")`,
the name javac's lint uses for this warning, are skipped, as are private nested classes that
nothing in the file extends, classes whose
constructors are all private (no subclass outside the
class is possible), enums and records.

### java/constructor-reference-capacity

**Constructor reference receives a number as capacity** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: collections, lambda

Detects a constructor reference of a collection or string builder with a
capacity constructor — `ArrayList::new`, `HashSet::new`, `HashMap::new`, `StringBuilder::new`,
`ArrayDeque::new`, … — used where it receives a number:

* `map.computeIfAbsent(key, ArrayList::new)` on a map whose keys are `Integer`, `Short`,
  `Byte` or `Character`;
* `intStream.mapToObj(ArrayList::new)`;
* `integerStream.map(HashSet::new)` on a `Stream<Integer>`.

**Why it matters.** The reference resolves to the `int` constructor: the number becomes the
initial capacity, not an element or a key. `computeIfAbsent(userId, ArrayList::new)` allocates
a backing array as large as the id — megabytes for large ids, an
`IllegalArgumentException` for negative ones — and `mapToObj(StringBuilder::new)` yields empty
builders instead of builders holding the number.

**How to fix.** Use a lambda that ignores the argument (`k -> new ArrayList<>()`), or pass the
value explicitly when it was meant as content.

```java
// Noncompliant
byUser.computeIfAbsent(userId, ArrayList::new).add(order);

// Compliant
byUser.computeIfAbsent(userId, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(order);
```

Only receivers whose key or element type the resolver proves are reported; maps keyed by
strings or collections (where the reference cannot compile or copies a collection) never
are.

### java/cyclomatic-complexity

**Cyclomatic complexity of functions should not be too high**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: complexity

Flags functions whose **cyclomatic complexity** (the number of independent paths through the function) is above a threshold (default 10). Off by default: cognitive complexity usually reflects readability better.

Many independent paths mean many test cases are needed to cover the function and a higher chance that some combination is wrong.

**How to fix:** split the function by responsibility, use lookup tables instead of long `if`/`else` chains, and move validation into dedicated helpers.

```text
// Noncompliant: one function handling every case
price(order) { if (a) ... else if (b) ... else if (c) ... /* 12 more */ }

// Compliant
price(order) { return RULES[order.kind](order); }
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `threshold` | `10` | Highest cyclomatic complexity allowed for one function |

### java/dangling-doc-comment

**Doc comment that documents nothing** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions, documentation

Detects documentation comments (`/** … */`) in places where the
documentation tool does not attach them to anything:

* between a declaration's annotations and the rest of the declaration;
* inside a method, constructor or initializer body, before a statement or a local variable;
* in a type body before an initializer block, or at the end of the body with no member after
  it.

**Why it matters.** A doc comment is only read when it directly precedes a declaration. In the
places above it is silently dropped from the generated documentation and from IDE hovers, so
the author believes something is documented when it is not. Inside a method body the `/**`
form also suggests an API comment where an ordinary note was meant.

**How to fix.** Move the comment before the declaration (above its annotations), or turn it
into a plain `/* … */` or `//` comment when it is a note for readers of the code.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Override
/** Returns the cached size. */
public int size() { … }

void run() {
    /** Retry three times. */
    int attempts = 3;
}

// Compliant
/** Returns the cached size. */
@Override
public int size() { … }

void run() {
    // Retry three times.
    int attempts = 3;
}
```

Not reported: comments before a declaration of any kind (local classes and records included),
comments before the `package` or `import` lines (file headers and package documentation),
banner comments that start with three or more stars (`/*****`), and `/**` comments inside
expressions. The rule is off by default: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

### java/date-field-out-of-range

**Date or time field out of range** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: dates, api-misuse

Detects constant date and time fields outside their valid range:

* `java.time` factories — `LocalDate.of`, `LocalDateTime.of`, `LocalTime.of`,
  `YearMonth.of`, `MonthDay.of`, `Month.of` — with a month outside 1–12, a day outside the
  month's days, an hour outside 0–23, a minute or second outside 0–59, or nanoseconds outside
  0–999,999,999;
* `java.util.Calendar` months above 11: `calendar.set(Calendar.MONTH, 12)`,
  `calendar.set(2024, 12, 1)`, `new GregorianCalendar(2024, 12, 31)`.

**Why it matters.** The `java.time` factories throw `DateTimeException` for such values, every
time. `Calendar` months are zero-based (January is 0, December is 11): writing the month
number people use (12 for December) makes a lenient calendar silently roll over into January
of the next year, which is the classic off-by-one in date code.

**How to fix.** Use the correct number, or better a named constant: `Month.DECEMBER`,
`Calendar.DECEMBER`.

```java
// Noncompliant
Calendar end = new GregorianCalendar(2024, 12, 31);
LocalTime closing = LocalTime.of(24, 0);

// Compliant
Calendar end = new GregorianCalendar(2024, Calendar.DECEMBER, 31);
LocalTime closing = LocalTime.MIDNIGHT;
```

Only integer literals are checked. Other `Calendar` fields are not reported: lenient
roll-over there is sometimes used on purpose (day 0 as "last day of the previous month").

### java/declaration-far-from-use

**Local variable declared long before its first use**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, readability

Detects local variables declared without a value, or with a literal value,
more than `max_statements` statements (5 by default) before the first statement of the same
block that mentions them.

**Why it matters.** A declaration far ahead of its use makes the reader carry the variable
through unrelated code, wondering whether something in between reads or changes it. It widens
the variable's scope for no benefit and is often left over from the habit of declaring
everything at the top of a method. Declared right where it is needed, the variable's purpose
is obvious from its context, and it can often get its real value at once.

**How to fix.** Move the declaration down to just before the statement that first uses it
(or into it, when it is only used inside a loop or a branch).

```java
// Noncompliant
int retries = 0;
log.info("starting");
connect();
loadSettings();
openSession();
registerHandlers();
warmUp();
while (!ready() && retries < 3) { retries++; }

// Compliant
log.info("starting");
connect();
loadSettings();
openSession();
registerHandlers();
warmUp();
int retries = 0;
while (!ready() && retries < 3) { retries++; }
```

Only declarations whose value is absent or a literal (a number, a string, a character, `true`,
`false`, `null`) are considered: moving them cannot change what the program does, whereas a
declaration such as `long start = System.nanoTime();` must stay where it is. Statements are
counted at the level of the block that holds the declaration, so a whole loop or `if` counts as
one; any mention of the name inside a statement (in a lambda or a comment within it too) counts
as a use. Variables never
mentioned again are left to `java/unused-local-variable`. The rule is off by default: it is
part of the `conventions` profile.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_statements` | `5` | Largest number of statements accepted between a declaration and the first statement that mentions the variable. |

### java/deep-nesting

**Control flow should not be nested too deeply**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: brain-overload, complexity

Flags functions whose control-flow statements (`if`, loops, `switch`, `try`) are nested more than `max` levels deep (default 4).

Deeply nested code forces readers to keep many conditions in mind at once and hides the main path of the function.

**How to fix:** use guard clauses and early returns, invert conditions, and extract inner blocks into helper functions.

```text
// Noncompliant
if (a) { for (...) { if (b) { while (c) { if (d) { ... } } } } }

// Compliant
if (!a) return;
for (...) processItem(...);
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max` | `4` | Deepest nesting of control-flow statements allowed in one function |

### java/default-charset

**Hash or resource read with the platform default charset** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: charset, i18n

Detects two conversions that depend on the JVM's default charset although their
result must not depend on the machine, in code compiled for a Java release older than 18:

- text hashed or signed through `getBytes()` without a charset:
  `digest.update(password.getBytes())`, `md.digest(input.getBytes())`, `mac.doFinal(s.getBytes())`;
- a bundled or remote resource read through `new InputStreamReader(…)` without a charset:
  `new InputStreamReader(getClass().getResourceAsStream("/template.txt"))`,
  `new InputStreamReader(url.openStream())`.

**Why it matters.** Up to Java 17 the default charset comes from the operating system and its
settings: UTF-8 on most Linux servers, windows-1252 on many Windows machines. A hash of
non-ASCII text then differs from one machine to the next, so stored password hashes, cache
keys or signatures stop matching when the application moves. A resource file has one fixed
encoding (usually UTF-8), so decoding it with whatever the machine uses garbles its non-ASCII
characters on some installations only.

**How to fix.** Name the charset: `getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)`,
`new InputStreamReader(in, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)`.

```java
// Noncompliant
byte[] hash = sha256.digest(password.getBytes());

// Compliant
byte[] hash = sha256.digest(password.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
```

Only reported when the Java release is known and below 18: from Java 18 on the default charset
is UTF-8 everywhere (JEP 400) unless explicitly overridden. Other default-charset conversions
(`new String(bytes)`, `FileWriter`, …) are not reported: the platform charset is often the
right one for console, process or local-file text, and that cannot be told from the code.
`getBytes()` on an ASCII string literal and test code are skipped.

### java/default-package

**Type in the default package** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: structure, convention

Detects a source file that declares types but has no `package` statement, so
its types live in the unnamed (default) package.

**Why it matters.** Types of the unnamed package cannot be imported by any class of a named
package, so nothing else in the code base can use them without reflection. Their simple names
are global and clash with any other default-package class on the class path, the module
system does not allow them in named modules, and tools that organize code by package (access
rules, architecture checks, coverage and logging configuration) cannot address them.

**How to fix.** Add a `package` declaration that matches the file's directory, and move the
file if needed.

```java
// Noncompliant (src/main/java/InvoiceParser.java)
public class InvoiceParser { … }

// Compliant (src/main/java/com/acme/billing/InvoiceParser.java)
package com.acme.billing;

public class InvoiceParser { … }
```

Not reported: a file with a `main` method (a program meant to be run directly, for instance
with the source launcher), test code (tests of how tools handle the unnamed package use it on
purpose), files at the root of the scanned tree, files under `resources`, test-data,
template and example directories (sources used as input data, and samples meant to be
compiled on their own), `package-info.java` and `module-info.java`, and files with syntax
errors.

### java/deprecated-annotation-missing

**Deprecation not marked with @Deprecated**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: deprecation, documentation

Detects a declaration whose Javadoc has a `@deprecated` tag but which is not
annotated `@Deprecated`. With the `require-javadoc-tag` parameter, also reports the reverse:
a `@Deprecated` declaration with a Javadoc comment that does not say why or what replaces it.

**Why it matters.** The compiler, IDEs and tools only see the annotation: without
`@Deprecated`, callers get no deprecation warning, the element is not struck through, and
removal-tracking tools miss it — the Javadoc tag alone only reaches people who read the
generated documentation. Conversely, the annotation without the tag warns callers but gives
them no replacement.

**How to fix.** Add `@Deprecated` (with `since` / `forRemoval` if useful) next to the tag;
document the replacement in the `@deprecated` tag.

```java
// Noncompliant
/**
 * @deprecated use {@link #connect(Endpoint)} instead
 */
public void connect(String host) { ... }

// Compliant
/**
 * @deprecated use {@link #connect(Endpoint)} instead
 */
@Deprecated
public void connect(String host) { ... }
```

Only Javadoc comments placed immediately before the declaration are considered; a
`@deprecated` mentioned inside the text (not at the start of a line) is not a tag.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `require-javadoc-tag` | `false` | Also report `@Deprecated` declarations whose Javadoc comment has no `@deprecated` tag explaining what to use instead. |

### java/deprecated-thread-methods

**Unsafe Thread.stop/suspend/resume**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~30 min · Tags: concurrency, deprecated

Detects calls to `stop()`, `suspend()`, and `resume()` on a `Thread`
(including `Thread.currentThread()`).

**Why it matters.** These methods are inherently unsafe and have been deprecated since Java
1.2; recent JDKs make them throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. `stop()` kills the thread at
an arbitrary point, releasing its locks while the objects they guard are half-updated.
`suspend()` keeps every lock the thread holds, so any other thread that needs one deadlocks
until a `resume()` that may never come.

**How to fix.** Make the thread cooperate: have it check a `volatile` flag or its interrupted
status (`Thread.interrupted()`) and exit on its own, and call `interrupt()` to ask it to stop.
Use `wait`/`notify`, `LockSupport`, or `java.util.concurrent` utilities to pause work.

```java
// Noncompliant
worker.stop();

// Compliant
worker.interrupt();     // the worker loop checks Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()
```

Only calls whose receiver is provably a `Thread` are reported (unqualified calls inside a
`Thread` subclass included).

### java/disabled-test-without-reason

**Disabled test without a reason**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: tests

Detects JUnit `@Disabled` / `@Ignore` (and TestNG `@Ignore`) annotations that
don't give a reason.

**Why it matters.** A disabled test silently stops protecting the code. Without a reason
nobody knows whether it is flaky, waiting for a fix, or obsolete, so it tends to stay disabled
forever. Test reports show the reason string next to the skipped test.

**How to fix.** Give the reason (ideally with an issue reference), or delete the test if it is
no longer relevant.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Disabled
@Test
void importsLargeFile() { … }

// Compliant
@Disabled("Flaky on Windows CI, see #1234")
@Test
void importsLargeFile() { … }
```

Only annotations that resolve to JUnit 4 (`org.junit.Ignore`), JUnit 5
(`org.junit.jupiter.api.Disabled`), or TestNG (`org.testng.annotations.Ignore`) through the
file's imports are checked; an empty or blank string counts as no reason.

### java/double-brace-initialization

**Double-brace initialization**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: collections, memory

Detects "double-brace initialization": an anonymous subclass of a collection
or map whose instance initializer fills it (`new ArrayList<>() {{ add(..); }}`).

**Why it matters.** Each occurrence creates a new class. Inside an instance method the
anonymous class also captures the enclosing object, so the collection keeps its creator alive
(a classic memory leak when the collection is cached or returned), and serializing it drags
the outer object along — or fails. The subclass also breaks `equals` symmetry with code that
compares classes and surprises serialization frameworks.

**How to fix.** Build the collection with ordinary statements, or use a factory method.

```java
// Noncompliant
Map<String, Integer> limits = new HashMap<>() {{
    put("users", 100);
    put("roles", 10);
}};

// Compliant
Map<String, Integer> limits = new HashMap<>();
limits.put("users", 100);
limits.put("roles", 10);
// or, when an unmodifiable map is fine:
Map<String, Integer> limits = Map.of("users", 100, "roles", 10);
```

Only anonymous classes whose body holds nothing but initializer blocks (and possibly a
`serialVersionUID`) are reported, and only when the created type is known to be a
`java.util.Collection` or `java.util.Map`.

### java/double-checked-locking

**Double-checked locking on a non-volatile field**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects double-checked locking on a field that is not `volatile`:

```java
if (instance == null) {
    synchronized (lock) {
        if (instance == null) {
            instance = new Service();
        }
    }
}
```

**Why it matters.** Without `volatile` there is no happens-before edge between the thread that
writes the field inside the lock and a thread that reads it in the first, unsynchronized check.
The reader can see a non-null reference to an object whose constructor effects are not yet
visible, and use a half-initialized instance. The bug is rare, timing dependent, and very hard
to reproduce.

**How to fix.** Declare the field `volatile`, or use the initialization-on-demand holder idiom
(a `static` nested class holding the instance), or simply synchronize the whole accessor.

```java
// Compliant
private volatile Service instance;

// Compliant: holder idiom
private static final class Holder {
    static final Service INSTANCE = new Service();
}
```

Only fields declared in the same class are checked. Fields of type `String` or a boxed
primitive are not reported (their state is final, so publishing them through a data race is
safe), and neither is the local-variable form of the idiom.

### java/double-checked-publish-early

**Double-checked initialization publishes the object before it is set up** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects double-checked lazy initialization (`if (f == null) { synchronized (…) {
if (f == null) { … } } }`) where the field is assigned first and the new object is then set
up through the field (`f = new Registry(); f.load();`, `f = new HashMap<>(); f.put(…)`).

**Why it matters.** The first, unsynchronized check lets other threads use the field as soon as
it is non-null. Assigning it before the set-up finishes publishes a half-built object: another
thread skips the lock, sees the field is set, and works with an object that is not loaded or
filled yet. `volatile` does not help, since the object really is incomplete at the moment it
becomes visible.

**How to fix.** Build and set up the object in a local variable, and assign the field last.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (registry == null) {
    synchronized (this) {
        if (registry == null) {
            registry = new Registry();
            registry.load(config);
        }
    }
}

// Compliant
if (registry == null) {
    synchronized (this) {
        if (registry == null) {
            Registry r = new Registry();
            r.load(config);
            registry = r;
        }
    }
}
```

Only statements that directly follow the assignment inside the inner check are considered: a
call on the field (`f.load()`) or a write to one of its fields (`f.size = 3`).

### java/duplicate-branch-body

**Branch repeats the code of another branch**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: suspicious, copy-paste

Detects a `switch` group whose code is the same as that of an earlier group of the
same `switch`, and an `else if` branch whose code is the same as that of the branch right
before it.

**Why it matters.** Two different cases leading to the same several statements is usually a
copy-paste slip: the second branch was pasted from the first and never adapted, so the second
case silently gets the first case's behaviour (a log message naming the wrong state, a value
read from the wrong source). When the duplication is deliberate, it still hides the fact that
the two cases are handled alike, and the copies drift apart the first time only one of them is
fixed.

**How to fix.** Adapt the branch that was meant to differ. If both cases really are handled
the same way, merge them: `if (a) X else if (b) X` becomes `if (a || b) X`, and two `switch`
groups become one group with both labels.

```java
// Noncompliant
switch (status) {
    case COMMITTED:
        log.warn("unexpected COMMITTED state for " + tx);
        return false;
    case COMMITTING:
        log.warn("unexpected COMMITTED state for " + tx);   // pasted, never adapted
        return false;
    default:
        return true;
}

// Compliant
switch (status) {
    case COMMITTED:
        log.warn("unexpected COMMITTED state for " + tx);
        return false;
    case COMMITTING:
        log.warn("unexpected COMMITTING state for " + tx);
        return false;
    default:
        return true;
}
```

Code is compared token by token, ignoring whitespace and comments. Branches shorter than
`min_statements` statements (default 2, a trailing `break` not counted) are not reported:
one-line branches such as `return true;` repeat on purpose in table-like code. In an `else if`
chain only neighbouring branches are compared, since a later branch may depend on the
conditions tested in between; the last `if`/`else` pair is left to `identical-branches`.
`switch` groups that fall through into the next one, and chains or switches whose conditions
bind pattern variables (the same text can then call different overloads), are not compared.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `min_statements` | `2` | Smallest number of statements (a trailing `break` not counted) a duplicated branch must have to be reported. |

### java/duplicate-condition

**Repeated condition in an if / else if chain**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, copy-paste

Detects an `if / else if` chain that tests the same condition more than once.

**Why it matters.** A branch is only reached when every earlier condition was false, so a
repeated condition can never be true there: its branch is dead code. This is usually a
copy-paste slip where the second test should check something else.

**How to fix.** Correct the repeated condition, or merge the branches if they really belong
together.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (type == FILE) {
    openFile();
} else if (type == DIRECTORY) {
    listDirectory();
} else if (type == FILE) {      // never true here
    openLink();
}

// Compliant
if (type == FILE) {
    openFile();
} else if (type == DIRECTORY) {
    listDirectory();
} else if (type == LINK) {
    openLink();
}
```

Conditions are compared ignoring whitespace, comments, and redundant outer parentheses.
Conditions that assign, increment, or create objects are not reported.

### java/duplicate-string-literal

**Duplicated string literal**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: duplication

Detects string literals that appear `threshold` (default 3) or more times in
the same file, with content at least `min_length` (default 5) characters long.

**Why it matters.** A repeated literal is usually a hidden constant — a column name, a
configuration key, a message. When it has to change, every copy must be found and updated,
and a single typo in one copy silently breaks behaviour.

**How to fix.** Extract the value into a named constant (or an enum) and use it everywhere.

```java
// Noncompliant
row.get("customer_id"); … row.put("customer_id", id); … log("customer_id");

// Compliant
private static final String CUSTOMER_ID = "customer_id";
row.get(CUSTOMER_ID); … row.put(CUSTOMER_ID, id); … log(CUSTOMER_ID);
```

The first occurrence is reported; the others are listed as secondary locations. Ignored:
literals inside annotations, text blocks, literals without any letter or digit (separators
such as `"-----"`), literals containing a run of four or more spaces (padded lines of
templates assembled by concatenation), and test files, where repeating readable sample
values is normal practice.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `min_length` | `5` | Shortest literal content (characters between the quotes, escapes counted as written) that is considered. |
| `threshold` | `3` | Number of occurrences in one file from which the literal is reported. |

### java/duplicated-block

**Blocks of code should not be duplicated**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: duplication

Flags blocks of code that appear, token for token, in more than one place (by default at least 100 tokens spanning at least 10 lines; literal values and whitespace are ignored).

Duplicated code must be changed in several places at once; sooner or later one copy is missed and the copies drift apart.

**How to fix:** extract the shared logic into a function, class or module and call it from each place.

### java/else-after-return

**Unnecessary else after return**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: readability, nesting

Detects an `else` block following an `if` branch that ends with `return` or
`throw`.

**Why it matters.** When the `if` branch always leaves the method, the `else` is redundant:
the code after the `if` only runs in the other case anyway. The extra block adds nesting and
hides the "early exit" structure of the method.

**How to fix.** Remove the `else` and move its content after the `if` statement.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (value == null) {
    return DEFAULT;
} else {
    return parse(value);
}

// Compliant
if (value == null) {
    return DEFAULT;
}
return parse(value);
```

Not reported: `else if` branches and `if` statements that are part of an `else if` chain,
where the symmetric form is often clearer.

### java/empty-block

**Empty block**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: unused, suspicious

Detects blocks with no statements and no comment: the body of an `if`,
`else`, loop, `try`, `finally`, `synchronized`, or `switch`, a static or instance initializer,
and a nested `{ }` block.

**Why it matters.** An empty block is either unfinished code (a forgotten implementation, an
`if` whose action was deleted) or a condition written the wrong way round (`if (ok) {} else
{ fail(); }`). Either way the reader has to guess what was intended.

**How to fix.** Add the missing code, invert the condition, or remove the block. If doing
nothing really is correct, say why in a comment inside the block.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (cache.isValid()) {
} else {
    cache.reload();
}

// Compliant
if (!cache.isValid()) {
    cache.reload();
}
```

Not reported: `catch` blocks (see `empty-catch-block`) and an empty `try` whose catch blocks
are all empty too (that no-op statement is already reported there), method, constructor and
lambda bodies,
arrow-switch cases `case X -> {}`, try-with-resources bodies (acquiring and releasing the
resource is the point), and loops that do their work in the header — a `while`/`do` whose
condition calls a method (`while (queue.poll() != null) {}`) or a `for` whose counter outlives
the loop (`for (i = 0; a[i] != 0; i++) {}`).

### java/empty-catch-block

**Empty catch block**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: error-handling

Detects `catch` blocks that contain no statements.

**Why it matters.** Swallowing an exception silently hides failures: the program continues in
an unknown state and the original cause is lost, which makes defects slow to diagnose.

**How to fix.** Handle the exception (recover, retry, translate and rethrow, or at least log it).
If ignoring it really is correct, say why in a comment inside the block, or name the variable
`ignored` / `expected` (or `_`) to make the intent explicit.

```java
// Noncompliant
try { cache.load(); } catch (IOException e) { }

// Compliant
try { cache.load(); } catch (IOException e) { log.warn("cache unavailable, starting cold", e); }
try { lock.close(); } catch (IOException ignored) { }
try { lock.close(); } catch (IOException e) { /* best effort: the lock file is recreated on start */ }
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `allow_comment` | `true` | Accept an empty catch block that contains a comment explaining why the exception is ignored. |

### java/empty-constructor

**Empty constructor without explanation**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: unused, documentation

Detects constructors whose body is empty and contains no comment.

**Why it matters.** An empty constructor is either redundant — when it is the only one and
takes no parameters, the compiler generates the same default constructor — or it exists for a
reason the code does not state: a framework or serializer that needs a no-argument
constructor next to the real ones, or an API that must stay source-compatible. Without a
comment, readers cannot tell which, and a later cleanup may remove one that a framework
needs, or keep one nobody uses.

**How to fix.** Remove a redundant constructor, or add a comment inside the body saying why
it is there.

```java
// Noncompliant
public class Invoice {
    public Invoice() {}
    public Invoice(String number) { this.number = number; }
}

// Compliant
public class Invoice {
    public Invoice() {
        // Required by the JSON mapper.
    }
    public Invoice(String number) { this.number = number; }
}
```

Off by default: many code bases keep empty no-argument constructors for frameworks as a
matter of course. Not reported: `private` constructors (the usual way to prevent
instantiation of utility classes and singletons), enum constructors, annotated constructors
(`@Inject`, `@JsonCreator`, …, whose purpose the annotation states), constructors that call
`super(…)` or `this(…)`, bodies followed by a comment on the same line
(`Money() {} // for JPA`), and test files.

### java/empty-method

**Empty method without explanation**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, documentation

Detects methods whose body is empty and contains no comment.

**Why it matters.** An empty method may be intentional (a no-op hook, an interface method
that does not apply) or a forgotten implementation. Readers cannot tell which, and callers may
silently rely on behaviour that never happens.

**How to fix.** Implement the method, throw `UnsupportedOperationException` if the operation
is not supported, or add a comment inside the body explaining why doing nothing is correct.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Override
public void onShutdown() {}

// Compliant
@Override
public void onShutdown() {
    // Nothing to release: this listener holds no resources.
}
```

Not reported: abstract and native methods, `default` interface methods, constructors,
methods with annotations other than `@Override` (for example AspectJ `@Pointcut` or test
lifecycle hooks, which are empty by design), and bodies followed by a comment on the same
line (`void reset() {} // no state`). Test code is not checked: mocks and stubs consist of
empty methods by design. Besides test files, that includes JUnit 3 test classes kept under a
main source root (a class extending `TestCase` or a `…TestCase` base class).

### java/empty-source-file

**Source file without any type declaration** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: unused, dead-code

Detects Java source files that contain no class, interface, enum, record or
annotation type: only a package line, imports, comments, or nothing at all.

**Why it matters.** Such a file compiles to nothing. It is usually what remains after the
type it held was moved, renamed or commented out, and it misleads whoever searches the
source tree: the file name promises a type that does not exist, and commented-out code in it
suggests it may come back.

**How to fix.** Delete the file (the version history keeps the old content).

```java
// Noncompliant: OrderMapper.java
package com.acme.orders;

import java.util.Map;

// Mapping moved to OrderConverter.
```

Not reported: `package-info.java`, `module-info.java` and other files whose name is not a
Java identifier (templates such as `license.header.java`), which are not meant to hold a type;
compact source files (top-level methods and fields, Java 25); files under a `resources`
folder (inputs of tests or generators, not compiled sources); and files with syntax errors,
where a declaration may have been lost by the parser.

### java/empty-statement

**Empty statement**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: suspicious, clutter

Detects empty statements — a lone `;` — such as `foo();;`, a `;` after a
member declaration (in a class, interface or enum body), or `if (x);`.

**Why it matters.** A doubled semicolon is only clutter, but a `;` right after `if (…)`,
`while (…)` or an enhanced `for (…)` header silently becomes the whole body: the block
that follows runs unconditionally (or once), which is a real bug that is easy to miss.

**How to fix.** Delete the stray semicolon. If a loop intentionally has no body, write an
empty block with a comment instead.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (list.isEmpty());
{
    return;             // always returns
}
counter++;;

// Compliant
if (list.isEmpty()) {
    return;
}
counter++;
```

Not reported: the semicolons inside a `for (;;)` header, a classic `for` loop whose header
does the work (`for (i = 0; a[i] != 0; i++);`), and a `while`/`do` whose condition calls a
method (`while (it.next() != null);`), and the `;` that ends the constants of an enum.

### java/equals-asymmetric-subclass

**Subclass equals is not symmetric with its superclass** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: equality

Detects a class whose `equals(Object)` checks `o instanceof Sub`, when its
superclass (declared in the same file) overrides `equals` with `o instanceof Super`.

**Why it matters.** `equals` must be symmetric. The superclass's method accepts any instance of
the superclass, including a `Sub`, so `superObj.equals(subObj)` can be `true`, while the
subclass's method rejects every object that is not a `Sub`, so `subObj.equals(superObj)` is
`false`. Hash sets, maps and `List.contains` then give answers that depend on which object
happens to be asked, and an object can be "found" in one collection and missing from another.

**How to fix.** Decide whether the two types can ever be equal. If not, compare classes with
`getClass() != o.getClass()` in the superclass. If they can, don't override `equals` in the
subclass (or use a `canEqual` handshake so both sides agree).

```java
// Noncompliant
class Point {
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Point p && x == p.x && y == p.y;
    }
}
class ColorPoint extends Point {
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof ColorPoint c && super.equals(c) && color == c.color;
    }
}

// Compliant
class Point {
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;
        Point p = (Point) o;
        return x == p.x && y == p.y;
    }
}
```

Only classes declared in the same file are compared. Methods that use `getClass()` or a
`canEqual` handshake are symmetric by design and are not reported.

### java/equals-overload

**equals() overloaded instead of overridden**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: equality

Detects an instance method `boolean equals(X)` whose parameter type is not
`Object`.

**Why it matters.** Such a method *overloads* `Object.equals(Object)` instead of overriding
it. Collections (`HashSet`, `HashMap`, `List.contains`), `Objects.equals`, assertion
libraries, and any caller holding the object as `Object` still use identity comparison, so
two "equal" values are treated as different — while direct calls with the static type `X`
behave differently. The result depends on the compile-time type of the argument.

**How to fix.** Declare `equals(Object)`, check the type inside, and add `@Override` so the
compiler verifies the signature.

```java
// Noncompliant
public boolean equals(Point other) {
    return x == other.x && y == other.y;
}

// Compliant
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    return o instanceof Point other && x == other.x && y == other.y;
}
```

Not reported: static methods, methods annotated `@Override` (they implement some interface
method), and classes that also declare `equals(Object)` (a deliberate typed helper next to
the real override).

### java/equals-unrelated-types

**equals() between unrelated types** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: equality, suspicious

Detects `a.equals(b)`, `Objects.equals(a, b)` and test assertions of equality
(`assertEquals(a, b)`, `assertNotEquals(a, b)`, AssertJ `assertThat(a).isEqualTo(b)` /
`isNotEqualTo(b)`) where the two values have
unrelated types, so the comparison is always `false`: a `Long` compared with an `int`, an
enum constant compared with a `String`, a `String` compared with a `StringBuilder`, an
`Optional` compared with the value it wraps.

**Why it matters.** `equals` takes an `Object`, so the compiler accepts any argument. The value
classes of the JDK (`String`, the wrappers, `UUID`, the `java.time` types, `Optional`, …) are
only ever equal to instances of their own class, and an enum constant only to itself. When the
argument's type can never be that class, the test is constant: the `if` never runs, the
lookup never matches, and the code silently does the wrong thing. Typical slips are autoboxing
(`count.equals(0)` on a `Long` compares with an `Integer`), comparing an enum with its name,
and comparing a wrapper with the object that holds the value.

**How to fix.** Compare values of the same type: convert one side (`count.equals(0L)`,
`status == Status.ACTIVE`, `status.name().equals("ACTIVE")`, `sb.toString().equals(s)`), or
compare the field that was meant.

```java
// Noncompliant
Long id = order.getId();
if (id.equals(42)) { … }                // Integer vs Long: always false
if (status.equals("ACTIVE")) { … }      // enum vs String: always false

// Compliant
if (id.equals(42L)) { … }
if (status == Status.ACTIVE) { … }
```

Reported only when the resolver proves both types and the receiver's `equals` is known to
accept only its own class: a JDK value class, an enum, a record, or a `final` class of this
file that inherits `Object.equals`. The argument's type must be provably unrelated (no object
can be an instance of both). Receivers of other types, whose `equals` could be written to
accept anything, are never reported; `null` arguments are left to `java/equals-with-null`.
For assertions, both sides must be such strict types (test libraries differ in which side's
`equals` they call), numeric, character and boolean pairs are skipped (a primitive overload may
widen instead of boxing), and only the two-argument forms are checked; an always-failing
`assertEquals` hides what the test meant to check, and an always-passing `assertNotEquals`
checks nothing. Comparisons where neither side's type shows in its syntax (a literal, or a variable with a
declared type), such as `a.getX().equals(b.getY())`, are not checked.

### java/equals-with-null

**equals() called with null**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: null-safety, equality

Detects `x.equals(null)`.

**Why it matters.** By the `equals` contract, `x.equals(null)` is always `false` for a
non-null `x` — and when `x` *is* null the call throws a `NullPointerException` before
`equals` even runs. So the expression can never detect a null value; the intended check was
almost certainly `x == null`.

**How to fix.** Compare the reference: `x == null` (or `Objects.isNull(x)`).

```java
// Noncompliant
if (result.equals(null)) { return fallback; }

// Compliant
if (result == null) { return fallback; }
```

Test code is not checked: `assertFalse(value.equals(null))` legitimately verifies the
`equals` contract.

### java/equals-without-hashcode

**equals() and hashCode() not overridden together**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: equality, collections

Detects classes that override `equals(Object)` without overriding
`hashCode()`, or the other way round.

**Why it matters.** Hash-based collections (`HashMap`, `HashSet`, caches) require that equal
objects have equal hash codes. With only `equals` overridden, two equal objects usually land in
different buckets: lookups miss, duplicates appear in sets. With only `hashCode` overridden,
the class still compares by identity, which is almost never what the author intended.

**How to fix.** Override both, based on the same fields (`Objects.hash(...)` helps), or use a
`record`, which generates consistent implementations.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Point {
    final int x, y;
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { ... }
}

// Compliant
class Point {
    final int x, y;
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { ... }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }
}
```

Records are not reported, nor an `equals` that only returns `super.equals(o)` (it keeps the
superclass's equality, which matches the inherited `hashCode`), an identity `equals`
(`return this == o;`, which every `hashCode` is consistent with), or a `hashCode` that only
returns `super.hashCode()`. Inherited methods are taken into account where they may matter: a
`hashCode` without `equals` in a class that extends another is only reported when every
superclass is declared in this file and none of them declares `equals` (an inherited `equals`
may compare the same fields), and an `equals` without `hashCode` is not reported when a
superclass of this file redeclares `hashCode()` abstract, or when the class is abstract and
extends a class of another file (which may do so). Lombok's `@EqualsAndHashCode`, `@Data` and
`@Value` do not help here: they generate both methods or neither, and neither as soon as the
class writes one of them, so a hand-written `equals` in such a class still lacks its
`hashCode`.

### java/equals-without-type-check

**equals() casts its argument without a type check**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: equality

Detects an `equals(Object)` implementation that casts its parameter without
any `instanceof` test or `getClass()` comparison.

**Why it matters.** The `equals` contract requires returning `false` for objects of other
types. A bare cast throws `ClassCastException` instead, so putting the object in a mixed
collection, comparing it with a proxy, or calling `list.contains("x")` blows up far away
from the actual mistake.

**How to fix.** Check the type first — `instanceof` (with a pattern variable) or
`getClass() != o.getClass()` when subclasses must never be equal.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    Point p = (Point) o;
    return x == p.x && y == p.y;
}

// Compliant
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    return o instanceof Point p && x == p.x && y == p.y;
}
```

Not reported when the method contains any `instanceof`, type pattern, `getClass()`,
`isInstance`/`isAssignableFrom` call, a `catch` clause, or passes the parameter to another
method first (for example `super.equals(o)` or a helper that may check the type).

### java/exception-logged-without-trace

**Exception logged without its stack trace**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: error-handling, logging

Detects a catch block that reports the caught exception at warning or error
level through a logger, but hands the logger only its text — `e.getMessage()`,
`e.getLocalizedMessage()`, `e.toString()` or `"…" + e` — and does nothing else with it: the
exception is not passed to the logger, not rethrown, not wrapped, not stored.

**Why it matters.** The handler is the last place that has the exception. Once only its
message is written, the stack trace and the chain of causes are gone for good: the log says
*that* something failed (sometimes only `null`, since many exceptions have no message) but not
*where*, and the root cause buried in `getCause()` is never seen. At warning or error level
the failure is by definition something someone will have to investigate.

**How to fix.** Pass the exception itself as the last argument of the logging call; every
logging API prints its stack trace and causes then.

```java
// Noncompliant
try {
    publisher.send(event);
} catch (IOException e) {
    log.error("could not publish event: " + e.getMessage());
}

// Compliant
try {
    publisher.send(event);
} catch (IOException e) {
    log.error("could not publish event {}", event.id(), e);
}
```

Loggers are recognized by their declared type (SLF4J, Log4j, Commons Logging, JBoss Logging,
`java.util.logging`) or by a conventional name in a file importing a logging API. Only
handlers after which the work is given up are considered: those in `void` methods,
constructors and initializers that assign nothing. Not reported: info, debug and trace
output; handlers that recover with a fallback value (a handler in a method returning a value
falls back to one, here or after the `try`; so does one that assigns a variable), since the
failure was expected and dealt with; handlers with an explanatory comment in their block (it
documents the failure as expected, and usually the fallback that follows: `// treat the same
as end of file`; tool markers and task tags written in capitals such as `// NOPMD` or `// TODO …`, and
commented-out code do not count);
handlers that throw, or use the exception in any way
other than for its text (the trace may be kept elsewhere); handlers inside lambdas; handlers
of `InterruptedException`, whose trace only shows where the thread was waiting; and test
code.

### java/exception-naming

**Exception class name without Exception suffix**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: naming, error-handling

Detects classes that extend an exception type but whose name doesn't end
in `Exception` or `Error`.

**Why it matters.** The suffix is how Java developers recognise throwables at a glance: in
`throws` clauses, catch blocks, imports, and stack traces. A class called `InvalidInput` or
`Timeout` reads like a value, not something that is thrown.

**How to fix.** Rename the class so its name ends in `Exception` (or `Error` for subclasses of
`java.lang.Error`).

```java
// Noncompliant
public class InvalidOrder extends RuntimeException { … }

// Compliant
public class InvalidOrderException extends RuntimeException { … }
```

The superclass is recognised by name (`…Exception`, `Throwable`) or, for names ending in
`Error`, only when the resolver proves it is a `Throwable` (many `…Error` classes are plain
data types).

### java/exception-not-thrown

**Exception created but not thrown**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: error-handling

Detects an exception object that is created as a statement of its own and then
dropped: `new IllegalArgumentException("bad id");` without `throw`.

**Why it matters.** Creating a `Throwable` does nothing by itself. The author almost certainly
meant to throw it, so the error condition the code was supposed to reject is silently
accepted and execution continues with invalid data.

**How to fix.** Add the missing `throw` (or remove the statement if it really is unneeded).

```java
// Noncompliant
if (id < 0) {
    new IllegalArgumentException("negative id: " + id);
}

// Compliant
if (id < 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative id: " + id);
}
```

The created type must be a proven `Throwable` subtype, or — for classes the resolver cannot
see (other files, libraries) — have a name ending in `Exception`. A name ending in `Error` is
not enough on its own, since plain classes are often named that way (error reports, error
response bodies, monitors that register themselves when constructed): such a type is reported
only when it is a JDK error (`java.lang.InternalError`, `java.io.IOError`, …) or a test-library
assertion error. Anonymous subclasses (`new Foo() { … };`) are not reported.

### java/explicit-finalize-call

**Explicit call to finalize()** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: finalization, resources

Detects explicit calls to `finalize()` (other than `super.finalize()`) and
calls to `System.runFinalizersOnExit(..)` / `Runtime.runFinalizersOnExit(..)`.

**Why it matters.** `finalize()` is the garbage collector's hook: calling it by hand does not
free the object, and the collector will still call it again later, so the cleanup runs twice
— closing a handle twice, releasing a native resource that another object now owns.
`runFinalizersOnExit` was deprecated from the start because it can run finalizers on live
objects while other threads still use them; it was removed in Java 11.

**How to fix.** Move the cleanup into a `close()` method (implement `AutoCloseable` and use
try-with-resources) and call that; use `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` as a safety net.

```java
// Noncompliant
connection.finalize();
System.runFinalizersOnExit(true);

// Compliant
connection.close();
```

Not reported: `super.finalize()` (the normal chaining inside a finalizer) and test code,
which may call a finalizer on purpose to exercise it.

### java/explicit-gc

**Explicit garbage collection request**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: performance, gc

Detects explicit requests for a garbage collection: `System.gc()` and
`Runtime.getRuntime().gc()` (or `gc()` on any `Runtime`) outside test code.

**Why it matters.** With the default collectors the call triggers a full, stop-the-world
collection of the whole heap: every application thread pauses, for seconds on large heaps,
at a moment the collector did not choose. It rarely fixes the problem it was added for (memory
that is still referenced is not freed; memory that is not referenced would have been freed
anyway), and its effect depends on JVM flags (`-XX:+DisableExplicitGC` turns it into a no-op,
`-XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent` changes it), so code that relies on it behaves differently
in each deployment.

**How to fix.** Remove the call and fix the underlying retention (clear references, close
resources, bound caches). Tune the collector with JVM options if pauses are the concern.

```java
// Noncompliant
cache.clear();
System.gc();

// Compliant
cache.clear();
```

Not reported: test code, where forcing a collection to observe weak or phantom references
is a legitimate technique, and benchmark code — files that use JMH (`org.openjdk.jmh`
imports) or sit in a `jmh` source set (`src/jmh/java`) — where collecting before measuring
memory or time is part of the method.

### java/explicit-varargs-array

**Array created for a varargs parameter**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: varargs, clutter

Detects an array created in the argument list (`new Object[] { a, b }`,
`new Class[0]`) and passed as the variable-arity (`...`) argument of a JDK method —
`String.format`, `printf`, `MessageFormat.format`, `Arrays.asList`, `List.of`, `Stream.of`,
`Paths.get`, `Method.invoke`, `Class.getMethod`, … — or of a method declared in the same class.

**Why it matters.** A varargs parameter builds that array itself: writing it out adds noise
(`new Object[] { … }` around the real arguments) and makes a call look like it needs an array
when it does not. It is usually a leftover of code written before Java 5 or of a library
version whose method took an array.

**How to fix.** Pass the elements directly, or nothing for an empty array.

```java
// Noncompliant
String msg = String.format("%s: %d", new Object[] { name, count });
Method m = type.getMethod("run", new Class[0]);

// Compliant
String msg = String.format("%s: %d", name, count);
Method m = type.getMethod("run");
```

Not reported: an array with a single element that could itself be an array or `null`
(unwrapping `invoke(target, new Object[] { args })` would spread `args` instead of passing it
as one argument), primitive arrays given to `Object...` or generic parameters (they are one
element there, see `java/ambiguous-varargs-argument`), methods of libraries (their parameter
may be a plain array in the version used), and same-class methods that are overloaded or
declared in a class that extends or implements anything (an inherited overload could take the
call).

### java/fail-swallowed-by-catch

**Test failure swallowed by its own catch**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: tests, exceptions

Detects `fail(..)`, or a test assertion (`assertEquals`, `assertThat`, …), inside a
`try` block whose first handler able to catch an `AssertionError` — `catch (Throwable ..)`,
`catch (Error ..)`, `catch (AssertionError ..)` — neither rethrows nor asserts anything.

**Why it matters.** `fail()` and failing assertions work by throwing `AssertionError`. The
"expected exception" idiom `try { call(); fail(); } catch (Throwable expected) { }` therefore
catches its own failure: when `call()` does *not* throw, `fail()` throws, the handler swallows
it, and the test passes. Likewise an `assertEquals` inside `try { … } catch (Throwable t) {
log(t); }` can never fail the test. The test cannot detect the regression it was written for.

**How to fix.** Catch the specific exception the code should throw, or use
`assertThrows` / `assertThatThrownBy`; keep assertions outside a catch-all.

```java
// Noncompliant
try {
    parser.parse("");
    fail("expected a parse error");
} catch (Throwable expected) {
}

// Compliant
assertThrows(ParseException.class, () -> parser.parse(""));
```

A handler that rethrows, throws something else, or makes an assertion about the caught
exception (which would fail on the `AssertionError`) is not reported, nor is a `fail()` that
an earlier, narrower `catch (AssertionError ..)` handles, nor one whose handler hands the
caught error on for a later check (`errors.add(e)`, `failure = e`). For assertions other than
`fail()`, a handler that does anything beyond logging or printing the error (adds it to a list,
counts it, stores it for a later check, calls other code) is not reported either, nor is a
`try` inside a loop (a retry loop that swallows failed attempts on purpose and fails after the
loop), nor a handler that ends with `return`/`break`/`continue` when the failure still has an
outcome: the handler returns a value the `try` block never returns (`return true` after the
assertion, `return false` in the handler: a polling check handed to a wait-until helper that
fails the test on time-out), or the code after the `try` fails the test (`catch
(AssertionError e) { return; } fail(..);` — the assertion is the code under test, expected to
throw).

### java/field-could-be-local

**Field could be a local variable**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: design, scope

Detects private instance fields that only one method uses, and that this
method always assigns before reading.

**Why it matters.** Such a field carries no state from one call to the next: it is a local
variable in disguise. As a field it widens the scope for no reason, keeps the value (and
anything it references) alive as long as the object, and makes the method unsafe to run from
two threads at once.

**How to fix.** Declare the variable inside the method and remove the field.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Exporter {
    private int written;

    void export(List<Row> rows) {
        written = 0;
        for (Row r : rows) { out(r); written++; }
        log(written);
    }
}

// Compliant
class Exporter {
    void export(List<Row> rows) {
        int written = 0;
        for (Row r : rows) { out(r); written++; }
        log(written);
    }
}
```

The check is deliberately strict: the first use in the method must be a plain assignment
(`x = …` or `this.x = …`) that is a top-level statement of the method body and does not read
the field; every other mention of the name in the file must be in the same method, outside
lambdas and inner classes, and refer to this field (a parameter or local variable of the same
name in another method, or the name inside a string or a comment, does not count). Not
reported: fields with an initializer other than the default value (`= null`, `= false`, `= 0`,
which the first assignment overwrites anyway), `static`, `volatile`, or annotated fields,
fields of classes with Lombok annotations that generate code reading or setting fields (`@Data`,
`@Getter`, `@Builder`, … — a logger annotation such as `@Slf4j` is fine), fields used by
constructors or initializers, methods that call themselves, and set-up callbacks
(`@BeforeEach`, `@Before`, `@PostConstruct`, …, and JUnit 3's `setUp()`), where fixtures are kept in
fields by convention.

### java/field-injection

**Field injection**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: spring, dependency-injection, design

Detects fields annotated with Spring's `@Autowired` or with `@Inject`
(`javax.inject` / `jakarta.inject`) in production code.

**Why it matters.** With field injection the container writes the dependencies into the
object after it has been built, through reflection. The class's constructor no longer states
what the class needs, the fields cannot be `final`, the object can exist in a half-wired
state (in a unit test, or when created with `new`), and circular or excessive dependencies
stay hidden. Constructor injection makes every dependency explicit, allows immutable
fields, and lets tests create the object with plain `new`; the framework documentation
recommends it for mandatory dependencies.

**How to fix.** Declare the dependencies as `final` fields and take them as constructor
parameters (a single constructor needs no annotation in Spring).

```java
// Noncompliant
@Service
class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository repository;
}

// Compliant
@Service
class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repository;

    OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }
}
```

Off by default: it is a design preference. Test classes are not reported (injecting fixtures
into test fields is the normal way to write container tests).

### java/field-naming

**Field naming convention**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: naming, convention

Detects fields that are not `static final` and whose name does not follow the
configured convention (by default camelCase: a lowercase letter followed by letters and digits,
no underscores).

**Why it matters.** Consistent field names make it obvious what is state and what is a
constant or a type. Prefixes and underscores (`m_count`, `_name`) or upper-case names on
mutable fields mislead readers.

**How to fix.** Rename the field. If it really is a constant, make it `static final`.

```java
// Noncompliant
private int Item_Count;
private String _name;

// Compliant
private int itemCount;
private String name;
```

Not reported: `static final` fields of any type (constants are covered by
`java/constant-naming`; the naming of `static final` loggers and collections varies between
teams), interface fields, record components, and fields in files that bind native code
through JNA (structure fields mirror native names). The `format` parameter takes a preset
name; regular expressions are not supported.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `format` | `"camelCase"` | Naming preset for fields: `camelCase` (`^[a-z][a-zA-Z0-9]*$`), `PascalCase`, `UPPER_SNAKE`, or `snake_case`. Arbitrary regular expressions are not supported; the regular expression of a preset is accepted as an alias. With an unknown value… |

### java/file-name-mismatch

**Top-level type named differently from its file** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, structure

Detects a source file whose only top-level type has a different name than
the file (`Helpers.java` declaring `class Utils`), compared case-sensitively.

**Why it matters.** The compiler insists on a matching name only for public types; a
package-private type can live in any file. Everyone who looks for `Utils` opens `Utils.java`,
which does not exist, and a later rename of the file or the type to "fix" the visibility then
breaks in surprising ways. On case-insensitive file systems a difference in case alone
(`Userservice.java` holding `UserService`) behaves differently from one machine to the next.

**How to fix.** Rename the file after the type, or the type after the file.

```java
// Noncompliant: Helpers.java
final class Utils { … }

// Compliant: Utils.java
final class Utils { … }
```

Not reported: files with several top-level types (see `java/multiple-top-level-types`),
`package-info.java`, `module-info.java`, compact source files without a class, files whose
name is not a Java identifier (templates), and files under a `resources` directory. The rule
is off by default: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

### java/file-too-long

**Files should not have too many lines of code**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~60 min · Tags: brain-overload, size

Flags files with more than `max_lines` lines of code (default 1000; blank and comment-only lines are not counted).

Very large files tend to mix responsibilities, are slow to navigate and review, and cause frequent merge conflicts.

**How to fix:** split the file along its responsibilities into smaller modules or classes.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_lines` | `1000` | Most lines of code allowed in one file |

### java/final-field-could-be-static

**Constant final field could be static**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: design, performance

Detects `final` instance fields of a primitive, boxed primitive or `String` type
initialized with a compile-time constant (`private final int retries = 3;`).

**Why it matters.** Every instance gets its own copy of a value that can never differ between
instances. Making the field `static` states that it is a class-wide constant, saves the
per-instance storage, and lets the compiler treat it as a constant everywhere.

**How to fix.** Add `static` (and, by convention, rename it in `UPPER_SNAKE` case).

```java
// Noncompliant
private final int maxRetries = 3;
private final String prefix = "job-";

// Compliant
private static final int MAX_RETRIES = 3;
private static final String PREFIX = "job-";
```

Only initializers made of literals and operators count (`60 * 1000`, `"a" + "b"`). Not
reported: annotated fields, fields of classes with Lombok annotations other than the logger ones
(`@Slf4j`, `@Log4j2`, … add a logger and nothing else) and of classes marked for persistence or
serialization frameworks (which read instance fields reflectively), and interface members
(already static). A non-static `serialVersionUID` is reported too: the
serialization mechanism ignores it unless it is `static`.

### java/finalize-override

**finalize() declared**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: resources, deprecated

Detects classes that declare a `finalize()` method.

**Why it matters.** Finalization is deprecated for removal. There is no guarantee when, or
whether, a finalizer runs; objects with finalizers slow down garbage collection, can be
resurrected, and run their cleanup on an unspecified thread. Resources released only in
`finalize()` leak under load.

**How to fix.** Make the class `AutoCloseable` and release resources in `close()` (used with
try-with-resources); for a safety net, register a `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` action.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Override
protected void finalize() throws Throwable {
    channel.close();
}

// Compliant
@Override
public void close() throws IOException {
    channel.close();
}
```

An empty `final` `finalize()` — the defensive idiom that stops subclasses from adding a
finalizer — is not reported, nor a `final` one whose only statement is `super.finalize();`
(the same idiom, delegating to the inherited no-op).

### java/fixme-comment

**FIXME, XXX and HACK comments should be resolved**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: todo

Flags comments containing `FIXME`, `XXX` or `HACK` markers.

A marker word used as placeholder text is not reported: quoted (`file name "XXX"`), as a member name (`Thread.XXX`), inside inline code or emphasis (`set<em>XXX</em>()`), or in a run of X placeholders (`XXXX XXX XX n`).

These markers admit that the code is known to be wrong or fragile. Unlike a TODO, the current behaviour itself is suspect.

**How to fix:** correct the code and delete the marker, or track the problem in the issue tracker with enough context to fix it later.

```text
// Noncompliant
total = total * 1.1; // FIXME rounding is wrong for negative amounts
```

### java/float-equality

**Floating-point values compared with == or !=**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: numbers, precision

Detects `==` and `!=` comparisons where an operand is a `float` or `double`
value.

**Why it matters.** Floating-point arithmetic rounds at almost every step, so two
computations that are mathematically equal often differ in the last bits: `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3`
is `false`. Exact comparisons therefore fail intermittently, depending on the inputs.

**How to fix.** Compare with a tolerance suited to the magnitudes involved
(`Math.abs(a - b) < EPSILON`), use `BigDecimal` for decimal quantities such as money, or
`Double.compare(a, b) == 0` when bitwise-exact equality really is wanted.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (total == expected) { ... }

// Compliant
if (Math.abs(total - expected) < 1e-9) { ... }
```

Not reported: `x != x` / `x == x` (the NaN test), comparisons with an integral constant such
as `0`, `-1`, or `1.0` (sentinels and exact guards like `if (divisor == 0.0)`) or with a
`static final` constant of this file holding one (`AUTO_DPI = -1f`), the two ends of a range
compared right before dividing by their difference (`if (max == min) return lo;` guarding
`/ (max - min)`, an exact test for a zero divisor), comparisons
with `MAX_VALUE`, `MIN_VALUE`, or the infinities, whole-number tests against the rounded value
(`x == Math.floor(x)`, `x == (long) x`), and operands whose type is unknown.

### java/float-loop-counter

**Floating-point loop counter** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, floating-point

Detects `for` loops whose counter is a `float` or `double` (declared in
the loop header, tested in its condition, and updated in its update part).

**Why it matters.** Most decimal steps (`0.1`, `0.01`) have no exact binary representation, so
the counter drifts: after ten steps of `0.1` it is `0.9999999999999999`, not `1.0`. The number
of iterations then depends on rounding — the loop may run once more or once less than
intended, or never end when it tests for equality. With `float`, large counters stop
changing altogether once the step is below their precision.

**How to fix.** Count with an integer and compute the floating-point value from it.

```java
// Noncompliant
for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) {
    plot(x);
}

// Compliant
for (int i = 0; i <= 10; i++) {
    plot(i / 10.0);
}
```
