Not reported: floating-point variables that the loop header declares but does not both test
and update (an accumulator in a loop that ends with `break`), and `for`-each loops over
collections of numbers.

### java/for-loop-counter-misuse

**for loop counter changed outside its header**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: loops, confusing

Detects `for` loops whose header does not say how the loop advances:

* the body assigns the counter (`i = …`) although the update clause changes it too, or steps
  it further (`i += 2`) on every pass, so the loop visits other elements than the header
  promises;
* the update clause changes only variables that the condition does not test
  (`for (int i = 0; i < n; j++)`), or the counter of an enclosing loop
  (`for (int col = 0; col < grid[row].length; row++)`), usually a slip when copying a nested
  loop.

**Why it matters.** The three parts of a `for` header are where readers look to learn which
values the counter takes. When the body moves the counter as well, that promise is wrong:
elements are skipped or visited twice depending on data, off-by-one errors hide in the
interplay of the two updates, and the loop's end is harder to prove. An update that doesn't
touch what the condition tests either never ends the loop or leaves the real advance to the
body.

**How to fix.** Let one place control the counter: use a `while` loop when the step depends on
the data, or restructure the body so that the header's update is the only change.

```java
// Noncompliant
for (int i = 0; i < records.length; i++) {
    process(records[i]);
    i += 2;                       // really a step of 3
}
for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
    if (queue.get(i).matches(id)) {
        found = true;
        i = size;                 // a disguised break
    }
}

// Compliant
for (int i = 0; i < records.length; i += 3) {
    process(records[i]);
}
for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
    if (queue.get(i).matches(id)) {
        found = true;
        break;
    }
}
```

Only counters declared in the loop header and compared with `<`, `<=`, `>` or `>=` are
considered (loops tested with `==` or `!=` are left to rules about skipping the bound). Not
reported: `++` and `--` on the counter in the body (the idiom that consumes the next element
while parsing, or that steps back after removing an element), compound steps (`i += 2`)
taken only under a condition (the same parsing idiom for longer tokens), writes inside a
lambda or an inner class, and loops whose update clause is empty (then the body is the only
place that advances the counter, which the header shows plainly).

### java/foreach-element-cast

**For-each variable widened and cast back** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: clarity, casts

Detects a for-each loop whose variable is declared with a wider type than the
known element type of the array or collection, when the loop body starts by casting the
variable back to that element type.

**Why it matters.** The cast only undoes the widening of the declaration: the elements already
have the type. The detour adds a line, a second name for the same element, and a cast that
readers must check and that hides a real mistake if the collection's type changes later.

**How to fix.** Declare the loop variable with the element type and drop the cast.

```java
// Noncompliant
for (Object o : names) {          // List<String> names
    String name = (String) o;
    print(name);
}

// Compliant
for (String name : names) {
    print(name);
}
```

Only element types the resolver knows are considered (arrays, and `Iterable` types with a
known type argument); raw collections, where the cast is needed, are not reported. Not
reported either: casts to a type other than the element type (a narrowing beyond it), and
casts that are not the first statement of the body.

### java/format-argument-mismatch

**Format placeholders and arguments don't match**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: format, logging

Detects a format call whose string-literal pattern expects a different number of
arguments than it is given:

* `String.format`, `"…".formatted(..)`, `PrintStream`/`PrintWriter` `printf` and `format`
  (`%s`, `%d`, … — `%%` and `%n` take no argument);
* `MessageFormat.format` (`{0}`, `{1}`, … — the highest index decides);
* SLF4J and Log4j 2 logger calls (`log.info("a {} b {}", x, y)`), where a final exception
  argument beyond the placeholders is allowed (it is logged with its stack trace).

**Why it matters.** A missing argument makes `String.format` throw
`MissingFormatArgumentException` at run time — typically in an error path, hiding the
original problem. Extra arguments are silently ignored, and logger messages print a literal
`{}`: in both cases the message lacks the information the author wanted to record.

**How to fix.** Make the placeholders and the arguments agree.

```java
// Noncompliant
String.format("%s: %s", user);
log.warn("Retry {} of {} failed", attempt);

// Compliant
String.format("%s: %s", user, reason);
log.warn("Retry {} of {} failed", attempt, max);
```

Not reported: patterns that are not string literals, explicit argument indexes (`%2$s`,
`%<s`), a single argument that may be an `Object[]` passed as the varargs array, logger
calls whose first argument is not the message (markers), and MessageFormat patterns with
quotes.

### java/function-too-long

**Functions should not have too many lines of code**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: brain-overload, size

Flags functions with more than `max_lines` lines of code (default 80; blank and comment-only lines are not counted).

Long functions usually do several things at once. They are harder to name, to understand and to reuse, and changes to them are riskier.

**How to fix:** extract cohesive steps into separate, well-named functions.

```text
// Noncompliant
importFile(path) { /* parse, validate, transform, save, notify — 150 lines */ }

// Compliant
importFile(path) { save(transform(validate(parse(path)))); notify(path); }
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_lines` | `80` | Most lines of code allowed in one function |

### java/generic-exception-thrown

**Generic exception thrown**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: error-handling

Detects `throw new RuntimeException(…)`, `throw new Exception(…)`,
`throw new Throwable(…)`, and `throw new Error(…)`.

**Why it matters.** Callers can only handle a generic exception by catching the generic type,
which also catches every unrelated failure. The type carries no meaning, so the only way to
tell failures apart is parsing messages.

**How to fix.** Throw a specific standard exception (`IllegalArgumentException`,
`IllegalStateException`, `UncheckedIOException`, …) or a dedicated domain exception.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (port < 0) {
    throw new RuntimeException("negative port " + port);
}

// Compliant
if (port < 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative port " + port);
}
```

Test code is not checked (tests throw generic exceptions to simulate failures).

### java/hard-coded-absolute-path

**Hard-coded absolute file-system path**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: portability, configuration

Detects string literals in production code that are absolute file-system paths
tied to one machine or one operating system:

* a Windows drive path to data or a user folder, in any use: `"C:\\data\\input.csv"`,
  `"D:/exports"`, `"c:/users/alice/report.pdf"`;
* a Windows system folder (`"C:\\Windows\\Fonts\\arial.ttf"`, `"C:\\Program Files\\…"`) or
  the Unix temporary folder (`"/tmp/cache"`, `"/var/tmp/x"`) given straight to a file API:
  `new File(..)`, `Paths.get(..)`, `Path.of(..)`, `Files.*(..)`, file streams, readers and
  writers;
* a macOS home folder (`"/Users/bob/work"`) given to a file API or stored in a variable, field
  or constant named like a path (`path`, `dir`, `file`, `folder`, `home`, `location`).

**Why it matters.** The path exists on the developer's machine, or on one operating system,
and nowhere else: the program fails on another workstation, in a container, on a build
server, or on Windows versus Unix. A hard-coded temporary folder also bypasses the platform's
setting and can collide with other users of a shared machine.

**How to fix.** Read the location from configuration (a property, an environment variable, a
command-line argument), or derive it: `System.getProperty("java.io.tmpdir")`,
`Files.createTempDirectory(..)`, `System.getProperty("user.home")`.

```java
// Noncompliant
File out = new File("C:\\reports\\daily.pdf");
Path cache = Paths.get("/tmp/app-cache");

// Compliant
File out = new File(config.reportDirectory(), "daily.pdf");
Path cache = Files.createTempDirectory("app-cache");
```

Not reported: test code; annotation values (documentation examples, defaults of injected
properties); the fallback value of a configuration lookup (`getProperty(key, "/tmp/x")`,
`orElse(..)`); literals compared with or searched in another string (`startsWith("C:\\")`,
path-parsing code); `case` labels; bare roots (`"C:\\"`); system folders and `/tmp` kept in
constants, which usually list the known locations of each platform on purpose, or used as a
path on a remote Unix host; `/home/…` and `/root/…` (the fixed layout of containers and
service accounts); and URIs (`file:///C:/…`), which do not start with the path.

### java/has-next-calls-next

**hasNext() calls next()** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: iterators, api-misuse

Detects a `hasNext()` method that calls the same object's `next()` (and
`hasMoreElements()` calling `nextElement()`).

**Why it matters.** `hasNext()` must be a side-effect-free query: callers may call it any
number of times before `next()`. Implementing it by fetching the next element consumes that
element, so every call to `hasNext()` silently skips one — `for`-each loops lose every other
element, and `hasNext(); hasNext();` runs off the end.

**How to fix.** Look ahead without consuming: compute and cache the next element in a field
(`hasNext()` fills it if empty, `next()` returns and clears it).

```java
// Noncompliant
public boolean hasNext() {
    return next() != null;
}

// Compliant
public boolean hasNext() {
    if (pending == null) {
        pending = fetch();
    }
    return pending != null;
}
```

Only unqualified or `this.` calls to a `next()` declared in the same class are reported; calls
on another iterator (delegation) are fine.

### java/hex-string-without-padding

**Byte converted to hex without zero padding** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: strings, encoding

Detects bytes converted with `Integer.toHexString(b & 0xFF)` (or
`Long.toHexString`) and appended back to back to a string or builder inside a loop, with no
padding to two digits.

**Why it matters.** `toHexString` drops leading zeros: the byte `0x0A` becomes `"a"`, not
`"0a"`. Hex strings built this way — digests, checksums, tokens, encoded keys — have a variable
length and are ambiguous (`0x01 0x23` and `0x12 0x03` both give `"123"`), so comparisons with
correctly encoded values fail for some inputs only.

**How to fix.** Pad each byte to two digits, or use a formatter.

```java
// Noncompliant
for (byte b : digest) {
    hex.append(Integer.toHexString(b & 0xFF));
}

// Compliant
for (byte b : digest) {
    hex.append(String.format("%02x", b));
}
String same = HexFormat.of().formatHex(digest);   // Java 17+
```

Not reported: results stored in a variable first (usually padded next), conversions outside
loops, and loop bodies that contain any string or character literal or check a `length()` —
the usual manual padding, or separators such as `':'` that keep the output unambiguous.

### java/hidden-declaration

**Declaration hides another one** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: confusing, naming, conventions

Detects declarations that hide another declaration of the same file, so that one
name means two things in the same place:

* a local variable of an instance method named like a field of its class;
* an instance field declared again, under the same name, in a subclass of a class of the same
  file that already has it (non-private);
* a type parameter of an instance method, constructor or inner class named like a type
  parameter of the enclosing class.

**Why it matters.** Inside the scope of the hiding declaration the plain name refers to the
new one, while readers (and the author a few weeks later) expect the other: an assignment
meant for the field only changes the local, a subclass method sees one copy of the state and
the parent's methods the other, and `T` in the method signature is not the class's `T`.

**How to fix.** Rename one of the two declarations (or, for a field, remove the duplicate and
use the parent's).

```java
// Noncompliant
class Order {
    private int total;
    void add(Line line) {
        int total = line.price() * line.quantity();   // hides the field
        …
    }
}

// Compliant
class Order {
    private int total;
    void add(Line line) {
        int lineTotal = line.price() * line.quantity();
        …
    }
}
```

Not reported: parameters (constructor, setter, builder and factory parameters named like the
field they initialize are the normal idiom), locals in constructors, static methods, lambdas,
anonymous classes and test code, locals holding a copy of the object's state
(`Thread worker = this.worker;`, the usual way to read a volatile field once, or
`Node root = getRoot();`) or whose value is later stored in the field
(`this.total = total`, or through the class's own setter: `setTotal(total)`), static fields (each class may define its own constants or logger),
static methods and static nested classes reusing a type parameter name (they cannot see the
enclosing one), types named like the type they extend (nested `Builder extends
Parent.Builder` classes and drop-in replacements of a library class are deliberate), and
hiding across files, which needs the other files' types.

Off by default: names shared between a local and a field are a style many code bases
accept.

### java/identical-branches

**Both branches of a conditional are identical**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, copy-paste

Detects an `if` statement whose `then` and `else` branches contain the same
code, and a conditional expression `c ? x : x` whose two results are the same.

**Why it matters.** The condition has no effect, which is either a copy-paste mistake (one
branch was meant to do something else) or leftover code that makes readers look for a
difference that isn't there.

**How to fix.** Fix the branch that should differ, or drop the condition and keep one copy of
the code.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (user.isAdmin()) {
    render(page);
} else {
    render(page);
}
String label = compact ? name : name;

// Compliant
render(page);
String label = compact ? shortName : name;
```

Branches are compared ignoring whitespace and comments. `else if` chains are checked link by
link: only an `if` whose `else` is a plain block or statement is compared. Two empty blocks are
left to `empty-block`.

### java/identical-catch-branches

**Identical catch branches**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: duplication, exceptions

Detects `catch` clauses of the same `try` statement whose bodies are
identical (the exception variable may have a different name in each).

**Why it matters.** Duplicated handlers have to be kept in sync by hand; sooner or later one
of them is changed and the other isn't. Since Java 7 a single multi-catch clause expresses
"handle these the same way" directly.

**How to fix.** Merge the clauses into one multi-catch.

```java
// Noncompliant
try {
    load(file);
} catch (IOException e) {
    log.warn("cannot load " + file, e);
} catch (ParseException e) {
    log.warn("cannot load " + file, e);
}

// Compliant
try {
    load(file);
} catch (IOException | ParseException e) {
    log.warn("cannot load " + file, e);
}
```

Reported only when merging is possible: the caught types must be provably unrelated (a
multi-catch may not list a subclass together with its superclass), so clauses catching types
unknown to the resolver are left alone. Neither are handlers that pass the caught exception to
a method or constructor whose overload may depend on its type (`throw wrap(ex);` with
`wrap(TimeoutException)` and `wrap(ExecutionException)`): the textually identical clauses
call different methods, and a multi-catch would call the most general one. That is assumed
for overloads declared in this file and for unqualified calls to methods this file does not
declare (inherited or statically imported). Empty handlers are not reported (see
`java/empty-catch-block`).

### java/identical-methods

**Methods with identical bodies**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: duplication

Detects two methods of one class whose bodies are the same code token for
token (comments and layout aside), with the same return type and the same parameter list.
Bodies shorter than three lines are not compared.

**Why it matters.** Two copies of the same logic have to be kept in step by hand: a fix or a
change applied to one of them is easily forgotten in the other, and the two then drift apart
silently. The duplicate also makes the reader compare the bodies to find out whether they
really are the same.

**How to fix.** Keep the code in one place: let one method call the other, or move the body
into a private method both call (safer when both are hooks subclasses may override
separately), or remove the second method and update its callers.

```java
// Noncompliant
String describeOrder(Order order) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(order.id());
    sb.append(": ").append(order.total());
    return sb.toString();
}
String describeInvoice(Order order) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(order.id());
    sb.append(": ").append(order.total());
    return sb.toString();
}

// Compliant
String describeInvoice(Order order) {
    return describeOrder(order);
}
```

Not reported: test files, methods of different classes (sibling implementations would need a
shared parent first), methods of anonymous classes and enum constant bodies (each implements
its own callback), two methods that both override (each fulfils its own contract, and stubs
often give the same answer to several questions), methods whose parameter or return types
differ (overloads for
different primitive types often have to repeat their body), and bodies whose statements span
fewer lines than `min_lines`. The larger token-level duplication across files is measured
separately.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `min_lines` | `3` | Smallest number of lines the statements of a body span for the method to be compared. |

### java/identical-operands

**Identical expressions on both sides of an operator**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, typo

Detects binary operations whose two operands are the same side-effect-free
expression — `a == a`, `x < x`, `flag && flag`, `n - n`, `mask | mask` — and `a.equals(a)`.

**Why it matters.** The result is fixed (`true`, `false`, `0`, `1`, or the operand itself), so
the expression doesn't test or compute what it appears to. It is nearly always a copy-paste
slip where one side should name a different variable (`a.x == b.x` written as `a.x == a.x`).

**How to fix.** Correct the operand that was meant to differ, or replace the expression with
its constant value if that really is the intent.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (left.getId() == left.getId() && width == width) { ... }
return this.start - this.start;

// Compliant
if (left.getId() == right.getId() && width == other.width) { ... }
return this.start - other.start;
```

Not reported: operands containing calls, `new`, assignments, or increments (they may yield
different values); two literals; `x == x` / `x != x` and other comparisons or arithmetic on
`float`/`double` values (the NaN-test idiom) or on values whose type is unknown; and
`a.equals(a)` in test code, where it checks that `equals` is reflexive.

### java/ignored-failure-return

**Failure-reporting result ignored**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: api-misuse, error-handling

Detects calls whose return value is the only report of failure or of partial
work, used as statements:

* `java.io.File`: `delete`, `createNewFile`, `renameTo`, `setLastModified`,
  `setReadable`, `setWritable`, `setExecutable`, `setReadOnly` return `false` instead of
  throwing;
* `Lock.tryLock(..)` returns `false` when the lock was *not* acquired;
* `InputStream.read(buf..)` / `Reader.read(buf..)` return how many elements were actually
  read (possibly fewer than asked, or `-1` at the end), and `skip(n)` how many were skipped.

**Why it matters.** Ignoring these results turns failures into silent misbehaviour: a file
that was not deleted or renamed, a critical section entered without the lock, a buffer
processed as if it were full although only part of it was filled.

**How to fix.** Check the result — throw or log when it signals failure, loop until the
buffer is filled (or use `readNBytes` / `DataInputStream.readFully`), and only enter the
critical section when `tryLock()` returned `true`. For files, `java.nio.file.Files`
(`delete`, `createDirectories`, `move`) throws a descriptive exception instead.

```java
// Noncompliant
tmp.delete();
in.read(header);

// Compliant
Files.delete(tmp.toPath());
in.readNBytes(header, 0, header.length);
```

`File` operations are not reported in test code (cleanup there is best-effort by design).
`mkdir()` / `mkdirs()` are deliberately left out: they also return `false` when the directory
already exists, so ignoring the result is the usual "make sure it exists" idiom (a real
failure surfaces at the next file operation).
Only receivers whose type the resolver proves are reported: variables, parameters, and
fields declared in this file with such a type, or objects created in place (`new File(..)`).

### java/ignored-return-value

**Result of a side-effect-free call ignored**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: api-misuse, immutability

Detects a call whose only effect is to return a new value, used as a statement
so that the value is thrown away:

* `String`: `trim`, `strip*`, `toUpperCase`, `toLowerCase`, `replace*`, `substring`,
  `concat`, `repeat`, `formatted`, `indent`, and the static `String.format` / `join` /
  `valueOf`;
* `BigDecimal` / `BigInteger` arithmetic (`add`, `subtract`, `multiply`, `divide`, `pow`,
  `negate`, `abs`, `setScale`, `max`, `min`, shifts, bit operations, …);
* `java.time` values: `plus*`, `minus*`, `with*`, `truncatedTo`, `negated`,
  `multipliedBy`, …;
* `Optional`: `filter`, `or`, `orElse`, and `map` / `flatMap` with a side-effect-free lambda;
* `Stream` / `IntStream` / `LongStream` / `DoubleStream` intermediate operations (`map`,
  `filter`, `sorted`, `peek`, `limit`, …).

**Why it matters.** These types are immutable (or, for streams, lazy): the call computes a
result and changes nothing else. `name.trim();` leaves `name` untouched, `total.add(tax);`
does not update `total`, and `stream.filter(..)` without a terminal operation runs nothing.
The code reads like an update that never happens.

**How to fix.** Use the returned value — usually by assigning it back.

```java
// Noncompliant
amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
date.plusDays(1);

// Compliant
amount = amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
date = date.plusDays(1);
```

Only receivers whose type the resolver proves are reported. `Optional.orElseThrow`,
`orElseGet`, and `String.intern` are deliberately not included, and calls that may be there to
provoke an exception are skipped: statements in a `try` body that has a `catch`, and, in test
code, statements inside lambdas (`assertThrows(.., () -> { s.substring(9); })`). The arm of a
`switch` expression whose value is used (`return switch (mode) { case UPPER ->
s.toUpperCase(); … };`) yields the call's result instead of discarding it and is not reported
either.

### java/immediately-returned-variable

**Variable returned immediately after its declaration**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: clutter, redundant

Detects a local variable that is declared with a value and then immediately
returned or thrown by the next statement.

**Why it matters.** The variable adds a name and a line without adding information; the
reader has to check that nothing happens to it in between.

**How to fix.** Return (or throw) the expression directly.

```java
// Noncompliant
String label = prefix + name;
return label;

IllegalStateException error = new IllegalStateException("closed");
throw error;

// Compliant
return prefix + name;

throw new IllegalStateException("closed");
```

Not reported: annotated declarations (for example `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` on a cast,
which cannot be placed on a `return`), array initializers, lambdas and method references
(which need the declared type as their target), and primitive variables whose declared type
differs from the value's type (the conversion would change what is returned).

### java/impossible-size-check

**Size compared with a value it can never have**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: collections, suspicious

Detects comparisons of a size or length with a constant whose result never
changes because a size is never negative: `list.size() < 0` (always false),
`name.length() >= 0` (always true), `array.length == -1`, `map.size() > -1`.

**Why it matters.** The condition doesn't test anything. Usually the author meant a
different check — emptiness (`isEmpty()`, `> 0`), a bound (`< max`), or an `indexOf` result
compared with `-1` — and the guarded code now runs always or never.

**How to fix.** Write the comparison that was intended, or remove the dead condition.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (items.size() >= 0) { process(items.get(0)); }

// Compliant
if (items.size() > 0) { process(items.get(0)); }
```

Only `size()` of a `Collection` or `Map`, `length()` of a `CharSequence` (`String`,
`StringBuilder`, …) and `length` of an array are checked, when the resolver proves the
receiver's type; custom `size()` methods may return -1 and are not reported.

### java/incompatible-collection-lookup

**Collection lookup with an incompatible type**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: collections, api-misuse

Detects collection and map lookups whose argument can never be equal to an
element or key: `Collection.contains/remove`, `List.indexOf/lastIndexOf`, and
`Map.get/containsKey/containsValue/remove/getOrDefault` called with a value of a type
unrelated to the declared element, key, or value type.

**Why it matters.** These methods take `Object`, so the compiler accepts any argument. A
`Set<Long>` never contains an `Integer`, and a `Map<String, User>` never has a key of type
`UUID` — the lookup always misses: `contains` is always `false`, `get` always `null`, and
`remove` silently removes nothing. The mismatch usually comes from autoboxing (`int` vs
`Long`) or from passing the wrong variable.

**How to fix.** Convert the argument to the element/key type (`set.contains((long) id)`,
`map.get(id.toString())`), or pass the variable that was meant.

```java
// Noncompliant
Set<Long> ids = loadIds();
int id = request.id();
if (ids.contains(id)) { … }   // Integer vs Long: always false

// Compliant
if (ids.contains((long) id)) { … }
```

Reported only when both types are known and one of them is a final JDK class (`String`,
the boxed primitives, `UUID`, `java.time` values, …) that is provably unrelated to the
other, so no object can ever be both. The receiver must be a variable, parameter, or field
declared in this file with a parameterized collection or map type whose element, key, or
value type is such a final class; the argument must be a literal, a cast, or a variable
(call results and `var` receivers are not checked). `List.remove(int)` (removal by index)
is not a lookup and is not considered.

### java/incomplete-fluent-assertion

**Fluent assertion without a check**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: tests, assertj

Detects fluent assertions (AssertJ, Truth, FEST) that are started but never
finished: a statement that is only `assertThat(actual)`, possibly followed by description
calls (`.as(..)`, `.describedAs(..)`, `.withFailMessage(..)`) or by calls that only
configure or transform what is checked (`.usingRecursiveComparison()`, `.usingComparator(..)`,
`.extracting(..)`), and the same for `assertThatCode(..)` and `assertThatExceptionOfType(..)`
without their check. Besides statements, the expression body of a lambda handed to a method
that discards its result (`satisfies(e -> assertThat(e.id()))`, `allSatisfy`, `forEach`, …)
is checked too.

**Why it matters.** In fluent libraries `assertThat(x)` only creates an assertion object;
nothing is verified until a check such as `isEqualTo(..)` or `isTrue()` is called on it. The
line looks like an assertion, passes unconditionally, and the test verifies less than it seems.

**How to fix.** Chain the intended check.

```java
// Noncompliant
assertThat(result.isValid());
assertThat(order.total()).as("total");

// Compliant
assertThat(result.isValid()).isTrue();
assertThat(order.total()).as("total").isEqualTo(expected);
```

Only calls that provably come from a fluent assertion library are reported: qualified by one
of its entry classes (`Assertions`, `Truth`, …), statically imported from `org.assertj`,
`com.google.common.truth` or `org.fest`, made on a `SoftAssertions`-typed variable, or in a
class implementing AssertJ's `WithAssertions`. Hamcrest's two-argument `assertThat(x, matcher)`
is complete and never reported; a one-argument `assertThat` helper declared in the file is
skipped too.

### java/index-loop-could-be-foreach

**Index loop could be an enhanced for**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: idiom, readability

Detects counting loops over an array or a `List` —
`for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)` or `for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++)` — whose body
uses the index only to read the current element (`a[i]`, `list.get(i)`).

**Why it matters.** The enhanced `for` says the same thing with less machinery: no index to
get wrong (`<=`, a wrong bound, a stray `i++` in the body), no repeated `list.get(i)`, and the
element gets a name. On linked lists it is also much faster than `get(i)`.

**How to fix.** Iterate over the elements directly.

```java
// Noncompliant
for (int i = 0; i < names.size(); i++) {
    print(names.get(i));
}

// Compliant
for (String name : names) {
    print(name);
}
```

Also detects the iterator form, `for (Iterator<T> it = items.iterator(); it.hasNext();)`, when
the body calls `it.next()` exactly once on every pass and uses the iterator for nothing else.

Only the plain patterns are reported. Counting loops: an `int` index starting at `0`, a `<`
bound on the same array's `length` or list's `size()`, a `++` step, and a body in which every
use of the index is `a[i]` / `list.get(i)` on that same variable, which is itself used for
nothing else. Writes to the element (`a[i] = …`) keep the loop as it is. Lists must be known
`java.util.List`s. Iterator loops: no update clause, a collection known to be `Iterable` (a
variable declared in this file with a JDK collection type, a map view such as `entrySet()`),
and a single `it.next()` that is not behind a condition, a `&&`/`||`, an inner loop, or a
lambda, with no `break`, `continue`, `return` or `throw` before it. Loops that call
`it.remove()` or pass the iterator on need it and are left alone.

### java/index-of-positive-check

**indexOf() result checked with > 0**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: strings, collections

Detects the result of `String.indexOf(..)` or `List.indexOf(..)` compared with
`> 0` (or `0 <`).

**Why it matters.** `indexOf` returns `-1` when nothing is found and `0` when the match is
at the very beginning. `> 0` therefore treats a match at index 0 as "not found": a string
that *starts* with the separator or a list whose *first* element matches takes the wrong
branch. The intended test is almost always `>= 0` (or `contains(..)`).

**How to fix.** Use `>= 0` / `!= -1`, or `contains(..)`. If a match at position 0 really
must be excluded, make that explicit (`idx > 0` on a named variable, with a comment).

```java
// Noncompliant
if (path.indexOf('/') > 0) { … }

// Compliant
if (path.indexOf('/') >= 0) { … }
if (path.contains("/")) { … }
```

Only direct comparisons of an `indexOf(..)` call on a receiver proven to be a `String`,
`StringBuilder`, or `List` are reported, and not when the guarded code works with positions
(`substring`, `indexOf`, `charAt`) — there `> 0` usually deliberately requires a non-empty
prefix, as in `if (s.indexOf(':') > 0) key = s.substring(0, s.indexOf(':'));`.

### java/inner-class-could-be-static

**Inner class could be static**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: memory, design

Detects private or package-private member classes that are not `static` although
nothing in them uses the enclosing instance: no field or method of the enclosing class, no
`Outer.this`, no creation of other inner classes.

**Why it matters.** Every instance of an inner (non-static) class carries a hidden reference to
the object that created it. When the class does not need that object, the reference only
costs memory and keeps the enclosing object alive as long as any inner instance exists (a
classic leak with listeners, caches and tasks handed to other threads). It also means the
class can only be created from an instance of the enclosing class, and misleads readers into
looking for a dependency that is not there.

**How to fix.** Declare the class `static`.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Cache {
    private class Entry {          // holds a hidden Cache reference it never uses
        String key;
        long expires;
    }
}

// Compliant
class Cache {
    private static class Entry {
        String key;
        long expires;
    }
}
```

The check is conservative: any name in the class that matches an instance member of an
enclosing class counts as a use, as does any reference to the enclosing class's type
parameters. Classes are skipped when an enclosing class extends another class or implements
interfaces (inherited members cannot be seen), when they are public or protected, annotated
`@Nested` (JUnit requires those to be inner), or nested in an interface, a local or an
anonymous class. Test code is not checked (a hidden reference in a test helper costs
nothing), nor are files that use Lombok, whose generated accessors cannot be seen.

### java/instanceof-in-catch

**instanceof check on a caught exception**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: exceptions, readability

Detects `instanceof` tests on the caught exception inside a `catch` block.

**Why it matters.** Sorting exceptions by type is exactly what separate `catch` clauses do.
Doing it by hand with `instanceof` (and usually a cast) is longer, easier to get wrong
(order, a missing `else`), and hides from the reader which exceptions get special treatment.

**How to fix.** Add a dedicated `catch` clause for each type that needs different handling,
before the broader one.

```java
// Noncompliant
try {
    sync();
} catch (Exception e) {
    if (e instanceof TimeoutException) {
        retryLater();
    } else {
        fail(e);
    }
}

// Compliant
try {
    sync();
} catch (TimeoutException e) {
    retryLater();
} catch (Exception e) {
    fail(e);
}
```

Only tests of the exception variable itself are reported (not of its cause, as in
`e.getCause() instanceof …`).

### java/instanceof-pattern-candidate

**instanceof followed by a cast**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: java16, clarity

Detects `if (x instanceof T)` whose then-branch casts the same variable to
the same type, `(T) x`.

**Why it matters.** Since Java 16, pattern matching for `instanceof` binds a typed variable in
the test itself. The separate cast repeats the type, can drift out of sync with the check
during refactoring, and adds noise.

**How to fix.** Declare a pattern variable in the `instanceof` and use it instead of the cast.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (shape instanceof Circle) {
    Circle c = (Circle) shape;
    return c.radius();
}

// Compliant
if (shape instanceof Circle c) {
    return c.radius();
}
```

Only reported when the file is known to be compiled for Java 16 or later: `java.release` in
`.mote.yaml`, or the release declared by the nearest `pom.xml` / `build.gradle(.kts)`
(`maven.compiler.release`, `sourceCompatibility`, …). When the release is unknown or older,
the rule stays silent — the suggested syntax would not compile. The variable must be a plain
name (or `this.name`), the `instanceof` must be the condition or a `&&` operand of the
condition, and the cast must use exactly the same type text.

### java/int-constant-overflow

**Constant int arithmetic overflows** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: numbers, overflow

Detects arithmetic on `int` literals (`*`, `+`, `-`) whose exact result does not
fit in an `int`: `24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 * 365`, `3 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024`.

**Why it matters.** All operands are `int`, so the computation is done in 32 bits and wraps
around before the result is stored — even when it is assigned to a `long`. A year in
milliseconds becomes `1471228928`; three gigabytes becomes a negative number. The compiler
does not warn.

**How to fix.** Make the first operand a `long` literal so the whole product is computed in
64 bits, or use a unit API.

```java
// Noncompliant
long yearMillis = 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

// Compliant
long yearMillis = 365L * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
long same = TimeUnit.DAYS.toMillis(365);
```

Only expressions made entirely of decimal `int` literals are checked (hexadecimal, octal and
binary literals are often deliberate bit patterns), and the smallest overflowing
sub-expression is reported.

### java/int-multiplication-overflow

**int multiplication overflows before widening**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: numbers, overflow

Detects a multiplication of `int` values by a large constant factor whose result is
then used as a `long`, `float` or `double`: stored in such a variable, returned from such a
method, cast to it, combined with a `long` (`System.currentTimeMillis() + timeout * 1000`) or
passed to a JDK method taking a `long` time or duration (`Thread.sleep`, `TimeUnit`,
`Duration.of…`, `Instant.ofEpoch…`, `new Date(…)`).

**Why it matters.** Java evaluates `seconds * 1000` in 32 bits because both operands are
`int`; the widening to `long` happens only afterwards, when the product has already wrapped
around. A timeout of 25 days in seconds becomes a negative number of milliseconds, a size of
2048 MB in bytes becomes zero. Declaring the target as `long` shows a large value was
expected, and the compiler says nothing.

**How to fix.** Make one factor a `long` before multiplying, typically the constant
(`seconds * 1000L`), or use a conversion API (`TimeUnit.SECONDS.toMillis(seconds)`,
`Math.multiplyExact`).

```java
// Noncompliant
long timeoutMillis = timeoutSeconds * 1000;
Thread.sleep(minutes * 60 * 1000);
long bytes = sizeMb * 1024 * 1024;

// Compliant
long timeoutMillis = timeoutSeconds * 1000L;
Thread.sleep(TimeUnit.MINUTES.toMillis(minutes));
long bytes = sizeMb * 1024L * 1024;
```

Only products whose constant factors multiply to at least `min_factor` (default 1000: unit
conversions of time and sizes) are reported, and only when the resolver proves every factor
is an `int` (or narrower). Products whose factors are all constants — literals, and `final`
fields or locals of this file initialized with a constant expression (`final int count = 10;`)
— have a fixed value and are not reported (literal-only products are left to
`int-constant-overflow`); additions and products of variables alone are not reported.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `min_factor` | `1000` | Smallest product of the constant factors of the multiplication for it to be reported (1 reports every int product that is widened). |

### java/int-to-long-bits-to-double

**Double.longBitsToDouble given an int** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: numbers, floating-point

Detects `Double.longBitsToDouble(x)` where `x` is an `int` (or a `short`,
`char`, `byte`, or their wrappers), including int literals written without the `L` suffix.

**Why it matters.** `longBitsToDouble` reads a 64-bit IEEE 754 pattern. An `int` is widened
first — zero-extended for non-negative values, sign-extended for negative ones — so the
sign, exponent and top of the mantissa end up in the wrong bits: the result is a tiny
subnormal number or NaN, not the intended value. The usual cause is a 32-bit float pattern
that should go through `Float.intBitsToFloat`, or a 64-bit constant missing its `L`.

**How to fix.** Use `Float.intBitsToFloat(bits)` for 32-bit patterns, or pass a `long`
(`0x3FF0000000000000L`).

```java
// Noncompliant
double d = Double.longBitsToDouble(buffer.getInt());
double one = Double.longBitsToDouble(0x3FF00000);

// Compliant
float f = Float.intBitsToFloat(buffer.getInt());
double one = Double.longBitsToDouble(0x3FF0000000000000L);
```

The literal `0` (the same bits either way) is not reported.

### java/integer-division-in-floating-context

**Integer division in a floating-point context**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: numbers, precision

Detects an integer division (both operands `int`/`long`/`short`/`byte`/`char`)
whose result is immediately stored in, returned as, or cast to a `float` or `double`.

**Why it matters.** Integer division truncates *before* the result is widened, so
`double half = 1 / 2;` is `0.0`, and `double ratio = done / total;` is `0.0` until the job is
complete. Declaring the target as `double` suggests a fractional result was expected.

**How to fix.** Convert an operand before dividing (`(double) done / total`, `done / 2.0`). If
truncation is intended, make it explicit (`Math.floorDiv`, or store the quotient in an integer
variable first).

```java
// Noncompliant
double ratio = done / total;
double average() { return sum / count; }

// Compliant
double ratio = (double) done / total;
double average() { return (double) sum / count; }
```

Only direct uses are reported: a variable or field initializer, an assignment (including
compound ones such as `+=`), a `return` from a method declared to return `float`/`double`, and a
cast `(double) (a / b)`. Returns inside lambdas and divisions nested in larger arithmetic are
not reported.

### java/internal-jdk-api

**JDK-internal API used** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~30 min · Tags: portability, jdk-internal

Detects imports and fully qualified type references of JDK-internal packages:
`sun.*`, `jdk.internal.*`, and the JDK's private copies of other libraries
(`com.sun.org.apache.*`, `com.sun.xml.internal.*`) and implementation packages
(`com.sun.crypto.provider.*`, `com.sun.imageio.*`, `com.sun.media.sound.*`).

**Why it matters.** These classes are implementation details of one JDK build, not an API:
they change or disappear between releases without notice (`sun.misc.BASE64Encoder` was
removed in Java 9), are missing on other vendors' runtimes, and since Java 16 strong
encapsulation makes most of them inaccessible without `--add-opens`/`--add-exports` flags.
The few kept reachable for compatibility (`sun.misc.Unsafe`, `sun.misc.Signal`) are
officially unsupported and are being replaced.

**How to fix.** Use the supported equivalent: `java.util.Base64` instead of the `sun.misc`
encoders, `VarHandle` and `MethodHandles` instead of `Unsafe`, the public `javax.xml` factories
instead of the internal Xerces and Xalan copies, `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` instead of
`sun.misc.Cleaner`.

```java
// Noncompliant
import sun.misc.BASE64Encoder;
String s = new BASE64Encoder().encode(bytes);

// Compliant
import java.util.Base64;
String s = Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(bytes);
```

Not reported: the supported `com.sun` APIs (`com.sun.net.httpserver`, `com.sun.management`,
`com.sun.source`, `com.sun.jdi`, …), packages that also exist outside the JDK
(`com.sun.jndi.ldap.ctl` came with a separate LDAP library, `com.sun.jmx.remote` with the
optional JMX remote package), third-party code published under `com.sun` names,
class names in strings (loading an optional internal class reflectively, with a fallback, is
a deliberate choice), and files that belong to such a package themselves.

### java/interrupt-status-lost

**InterruptedException handled without restoring the interrupt status**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: concurrency, error-handling

Detects a `catch` block for `InterruptedException` that does something (logs,
counts, retries) but neither calls `interrupt()` to restore the thread's interrupt status nor
throws.

**Why it matters.** Interruption is how Java asks a thread to stop: executors use it to cancel
tasks and shut down, and code further up the stack checks `isInterrupted()` to know it should
wind down. Throwing `InterruptedException` clears the thread's interrupt flag, so a handler that
just logs and carries on erases the request: the loop keeps running, the task ignores its
cancellation, and a shutdown waits for a thread that will never notice it was asked to stop.

**How to fix.** Either let the exception propagate (declare it, or wrap and rethrow it), or
restore the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` before continuing, so that the
callers still see the request.

```java
// Noncompliant
while (running) {
    try {
        queue.take().run();
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        log.warn("interrupted", e);   // the stop request is lost; the loop goes on
    }
}

// Compliant
while (running) {
    try {
        queue.take().run();
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        return;
    }
}
```

Only handlers that carry on as if nothing happened are reported. Not reported: empty handlers
(left to `empty-catch-block`); handlers that end with `break` or `return` (the code stops what
it was doing) or set a boolean flag (`interrupted = true`, `running = false`) the surrounding
code acts on; handlers that hand the exception to another method or object (other than a
logger) or store it; methods that restore the flag elsewhere (`interrupt()` in a `finally`);
`SwingWorker.done()` methods, where `get()` cannot block; a `try` that is the last thing a
thread's `run()` method does (the thread ends right after); and test code.

### java/intrinsic-lock-on-lock-object

**Monitor operation on a java.util.concurrent lock** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects the built-in monitor operations applied to a
`java.util.concurrent.locks` object:

* `synchronized (lock) { … }` where `lock` is a `Lock`, `ReadWriteLock`, `StampedLock` or
  `Condition`;
* `wait()`, `notify()` or `notifyAll()` called on a `Lock` or a `Condition`.

**Why it matters.** A `ReentrantLock` and the object's built-in monitor are unrelated.
`synchronized (lock)` does not acquire the lock, so it excludes nothing with code that calls
`lock.lock()`. `condition.wait()` / `condition.notify()` use the monitor of the `Condition`
object, not the condition itself: without `synchronized (condition)` they throw
`IllegalMonitorStateException`, and with it they never wake threads blocked in `await()`.
The intended methods are `await()`, `signal()` and `signalAll()`.

**How to fix.** Use the lock's own API.

```java
// Noncompliant
synchronized (lock) { balance += amount; }
notEmpty.notify();

// Compliant
lock.lock();
try { balance += amount; } finally { lock.unlock(); }
notEmpty.signal();
```

Only receivers the resolver proves to be one of these types are reported.

### java/invalid-range-arguments

**Range bounds that always throw** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: api-misuse, strings, collections

Detects range arguments written as constants that can never be valid:

* `substring`/`subSequence` on a string or builder, and `subList` on a list, with a negative
  bound or a start greater than the end (`s.substring(5, 2)`, `list.subList(-1, 3)`);
* `Arrays.copyOfRange(a, from, to)` with `from` negative or greater than `to`;
* `Math.clamp(value, min, max)` with `min` greater than `max`.

**Why it matters.** Each of these calls throws (`StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`,
`IndexOutOfBoundsException`, `IllegalArgumentException`) every time it runs. Swapped or
mistyped bounds are easy to miss when the code path is rare, such as error handling.

**How to fix.** Put the bounds in the right order and make them non-negative.

```java
// Noncompliant
String year = date.substring(4, 0);

// Compliant
String year = date.substring(0, 4);
```

Only integer literals are evaluated, and only receivers the resolver proves (`String`,
`CharSequence`, `List`, `java.util.Arrays`, `Math`).

### java/invalid-regex-literal

**Invalid regular expression literal**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: regex

Detects a string literal passed as a regular expression — to
`Pattern.compile`, `Pattern.matches`, or `String.matches`, `replaceAll`, `replaceFirst`,
`split` — that is not valid `java.util.regex` syntax: unbalanced parentheses, an unclosed
character class, a quantifier with nothing to repeat (`*abc`, `a|+b`), a `{` that does not
start a repetition (`"{name}"`, `"${user}"`), a reversed range (`[z-a]`), or a trailing
lone backslash.

**Why it matters.** The pattern is only compiled at run time, so the mistake surfaces as a
`PatternSyntaxException` on the first execution — often on an error path or a rarely used
feature. A frequent case is treating `replaceAll` / `split` as plain-text operations:
`s.replaceAll("{name}", value)` always throws.

**How to fix.** Escape the metacharacters (`"\\{name\\}"`), quote the text with
`Pattern.quote(..)`, or use `String.replace` for literal replacements.

```java
// Noncompliant
template.replaceAll("${user}", name);
line.split("*");

// Compliant
template.replace("${user}", name);
line.split("\\*");
```

The checker is conservative: patterns using constructs it does not model (`\Q…\E`, nested
or intersected classes, comments mode, flags passed to `compile`) are never reported.

### java/invisible-character

**Invisible or control character in source**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: unicode, confusing, security

Detects characters in the source that readers cannot see but the compiler
does:

* bidirectional control characters (U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069, U+200E, U+200F, U+061C)
  anywhere, comments included: they reorder how the following text is displayed, so code can
  look different from what is compiled;
* raw zero-width and other invisible characters (zero-width space and joiners, word joiner,
  soft hyphen, byte order mark inside the file, Hangul fillers), non-breaking spaces and raw
  control characters in string and character literals and in code;
* Unicode escapes (`\u0022`) outside string, character literals and comments, and escapes of
  line breaks in comments: the compiler translates them before anything else, so an escape
  can end a comment or a string early.

**Why it matters.** Two strings that print the same but differ by an invisible character
compare unequal; an identifier with a zero-width character is a different identifier; a
bidirectional override can make a comment appear to end where it doesn't. None of this shows
in a code review.

**How to fix.** Remove the character, or write it as an escape inside the literal
(`"\u00A0"`), where the intent is visible.

```java
// Noncompliant: the space before the euro sign is a raw no-break space (U+00A0)
String price = amount + " €";

// Compliant
String price = amount + "\u00A0€";
```

Not reported: escapes inside string and character literals (they keep the source ASCII),
other escapes in comments (the character they denote stays inside the comment), non-breaking
spaces, zero-width and control characters in comments (pasted documentation), a byte
order mark at the start of the file, and the end-of-file control character some old editors
append.

### java/iterator-contract

**Iterator implementation breaks the iterator contract**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: iterators, api-misuse

Detects two breaches of the iterator contracts in classes that implement
`java.util.Iterator`:

- a `next()` that cannot throw `NoSuchElementException`: it has no `throw` and does not
  delegate to anything that would (`return items[index++];`, `if (!hasNext()) return null;`);
- an `iterator()` method that returns `this`.

**Why it matters.** Callers and library code rely on `next()` throwing
`NoSuchElementException` once the iteration is exhausted. An implementation that returns
`null` instead lets a consumer loop on silently with a `null` element, and one that indexes
past the end throws an unrelated exception that callers don't expect. An `Iterable` whose
`iterator()` returns itself can be traversed only once: a second or nested `for` loop over it
sees no elements, or steals elements from the first.

**How to fix.** Start `next()` with `if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();`.
Return a new iterator object from `iterator()`.

```java
// Noncompliant
public T next() {
    return items[position++];
}

// Compliant
public T next() {
    if (position >= items.length) {
        throw new NoSuchElementException();
    }
    return items[position++];
}
```

`next()` methods that call another `next…()` (`nextInt()`, `nextToken()`), a queue method that throws when empty
(`remove()`, `pop()`, …) or a helper method of the same class are not reported: the exception
may come from there. That includes such a call in a field initializer of an anonymous object
that `next()` creates (`return new Entry<>() { final E e = it.next(); … }`), which runs during
`next()`. Infinite iterators, whose `hasNext()` is `return true;`, are not reported either:
they are never exhausted, so `next()` has no reason to throw.

### java/javadoc-empty-tag

**Javadoc tag without a description**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, documentation

Detects block tags of a documentation comment that carry no description:
`@param` with only the parameter name, `@throws` / `@exception` with only the exception type,
and `@return` or `@deprecated` with nothing after them.

**Why it matters.** An empty tag looks like documentation but says nothing: the generated
page lists the parameter with a blank explanation, and the `@deprecated` note gives users no
replacement to move to. It usually means the tag was generated by an IDE and never filled in.
Either the tag has something to say, or it can go.

**How to fix.** Write the description, or delete the tag.

```java
// Noncompliant
/**
 * Moves the cursor.
 *
 * @param steps
 * @return
 * @throws IOException
 */

// Compliant
/**
 * Moves the cursor.
 *
 * @param steps how far to move; negative values move backwards
 * @return the new position
 * @throws IOException if the underlying stream fails
 */
```

A description may continue on the following lines; it is empty only when the next tag or the
end of the comment comes first. Lines inside `<pre>` blocks and inside inline tags such as
`{@code …}` are not read as tags. Other block tags (`@see`, `@since`, `@author`, custom tags)
are not checked. The rule is off by default: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

### java/jdbc-statement-in-loop

**JDBC statement executed row by row in a loop** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: jdbc, performance

Detects two inefficiencies of a `PreparedStatement` reused in a loop:

* `executeUpdate()` / `execute()` called on every pass, after binding that pass's parameters,
  in a method that never uses `addBatch`;
* a parameter bound to the same constant on every pass (`ps.setString(1, "ACTIVE")` inside the
  loop), with no `clearParameters()` in the loop.

**Why it matters.** Each `executeUpdate` is a round trip to the database — for a thousand rows,
a thousand network exchanges and statement executions. `addBatch` collects the rows and
`executeBatch` sends them together, which is typically an order of magnitude faster. Parameter
values stay bound until they are replaced or cleared, so binding a constant again on every pass
is wasted work that also hides which values actually change.

**How to fix.** Call `addBatch()` in the loop and `executeBatch()` after it (in chunks for very
large inputs); bind constant parameters once, before the loop.

```java
// Noncompliant
for (Order o : orders) {
    ps.setString(1, "SHIPPED");
    ps.setLong(2, o.getId());
    ps.executeUpdate();
}

// Compliant
ps.setString(1, "SHIPPED");
for (Order o : orders) {
    ps.setLong(2, o.getId());
    ps.addBatch();
}
ps.executeBatch();
```

Not reported: statements prepared inside the loop, updates whose result is used (an update
count that decides what to do next, as in insert-or-update), loops that read generated keys, results or
update counts, or commit on every pass, updates followed by `break`, `return` or `throw` (retry loops), methods
that already use batching, and receivers not provably a `PreparedStatement`. A parameter bound
conditionally or to different values in the same loop is not a constant.

### java/jdbc-zero-index

**JDBC index 0 (indexes start at 1)** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: jdbc, api-misuse

Detects JDBC calls that pass index `0` (or a negative index) where JDBC counts
from 1: `PreparedStatement.setXxx(0, …)`, `CallableStatement.registerOutParameter(0, …)`,
`ResultSet.getXxx(0)` / `updateXxx(0, …)`, and `ResultSetMetaData.getColumnXxx(0)`.

**Why it matters.** Parameter and column positions in JDBC are 1-based. Index 0 does not
exist, so the driver throws `SQLException` ("parameter index out of range", "invalid column
index") every time the statement runs — or, with a shifted loop, binds every value to the
wrong placeholder.

**How to fix.** Start at 1.

```java
// Noncompliant
ps.setString(0, name);
long id = rs.getLong(0);

// Compliant
ps.setString(1, name);
long id = rs.getLong(1);
```

Only receivers the resolver proves to be a `java.sql` statement, result set, or result-set
metadata are reported. Methods whose `int` argument is not an index (`setFetchSize`,
`setMaxRows`, `absolute`, …) are not checked.

### java/junit5-test-visibility

**Public JUnit 5 test class or method**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: tests, junit

Detects the `public` modifier on JUnit 5 test classes and on test and
lifecycle methods (`@Test`, `@ParameterizedTest`, `@RepeatedTest`, `@TestFactory`,
`@TestTemplate`, `@BeforeEach`, `@AfterEach`, `@BeforeAll`, `@AfterAll`).

**Why it matters.** JUnit 4 required public tests; JUnit 5 finds package-private classes and
methods just as well. The leftover `public` is noise, and it wrongly suggests that other code
is meant to call the test.

**How to fix.** Remove `public`.

```java
// Noncompliant
public class InvoiceTest {
    @BeforeEach
    public void setUp() { ... }

    @Test
    public void computesTotal() { ... }
}

// Compliant
class InvoiceTest {
    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() { ... }

    @Test
    void computesTotal() { ... }
}
```

Only test files that import `org.junit.jupiter` (and no JUnit 4 test API) are checked. A test
class is not reported when it is abstract or has other public members (constants, helpers,
nested types) that code elsewhere may use; `@Override` methods, interface methods, and
lifecycle methods of classes that extend another class (they may override a public hook) are
not reported.

### java/keyset-lookup-in-loop

**Map values looked up while iterating its keys**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: performance, collections

Detects a for-each loop over `map.keySet()` whose body looks each key up again
with `map.get(key)` on the same map.

**Why it matters.** The loop already walks the map's entries to produce the keys; looking
each one up again repeats the work — a hash computation and bucket search per key for a
`HashMap`, a tree descent for a `TreeMap`. Iterating `entrySet()` gives the key and the value
together, reads more directly, and for a `TreeMap` turns an `n log n` loop into a linear one.

**How to fix.** Iterate the entries and use `getKey()` / `getValue()` (or `forEach((k, v) ->
…)`).

```java
// Noncompliant
for (String name : settings.keySet()) {
    apply(name, settings.get(name));
}

// Compliant
for (Map.Entry<String, String> e : settings.entrySet()) {
    apply(e.getKey(), e.getValue());
}
```

Only maps the resolver proves to be a `java.util.Map` are considered (multimaps and other
map-like types, where `get` and `entrySet` mean something else, are left alone). Not reported:
lookups in another map, lookups with anything other than the loop variable itself, and
lookups inside lambdas or anonymous classes in the body.

### java/labeled-statement

**Labeled statement**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: control-flow

Detects labeled statements (`outer: for (…)`).

**Why it matters.** Labels exist to support `break label` / `continue label` jumps across
several nesting levels. That control flow is hard to follow: the reader must find the label to
know where execution continues, and the deep nesting that made the label necessary is itself a
readability problem.

**How to fix.** Extract the nested loops into a method and `return` from it, or restructure the
loop condition.

```java
// Noncompliant
search:
for (Row row : rows) {
    for (Cell cell : row) {
        if (cell.matches(query)) {
            found = cell;
            break search;
        }
    }
}

// Compliant
found = findFirstMatch(rows, query);   // the inner loops `return cell;`
```

### java/lambda-could-be-method-reference

**Lambda could be a method reference**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: idiom, readability

Detects lambdas whose body does nothing but pass the lambda's parameters, in
order, to one method or constructor: `x -> service.handle(x)`, `(a, b) -> merge(a, b)`,
`s -> s.trim()`, `name -> new Label(name)`, `() -> list.clear()`.

**Why it matters.** A method reference names the operation directly (`service::handle`,
`String::trim`, `Label::new`) without inventing parameter names that carry no meaning. It is
shorter and reads as "what", not "how".

**How to fix.** Replace the lambda with the corresponding method reference.

```java
// Noncompliant
names.forEach(n -> System.out.println(n));
orders.stream().map(o -> o.getTotal()).forEach(t -> ledger.add(t));

// Compliant
names.forEach(System.out::println);
orders.stream().map(Order::getTotal).forEach(ledger::add);
```

Only receivers that a method reference evaluates the same way are accepted: `this`, `super`,
a type name, a local variable or parameter, a `final` field, `System.out` / `System.err`, or
the lambda's first parameter. Receivers computed by a call (`() -> getService().run()`) are
evaluated once by a method reference but at every call by the lambda, so they are left alone,
as are generic calls with explicit type arguments and names that are ambiguous as unbound
references (`toString`, `hashCode`, …).

### java/linear-access-in-loop

**Linear-time list access inside a loop**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: performance, collections

Detects, inside a loop, list operations whose cost grows with the size of the
list:

* `get(i)` on a `LinkedList`, with `i` the counter of the enclosing `for` loop: every call walks
  the nodes from one end of the list up to `i`;
* `remove(0)` or `add(0, x)` on an `ArrayList`: every call shifts all other elements by one
  place.

The list's class must be known from its declaration: a variable or field declared as
`LinkedList` / `ArrayList`, or declared with an interface type, initialized with `new` of that
class and never reassigned (a local) or `final` (a field).

**Why it matters.** Each call is linear in the size of the list, so the loop is quadratic: a
loop over 100 000 elements performs billions of steps where a linear pass would do. The cost
stays invisible in tests with small lists and appears in production.

**How to fix.** Iterate a `LinkedList` with a for-each loop or an iterator. Use an
`ArrayDeque` for a queue (`poll()`, `addFirst(x)`), or build the list in the other order and
reverse it once.

```java
// Noncompliant
for (int i = 0; i < names.size(); i++) {   // names is a LinkedList
    print(names.get(i));
}
while (!pending.isEmpty()) {               // pending is an ArrayList
    handle(pending.remove(0));
}

// Compliant
for (String name : names) {
    print(name);
}
Deque<Task> pending = new ArrayDeque<>(tasks);
while (!pending.isEmpty()) {
    handle(pending.poll());
}
```

Not reported: `get(0)` and other constant positions of a `LinkedList` (they are found at once),
lists whose class is not known from the declaration, calls in a lambda or class declared in
the loop, and calls followed by a `break`, `return` or `throw` in the same block (they run at
most once per loop).

### java/list-remove-in-index-loop

**List element removed in an ascending index loop**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: collections, loops

Detects `list.remove(i)` inside a `for` loop that counts `i` upwards (`i++`),
when nothing compensates for the removal.

**Why it matters.** Removing the element at `i` shifts every following element one position
to the left. The loop then increments `i` and never looks at the element that moved into
position `i`: two matching elements in a row leave the second one in the list. The bug only
shows with adjacent matches, so tests with sparse data pass.

**How to fix.** Use `removeIf`, an explicit `Iterator.remove()`, or iterate backwards.

```java
// Noncompliant
for (int i = 0; i < names.size(); i++) {
    if (names.get(i).isBlank()) {
        names.remove(i);
    }
}

// Compliant
names.removeIf(String::isBlank);
```

Not reported: loops whose body also changes `i` (the `i--` compensation), removals followed by
`break`, `return` or `throw` in the same block, and receivers or counters whose types are not
proven (`List` and `int`; with an `Integer` counter `remove` removes by value).

### java/literal-first-in-equals

**String literal should be the receiver of equals**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: null, strings

Detects `s.equals("literal")` and `s.equalsIgnoreCase("literal")` where `s`
may be `null`, and the same with a `String` constant declared in this file
(`static final String ADMIN = "admin"`) as the argument.

**Why it matters.** Called on a `null` string, `equals` throws a `NullPointerException`. With
the literal as the receiver the comparison is simply `false` for `null`, which is almost
always what the code means ("is it this value?").

**How to fix.** Swap the operands (or use `Objects.equals`).

```java
// Noncompliant
if (role.equals("admin")) { ... }
if (role.equals(ADMIN)) { ... }

// Compliant
if ("admin".equals(role)) { ... }
if (ADMIN.equals(role)) { ... }
```

The receiver is reported when it is known to be a `String`, and also when its type is unknown
(the result of a call into another class, an inherited field, a lambda parameter): with a
string literal as the argument, swapping the operands gives the same answer for any string.
Receivers of a known type other than `String` are skipped (`Object`, numbers, enums, or a
variable declared in this file with another type). Receivers that cannot be `null` are
skipped too: literals, constants, `this`, `new` expressions, concatenations, and the
results of `String` methods such as `trim()`, `toLowerCase()`, `name()`, or
`String.valueOf(..)` (for those, a `null` would already have failed earlier), local variables
initialized with such a value and never assigned anything that may be `null`
(`String t = key.trim(); … t.equals("|")`), and the elements of `main`'s argument array
(`args[0].equals("start")`), which the JVM never fills with `null`. Receivers that an
enclosing condition has just checked (`s != null && s.equals("x")`, `if (!isEmpty(s)) { … }`)
are not reported either. A constant argument counts only when this file declares it
`static final` with a `String` type and a literal value (also `Nested.NAME` of a class of this
file); constants of other classes are not visible, unless `external_constants` is set: then
`lookup(key).equals(Names.TYPE)` is reported too, on the convention that an `UPPER_SNAKE` field
of a class is a non-null constant.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `external_constants` | `false` | Also report a call on the result of a method call whose argument is an `UPPER_SNAKE` constant of a class declared in another file (`lookup(key).equals(Names.TYPE)`), whose value and type are not visible. |

### java/local-variable-naming

**Local variable and parameter naming convention**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: naming, convention

Detects local variables and parameters whose name does not follow the
configured convention (by default camelCase: a lowercase letter followed by letters and
digits). Checked: local variables, method/constructor/lambda/catch parameters, record
components, enhanced-`for` variables, try-with-resources resources, and pattern variables.

**Why it matters.** Local names are the most frequently read identifiers in a method. Mixing
conventions (`user_id`, `UserName`, `MAX`) makes it harder to tell locals from constants,
types and fields.

**How to fix.** Rename the variable.

```java
// Noncompliant
int Item_Count = items.size();
for (String Name : names) { … }

// Compliant
int itemCount = items.size();
for (String name : names) { … }
```

Single-character names (`i`, `x`, `T`) and the unnamed variable `_` are always accepted. The
`format` parameter takes a preset name; regular expressions are not supported.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `format` | `"camelCase"` | Naming preset for local variables and parameters: `camelCase` (`^[a-z][a-zA-Z0-9]*$`), `PascalCase`, `UPPER_SNAKE`, or `snake_case`. Arbitrary regular expressions are not supported; the regular expression of a preset is accepted as an alia… |

### java/log-and-rethrow

**Exception logged and rethrown**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: error-handling, logging

Detects a catch block that writes the caught exception (or its message) to a
logger at info level or above, and ends by throwing it on: the exception itself (`throw e`)
or a new exception that carries it as its cause (`throw new ServiceException("…", e)`).
Both the logging call and the `throw` are statements of the catch block itself.

**Why it matters.** An exception that keeps propagating will be handled somewhere up the
stack, and that handler usually logs it too. Logging it at every layer it crosses fills the log
with the same failure several times, often with the full stack trace each time, which makes it
look like several problems and buries the one line that matters. The layer that finally deals
with the failure is the one that knows how serious it is and should be the one that logs it.

**How to fix.** Either handle the exception here and log it, or let it propagate (add context
by wrapping it) and leave the logging to whoever handles it.

```java
// Noncompliant
try {
    store.save(order);
} catch (IOException e) {
    log.error("could not save order {}", order.id(), e);
    throw new StorageException("could not save order " + order.id(), e);
}

// Compliant: the message travels with the exception and is logged once, where it is handled
try {
    store.save(order);
} catch (IOException e) {
    throw new StorageException("could not save order " + order.id(), e);
}
```

Loggers are recognized by their declared type (SLF4J, Log4j, Commons Logging, JBoss Logging,
`java.util.logging`) or by a conventional name in a file importing a logging API. Not
reported: debug and trace output (diagnostics that are off in production), a rethrow that
only happens on some paths (`if (fatal) throw e;` — the handler decided which failures to
pass on, and may add context for them), logging inside such a branch, exceptions thrown
without the caught one as their cause (see `java/lost-exception-cause`), and throws inside
lambdas or nested `try` statements.

### java/log-message-concatenation

**Eagerly built debug log or precondition message**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: logging, performance

Detects debug- and trace-level logging calls (`debug`, `trace`; `fine`,
`finer`, `finest` for `java.util.logging`) whose message is built eagerly — by string
concatenation or `String.format` with non-constant parts — outside an `isDebugEnabled()` /
`isTraceEnabled()` / `isLoggable(..)` check, and precondition checks whose failure message is
built the same way although it is only needed when the check fails:
`Objects.requireNonNull(x, "no " + name)`, Guava's `checkArgument` / `checkState` /
`checkNotNull` / `verify`, Spring's `Assert` methods, and Commons Lang's `Validate` methods.

**Why it matters.** Debug and trace output is normally switched off in production, yet the
message is built before the logger gets a chance to discard it: every call pays for string
building, `toString()` calls, and garbage. On hot paths this cost is measurable.

The same holds for a precondition: the check almost always passes, yet its message is
concatenated every time.

**How to fix.** Use the logger's parameterized form (SLF4J and Log4j 2 `{}` placeholders,
`java.util.logging` `{0}` parameters or a `Supplier`), or wrap the call in a level check. For
preconditions, pass the message lazily: a `Supplier` (`requireNonNull(x, () -> "no " + name)`,
Spring's `Assert`) or template arguments (Guava's `checkArgument(ok, "bad %s", name)`,
`Validate.isTrue(ok, "bad %s", name)`).

```java
// Noncompliant
log.debug("Loaded " + rows.size() + " rows for " + table);

// Compliant
log.debug("Loaded {} rows for {}", rows.size(), table);
if (log.isDebugEnabled()) {
    log.debug("Loaded " + rows.size() + " rows for " + table);
}
```

The logger is recognized by its declared type (SLF4J, Log4j 1/2, Commons Logging, JBoss
Logging, `java.util.logging`) or, for inherited fields, by a conventional name (`log`,
`logger`, `LOG`, `LOGGER`) in a file importing a logging API. Precondition calls count when they
provably go to one of the classes above (qualified by it, or statically imported from it). Other
log levels (`info`, `warn`, `error`) are deliberately not reported: they are normally enabled,
so their message is needed anyway. Concatenations of literals and
constants are not reported, and neither is any call in a method that tests the level
(`isDebugEnabled`, `isTraceEnabled`, `isLoggable`, `isEnabled`) before it.

### java/logger-for-wrong-class

**Logger created for another class**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: logging, copy-paste

Detects a logger field initialized for another class than the one declaring it:
`private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderService.class);` inside
`class InvoiceService` (SLF4J, Log4j 2, Log4j 1, Commons Logging, JBoss Logging and
`java.util.logging` factories, with a class literal or its `getName()`).

**Why it matters.** The class passed to the factory names the log category: it is what the log
lines show as their origin and what logging configuration uses to turn levels up or down. A
logger copied from another class together with the code around it files every message under
the wrong class, so the messages are searched for in the wrong place and level settings meant
for one class silently apply to the other.

**How to fix.** Pass the declaring class.

```java
// Noncompliant
class InvoiceService {
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderService.class);
}

// Compliant
class InvoiceService {
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(InvoiceService.class);
}
```

Not reported: nested classes using an enclosing class (a common way to share one category),
