classes using one of their declared supertypes (a subclass logging under its base class's
category is a deliberate choice), loggers created from a string or from `getClass()`, loggers
created outside field initializers, and test code.

### java/lone-block

**Nested block without declarations**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: confusing, structure

Detects a block statement `{ … }` nested directly in a method, constructor or
initializer body (or in another such block) that declares no local variable or class.

**Why it matters.** A bare block only limits the scope of what is declared inside it. When
nothing is declared it has no effect at all, and it reads like the body of a statement that
went missing — an `if`, a loop or an `else` deleted by an edit or a merge — so readers stop to
work out whether code was lost.

**How to fix.** Remove the braces, or restore the statement the block belongs to. To group
steps, extract a method with a descriptive name.

```java
// Noncompliant
void reset() {
    counter = 0;
    {
        cache.clear();
        listeners.clear();
    }
}

// Compliant
void reset() {
    counter = 0;
    cache.clear();
    listeners.clear();
}
```

Not reported: blocks that declare a local variable or a local class (limiting their scope is
the point), empty blocks (`java/empty-block`), labeled blocks (`label: { … break label; }`),
blocks that are a `case` group's body, and blocks of lambdas, `switch` rules, `synchronized`
and other statements.

### java/long-literal-lowercase

**Long literal with lowercase suffix**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: readability, convention

Detects `long` integer literals written with a lowercase `l` suffix.

**Why it matters.** In most fonts a lowercase `l` is almost indistinguishable from the digit
`1`: `10l` easily reads as `101`. The uppercase `L` is unambiguous.

**How to fix.** Use the uppercase suffix.

```java
// Noncompliant
long timeout = 30000l;

// Compliant
long timeout = 30000L;
```

### java/loop-counter-wrong-direction

**Loop counter moves away from its bound** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: loops, suspicious, typo

Detects a `for` loop whose update moves the counter away from the bound tested
by its condition: `i < n` with `i--`, or `i >= 0` with `i++` (also `+=` / `-=` by a constant
and `i = i + 1` forms).

**Why it matters.** The condition stays true while the counter runs off in the wrong
direction, so the loop does not stop where it should: it runs until the counter overflows,
indexes an array with a negative position, or never ends. It is almost always a slip made
while turning an ascending loop into a descending one (or the reverse) and changing only one
of the three clauses.

**How to fix.** Make the update and the condition agree.

```java
// Noncompliant
for (int i = items.length - 1; i < items.length; i--) { … }

// Compliant
for (int i = items.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) { … }
```

Only counters that are plain local names are considered. Loops whose body also assigns the
counter, conditions that are not `<`, `<=`, `>` or `>=`, steps that are not constants, and
loops whose update also changes the bound are not reported.

### java/loop-exits-first-pass

**Loop body always exits on the first pass**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: loops, suspicious

Detects loops (`for`, enhanced `for`, `while`, `do`) whose body ends with an
unconditional `break`, `return` or `throw` and contains no `continue` for that loop, so the
body can never run a second time.

**Why it matters.** Every path through such a body leaves the loop: either it reaches the
final jump, or it exits earlier through another `break`, `return` or exception. The update
clause never runs and the condition is tested once. Either the loop is an `if` in disguise,
which misleads the reader into looking for the iteration, or the final jump was meant to be
conditional (placed one brace too low, or left over from debugging) and the loop silently
processes only its first element.

**How to fix.** If one pass is intended, write it as an `if` (for the first element of a
collection: `if (!items.isEmpty()) … items.get(0)`, or `iterator().next()` after a check). If
the loop should go on, make the jump conditional.

```java
// Noncompliant
for (Order order : orders) {
    if (order.isOpen()) {
        close(order);
    }
    break;              // only the first order is ever looked at
}

// Compliant
for (Order order : orders) {
    if (order.isOpen()) {
        close(order);
        break;
    }
}
```

Not reported: loops with a `continue` that targets them (search and retry loops, where the
final jump is the normal exit after the retries), `do { … } while (false)` blocks, and jumps
that are not the last statement of the body.

### java/loop-may-skip-bound

**Loop tested with != may skip its bound** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: loops, suspicious

Detects `for` loops whose condition is `i != bound` while the counter does not
move by exactly one each time: the update adds or subtracts a constant other than 1
(`i += 2`), or the body changes the counter as well.

**Why it matters.** With `!=` the loop only stops when the counter lands exactly on the
bound. A counter that moves in bigger steps, or is bumped again inside the body, can step
over it; the loop then runs on until the counter overflows or an index goes out of range.
`<` or `>` stop the loop whatever the step.

**How to fix.** Use an ordering comparison (`i < bound`, `i > bound`).

```java
// Noncompliant
for (int i = 0; i != data.length; i += 2) { … }   // odd length: never stops

// Compliant
for (int i = 0; i < data.length; i += 2) { … }
```

Off by default: `!=` loops are a style some code bases use on purpose. Not reported: loops
whose start and bound are constants that the step reaches exactly, and counters that are not
plain integer locals.

### java/loop-never-entered

**Loop condition false on entry** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: loops, suspicious, dead-code

Detects `for` and `while` loops whose condition is false on entry, judging
from the constant values the variables in it have just been given: `for (int i = 10; i < 5;
i++)`, or `int n = 0;` directly followed by `while (n > 0)`.

**Why it matters.** The body never runs. The code looks like it iterates, but it is dead: a
reversed comparison, a wrong start value, or a bound copied from another loop. Since the
variables are not compile-time constants, the compiler accepts the loop without a warning.

**How to fix.** Correct the start value or the comparison (often the loop was meant to count
down: `for (int i = 10; i > 5; i--)`), or delete the dead loop.

```java
// Noncompliant
for (int i = 10; i < 5; i++) {
    process(i);
}

// Compliant
for (int i = 10; i > 5; i--) {
    process(i);
}
```

Only integer and boolean variables initialized with literals are considered: in the `for`
initializer itself, or in the declaration immediately before a `while` loop. Conditions that
involve anything else (fields, method calls, other variables) are not evaluated.

### java/lost-exception-cause

**Exception cause lost when rethrowing**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: error-handling

Detects exceptions thrown from a `catch (E e)` block — `throw new X(…)` or an
exception built by a helper, `throw invalidInput(…)` — that do not receive `e` itself: either
`e` is not mentioned at all, or only its text is (`e.getMessage()`, `e.toString()`,
`"failed: " + e`).

**Why it matters.** The caught exception carries the stack trace and message of the real
failure, and the chain of its own causes. Throwing a fresh exception without chaining it
discards that information: the logs show where the translation happened, not what went wrong.
Copying the message keeps a line of text but still loses the stack trace and the causes.

**How to fix.** Pass the caught exception as the cause (most exception types have a
`(String, Throwable)` constructor), or call `initCause(e)` / `addSuppressed(e)` when the
constructor doesn't accept one.

```java
// Noncompliant
try {
    return Integer.parseInt(text);
} catch (NumberFormatException e) {
    throw new ConfigException("invalid port: " + e.getMessage());
}

// Compliant
try {
    return Integer.parseInt(text);
} catch (NumberFormatException e) {
    throw new ConfigException("invalid port: " + text, e);
}
```

Not reported: catch blocks that call `initCause` or `addSuppressed`, caught variables named
`ignored`/`ignore`/`expected`, throws inside a nested `try` that has its own handlers, throws
inside lambdas or anonymous classes declared in the catch block, rethrowing a variable
(`throw e`, `throw cause`), and exceptions that receive the caught variable in any other way
than for its text — as an argument (`new X(e)`, `wrap(e)`, `ExceptionUtils.getStackTrace(e)`),
through `e.getCause()`, through the variable of an enclosing catch clause, or through a local
derived from them (`Throwable root = e.getCause()`). A helper-built exception is also not
reported when the catch block stores the caught exception somewhere (`this.failure = e`).

### java/magic-number

**Magic number**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: readability, conventions

Detects numeric literals ("magic numbers") used directly in code instead of
through a named constant.

**Why it matters.** A bare `86400` or `0.075` says nothing about what it means, and when the
same value appears in several places, changing it means finding every copy — and not
changing an unrelated literal that happens to have the same value.

**How to fix.** Introduce a `static final` constant (or an enum) whose name explains the
value.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (retries > 5) { sleep(86400); }

// Compliant
private static final int MAX_RETRIES = 5;
private static final int SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86_400;
if (retries > MAX_RETRIES) { sleep(SECONDS_PER_DAY); }
```

Not reported: the numbers listed in `ignore` (default `-1, 0, 1, 2`), literals in initializers
of `static final` fields and interface constants, in static initializer blocks, and in private
static helpers that only build the value of such a field (`static final Map<..> CODES =
buildCodes();`), in data tables (an array initializer with three or more elements, or a row of
a nested one, such as `{161, "degree"}`, or a table written as calls: three or more
consecutive statements calling the same method on the same receiver with only literals,
constants and objects built from them as arguments, such as `codes.put(404, "Not Found");`;
a call that also takes a variable is an operation, not a row), in annotations, in enum constant arguments, in
`hashCode()` implementations, and in test files. Off by default: the rule is useful for
focused clean-ups but noisy on most code bases.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ignore` | `"-1,0,1,2"` | Comma-separated numbers that are never reported (compared by value, so `1` also accepts `1L` and `1.0`). |

### java/manual-array-copy

**Loop that copies elements one by one**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: performance, clutter, arrays

Detects loops whose only statement copies elements:

* an index loop `for (int i = a; i < b; i++) dst[i + k] = src[i + m];` between two different
  arrays of the same element type;
* a for-each loop `for (T x : source) target.add(x);` adding every element of a collection or
  of an array of objects to a collection.

**Why it matters.** `System.arraycopy`, `Arrays.copyOf`, `addAll` and `Collections.addAll`
state the intent in one call, are checked once instead of per element, and are faster:
`System.arraycopy` is a single memory move, and `addAll` grows the target once instead of
once per element. The hand-written loop hides an easy off-by-one in its bounds.

**How to fix.**

```java
// Noncompliant
for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    copy[i] = values[i];
}
for (String name : names) {
    all.add(name);
}

// Compliant
System.arraycopy(values, 0, copy, 0, count);
all.addAll(names);
```

Not reported: copies within one array (a shifting loop and `System.arraycopy` treat
overlapping ranges differently), arrays of different element types (the loop converts each
element, `System.arraycopy` would throw), loops that also do something else or convert the
element (a cast, unboxing into a primitive loop variable), counters stepping by more than one
or declared before the loop (their final value may be used afterwards), and receivers or
sources whose types are not known.

### java/map-callback-returns-null

**Map callback always returns null** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: collections, null, api-misuse

Detects `Map` callbacks that always return `null` where that cannot be what the
author wants:

* a `computeIfAbsent` mapping function that always returns `null`: the map never stores
  anything, so the call is an expensive `get`;
* a `compute`, `computeIfPresent` or `merge` function that changes the current value (adds
  to it, puts into it, appends to it) and then returns `null`: returning `null` *removes* the
  entry, so the change is thrown away together with it.

**Why it matters.** For these methods `null` is not a value that can be stored: it means
"no mapping". Code written as if the callback's side effects or its `null` were kept loses
data silently, and the next lookup finds nothing.

**How to fix.** Return the value to store (the new or the updated object). To remove an
entry, call `remove` so the intent is visible.

```java
// Noncompliant
index.compute(key, (k, list) -> {
    list.add(item);
    return null;                  // removes the entry, item is lost
});

// Compliant
index.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(item);
```

Only callbacks written as lambdas whose every `return` is the `null` literal, on receivers the
resolver proves to be a `java.util.Map`, are considered. A `compute` function that returns
`null` after closing or releasing the old value (an atomic remove-and-clean-up) is not
reported.

### java/member-order

**Members out of the conventional order**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, structure

Detects members of a class, enum, record or interface declared out of the
conventional order: static fields first, then instance fields, then constructors, then methods.

**Why it matters.** When every type is laid out the same way, a reader knows where to look for
its state and how it is created without scanning the whole file. A field declared between two
methods near the bottom of a class is state that most readers will not notice, and a
constructor among the methods hides how instances come to exist.

**How to fix.** Move the member up to its group.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Account {
    private final String id;
    Account(String id) { this.id = id; }
    String id() { return id; }
    private static final int MAX_NAME = 64;   // a static field after the methods
}

// Compliant
class Account {
    private static final int MAX_NAME = 64;
    private final String id;
    Account(String id) { this.id = id; }
    String id() { return id; }
}
```

Each member that comes after a member of a later group is reported, with that member as
secondary location. Nested types, initializer blocks and enum constants are not ordered by this
rule, and anonymous classes are not checked. Visibility order within a group is not checked.
The rule is off by default and reports a lot on code that groups members by feature instead:
it is part of the `conventions` profile.

### java/method-naming

**Method naming convention**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: naming, convention

Detects methods whose name does not follow the configured convention (by
default camelCase: a lowercase letter followed by letters and digits).

**Why it matters.** Consistent names make code predictable: in Java, a lowercase identifier
followed by `(` is a method call, an uppercase one is a type. Deviations slow readers down and
look like mistakes.

**How to fix.** Rename the method.

```java
// Noncompliant
public int Get_Count() { … }

// Compliant
public int getCount() { … }
```

Not reported: constructors, methods annotated `@Override` (the name is dictated by the
supertype), `native` methods, and methods in files that bind native code through JNA (the
names mirror native functions such as `ShellExecuteEx`). In test files underscores are
accepted (`rejects_empty_input`, `Parser_emptyInput_throws`). An underscore between two digits
(a version number such as `isBefore3_8`) is always accepted. The `format` parameter takes a
preset name; regular expressions are not supported.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `format` | `"camelCase"` | Naming preset for method names: `camelCase` (`^[a-z][a-zA-Z0-9]*$`), `PascalCase`, `UPPER_SNAKE`, or `snake_case`. Arbitrary regular expressions are not supported; the regular expression of a preset is accepted as an alias. With an unknown… |

### java/misleading-if-layout

**if laid out as if it were an else branch** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: confusing, braces

Detects two layouts that make an `if` read differently from how it runs:

- an `if` that starts on the line of the closing brace of the previous `if` statement
  (`} if (…) {`): it reads like `else if`, but it is a separate statement that is evaluated
  even when the previous branch ran;
- a dangling `else` placed under an outer braceless `if`: `else` always belongs to the nearest
  `if`, so the branch runs when the *inner* condition is false, not the outer one.

**Why it matters.** Both are typical slips: a forgotten `else` turns a chain of exclusive
cases into independent tests (the first case falls into the checks of the next ones), and an
`else` indented for the wrong `if` runs in exactly the situations the reader thinks it
doesn't.

**How to fix.** Add the missing `else`, or put the second `if` on its own line if the tests
really are independent. For a dangling `else`, add braces around the inner `if`.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (value instanceof Map) {
    return fromMap(value);
} if (value instanceof List) {      // meant: else if
    return fromList(value);
}

if (user != null)
    if (user.isAdmin())
        grant();
else                                // belongs to `if (user.isAdmin())`
    login();

// Compliant
if (value instanceof Map) {
    return fromMap(value);
} else if (value instanceof List) {
    return fromList(value);
}

if (user != null) {
    if (user.isAdmin())
        grant();
} else {
    login();
}
```

Only an `if` directly following another `if` statement whose last branch is a block is
checked for the first shape; for the second, the `else` must start its line in the column of
the outer `if`.

### java/misleading-indentation

**Misleading indentation after a braceless body**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: confusing, braces

Detects a statement that follows a braceless `if`, `else`, `for`, or `while`
body and is indented exactly like that body, so it looks guarded but always runs.

**Why it matters.** Without braces only the first statement belongs to the body. A second
line added at the same indentation — often during a quick fix — reads as part of the
branch or loop, but executes unconditionally (or once, after the loop). This is the shape
of several well-known security bugs.

**How to fix.** Add braces around the body, or fix the indentation of the following
statement if it really is meant to run unconditionally.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (user.isAdmin())
    grantAccess();
    auditLog.record(user);

// Compliant
if (user.isAdmin()) {
    grantAccess();
    auditLog.record(user);
}
```

Only bodies that start on their own line are considered, and indentation is compared as
the literal leading whitespace of each line (tabs and spaces are never equated).

### java/missing-braces

**Control statement body without braces**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions, braces

Detects `if`, `else`, `for`, `while` and `do` statements whose body is a
single statement written without braces.

**Why it matters.** A body without braces ends after its first statement, whatever the
indentation says. A second statement added later "inside" the `if` runs unconditionally, and a
debugging line slipped in before the body silently becomes the body. Braces make the extent of
every body explicit, and a code base that always uses them never has to wonder. Formatters
re-indent code but do not add the braces.

**How to fix.** Put the body in a block, even when it is one statement.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (items.isEmpty())
    return Collections.emptyList();
for (Item item : items) total += item.price();

// Compliant
if (items.isEmpty()) {
    return Collections.emptyList();
}
for (Item item : items) {
    total += item.price();
}
```

Not reported: `else if` chains (the nested `if` is checked itself), and an empty body written
as a lone `;` (see `java/empty-statement`). The rule is off by default: it is part of the
`conventions` profile. Layouts that misstate the control flow are reported by
`java/misleading-indentation` and `java/misleading-if-layout`, which are on by default.

### java/missing-javadoc

**Visible declaration without documentation**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: conventions, documentation

Detects declarations that other code can see but that carry no
documentation comment (`/** … */`): public top-level types, and the public and protected
nested types, methods, constructors and fields of such types (members of interfaces and
annotation types are public unless declared `private`).

**Why it matters.** The visible declarations of a type are its contract. Without
documentation, every caller has to read the implementation to learn what a method expects,
returns, throws or guarantees, and the implementation then becomes the specification: any
change to it may break someone. A short comment stating the purpose and the edge cases is far
cheaper to write than to reconstruct.

**How to fix.** Add a doc comment above the declaration (and above its annotations).

```java
// Noncompliant
public final class RateLimiter {
    public boolean tryAcquire(int permits) { … }
}

// Compliant
/** Limits how often an operation may run, with a fixed number of permits per second. */
public final class RateLimiter {
    /**
     * Takes permits if they are available right now.
     *
     * @param permits how many permits to take; must be positive
     * @return whether the permits were taken
     */
    public boolean tryAcquire(int permits) { … }
}
```

Not reported: test files; members of private, package-private, local and anonymous classes;
methods annotated `@Override` (they inherit the documentation of the method they override);
simple accessors (a getter `getX()` / `isX()` / `hasX()` whose body only returns a field, a
setter `setX(v)` whose body only assigns it, optionally followed by `return this;`); compact
record constructors; and enum constants. A doc comment placed after the annotations counts
here (`java/dangling-doc-comment` reports its position). The rule is off by default and
reports a lot on code that is not documented: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

### java/missing-override

**Missing @Override on an overriding method**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: convention, overrides

Detects methods that override or implement a method of a supertype without being
annotated with `@Override`.

**Why it matters.** `@Override` makes the compiler verify that the method really overrides
the inherited one. Without it, a slip such as `equals(Point other)`, `hashcode()`, or a changed
parameter type in the supertype compiles fine as an unrelated new method, and the inherited
behaviour silently stays in place. The annotation also tells readers at a glance that the
method is part of a contract.

**How to fix.** Add `@Override`.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Job implements Runnable {
    public void run() { work(); }
}

// Compliant
class Job implements Runnable {
    @Override
    public void run() { work(); }
}
```

The supertype must be known: a class or interface declared in the same file, or a common JDK
type (`Object`, `Runnable`, `Callable`, `Comparable`, `Comparator`, `Iterator`, `Iterable`,
`AutoCloseable`, `Thread`, `Throwable`, collection and map types, functional interfaces, I/O
streams, AWT/Swing listeners, SAX handlers, the JDBC and DOM interfaces, …). The method must
match by name, number of parameters, and parameter types. Methods overriding supertypes from other files or libraries
are not reported, nor are methods without a body (abstract or interface declarations), static
and private methods, and methods declared in interfaces (including `default` methods).

### java/missing-switch-default

**switch statement without default**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: switch, defensive

Detects `switch` statements (classic `case X:` or arrow `case X ->` labels) that
have no `default` label, and `switch` statements over an enum declared in the same file that
neither cover all of its constants nor have a `default`.

**Why it matters.** Without `default`, a value that no `case` matches is silently ignored.
When a new value appears later (a new status code, a new string key, a new enum constant)
nothing points at the `switch` that should handle it.

**How to fix.** Add a `default` that handles the remaining values — or throws, if they are
impossible — or document that ignoring them is intended with an empty `default: break;` and
a comment. For an enum, adding the missing constants also works.

```java
// Noncompliant
switch (code) {
    case 200: ok(); break;
    case 404: notFound(); break;
}

// Compliant
switch (code) {
    case 200: ok(); break;
    case 404: notFound(); break;
    default: throw new IllegalStateException("unexpected status " + code);
}
```

Not reported: `switch` expressions (the compiler already requires them to be exhaustive),
pattern switches, switches whose labels are bare names (the names may be enum constants
declared elsewhere, whose complete list is unknown) unless the selector is an enum declared in
this file, or a variable of this file with a primitive or `String` type whose labels are all
constants declared in this file, and enum switches that list every constant.

### java/mockito-mixed-matchers

**Mockito matchers mixed with plain values** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: tests, mockito

Detects calls whose arguments mix Mockito argument matchers (`any()`, `eq(..)`,
`anyString()`, `argThat(..)`, …) with plain values (literals, variables, `new` objects), as in
`when(repo.find(anyLong(), "active"))` or `verify(mailer).send(eq(to), subject)`.

**Why it matters.** Mockito records matchers on a stack while the arguments are evaluated and
then pairs them with the call's parameters. It needs either a matcher for every argument or
none at all: with a mix it cannot tell which matcher belongs to which argument and throws
`InvalidUseOfMatchersException` at run time (sometimes in a later, unrelated test, which makes
the failure confusing).

**How to fix.** Wrap the plain values in `eq(..)` (or `same(..)`), or use plain values for all
arguments.

```java
// Noncompliant
when(repo.find(anyLong(), "active")).thenReturn(user);

// Compliant
when(repo.find(anyLong(), eq("active"))).thenReturn(user);
```

Only matchers that provably come from Mockito (statically imported from `org.mockito`, or
qualified with `Mockito`, `ArgumentMatchers` or `Matchers`) are recognised, and only
literals, variables, field reads, `new` expressions and `this` count as plain values: a call
to a helper method may itself return a matcher and is never counted.

### java/mocks-not-initialized

**Mockito annotations never processed** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: tests, mockito

Detects test classes whose fields carry Mockito's `@Mock`, `@Spy`, `@Captor` or
`@InjectMocks` while nothing in the file asks Mockito to process them: no
`@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`, no `@RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class)`, no
`MockitoJUnit.rule()`, no `MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this)` / `initMocks(this)`.

**Why it matters.** The annotations do nothing by themselves: some runner, extension, rule or
explicit call must create the mocks. Without it the fields stay `null`; tests that use them
fail with a `NullPointerException` far from the cause, and tests that only pass them along
(to `@InjectMocks` or a constructor) silently test against `null` collaborators.

**How to fix.** Add the Mockito extension (JUnit 5) or runner (JUnit 4), or initialize the
mocks in a set-up method.

```java
// Noncompliant
class OrderServiceTest {
    @Mock OrderRepository repository;
    @Test void saves() { … }
}

// Compliant
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderServiceTest {
    @Mock OrderRepository repository;
    @Test void saves() { … }
}
```

Only top-level, non-abstract classes that declare `@Test` methods and extend nothing are
checked (a superclass may set the mocks up); classes with any annotation other than a few
descriptive ones (`@DisplayName`, `@Tag`, `@Disabled`, …) are skipped, since a custom
annotation may carry the extension, and so are files that mention Spring's test support.

### java/modifier-order

**Modifiers out of the usual order**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions, readability

Detects keyword modifiers written out of the customary order, which is the
order the Java Language Specification lists them in: `public` / `protected` / `private`,
`abstract`, `default`, `static`, `final`, `sealed` / `non-sealed`, `transient`, `volatile`,
`synchronized`, `native`, `strictfp`.

**Why it matters.** The compiler accepts any order, but readers do not scan modifiers one by
one: they expect the visibility first and `static final` together. `final static public`
or `static public` slows every reader down a little and makes searches such as
`public static final` miss the declaration.

**How to fix.** Reorder the keywords; annotations on the declaration stay in front of them.

```java
// Noncompliant
final static public int LIMIT = 10;
synchronized public void reset() { … }

// Compliant
public static final int LIMIT = 10;
public synchronized void reset() { … }
```

With the parameter `type_use_annotations`, the rule also reports a nullness annotation that
targets types (JSpecify's or the Checker Framework's `@Nullable` / `@NonNull`, recognized by
their imports) placed before the keyword modifiers: such an annotation describes the type, so it
is written right before it (`public @Nullable String name()`). Annotations in other positions
are never reported. The rule is off by default: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `type_use_annotations` | `false` | Also report a nullness type annotation of JSpecify or the Checker Framework written before the keyword modifiers (`@Nullable public String name()`) instead of right before the type it annotates. |

### java/multiple-top-level-types

**Several top-level types in one file**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: conventions, structure

Detects source files that declare more than one top-level class, interface,
enum, record or annotation type.

**Why it matters.** Tools and people find a type by its file: `Order.java` holds `Order`. A
second top-level type in that file is invisible from the file list, cannot be found by the
usual "open type by file name" habits, and makes the compiler's output (one `.class` file per
type) disagree with the source tree. When two files both declare a package-private type of the
same name, the build fails depending on which files are compiled together.

**How to fix.** Move the extra type to its own file, or nest it inside the main type
(`static` when it does not need an instance of the outer class).

```java
// Noncompliant: Order.java
public class Order { … }
class OrderLine { … }

// Compliant: Order.java
public class Order {
    static class Line { … }
}
```

The type kept in place is the one named after the file, else the public one, else the first;
every other top-level type is reported. Parameter `allow_package_private` accepts
package-private helper types next to a public type, a layout older conventions tolerate.
Files whose name is not a Java identifier (templates) and files under a `resources` directory
are not checked. The rule is off by default: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `allow_package_private` | `false` | Accept package-private helper types next to the file's public type. A file without a public type is still reported. |

### java/multiple-unary-operators

**Stacked unary operators** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: suspicious, confusing

Detects unary operators applied directly to another unary expression:
`!!ready`, `- -delta`, `~~mask`, `-~n`.

**Why it matters.** A doubled `!`, `-`, or `~` cancels itself out, so the expression is either
a roundabout way of writing the operand or — more often — a typo or an edit that went wrong
(one operator too many, a missing operand in between). Mixed stacks such as `-~n` are bit
tricks that few readers decode correctly.

**How to fix.** Remove the extra operators, or write the intended expression plainly.

```java
// Noncompliant
boolean active = !!flags.contains(ACTIVE);
int n = - -offset;

// Compliant
boolean active = flags.contains(ACTIVE);
int n = offset;
```

Not reported: increments and decrements (`--x` is an update, not two minus signs), and
stacked operators separated by parentheses (`-(-x)`), which mark the nesting as deliberate.

### java/mutable-exception-field

**Mutable field in an exception class**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: exceptions, immutability

Detects instance fields that are not `final` in a class whose superclass chain
provably reaches `Throwable` (through classes of this file or JDK exceptions).

**Why it matters.** An exception is a report of something that happened: it is created at one
place, travels up the stack, is often handed to other threads (futures, executors, log
appenders) and may be serialized. A handler that changes it — or a field set later through a
setter — changes the report for every other holder, and a field written without
synchronization may not even be visible to the thread that reads it. Final fields make the
exception a safe, self-describing value.

**How to fix.** Declare the fields `final` and set them in the constructor; if a value is only
known later, create a new exception (with the original as its cause) instead of mutating it.

```java
// Noncompliant
class OrderFailedException extends RuntimeException {
    private String orderId;
    void setOrderId(String id) { this.orderId = id; }
}

// Compliant
class OrderFailedException extends RuntimeException {
    private final String orderId;
    OrderFailedException(String orderId, Throwable cause) {
        super(cause);
        this.orderId = orderId;
    }
}
```

Not reported: `static` fields, classes whose superclass is declared in another file (whether
they are exceptions is not visible here), classes using Lombok (it may generate final
fields and constructors), and classes with a custom `readObject` (deserialization assigns
their fields after construction).

### java/negated-comparison

**Negated comparison instead of the opposite operator**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: readability

Detects a negated comparison that can be written with the opposite
operator: `!(a == b)` is `a != b`, `!(a != b)` is `a == b`, and — for integer operands —
`!(i < n)` is `i >= n` (likewise `<=`, `>`, `>=`).

**Why it matters.** The negation wrapped around the parentheses is one more step for the
reader, and it is easy to miss when scanning a condition. The direct operator states the
condition as it is.

**How to fix.** Drop the `!` and the parentheses, and use the opposite operator.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (!(count == 0)) { ... }
while (!(index >= size)) { ... }

// Compliant
if (count != 0) { ... }
while (index < size) { ... }
```

Ordering comparisons are only reported when both operands are proven integers (`int`,
`long`, `short`, `byte`, `char` or their wrappers): with `float` or `double`, `!(a < b)` is
also true when either value is NaN, so it is not the same as `a >= b`. Off by default: this
is a readability preference.

### java/nested-code-too-long

**Lambda, anonymous class or nested type too long**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: brain-overload, size

Detects code nested inside another unit that has grown too long to stay there:

* a lambda expression with more than `max_lambda_lines` lines of code (20 by default);
* an anonymous class with more than `max_anonymous_class_lines` (40);
* a nested, inner or local class, interface, enum or record with more than
  `max_nested_class_lines` (300).

Lines of code are lines holding something other than blanks and comments.

**Why it matters.** Lambdas and anonymous classes are meant for small pieces of behavior
passed along where they are used; the method-length limit counts them as part of the
enclosing method, where a long one makes the method hard to read and cannot be tested or
named on its own. A nested type that grows to hundreds of lines has become a unit in its own
right, sharing the file (and often the private state) of its outer class.

**How to fix.** Move the lambda's body to a named method and pass a method reference; turn
the anonymous class into a named class; move the nested type to its own file.

```java
// Noncompliant
orders.forEach(order -> {
    // 30 lines of validation, pricing and persistence
});

// Compliant
orders.forEach(this::process);

private void process(Order order) {
    // …
}
```

Nested units are measured on their own; the enclosing method still counts their lines for
`function-too-long`. Top-level types are not measured here (see `file-too-long`).

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_lambda_lines` | `20` | Most lines of code allowed in one lambda expression. |
| `max_anonymous_class_lines` | `40` | Most lines of code allowed in one anonymous class. |
| `max_nested_class_lines` | `300` | Most lines of code allowed in one nested, inner or local type. |

### java/nested-ternary

**Nested conditional expression**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: readability

Detects a conditional (ternary) expression nested inside another conditional
expression — in its condition, in one of its branches, or in an argument of a call there.

**Why it matters.** One `?:` reads well; two or more force readers to work out which `:`
belongs to which `?`, and the precedence is easy to get wrong when editing.

**How to fix.** Use `if`/`else` statements, a `switch` expression, or extract the inner
expression into a well-named local variable or method.

```java
// Noncompliant
String size = n > 100 ? "large" : n > 10 ? "medium" : "small";

// Compliant
String size;
if (n > 100) {
    size = "large";
} else if (n > 10) {
    size = "medium";
} else {
    size = "small";
}
```

Each nested conditional is reported once. A conditional inside a lambda or an anonymous
class body that is itself inside a conditional is not considered nested.

### java/nested-test-class-not-run

**Inner test class without @Nested is never run** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: tests, junit

Detects a non-static inner class that declares JUnit 5 test methods (`@Test`,
`@ParameterizedTest`, `@RepeatedTest`, `@TestFactory`, `@TestTemplate`) but is not annotated
`@Nested`.

**Why it matters.** JUnit 5 only runs the tests of an inner (non-static member) class when the
class is marked `@Nested`. Without the annotation the class is skipped without a warning: the
build is green, the test report simply does not mention those tests, and the behaviour they
were written to check is not verified.

**How to fix.** Annotate the inner class with `@Nested`.

```java
// Noncompliant
class CartTest {
    class WhenEmpty {
        @Test
        void totalIsZero() { … }
    }
}

// Compliant
class CartTest {
    @Nested
    class WhenEmpty {
        @Test
        void totalIsZero() { … }
    }
}
```

Only inner classes are checked: whether a `static` nested class is run depends on the build
tool's test filters. Abstract inner classes (templates for `@Nested` subclasses) are not
reported, and only annotations that resolve to JUnit 5 through the imports count.

### java/nested-try

**Nested try-catch**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: exceptions, structure

Detects a `try` statement that is a statement of the body of another `try`
statement when both have `catch` clauses for overlapping exception types: the same type, one
a subtype of the other, or a catch-all (`Exception`, `Throwable`).

**Why it matters.** Code in the inner body is covered by two sets of handlers that could both
take the same failure. To know what happens when it throws, a reader has to match the
exception against the inner catches, then the outer ones, and keep in mind that the inner
handlers can themselves throw into the outer ones. The nesting also usually means one method
is handling failures of two different operations.

**How to fix.** Extract the inner `try` into a method named after what it does, or merge the
handlers into one `try` when they handle the same failure.

```java
// Noncompliant
try {
    Config config = load(path);
    try {
        connect(config);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        useOfflineMode();
    }
} catch (IOException e) {
    reportUnreadable(path, e);
}

// Compliant
try {
    Config config = load(path);
    connectOrGoOffline(config);
} catch (IOException e) {
    reportUnreadable(path, e);
}
```

Not reported: handlers for unrelated exception types (each failure has one obvious handler),
an inner or outer `try` without `catch` clauses (`try`-`finally` and
try-with-resources used for cleanup), and tries nested in a `catch` or `finally` block, in a
loop or in a conditional inside the outer body (cleanup that can fail and per-item handling
are common and deliberate).

### java/non-atomic-volatile-update

**Non-atomic update of a volatile field**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects `++`, `--`, and compound assignments (`+=`, `|=`, …) applied to a
`volatile` field declared in this file.

**Why it matters.** `volatile` makes each individual read and write visible to other
threads, but `count++` is three steps — read, add, write. Two threads can read the same
value and both write back `value + 1`, losing an update. Counters, sequence numbers, and
flags updated this way drift under load, and the bug almost never reproduces in tests.

**How to fix.** Use an atomic type (`AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()`,
`AtomicLong.addAndGet(n)`, `LongAdder` for hot counters), or guard every update with the
same lock.

```java
// Noncompliant
private volatile int requests;
void onRequest() { requests++; }

// Compliant
private final AtomicInteger requests = new AtomicInteger();
void onRequest() { requests.incrementAndGet(); }
```

Updates inside `synchronized` methods or blocks (volatile for lock-free readers, writers
serialized by the lock) and inside constructors and static initializers (the object is not
shared yet) are not reported.

### java/non-short-circuit-boolean

**Non-short-circuit boolean operator**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious, null-safety

Detects the non-short-circuit operators `&` and `|` applied to two `boolean`
operands.

**Why it matters.** Unlike `&&` and `||`, these operators always evaluate the right-hand side.
Guards such as `s != null & s.isEmpty()` then throw exactly when the guard was supposed to
protect, and expensive right-hand sides run needlessly. When both sides really must run (for
their side effects) the intent is invisible to the reader.

**How to fix.** Use `&&` / `||`. If both operands must be evaluated, compute them into local
variables first and combine those.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (user != null & user.isActive()) { ... }

// Compliant
if (user != null && user.isActive()) { ... }
```

Compound assignments (`ok &= step()`, `changed |= update()`) are not reported; neither are
integer bit operations or operands whose type is unknown.

### java/nondeterministic-test

**Test depends on randomness or retries**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: tests, flaky

Detects test code whose outcome can change from one run to the next:

* data drawn from an unseeded random source: `new Random()`, `Math.random()`,
  `ThreadLocalRandom.current()`, `Collections.shuffle(list)` without a `Random`, and the
  Commons Lang `RandomStringUtils` / `RandomUtils` helpers;
* tests marked to be run again until they pass: JUnit Pioneer's `@RetryingTest`,
  `@RepeatedIfExceptionsTest`, TestNG's `retryAnalyzer`.

**Why it matters.** A test is only useful if a failure can be reproduced. With a fresh random
seed on every run, a failing input shows up once on a build server and cannot be replayed
while debugging; the test becomes "flaky" and the team learns to re-run it instead of reading
it. Retrying until green is the same problem made official: a real intermittent bug (a race,
an ordering assumption) is hidden behind the retries.

**How to fix.** Use a fixed seed (`new Random(42)`), or a random seed that the test logs and
accepts as a parameter so a failure can be replayed; make the flaky behavior deterministic
instead of retrying.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Test
void sortsAnyInput() {
    int[] data = new Random().ints(100).toArray();
    …
}

// Compliant
@Test
void sortsAnyInput() {
    int[] data = new Random(20260928L).ints(100).toArray();
    …
}
```

Only test files are checked. Not reported: seeded generators (also when `setSeed` follows,
or when an unseeded generator only draws the seed, `long seed = new Random().nextLong()`, the
usual start of a replayable test), `SecureRandom` (used for keys
and tokens, not for test data), `UUID.randomUUID()` (unique names, not data a result depends
on), random values only used to build a unique name for a file, table or queue or to pick a
network port (`int listenPort = RandomUtils.nextInt(10000, 20000)`, a `createRandomPort()`
helper: a clash is fixed by a port the system assigns, not by a seed), and generators stored
in a variable that nothing reads (no data is drawn from them).

### java/notify-instead-of-notify-all

**notify() instead of notifyAll()**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects calls to `notify()`.

**Why it matters.** `notify()` wakes exactly one thread, chosen arbitrarily, among those
waiting on the monitor. When threads wait for *different* conditions on the same object (a
bounded buffer's "not full" and "not empty"), the wrong one can be woken, go back to
waiting, and leave the thread that could make progress asleep — a lost wake-up that shows
up as a rare hang. `notifyAll()` lets every waiter re-check its own condition.

**How to fix.** Use `notifyAll()`, or move to `java.util.concurrent` (`Condition.signal`
with one condition per predicate, `BlockingQueue`, `CountDownLatch`, …).

```java
// Noncompliant
synchronized void put(Item item) {
    queue.add(item);
    notify();
}

// Compliant
synchronized void put(Item item) {
    queue.add(item);
    notifyAll();
}
```

`notify()` is correct when every waiter waits for the same condition and any one of them
can handle it; this rule is informational in that case.

### java/null-check-after-dereference

**Null check after the value was dereferenced**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: null, suspicious

Detects an `if` that compares a local variable or parameter with `null` after an
earlier statement of the same block has already dereferenced it (called a method on it, read
a field or an element, iterated over it, locked on it), with no assignment to the variable in
between.

**Why it matters.** Had the variable been `null`, the earlier dereference would have thrown a
`NullPointerException` and the check would never run. So one of the two is wrong: either the
value can be `null` and the dereference comes too early (the check was meant to protect it),
or it cannot and the check is dead code that misleads readers into thinking `null` is
possible here.

**How to fix.** Move the check before the first use, or remove it when the value can never be
`null`.

```java
// Noncompliant
String name = user.getName();
int length = name.length();
if (name != null) { … }          // too late: length() already failed on null

// Compliant
String name = user.getName();
if (name != null) {
    int length = name.length();
    …
}
```

Only the 16 statements before the check are examined, only locals and parameters are
considered (a field can be changed by the calls in between),
and only dereferences that always run: those inside lambdas, anonymous classes, the right
side of `&&` / `||`, a branch of `?:`, a loop body, a `try` block, or an `assert` are ignored.

### java/nullability-annotation-misuse

**Nullability annotation that cannot apply** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: null, annotations, confusing

Detects nullability annotations that say something impossible or wrong:

* `@Nullable`, `@NonNull`, `@NotNull`, `@CheckForNull` (and their spellings in the common
  annotation libraries) on a field, parameter, local variable, record component or method
  return of a primitive type (`int`, `long`, `boolean`, …) or `void`;
* a non-null marker (`@NonNull`, `@Nonnull`, `@NotNull`) on the parameter of
  `equals(Object)`;
* an override that turns a `@Nullable` parameter of the method it overrides into a non-null
  one, or a non-null return into a `@Nullable` one, when the overridden method is declared in
  the same file.

**Why it matters.** A primitive can never be `null`: the annotation is noise at best, and at
worst tells the reader (or a null checker) that `null` is a possible value when it is not —
often the leftover of a change from `Integer` to `int`. The `equals` contract requires
`x.equals(null)` to return `false`, so a non-null parameter promises callers something the
method must not demand. An override may accept more than its parent and return less, never
the reverse: callers that follow the parent's contract would pass `null` where the override
rejects it, or get `null` where the parent promised a value.

**How to fix.** Remove the annotation from primitives (or go back to the boxed type if `null`
really is a state), drop the non-null marker from `equals`, and keep an override's contract at
least as permissive as its parent's.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Nullable int retries;
public boolean equals(@NonNull Object other) { … }

// Compliant
int retries;
public boolean equals(@Nullable Object other) { … }
```

Not reported: arrays of primitives (a declaration annotation on `int[]` describes the array,
which can be `null`), boxed types, overrides of methods declared in other files (their
contract is not visible here), and test code (tests of validation and null-checking tools
use such declarations on purpose).

### java/numeric-escape-for-named-char

**Numeric escape for a character with a named escape**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions, strings

Detects octal escapes (`\11`, `\12`, `\42`, `\134`, …) and Unicode escapes
(`\u0009`, `\u0008`, `\u000c`) in string, text block and character literals for characters
that have a short named escape: backspace `\b`, tab `\t`, line feed `\n`, form feed `\f`,
carriage return `\r`, double quote `\"`, single quote `\'` and backslash `\\`.

**Why it matters.** Few readers know that `\12` is a line feed or `\42` a double quote; the
named escapes say what the character is. A Unicode escape is worse: it is replaced before the
code is even tokenized, so `"\u0009"` is a raw tab inside the literal, and the same trick with
`\u000a` or `"` does not even compile.

**How to fix.** Use the named escape.

```java
// Noncompliant
String row = name + "\11" + value + "\12";
char tab = '\u0009';

// Compliant
String row = name + "\t" + value + "\n";
char tab = '\t';
```

Not reported: numeric escapes for characters without a named escape (`\0`, `\u001b`), escaped
backslashes followed by digits (`"\\12"`), and the space character (its named escape `\s`
needs Java 15). The rule is off by default: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

### java/object-method-name-typo

**Misspelled Object method** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: typo, equality, overrides

Detects instance methods whose name and parameters almost match an `Object`
method: `hashcode()` / `HashCode()`, `tostring()` / `ToString()`, `Equals(Object)`, and
`equal(Object)` returning `boolean`; and a `finalize(..)` with parameters that is written as a
finalizer (it declares `throws Throwable` or calls `super.finalize()`), which the garbage
collector never calls.

**Why it matters.** The method was meant to override `hashCode`, `toString` or `equals`, but
Java names are case-sensitive, so it is a new, unrelated method that nothing calls. The class
keeps the identity-based `Object` behavior: equal objects get different hash codes, hash-based
collections lose entries, and logs print `Order@1b6d3586`.

**How to fix.** Use the exact name and add `@Override`, which makes the compiler catch the
next typo.

```java
// Noncompliant
public int hashcode() { return Objects.hash(id); }

// Compliant
@Override
public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(id); }
```

Static methods and classes that also declare the correctly spelled method are not
reported.

### java/octal-literal

**Octal integer literal** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious, numbers

Detects integer literals written with a leading zero, such as `010` or
`030`. In Java a leading zero makes the literal octal: `010` is eight, not ten.

**Why it matters.** Most readers — and most authors padding numbers to line them up — read
`010` as ten. When the octal value was not intended, the program silently uses a different
number (a month, a port, a size); when it was intended, the next maintainer is likely to
"fix" or copy it wrongly. Octal is rarely the clearest way to write a value in Java.

**How to fix.** Drop the leading zero for a decimal value. For bit patterns and file modes
use hexadecimal or binary, or a named constant; `Integer.parseInt("755", 8)` makes an octal
value explicit.

```java
// Noncompliant
int timeoutSeconds = 030;      // 24, not 30
record.setMonth(012);          // 10, not 12

// Compliant
int timeoutSeconds = 30;
record.setMonth(12);
```

The rule looks for octal that looks accidental — a decimal-looking number with a leading zero
— and leaves alone the places where octal is written on purpose:

* `0` itself and the single digits `00` to `07` (octal and decimal agree);
* files that use octal as their notation: at least `file_convention` (default 3) octal
  literals of 8 and above in the file (archive headers, file-mode tables, generated scanners);
* unless `report_tables` is set, literals in an array initializer that holds several octal
  literals (a lookup table such as a character-code map written in octal deliberately);
* file modes: permission-shaped values (`0644`, `0755`, `0600`, `04755`: an owner digit of
  4 to 7 and every permission digit 0, 4, 5, 6 or 7; special bits such as `04000`), Unix mode
  words (`0100644`, `040755`, `0170000`), and any octal value up to `07777` assigned to, compared or combined with,
  returned from, or passed to a name about modes or permissions (`fileMode`, `umask`,
  `setMode(0123)`, `chmod(path, 0700)`, `assertEquals(0644, entry.getMode())`);
* bit patterns: operands of `&`, `|`, `^` and shifts (`c & 077`), masks made of sevens
  (`0777`, `07777777L`), literals with five or more significant digits (`070707`,
  `0100000000000L`), and literals grouped with underscores (`0777_776`), none of which reads
  like a decimal number that lost its meaning to a leading zero.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `report_tables` | `false` | Also report octal literals in array initializers that hold several of them (lookup tables written in octal on purpose). Such a table usually makes the whole file count as octal by convention: set `file_convention` to 0 as well to see them. |
| `file_convention` | `3` | A file holding at least this many octal literals (of 8 and above) uses octal on purpose (archive formats, file modes, generated tables): none of them is reported. 0 turns the file-level test off. |

### java/one-variable-per-declaration

**Several variables in one declaration**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions, readability

Detects field, constant and local variable declarations that declare more
than one variable (`int width, height;`).

**Why it matters.** One name per declaration gives every variable its own line for its type,
its initial value, its annotations and its comment. Grouped declarations hide which names are
initialized (`int a, b = 0;` leaves `a` without a value), make the type of later names easy to
misread when array brackets are mixed in (`int a, b[];` declares an `int` and an `int[]`), and
turn a change to one variable into an edit of a line that also declares others.

**How to fix.** Write one declaration per variable.

```java
// Noncompliant
private int width, height;
String first = null, last = null;

// Compliant
private int width;
private int height;
String first = null;
String last = null;
```

Not reported: the initialization part of a classic `for` loop (`for (int i = 0, n = size(); i <
n; i++)`), where several loop variables in one declaration are the usual form. The rule is off
by default: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

### java/optional-get-without-check

**Optional.get() without a presence check**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: optional, null-safety

Detects `get()` on an `Optional` variable (and `getAsInt()`, `getAsLong()`,
`getAsDouble()` on `OptionalInt`, `OptionalLong`, `OptionalDouble`) when the same method never
checked it earlier with `isPresent()`, `isEmpty()`, `ifPresent(..)`, or `ifPresentOrElse(..)`.

**Why it matters.** `get()` throws `NoSuchElementException` on an empty optional. Calling it
unchecked brings back exactly the failure `Optional` was meant to make explicit — just with a
different exception than `NullPointerException`.

**How to fix.** Handle the empty case: `orElse(..)`, `orElseGet(..)`, `map(..)`, `ifPresent(..)`,
or `orElseThrow(..)` with a meaningful exception. If emptiness is truly impossible, say so with
`orElseThrow()`, which reads as an assertion.

```java
// Noncompliant
Optional<User> user = repository.findById(id);
return user.get().getName();

// Compliant
Optional<User> user = repository.findById(id);
return user.map(User::getName).orElse("unknown");
```

Only local variables, parameters, and fields (`opt` or `this.opt`) are tracked, and a check
anywhere earlier in the same method (including code around a lambda or anonymous class, and
conditions such as `opt.isPresent() ? opt.get() : x`) counts. Optionals initialized with
`Optional.of(..)` and test code (where a failing `get()` just fails the test) are not
reported.

### java/optional-null

**Optional compared with or set to null**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: optional, null-safety

Detects an `Optional` (`java.util.Optional`, `OptionalInt`, `OptionalLong`,
`OptionalDouble`, or Guava's `Optional`) that is compared with `null` (`opt == null`,
`opt != null`) or given the value `null` (`Optional<User> user = null;`, `user = null;`).
With `report_parameters`, method and constructor parameters declared as `Optional` are
reported as well.

**Why it matters.** An `Optional` exists to represent "no value" without `null`. A variable of
that type holding `null` breaks the contract every caller relies on: `isPresent()`, `map(..)`
or `orElse(..)` on it throw `NullPointerException` instead of handling the empty case. A
comparison with `null` is either dead code or a sign that such a `null` does circulate, and it
often stands where `isPresent()` / `isEmpty()` was meant. An `Optional` parameter forces every
caller to wrap its argument and still admits `null`, so overloads or a nullable parameter are
usually clearer.

**How to fix.** Use `Optional.empty()` instead of `null`, test with `isPresent()` /
`isEmpty()`, and make sure no method returns `null` for an `Optional`.

```java
// Noncompliant
Optional<User> user = null;
if (lookup != null && lookup.isPresent()) { … }

// Compliant
Optional<User> user = Optional.empty();
if (lookup.isPresent()) { … }
```

Only expressions whose type the resolver proves to be one of these optional types are
reported; `return null` from a method returning `Optional` is `optional-return-null`'s. Parameter
reporting skips `@Override` methods, whose signature is inherited, and annotated parameters
(`@RequestParam Optional<String> q`), which frameworks fill in.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `report_parameters` | `false` | Also report method and constructor parameters declared as `Optional` (a design choice rather than a defect). |

### java/optional-return-null

**null returned from a method returning Optional**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: optional, null-safety

Detects `return null;` in a method whose declared return type is `Optional<…>`,
`OptionalInt`, `OptionalLong`, or `OptionalDouble` (the JDK types, or Guava's `Optional`).

**Why it matters.** Callers of a method returning `Optional` rely on never getting `null` —
that is the whole contract of the type. They call `isPresent()`, `map(..)`, or `orElse(..)`
directly on the result and fail with a `NullPointerException` instead of handling the "no
value" case.

**How to fix.** Return an empty optional: `Optional.empty()` (`OptionalInt.empty()`, …, or
Guava's `Optional.absent()`).

```java
// Noncompliant
Optional<User> find(String id) {
    if (id == null) {
        return null;
    }
    return Optional.ofNullable(users.get(id));
}

// Compliant
Optional<User> find(String id) {
    if (id == null) {
        return Optional.empty();
    }
    return Optional.ofNullable(users.get(id));
}
```

`return null` inside a lambda or an anonymous class within such a method is not reported (it
returns from that inner function, whose type is not the method's).

### java/overload-instead-of-override

**Overload that looks like an override** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: inheritance, suspicious

Detects methods of a subclass that have the name and the number of parameters of
a superclass method, but where a parameter type differs only by boxing (`int` versus
`Integer`) or only by package (two different classes with the same simple name, such as
`java.util.Date` and `java.sql.Date`). The superclass must be declared in the same file.

**Why it matters.** Such a method does not override: it adds an overload. Code that calls the
method through a reference of the superclass type still runs the superclass version, so the
subclass's behaviour is silently skipped. Without `@Override` the compiler does not
complain, and the near-identical signature hides the difference from readers.

**How to fix.** Use exactly the superclass parameter types (and add `@Override`, so that the
compiler checks it), or give the method a different name if an overload is really meant.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Handler {
    void handle(Integer code) { … }
}
class RetryHandler extends Handler {
    void handle(int code) { … }       // never called through a Handler reference
}

// Compliant
class RetryHandler extends Handler {
    @Override
    void handle(Integer code) { … }
}
```

Methods annotated `@Override` (the compiler already checks them), static and private
methods, methods of the superclass using its type parameters, and superclasses declared in
other files are not considered.

### java/overloads-not-adjacent

**Overloads separated by other members**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, structure

Detects overloads that are not kept together: a method with the same name
as an earlier method of the same type, or a constructor, with other members in between.

**Why it matters.** Overloads are variations of one operation, and a reader choosing between
them, or changing their shared behavior, needs to see all of them at once. Scattered through a
long class, the third `parse` is missed when the first two are fixed, and a reviewer cannot
tell whether the overloads still agree with each other.

**How to fix.** Move the overload next to the others with that name (or the constructor next
to the other constructors), with no other member in between.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Parser {
    Node parse(String text) { … }
    void reset() { … }
    Node parse(Reader in) { … }
}

// Compliant
class Parser {
    Node parse(String text) { … }
    Node parse(Reader in) { … }
    void reset() { … }
}
```

Every member counts as a separator: fields, nested types, initializers and other methods.
Each overload that does not follow the previous one of its name is reported, with the
previous one as secondary location. The rule is off by default: it is part of the
`conventions` profile.

### java/override-drops-synchronized

**Override drops synchronized** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: concurrency

Detects a method overriding a `synchronized` method of a superclass declared
in the same file, without being `synchronized` itself.

**Why it matters.** `synchronized` is not inherited. The superclass made the method
thread-safe by locking the object, and its other synchronized methods rely on that lock; the
override silently runs without it, so it can interleave with them and see or leave
half-updated state.

**How to fix.** Declare the override `synchronized` too (or wrap its body in
`synchronized (this)`), or document why the lock is not needed.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Counter {
    protected int count;
    public synchronized void increment() { count++; }
}
class LoggingCounter extends Counter {
    @Override public void increment() { log(); count++; }
}

// Compliant
class LoggingCounter extends Counter {
    @Override public synchronized void increment() { log(); count++; }
}
```

Not reported: overrides whose body only delegates to `super` (the superclass method takes
the lock), only throws, only returns a literal, is empty, or is entirely a
`synchronized (this)` block — or ends with one, after statements that assign no field (a
read-only check before taking the lock: `verify(file); synchronized (this) { … }`); static
methods; superclasses declared in other files.

### java/overwritten-before-read

**Value overwritten before it is read**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, copy-paste

Detects two consecutive statements that write the same target, so the first
value is replaced before anything can read it:

* `map.put(KEY, a); map.put(KEY, b);` — same map, same key (a JDK `Map`);
* `values[i] = a; values[i] = b;` — same array element with a side-effect-free index;
* `this.name = a; this.name = b;` or `x = a; x = b;` — same field or variable.

**Why it matters.** The first write is dead. In practice this is nearly always a copy-paste
slip where the second statement was meant to use a different key, index, or field
(`put("width", w); put("width", h);`), so one value is silently lost and another is never
set.

**How to fix.** Correct the key, index, or target of one of the statements, or delete the
redundant write.

```java
// Noncompliant
size.put("width", width);
size.put("width", height);

// Compliant
size.put("width", width);
size.put("height", height);
```

Not reported: when the second value reads the target (`x = x + 1`, `m.put(k, m.get(k) + 1)`),
when a field or array write is followed by a value that calls methods of this object (they
could read it), volatile fields, compound assignments, and plain variable writes whose
first value has side effects (`line = reader.readLine(); line = reader.readLine();`).

### java/package-directory-mismatch

**Package does not match directory** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: structure, convention

Detects a `package` declaration whose names do not match the last directories of
the file's path: `package com.acme.billing;` in `src/main/java/com/acme/orders/Invoice.java`.

**Why it matters.** Build tools, IDEs and the compiler's source path look for a class of
package `com.acme.billing` under `com/acme/billing/`. A file elsewhere compiles only when it
is passed explicitly, is not found by incremental builds and by tools that locate sources
from class names (debuggers, coverage reports, navigation), and misleads readers who browse
the directory tree.

**How to fix.** Move the file to the directory of its package, or correct the declaration.

Only the directories the path shows are compared (a scan of a sub-directory sees a shortened
path). Not reported: files at the root of the scanned tree, files under `resources`
directories or test-data directories (sources used as input data), and package names that are
template placeholders.

### java/package-naming

**Package naming convention**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: naming, convention

Detects `package` declarations whose name is not all lowercase: each
dot-separated segment must start with a lowercase letter or underscore and contain only
lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

**Why it matters.** Package names map to directories; mixed case causes trouble on
case-insensitive file systems and can collide with class names (`com.acme.Util` the package
vs. `com.acme.Util` the class). Lowercase packages are the universal Java convention.

**How to fix.** Rename the package (and move its directory).

```java
// Noncompliant
package com.acme.OrderService;

// Compliant
package com.acme.orderservice;
```

The `format` parameter takes a preset name (`lower.dotted`); regular expressions are not
supported.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `format` | `"lower.dotted"` | Naming preset for package names: `lower.dotted` (`^[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*(\.[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*)*$`). Arbitrary regular expressions are not supported; the regular expression of the preset is accepted as an alias. With an unknown value the rule repo… |

### java/parameter-overwritten-before-read

**Parameter overwritten before it is read** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, unused

Detects a method, constructor or lambda parameter, a `catch` parameter, or an
enhanced-`for` variable that is assigned a new value before its incoming value has been read.

**Why it matters.** The value the caller passed (the exception that was caught, the element of
the current iteration) is thrown away unseen. Either the parameter is useless and misleads
callers into thinking their argument matters, or, far more often, the assignment is a slip:
it was meant to go the other way (`this.name = name`), to target a field or another variable,
or to happen after the value was used.

**How to fix.** Use the incoming value, fix the target of the assignment, or remove the
parameter and declare a local variable instead.

```java
// Noncompliant
Account(String owner, int limit) {
    owner = "unknown";            // the caller's owner is ignored
    this.owner = owner;
    this.limit = limit;
}

// Compliant
Account(String owner, int limit) {
    this.owner = owner == null ? "unknown" : owner;
    this.limit = limit;
}
```

Only an assignment that is a statement of the body itself (not nested in a branch or loop)
and comes before any other mention of the name is reported; `final` parameters cannot be
reassigned and are skipped, as are values computed from the name itself (`s = s.trim()`).

### java/parameter-reassignment

**Parameter reassigned**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: readability, confusing

Detects assignments (`=`, compound assignments, `++`, `--`) to a parameter of
the enclosing method or constructor.

**Why it matters.** Readers expect a parameter to hold the value the caller passed for the
whole method. Reassigning it makes the method harder to follow (which value is used where?),
hides the original argument from later code and from debuggers, and is easily mistaken for
changing the caller's variable, which Java never does.

**How to fix.** Introduce a local variable for the computed value. Declaring parameters
`final` prevents the problem.

```java
// Noncompliant
String normalize(String name) {
    name = name.trim();
    return name.toLowerCase();
}

// Compliant
String normalize(String name) {
    String trimmed = name.trim();
    return trimmed.toLowerCase();
}
```

Not reported: lambda parameters, assignments in record compact constructors, where
reassigning the parameters is the intended way to normalize component values, and `p = p`
(reported by `java/self-assignment`).

### java/peek-side-effect

**Stream.peek used for side effects** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: streams, side-effects

Detects `peek(..)` on a `java.util.stream` pipeline whose action does real work —
changes an element or some other state, collects into a list, validates, counts — instead of
only logging or printing what flows by.

**Why it matters.** A stream runs `peek`'s action only for the elements the terminal operation
actually pulls through the pipeline, and the library is free to skip it altogether. Since
Java 9, `list.stream().peek(action).count()` does not run the action at all, because the count
is known from the source; `findFirst`, `anyMatch` or `limit` stop after a few elements; a
parallel stream runs the action on several threads in any order. Code that relies on the
action happening works until one of these conditions changes, then fails quietly. The API
itself describes `peek` as a debugging aid.

**How to fix.** Do the work where the stream guarantees it runs: in `map` (returning the
element), in the terminal `forEach`, or in a separate loop before or after the pipeline.

```java
// Noncompliant
List<Order> sent = orders.stream()
        .filter(Order::isReady)
        .peek(o -> o.setStatus(SENT))
        .collect(Collectors.toList());

// Compliant
List<Order> sent = orders.stream()
        .filter(Order::isReady)
        .collect(Collectors.toList());
sent.forEach(o -> o.setStatus(SENT));
```

Only pipelines that start with a `stream()` / `parallelStream()` call or that the resolver
proves to be `java.util.stream` streams are considered. Not reported: actions that only print
(`System.out::println`, `print`, `printf`) or log (`log.debug(..)`, also behind an
`isDebugEnabled()` test), empty actions, and actions passed as a variable (their body is not
visible).

### java/post-increment-self-assignment

**Variable assigned its own post-increment** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: suspicious, typo

Detects `x = x++;` and `x = x--;`: a variable assigned the value of its own
postfix increment or decrement.

**Why it matters.** A postfix `x++` yields the *old* value and then increments `x`; the
assignment runs last and stores that old value back. The increment is lost, so the statement
does nothing — a counter that never advances, a loop that never ends. The author meant
`x++` or `x = x + 1`.

**How to fix.** Drop the assignment (`x++;`) or write the new value explicitly.

```java
// Noncompliant
retries = retries++;

// Compliant
retries++;
```

`x = ++x` (prefix, which does store the new value) and assignments to a different target are
not reported.

### java/prefer-enum-map

**Enum-keyed map or set that could be an EnumMap or EnumSet** (incubating)
