Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: performance, collections, enum

Detects a new `HashMap` or `TreeMap` whose keys are an enum, and a new `HashSet`
or `TreeSet` of an enum, when the enum is declared in the same file or is a JDK enum
(`TimeUnit`, `DayOfWeek`, …).

**Why it matters.** `EnumMap` and `EnumSet` are built for enum keys: an `EnumMap` is an array
indexed by the constant's ordinal and an `EnumSet` a bit mask, so they use a fraction of the
memory of a hash table, never hash or box anything, and iterate in the enum's declaration
order — the same order a `TreeMap` or `TreeSet` of an enum gives, and a stable one instead of
a `HashMap`'s unspecified order.

**How to fix.** `new EnumMap<>(Color.class)` for a map, `EnumSet.noneOf(Color.class)` for a
set. Note that they reject `null` keys.

```java
// Noncompliant
Map<Color, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
Set<Color> seen = new HashSet<>();

// Compliant
Map<Color, Integer> counts = new EnumMap<>(Color.class);
Set<Color> seen = EnumSet.noneOf(Color.class);
```

Not reported: enums declared in other files (not visible here), `LinkedHashMap` and
`LinkedHashSet` (their order is the insertion order), concurrent maps, a `TreeMap` or
`TreeSet` given a comparator (a custom order), copies of another collection
(`EnumSet.copyOf` rejects an empty collection that is not an `EnumSet`), and anonymous
subclasses.

### java/prefer-try-with-resources

**Resource closed in finally instead of try-with-resources**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: resources, modernization

Detects local variables holding a file or database resource (the kinds tracked by
`resource-not-closed-with-try`: file streams, readers and writers, `Files.newInputStream(…)`
and similar, JDBC connections, statements and result sets) that are closed in a `finally`
block — by `close()` or by a helper such as `closeQuietly(in)` — instead of being declared in a
try-with-resources statement.

**Why it matters.** The `finally` version is correct but fragile: the variable must be declared
outside the `try` (often as `null`), every close needs a null check, an exception thrown by one
`close()` skips the ones after it, and an exception from `close()` replaces the one that caused
the failure. Try-with-resources closes every resource in reverse order on every path and keeps
exceptions from `close()` as suppressed exceptions of the original one.

**How to fix.** Declare the resource in the header of a try-with-resources statement and drop
the `finally` cleanup.

```java
// Noncompliant
PreparedStatement ps = null;
try {
    ps = connection.prepareStatement(sql);
    ps.executeUpdate();
} finally {
    if (ps != null) {
        ps.close();
    }
}

// Compliant
try (PreparedStatement ps = connection.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ps.executeUpdate();
}
```

Not reported: resources that may leave the method (returned, stored in a field or another
variable, passed to a method outside the `finally` block, captured by a lambda or inner class),
variables that sometimes hold something other than a tracked resource (`in = System.in`),
resources that are not closed in a `finally` block at all (a leak, reported by
`resource-not-closed-with-try`), JDBC objects in test code, and a `ResultSet` obtained from a
statement variable (closed together with the statement).

### java/presized-to-array

**Pre-sized array passed to toArray**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: collections, performance

Detects `c.toArray(new T[c.size()])`: a collection converted to an array
through a pre-sized array.

**Why it matters.** Pre-sizing looks like an optimization but isn't one: current JVMs fill an
empty array (`new T[0]`) at least as fast, because the pre-sized array has to be zeroed before
it is overwritten. The pre-sized form also has a race: on a concurrent or synchronized
collection the size can change between `size()` and `toArray(..)`, leaving `null`s at the
end of the result.

**How to fix.** Pass an empty array (or, on Java 11+, the generator form).

```java
// Noncompliant
String[] names = list.toArray(new String[list.size()]);

// Compliant
String[] names = list.toArray(new String[0]);
String[] names = list.toArray(String[]::new);
```

Only the exact pattern is reported — the array sized by `size()` of the same receiver, or a
map view (`m.keySet()`, `m.values()`, `m.entrySet()`) sized by `m.size()` — and not when the
receiver is known not to be a `java.util.Collection` (for a view: when `m` is not known to be a
`java.util.Map`).

### java/print-stack-trace

**printStackTrace() instead of logging**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: logging, error-handling

Detects `e.printStackTrace()` (without arguments) on exceptions.

**Why it matters.** `printStackTrace()` writes to the process's standard error stream: the
output bypasses the logging configuration (levels, formats, destinations, correlation ids), is
often lost entirely in containers and application servers, and can leak internal details to
users of console applications.

**How to fix.** Log the exception through the application's logger, passing the exception
itself so the stack trace is kept — or rethrow it.

```java
// Noncompliant
try { sync(); } catch (IOException e) { e.printStackTrace(); }

// Compliant
try { sync(); } catch (IOException e) { log.error("sync failed", e); }
```

Test code is not checked. The receiver must be a caught exception or have a known `Throwable`
type.

### java/private-constructor-class-not-final

**Class with only private constructors is not final**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: design

Detects classes whose constructors are all `private` but that are not
declared `final`.

**Why it matters.** With only private constructors, no class outside this file can extend it
anyway. Saying so with `final` documents the intent (a utility class, a singleton, a class
built through a factory method), lets tools and readers rely on it, and turns an accidental
nested subclass into a compile error.

**How to fix.** Add `final`.

```java
// Noncompliant
public class Strings {
    private Strings() { }
    public static boolean isBlank(String s) { ... }
}

// Compliant
public final class Strings {
    private Strings() { }
    public static boolean isBlank(String s) { ... }
}
```

Not reported: classes without any explicit constructor, `abstract`, `sealed`, and
`non-sealed` classes, classes with Lombok annotations that may generate constructors or subclasses
(`@Data`, `@Value`, `@Builder`, `@AllArgsConstructor`, … — accessor, `toString` and logger
annotations such as `@Getter` or `@Slf4j` are fine), and classes extended in the same file (by a
nested, local, or anonymous class).

### java/protected-in-final-class

**Protected member in a final class**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: design, visibility

Detects `protected` fields, constructors, methods, and nested types declared
in a `final` class or a record.

**Why it matters.** `protected` means "for subclasses (and the package)". A final class has
no subclasses, so the modifier promises an extension point that cannot exist and confuses
readers about the intended visibility.

**How to fix.** Use `private` or package-private visibility (package-private keeps the access
other classes of the package already have).

```java
// Noncompliant
public final class Invoice {
    protected BigDecimal total;
    protected void recompute() { ... }
}

// Compliant
public final class Invoice {
    private BigDecimal total;
    void recompute() { ... }
}
```

Methods annotated `@Override` are not reported (an override cannot reduce visibility), and
neither are methods of a final class that extends another class, since they may override a
protected method without saying so; `finalize` and `clone` are never reported.

### java/public-instance-field

**Mutable public instance field**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: design, encapsulation

Detects `public` instance fields that are not `final`, in classes.

**Why it matters.** A public mutable field exposes the internal representation of a class:
any caller can change it without the class knowing, so invariants cannot be enforced, the
representation cannot change later without breaking callers, and there is no single place to
add validation, lazy computation, or change notification.

**How to fix.** Make the field `private` and add accessors as needed, make it `final` if it
never changes, or turn the class into a `record` if it is a plain data carrier.

```java
// Noncompliant
public class Range {
    public int low;
    public int high;
}

// Compliant
public record Range(int low, int high) { }
```

Not reported: annotated fields (frameworks such as JUnit's `@Rule` or command-line parsers
require public fields), fields of private, local, or anonymous classes, fields of enums and
records, and files that bind native code through JNA (which maps the public fields of a
`Structure` onto native memory).

### java/public-static-mutable-field

**Mutable public static field**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: design, encapsulation, multi-threading

Detects global state that any code can change: `public static` fields that
are not `final`, `public static final` fields (and interface constants) whose value is still
mutable — a non-empty array, or a mutable JDK collection created in place (`new ArrayList<>()`,
`new HashMap<>()`, `Arrays.asList(..)`) — and public fields of enums that are not `final` (an
enum constant is a single instance shared by the whole program).

**Why it matters.** Such a field is global mutable state: any code anywhere can replace its
value at any time, without synchronization or validation. Bugs caused by it are hard to trace,
the value is not safely published between threads, and tests influence each other through it.

`final` only fixes the reference: `NAMES[0] = null` or `CODES.clear()` still changes what every
other user of the constant sees.

**How to fix.** Make the field `final` if it is a constant; otherwise make it `private` and,
if outside access is really needed, expose it through methods that can validate and
synchronize. For arrays and collections, publish an unmodifiable view or copy (`List.of(..)`,
`Collections.unmodifiableMap(..)`), or keep the array private and return a copy.

```java
// Noncompliant
public static int timeoutMillis = 5_000;

// Compliant
public static final int DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS = 5_000;
private static volatile int timeoutMillis = DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS;
public static void setTimeoutMillis(int t) { timeoutMillis = t; }

// Noncompliant
public static final String[] LEVELS = {"low", "high"};
// Compliant
public static final List<String> LEVELS = List.of("low", "high");
```

Not reported: annotated fields (some frameworks, such as JUnit 4's `@ClassRule`, require
`public static` fields), fields of private, local, or anonymous classes, which are not
visible outside the file anyway, empty arrays (`{}`, `new String[0]`: nothing to change),
and collections whose initializer is not a known mutable JDK collection (`List.of(..)`,
`Collections.unmodifiableList(..)`, a factory method of another class).

### java/random-cast-to-int

**Random fraction cast to an integer** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: numbers, random

Detects `Math.random()`, `Random.nextDouble()` or `Random.nextFloat()` cast
directly to an integer type: `(int) Math.random()`.

**Why it matters.** These methods return a value in `[0, 1)`, which truncates to `0`. The
usual form is `(int) Math.random() * n`: the cast binds tighter than the multiplication, so the
expression is `0 * n` and the "random" number is always zero.

**How to fix.** Scale before casting, or ask for an integer directly.

```java
// Noncompliant
int slot = (int) Math.random() * buckets;

// Compliant
int slot = (int) (Math.random() * buckets);
int other = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(buckets);
```

Only calls whose receiver is `Math`/`StrictMath` or provably a `java.util.Random` are
reported; `nextGaussian()` (which is not bounded by 1) is not.

### java/raw-type

**Raw use of a generic type**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: generics, type-safety

Detects generic JDK types used without type arguments — `List items`,
`new HashMap()`, `Map<String, List> index`, `Class type` — in the types of fields, local
variables, parameters, method results and `new` expressions, and the untyped constants
`Collections.EMPTY_LIST`, `EMPTY_SET` and `EMPTY_MAP`.

**Why it matters.** A raw type switches off the compiler's checks for everything that goes
through it: any object can be added to a raw `List`, and what comes out has to be cast back,
so a wrong element type is only discovered at run time as a `ClassCastException`, far from
the code that inserted it. Raw types exist only for compatibility with code written before
Java 5.

**How to fix.** Give the type arguments (`List<Order>`, `new HashMap<>()`, `Class<?>` when
any class will do), or use `Collections.emptyList()`, `emptySet()`, `emptyMap()`.

```java
// Noncompliant
List names = new ArrayList();
Map<String, List> byCity = new HashMap<>();
return Collections.EMPTY_LIST;

// Compliant
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
Map<String, List<Customer>> byCity = new HashMap<>();
return Collections.emptyList();
```

Off by default: legacy code bases use raw types in large numbers. Not reported: `instanceof`,
class literals and casts (where a raw type is the norm or the point), array types and array
creation (`new List[n]` cannot be parameterized), a raw type argument of a declaration that
passes the matching class literal (`ArgumentCaptor<List> c = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(List.class)`
cannot be written otherwise), supertypes in `extends` / `implements`, parameters and results of methods marked
`@Override` (their signature is dictated by the overridden method), declarations under
`@SuppressWarnings("rawtypes")`, and types other than the JDK's.

### java/record-array-component

**Record with an array component uses identity equality**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: equality, records, arrays

Detects a `record` with an array component (`int[] values`, `String... parts`)
that does not declare both `equals(Object)` and `hashCode()`.

**Why it matters.** The methods a record generates compare each component with `equals`,
and arrays inherit identity equality from `Object`. Two records holding arrays with the same
contents are therefore *not* equal, hash differently, and can't be found in sets or used as
map keys — the opposite of what a value type promises. `toString()` prints the array's
identity (`[I@1b6d3586`) too.

**How to fix.** Override `equals` and `hashCode` (and usually `toString`) with
`Arrays.equals` / `Arrays.hashCode` / `Arrays.toString`, or use an immutable `List`
component instead of an array.

```java
// Noncompliant
record Samples(String name, double[] values) { }

// Compliant
record Samples(String name, List<Double> values) { }
```

Records that declare both `equals` and `hashCode` are not reported.

### java/redundant-annotation-value

**Redundant `value =` in an annotation**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: clutter, annotations

Detects annotations written as `@Anno(value = x)` when `value` is the only
element given.

**Why it matters.** Java lets the element named `value` be passed without its name when it
is the only one. Spelling it out adds noise and makes the usage look different from the
common form readers expect.

**How to fix.** Drop `value =`.

```java
// Noncompliant
@SuppressWarnings(value = "unchecked")
@RequestMapping(value = "/orders")

// Compliant
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
@RequestMapping("/orders")
```

Annotations that set any other element next to `value` are not reported.

### java/redundant-cast

**Cast to the expression's own type**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: clutter, types

Detects a cast to exactly the static type its operand already has: a local
variable, field or parameter cast to its own declared type, a JDK method result cast to the
type the method returns, `(int)` applied to an `int` expression, `(String)` applied to a
string concatenation.

**Why it matters.** Such a cast converts nothing and can never fail, yet it reads as if a
conversion or a runtime check were taking place. It is usually left over from an earlier
version of the code, where the operand had another type (a raw collection, an `Object`
field), and it hides that history: the next reader wonders what it protects against. A
redundant numeric cast also suggests a narrowing that isn't there.

**How to fix.** Remove the cast.

```java
// Noncompliant
List<String> names = catalog.names();
String first = (String) names.get(0);
long total = (long) count * size;   // count is already a long

// Compliant
String first = names.get(0);
long total = count * size;
```

Only casts whose type and operand type the resolver knows completely are considered, down to
the arguments of the calls and the operands of the arithmetic inside the operand (an argument
of unknown type could select another overload). Not
reported: casts that change the type in any way (widening, narrowing, boxing, unboxing, from a
raw to a parameterized type or back), casts of `null`, of lambdas and of method references
(the cast gives them their type), casts to intersection types, and the inner cast of a double
cast (`(List<String>) (List) objects`, a deliberate unchecked conversion).

### java/redundant-close-in-try-with-resources

**Redundant close() of a try-with-resources resource** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: resources, redundant

Detects an explicit `close()` on a resource of a try-with-resources statement
when that call is the last statement of the statement's body.

**Why it matters.** The try-with-resources statement closes each resource as soon as its
body ends, in reverse order, and also when an exception is thrown. The explicit call adds
nothing: the resource is closed twice in a row, which is only harmless when the class makes
`close()` idempotent (`AutoCloseable` does not require it), and it suggests the author did not
trust — or did not notice — the automatic close.

**How to fix.** Remove the call.

```java
// Noncompliant
try (BufferedWriter out = Files.newBufferedWriter(path)) {
    out.write(report);
    out.close();
}

// Compliant
try (BufferedWriter out = Files.newBufferedWriter(path)) {
    out.write(report);
}
```

Not reported: a `close()` followed by other statements of the body — closing early, for
instance to flush a stream before reading what it wrote, has an effect — and bodies that
exercise `close()` itself: a body made only of the call, two calls in a row, or a test method
whose name is about closing (tests of idempotent or delegated closing).

### java/redundant-default-constructor

**Redundant default constructor**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: clutter, redundant

Detects a class whose only constructor takes no arguments, has an empty body
(or just `super();`), and has the same access as the class — exactly the default constructor
the compiler generates when none is written.

**Why it matters.** The constructor is dead weight: it has to be read and scrolled past, and
it looks as if it did something special.

**How to fix.** Delete it.

```java
// Noncompliant
public class Report {
    public Report() {
    }

    public String render() { ... }
}

// Compliant
public class Report {
    public String render() { ... }
}
```

Not reported: constructors with a comment (right before them, inside the body, or at the end of
their last line), which is often kept to explain why they exist — a comment separated from the
constructor by a blank line heads a section and does not count; annotated constructors and
those with a `throws` clause or type parameters; constructors whose access differs from the
class (e.g. a `private` constructor that prevents instantiation; a class declared in an
interface is implicitly `public`); enums and records; and
classes with other constructors. `java/empty-constructor` (off by default) covers empty
constructors in general.

### java/redundant-inheritance-declaration

**Redundant supertype or inherited method declaration**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: redundant, clarity

Detects parts of a type declaration that restate what the type already has:

* `extends Object` (every class extends `Object`);
* an interface in the `implements` (or an interface's `extends`) list that the superclass or
  another listed interface already implements, according to the declarations of this file and
  the JDK: `class Failure extends RuntimeException implements Serializable`,
  `interface Store extends Collection<Item>, List<Item>`, `enum Mode implements Comparable<Mode>`
  (every enum is `Comparable` and `Serializable`);
* an abstract method of an abstract class or an interface that repeats, word for word and
  without documentation, an abstract method of an interface declared in this file that the type
  lists: same name, parameter types, return type and `throws` clause.

**Why it matters.** The repetition adds nothing the compiler does not already know, yet it
makes the declaration look as if it did something: readers check why `Serializable` is listed
again, or whether the repeated method changes the contract. When the superclass later stops
implementing the interface, the stale mention silently keeps it.

**How to fix.** Remove the redundant part.

```java
// Noncompliant
public class Failure extends RuntimeException implements Serializable { … }
public abstract class Job implements Task {
    public abstract void run();   // Task declares: void run();
}

// Compliant
public class Failure extends RuntimeException { … }
public abstract class Job implements Task {
}
```

Not reported: supertypes declared in other files or libraries the resolver does not know (their
hierarchy cannot be checked); an interface that a JDK type gained only in a later release when
the project's Java release is older or unknown (`ExecutorService` is `AutoCloseable` from Java
19: `class Pool extends ThreadPoolExecutor implements AutoCloseable` is needed before); a repeated method that adds Javadoc or a comment, an annotation
other than `@Override`, a narrower return type or a shorter `throws` clause (those change or
document the contract); methods of generic interfaces or generic methods; abstract classes with
a superclass and types that also list an interface of another file (redeclaring the method
abstract can deliberately override an inherited implementation or `default` method); and
methods that another listed interface also declares.

### java/redundant-null-check-before-instanceof

**Redundant null check before instanceof**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: clutter, redundant

Detects a `null` check followed by an `instanceof` test of the same
expression: `x != null && x instanceof T`, and its negated form `x == null || !(x instanceof
T)`.

**Why it matters.** `instanceof` is already `false` for `null` (so its negation is `true`),
so the null check adds nothing but length and suggests the author expected otherwise.

**How to fix.** Drop the null check.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (value != null && value instanceof String s) { use(s); }

// Compliant
if (value instanceof String s) { use(s); }
```

The check is also recognised in a longer chain (`a && x != null && x instanceof T`), also
when other terms stand between the two tests, as long as they have no side effects and don't
mention the tested expression (dropping the null check must not change what they do). The
tested expression may be a variable, a field, an array element, or a chain of argument-less
getters (`e.getCause() != null && e.getCause() instanceof IOException`); other method calls
may return a different value the second time and are not compared.

### java/redundant-parentheses

**Parentheses that group nothing**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions, clutter

Detects parentheses that group nothing:

* around the whole value of a `return`, `throw` or `yield` (`return (count);`,
  `return (a + b);`);
* around a single operand: a name, a literal, a field access, a call, an object creation or an
  array element (`(name).length()`, `total += (price);`, `values[(i)]`);
* doubled parentheses (`((a + b))`, `if ((ready))`).

**Why it matters.** Parentheses tell the reader that grouping matters here. Where there is
nothing to group, the reader looks for the precedence problem they solve and finds none, and
`return (x);` makes `return` look like a function call. Java formatters keep such parentheses,
so they stay until someone removes them.

**How to fix.** Remove the parentheses.

```java
// Noncompliant
return (result);
String label = (name).trim();
if ((enabled)) { … }

// Compliant
return result;
String label = name.trim();
if (enabled) { … }
```

Not reported: parentheses around an operation inside another expression, which may clarify
precedence even where it is not needed (`a + (b * c)`, `(a && b) || c`); a returned
conditional expression or assignment (`return (ok ? a : b);`), which some conventions
parenthesize on purpose; parentheses around a whole condition assigned to a variable
(`boolean empty = (size == 0);`); and parentheses that contain a comment. The rule is off by
default: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

### java/redundant-qualified-this

**Redundant qualified this**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: clutter, redundant

Detects `Name.this` where `Name` is the class the code is directly in, so
`Name.this` and `this` are the same object.

**Why it matters.** A qualified `this` is how inner and anonymous classes reach their
enclosing instance; using it where no such distinction exists sends the reader looking for an
inner class that isn't there.

**How to fix.** Write `this` (or drop it where it isn't needed).

```java
// Noncompliant
class Counter {
    private int count;
    void increment() {
        Counter.this.count++;
    }
}

// Compliant
class Counter {
    private int count;
    void increment() {
        this.count++;
    }
}
```

Inside an inner, local, or anonymous class, `Outer.this` refers to a different object and is
never reported. Lambdas don't introduce a new `this`, so the qualification is redundant there
as well.

### java/redundant-record-member

**Record member that repeats the generated one**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: redundant, record

Detects members of a `record` that repeat what the compiler already generates:

* an accessor that only returns its component (`public String name() { return name; }`);
* a canonical constructor that only assigns each parameter to its field, and a compact
  constructor with an empty body;
* a `serialVersionUID` field: records are serialized through their components, and the
  serialization mechanism does not compare this value for them.

**Why it matters.** The generated members are exactly these. Writing them out adds lines that
look meaningful, so readers search them for the validation, normalization or defensive copy
they expect a hand-written member to contain — and a later change to a component has more
places to update.

**How to fix.** Remove the member.

```java
// Noncompliant
record Point(int x, int y) {
    Point(int x, int y) {
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }
    public int x() { return x; }
}

// Compliant
record Point(int x, int y) { }
```

Not reported: members with annotations other than `@Override` (they may be there for a
framework), members documented with a Javadoc comment, accessors or constructors that do
anything else (normalize, validate, copy), and constructors whose parameters carry
annotations.

### java/redundant-regex-syntax

**Regular expression written the long way**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: regex, clarity

Detects constant regular expressions (given to `Pattern.compile`,
`Pattern.matches`, `String.matches`, `replaceAll`, `replaceFirst`, `split`, or Bean Validation's
`@Pattern`) that contain syntax with a shorter or plainer equivalent:

* a quantifier written with braces where a symbol or nothing says the same: `{1}` (remove it),
  `{0,}` (`*`), `{1,}` (`+`), `{0,1}` (`?`);
* an empty group: `(?:)`, `(?i:)`, `(?>)`, and `()` when the groups of the match cannot be read
  (`matches`, `split`, `@Pattern`, a replacement without `$`);
* a character class holding a single plain character or a single predefined class: `[a]`,
  `[,]`, `[\d]`;
* a member of a character class that another member already covers: `[\w_]`, `[a-z0-9a]`,
  `[\s\n]`;
* an alternation of single characters or predefined classes, which a character class states
  in one step: `a|b|c` is `[abc]`, `\s|,` is `[\s,]`;
* two or more spaces in a row, which are hard to count: ` {3}` states the number;
* a named group whose name is never used: the pattern is only tested (`matches`, `split`,
  `@Pattern`) or the replacement does not refer to `${name}`, and the pattern has no
  `\k<name>`.

**Why it matters.** Regular expressions are dense; every redundant construct is one more thing
the reader must decode and check, and a redundant class member suggests the author expected
it to add something (`[\w_]` reads as if `\w` did not include `_`).

**How to fix.** Use the shorter form shown in the message.

```java
// Noncompliant
String[] words = line.split("[,]|[;]");
boolean ok = code.matches("[A-Z]{1}[\\w_]{0,}");

// Compliant
String[] words = line.split("[,;]");
boolean ok = code.matches("[A-Z]\\w*");
```

Not reported: single-character classes used to quote a metacharacter or a space (`[.]`, `[$]`,
`[ ]`), classes whose repetition is a `|` misread as an alternation (see
`java/regex-suspicious-character-class`), duplicates that only appear under case-insensitive
matching, empty lookarounds (`(?!)` is a deliberate "never matches"), named groups of a pattern
compiled with `Pattern.compile` (the matcher may read them), patterns that are not constant, and
patterns the parser does not model (comments mode, `LITERAL`).

### java/redundant-tostring

**toString() called on a String**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: clutter, strings

Detects `toString()` called on an expression whose type is already `String`.

**Why it matters.** `String.toString()` returns the string itself, so the call is noise that
suggests the author wasn't sure of the type. It also throws on `null`, which a plain reference
wouldn't.

**How to fix.** Remove the call.

```java
// Noncompliant
String name = user.getName().toString();

// Compliant
String name = user.getName();
```

Only receivers whose type is provably `String` are reported.

### java/regex-case-insensitive-non-ascii

**Case-insensitive regex with non-ASCII letters but no Unicode case** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: regex, i18n

Detects a constant regular expression compiled case-insensitively — the
`CASE_INSENSITIVE` flag or inline `(?i)` — without `UNICODE_CASE`, that contains a non-ASCII
letter having another case form (`é`/`É`, `ä`/`Ä`, Cyrillic, Greek…).

**Why it matters.** By default, Java's case-insensitive matching only folds US-ASCII
letters. `Pattern.compile("café", CASE_INSENSITIVE)` matches `CAFé` but not `CAFÉ`, and
`(?i)[а-я]+` does not match capital Cyrillic letters. The pattern looks right and works on
the test data, then misses real input.

**How to fix.** Add `Pattern.UNICODE_CASE` to the flags (`(?iu)` inline), or list both cases
explicitly.

```java
// Noncompliant
Pattern p = Pattern.compile("^straße|münchen$", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE);

// Compliant
Pattern p = Pattern.compile("^straße|münchen$", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE | Pattern.UNICODE_CASE);
```

Not reported: character classes that already list the other case (`[äÄ]`), negated classes,
letters whose other case is several characters (`ß`), and patterns whose flags are not
constant.

### java/regex-compiled-per-call

**Constant regular expression compiled repeatedly**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: performance, regex

Detects a constant regular expression that is compiled again and again:

* `Pattern.compile("…")` or `Pattern.matches("…", input)` with a constant pattern inside a
  method body, so the pattern is compiled on every call;
* `String.matches`, `replaceAll`, `replaceFirst` or `split` with a constant pattern that
  needs the regular-expression engine, inside a loop, so the pattern is compiled on every
  pass.

**Why it matters.** Compiling a pattern parses it and builds a matcher program; for anything
but trivial patterns that costs far more than matching a short string. The `String`
convenience methods hide a `Pattern.compile` on every call. A pattern that never changes can
be compiled once, in a `static final` field, and reused (a compiled `Pattern` is immutable
and safe to share between threads).

**How to fix.** Compile the pattern once into a constant and use it.

```java
// Noncompliant
boolean valid(String code) {
    return Pattern.compile("[A-Z]{3}-\\d{4}").matcher(code).matches();
}
for (String line : lines) {
    String[] cols = line.split("\\s*,\\s*");
}

// Compliant
private static final Pattern CODE = Pattern.compile("[A-Z]{3}-\\d{4}");
private static final Pattern COMMA = Pattern.compile("\\s*,\\s*");
boolean valid(String code) {
    return CODE.matcher(code).matches();
}
for (String line : lines) {
    String[] cols = COMMA.split(line);
}
```

Constant patterns are string literals, concatenations of them and `static final` string
constants of the file. Not reported: patterns built at run time, compilation in field and
static initializers, constructors and `main`, a compiled pattern stored into a field (lazy
initialization), `split` on a single ordinary character or an escaped punctuation character
(`split(",")`, `split("\\|")`, which the JDK handles without the regular-expression engine),
`String` calls outside loops and patterns without any regular-expression syntax (see
`java/replace-all-without-regex`), and test code.

### java/regex-control-escape

**Regex control escape that is not a control character** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: regex

Detects a `\c` control escape in a constant regular expression followed by a
character other than `@`, an upper-case ASCII letter, `[`, `\`, `]`, `^`, `_` or `?`: `\ca`,
`\cz`, `\c1`.

**Why it matters.** Java computes `\cX` by flipping one bit of the next character (`X ^ 64`),
whatever that character is. Only `@`, `A`–`Z` and `[ \ ] ^ _` give the control characters
`\x00`–`\x1F` (and `?` gives DEL); `\ca` is the character `!`, not Ctrl-A, and `\c1` is the
letter `q`. Other regex dialects accept the lower-case form, so the pattern looks right but
looks for a printable character instead of the control character.

**How to fix.** Write the letter in upper case (`\cA`), or use a hexadecimal escape
(`\x01`).

```java
// Noncompliant
Pattern bell = Pattern.compile("\\cg");   // matches an apostrophe (0x67 ^ 0x40), not BEL

// Compliant
Pattern bell = Pattern.compile("\\cG");   // U+0007
Pattern bel2 = Pattern.compile("\\x07");
```

Only constant patterns are checked; text inside `\Q…\E` is literal and ignored.

### java/regex-empty-alternative

**Empty alternative in a regular expression** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: regex

Detects an explicit empty alternative in a constant regular expression:

* two `|` in a row (`a||b`), anywhere: the gap is an alternative that matches the empty
  string;
* a leading or trailing `|` at the top of a pattern that is searched for — `split`,
  `replaceAll` / `replaceFirst` with a non-empty replacement, or `Pattern.compile(..)`
  followed directly by `split`, `matcher(..).find()` and the like (`",|;|"`).

**Why it matters.** A pattern with an empty alternative matches the empty string at every
position. `"a,b".split(",|")` does not split on commas only: it cuts the input between every
pair of characters. `replaceAll("x|", "-")` inserts `-` everywhere. `||` usually comes from
thinking of the logical OR operator.

**How to fix.** Remove the stray `|`; if an optional part was meant, use `?`.

```java
// Noncompliant
String[] parts = line.split(",|;|");
String cleaned = text.replaceAll("\\s||-", "_");

// Compliant
String[] parts = line.split(",|;");
String cleaned = text.replaceAll("\\s|-", "_");
```

Not reported: a leading or trailing empty alternative inside a group (`(a|)`, an optional
part), in a pattern matched as a whole (`matches`, `@Pattern`), or in a `replaceAll` whose
replacement is the empty string (the extra empty matches then change nothing).

### java/regex-lazy-quantifier-at-end

**Lazy quantifier at the end of a searched regular expression** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: regex

Detects a lazy quantifier (`*?`, `+?`, `??`, `{n,m}?`) at the very end of a
constant regular expression that is searched for in the input — `split`, `replaceAll`,
`replaceFirst`, or `Pattern.compile(..)` followed directly by `matcher(..).find()`, `split`
and the like: `"<!--.*?"`, `"key=\\w+?"`.

**Why it matters.** A lazy quantifier takes as few repetitions as it can and only takes more
when what follows it fails to match. At the end of a searched pattern nothing follows, so it
always stops at its minimum: `.*?` matches nothing, `\w+?` exactly one character, `{2,5}?`
exactly two. The pattern looks as if it captures "the rest", but it never does; usually the
part that should end the match (`-->`, a delimiter, `$`) was forgotten.

**How to fix.** Write what ends the match after the quantifier (`<!--.*?-->`), or make the
quantifier greedy if the longest run was meant.

```java
// Noncompliant
String plain = html.replaceAll("<!--.*?", "");   // removes only "<!--"

// Compliant
String plain = html.replaceAll("<!--.*?-->", "");
```

Not reported: patterns matched as a whole (`matches`, `@Pattern`), where the end of the input
forces the quantifier to go on, and compiled patterns whose use is not visible at the
`compile` call.

### java/regex-never-matches

**Regular expression part that can never match** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: regex

Detects a constant regular expression — passed to `Pattern.compile`,
`Pattern.matches`, `String.matches` / `replaceAll` / `replaceFirst` / `split`, or given to a
Bean Validation `@Pattern` — containing a part that can never match:

* an anchor in a place it cannot hold: `^` or `\A` after text that must already have been
  matched (`a^b`), `$` followed by a character that is not a line break (`$abc`), `\z`
  followed by more text;
* a word boundary between two characters of the same kind (`\w\b\w`, `,\b `), or `\B`
  between a word and a non-word character;
* a lookaround contradicting its surroundings: `(?=\d)[a-z]`, `(?!a)a`, `a(?<=b)`;
* a back-reference to a group that does not exist (`(a)\2`) or that cannot have matched yet
  (`\1(a)`, `(a)|\1`, `(a\1)`);
* an unbounded possessive repetition followed by a character it would have taken (`\d++\d`,
  `[a-z]*+s`): it keeps every such character and never gives one back;
* a `\b` written in the Java string (`"\bword"`): that is a backspace character, not a word
  boundary.

**Why it matters.** The pattern compiles, so nothing fails loudly: the branch or the whole
pattern simply never matches, and the code silently takes the "no match" path — validation
that rejects everything, a `split` that never splits, a `replaceAll` that changes nothing.

**How to fix.** Move the anchor to where it can hold (or enable `MULTILINE` if line
anchors were meant), fix the lookaround or the group number, and write `\\b` in Java
strings for a word boundary.

```java
// Noncompliant
Pattern.compile("^\\d+^");          // the second ^ can never match
Pattern.compile("\\d+$px");         // $ followed by more text
line.matches("\\bid\\b=(\\d+)\\2"); // there is no group 2

// Compliant
Pattern.compile("^\\d+$");
Pattern.compile("\\d+px$");
line.matches("\\bid\\b=(\\d+)");
```

Only constant patterns are checked (string literals, possibly concatenated). Case-insensitive
and Unicode-class modes are taken into account; patterns using comments mode, `LITERAL`,
`CANON_EQ`, or constructs the checker does not model are skipped, as are syntax errors (see
`java/invalid-regex-literal`).

### java/regex-shadowed-alternative

**Regular expression alternative that is never used** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: regex

Detects an alternative of a constant regular expression that can never be
chosen:

* an exact duplicate of an earlier alternative of the same alternation (`jpg|png|jpg`);
* where the pattern is searched for (`split`, `replaceAll`, `replaceFirst`, or a compiled
  pattern used right away with `split` / `matcher(..).find()`), a literal alternative that
  starts with an earlier literal alternative, when nothing follows the alternation
  (`",|, "`): Java tries alternatives from left to right and stops at the first that matches,
  so the shorter one always wins.

**Why it matters.** The longer alternative was written for a reason — to also consume the
space after a comma, to replace a whole word — and it silently never takes effect:
`"a, b".split(",|, ")` leaves a leading space on `" b"`. A duplicate alternative is dead
code that usually hides a typo in the one that was meant.

**How to fix.** Put longer alternatives first (`", |,"`), or make the difference optional
(`",\\s?"`); remove duplicates.

```java
// Noncompliant
String[] parts = line.split(";|;\\s");
String out = text.replaceAll("cat|dog|cat", "pet");

// Compliant
String[] parts = line.split(";\\s|;");
String out = text.replaceAll("cat|dog", "pet");
```

Not reported: prefix-shadowed alternatives in patterns matched as a whole (`matches`,
`@Pattern`: when the short alternative leaves input unmatched, Java backtracks into the
longer one) or followed by more pattern (`(a|ab)c`); duplicates involving capturing groups,
back-references or inline flags, whose meaning can differ between the copies.

### java/regex-stack-overflow-risk

**Repeated alternation that can overflow the stack** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: regex, performance

Detects a constant regular expression that repeats, without an upper
bound, a group alternating between single characters: `(a|b)*`, `(?:\s|,)+`, and the classic
"anything including newlines" `(.|\n)*`.

**Why it matters.** `java.util.regex` is a backtracking matcher. A repeated group containing
an alternation is matched recursively, one level of Java stack per iteration, so the depth
grows with the length of the input. Input of a few thousand characters — a large text field,
a file, a request body — throws `StackOverflowError`, which is usually not caught and kills
the thread. A character class matches the same text iteratively.

**How to fix.** Replace the alternation with a character class (`[ab]*`, `[\s,]+`), use
`[\s\S]*` or the `DOTALL` flag for "anything", or make the repetition possessive (`*+`) when
backtracking into it is not needed.

```java
// Noncompliant
Pattern block = Pattern.compile("BEGIN(.|\\n)*END");
boolean ok = code.matches("(\\d|-)+");

// Compliant
Pattern block = Pattern.compile("BEGIN.*END", Pattern.DOTALL);
boolean ok = code.matches("[\\d-]+");
```

Not reported: bounded repetitions (`{1,5}`), possessive ones, and alternations with longer
alternatives (`(ab|cd)*`), which cannot become a character class.

### java/regex-suspicious-character-class

**Suspicious character class in a regular expression** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: regex

Detects character classes of constant regular expressions that match
something else than they appear to:

* a range from an upper-case to a lower-case letter, or from a digit to a letter (`[A-z]`,
  `[0-z]`): it also covers the ASCII punctuation in between (`[`, `\`, `]`, `^`, `_`, the
  backtick; `:` to `@`);
* a letter followed by a combining mark (`é` written as `e` + U+0301, an emoji with a
  modifier): the class holds two separate members, each matched on its own;
* `|` used as if it separated alternatives, with repeated characters (`[jpg|png]`): in a
  class `|` is an ordinary character and the class matches one character.

**Why it matters.** The pattern accepts input it should reject (`[A-z]+` accepts `_^[]`,
`[jpg|png]` accepts a lone `p` or `|`) or splits a user-perceived character in two.

**How to fix.** Write the ranges separately (`[A-Za-z]`), use a group for alternatives
(`(?:jpg|png)`), and put multi-code-point characters in an alternation instead of a class.

```java
// Noncompliant
boolean ok = name.matches("[A-z0-9]+");
Pattern images = Pattern.compile(".*\\.[jpg|png]");

// Compliant
boolean ok = name.matches("[A-Za-z0-9]+");
Pattern images = Pattern.compile(".*\\.(?:jpg|png)");
```

Not reported: classes with nesting or intersections (`[a-z&&[^e]]`), ranges between
punctuation characters (`[!-~]`), and a single `|` among distinct characters (`[|,;]`),
which is a legitimate way to list separators.

### java/regex-too-complex

**Regular expression too complex** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: regex, complexity

Detects a constant regular expression — passed to `Pattern.compile`,
`Pattern.matches`, `String.matches`, `replaceAll`, `replaceFirst`, `split` or Bean Validation's
`@Pattern(regexp = …)` — whose structure scores above a threshold (`max`, 20 by default).

The score uses the same scale as `js/regex-too-complex`. Each of the following adds one point
plus one per level of group nesting around it: an alternative after the first (a list of plain
words such as `(GET|PUT|POST)` counts as one alternative), a variable repetition of a group
(`(…)*`, `(…)?`) and a lookaround. A variable repetition of a single character, class or
escape (`\s+`, `[0-9]*`), a character class and a back-reference add one point each. Fixed
repetitions (`\d{4}`), literal characters, escapes and anchors are free, so a long but flat
pattern scores low while nested alternations of repeated groups score high.

**Why it matters.** A regular expression has no names, comments or structure to guide the
reader: every nested group and alternative multiplies the cases to keep in mind. Complex
patterns are where subtle mistakes hide (an alternative that never matches, a quantifier that
backtracks for seconds on long input), and they are the part of the code people least dare to
change.

**How to fix.** Split the pattern into several simpler checks, build it from named constants
(`String DATE = "\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}";`), use comments mode (`Pattern.COMMENTS`) to lay it out
with explanations, or replace it with a small parser.

```java
// Noncompliant
Pattern.compile("^(?:(?:25[0-5]|2[0-4]\\d|1\\d\\d|[1-9]?\\d)\\.){3}(?:25[0-5]|2[0-4]\\d|1\\d\\d|[1-9]?\\d)$");

// Compliant
private static final String OCTET = "(?:25[0-5]|2[0-4]\\d|1\\d\\d|[1-9]?\\d)";
Pattern.compile("^" + OCTET + "(?:\\." + OCTET + "){3}$");
```

The compliant form builds the same pattern, and is still reported when its total score is
above the threshold: split it into separate checks, or raise `max`, when the parts are named.
Not reported: patterns built at run time, patterns compiled with `Pattern.COMMENTS` (they are
already laid out for reading) or `LITERAL`, and patterns the parser does not model.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max` | `20` | Highest complexity score accepted for one regular expression. |

### java/replace-all-without-regex

**replaceAll() with a plain-text pattern**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: regex, performance, clarity

Detects `String.replaceAll(pattern, replacement)` where the pattern is a string
literal without any regular-expression metacharacter and the replacement is a literal
without `$` or `\`.

**Why it matters.** `replaceAll` compiles its first argument as a regular expression on
every call and interprets `$` and `\` in the replacement. When the pattern is plain text,
`replace(..)` does exactly the same replacement (all occurrences) without the compilation
cost — and states the intent clearly. Readers of `replaceAll` must otherwise check whether
some character in the pattern is special.

**How to fix.** Call `replace(..)`.

```java
// Noncompliant
String csv = line.replaceAll(";", ",");

// Compliant
String csv = line.replace(";", ",");
```

Patterns containing any of `\ ^ $ . | ? * + ( ) [ ] { }`, empty patterns, and non-literal
replacements are not reported.

### java/resource-not-closed-with-try

**Resource not closed with try-with-resources**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: resources, leak

Detects local variables that open a file or database resource —
`new FileInputStream/FileOutputStream/FileReader/FileWriter/RandomAccessFile/ZipFile(…)`,
`new FileImageOutputStream(…)`, a JDK decorator (`BufferedReader`, `OutputStreamWriter`,
`BufferedInputStream`, `ZipOutputStream`, `DataOutputStream`, …) over a newly opened file,
`new Scanner(File|Path)`, `getResourceAsStream(…)` on a `Class` or `ClassLoader`,
`Files.newInputStream/newOutputStream/newBufferedReader/newBufferedWriter/lines/list/walk(…)`,
or a `Connection`/`Statement`/`ResultSet` obtained from `getConnection`, `prepareStatement`,
`prepareCall`, `createStatement`, `executeQuery`, or a `DatabaseMetaData` query such as
`getTables` — when the variable is not managed by a try-with-resources statement and is not
closed in a `finally` block. A variable declared as `null` (or without a value) and assigned the resource
later (`in = null; … in = new FileInputStream(f);`) is checked the same way. Resources closed in a
`finally` block are closed on every path and not reported here; `prefer-try-with-resources`
suggests converting them.

**Why it matters.** If any statement between opening and `close()` throws, the close is skipped
and the file handle or connection leaks. Leaks accumulate until the process runs out of file
descriptors or the connection pool is exhausted.

**How to fix.** Declare the resource in a try-with-resources header; it is closed on every
path, including exceptions.

```java
// Noncompliant
BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(path));
String first = in.readLine();
in.close();

// Compliant
try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(path))) {
    String first = in.readLine();
}
```

To stay precise, the rule is silent when ownership may move elsewhere: the variable is
returned (or an object derived from it is, as in `return stmt.executeQuery(sql)`), assigned to
another variable or field, passed as an argument (e.g. wrapped by another stream or closed by a
helper) — unless the method itself closes it afterwards, outside a `finally` block, which shows
it kept the ownership (a close only in a `catch` block does not show that) — or captured by a
lambda or inner class. JDBC results are only considered when the
variable's declared type is a known `java.sql` type (not `var`), and not in test code (where
they are usually mocks). A `ResultSet` obtained from a statement variable is closed with that
statement, so only the statement is checked. Wrappers over non-file streams (`System.in`,
`StringReader`, a servlet writer) are ignored.

Also not reported:

* A connection lent by an object that manages its lifecycle. `getConnection()` counts as
  opening a connection only on `DriverManager` or on a data source (a receiver whose static
  type is a `javax.sql.DataSource` or a class named `…DataSource`). A connection taken from a
  transaction, session or unit-of-work object, from a statement, from a static helper such
  as `DataSourceUtils.getConnection(ds)`, or from a receiver of unknown type belongs to that
  owner, and closing it would be the bug.
* A resource whose `close()` is the very next statement (`Connection c = ds.getConnection();
  c.close();`, also behind `if (c != null)`): nothing can throw in between.
* A statement or result set created from a connection variable (`conn.prepareStatement(..)`,
  `conn.createStatement().executeQuery(..)`, `conn.getMetaData().getTables(..)`) when that
  connection is closed on the failure path: it is a try-with-resources resource of an
  enclosing `try`, or a `catch` or `finally` clause of an enclosing `try` closes it
  (`conn.close()` or a `close…(conn)` helper). Closing a connection closes its statements and
  result sets.

### java/restricted-identifier

**Identifier restricted in newer Java releases** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: portability, java-upgrade

Detects names that later Java releases restrict, used in a position where
the newer compiler rejects them:

* a class, interface, enum, record, annotation type or type parameter named `var` (restricted
  from Java 10), `yield` (Java 14), `record` (Java 16), `sealed` or `permits` (Java 17);
* an unqualified call of a method named `yield` (`yield()`, `yield(x)`): from Java 14 the
  compiler reads it as a `yield` statement;
* `_` as a variable or parameter name in code compiled for Java 8 or older (an error from
  Java 9 on).

**Why it matters.** The code compiles today and stops compiling when the project moves to a
newer Java release, so the upgrade starts with renaming work in unexpected places (and in
public types, for every caller).

**How to fix.** Rename the type or type parameter; qualify the call (`this.yield()`,
`Thread.yield()`); give the variable a real name.

```java
// Noncompliant
class record { … }
public void run() { yield(); }

// Compliant
class Record { … }
public void run() { Thread.yield(); }
```

Findings depend on the Java release the file is compiled for (from `java.release` in the
configuration, or the build file): a name is only reported when the release is older than the
one that restricts it, or unknown. `_` is only reported when the release is known to be 8 or
older, because Java 22 gave it a new, valid meaning (an unnamed variable). Variables, fields
and methods named `var`, `yield`, `record`, `sealed` or `permits` are not reported: they
remain legal.

### java/return-in-finally

**Jump out of a finally block**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: error-handling, control-flow

Detects `return`, `throw`, `break`, and `continue` statements that leave a
`finally` block.

**Why it matters.** When control jumps out of a `finally` block, whatever the `try` block was
doing is silently discarded: an exception in flight disappears, and a value already being
returned is replaced. Failures become invisible and results surprising.

**How to fix.** Let the `finally` block complete normally; move the `return`/`throw` after the
`try` statement or into the `try`/`catch` blocks.

```java
// Noncompliant
try {
    return compute();
} finally {
    return -1;          // hides any exception from compute()
}

// Compliant
int result;
try {
    result = compute();
} finally {
    cleanup();
}
return result;
```

Jumps that stay inside the `finally` block (a `break` of a loop inside it, a `return` inside a
lambda or anonymous class declared there, a `throw` caught within it) are not reported.

### java/reversed-compound-assignment

**Compound assignment operator typed backwards** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: suspicious, typo

Detects assignments written `x =+ y`, `x =- y`, or `x =! y`: the `=` is glued
to a unary `+`, `-` or `!` while a space separates that sign from its operand.

**Why it matters.** Java reads `x =+ 5` as `x = +5` and `x =- 5` as `x = -5`, so the
variable is overwritten instead of incremented or decremented. `done =! ok` is `done = !ok`,
probably meant as the comparison `done != ok`. The code compiles, and the spacing makes the
typo easy to read past.

**How to fix.** Swap the characters (`+=`, `-=`, `!=`), or, if a plain assignment of a
negated value was intended, put the space after the `=`.

```java
// Noncompliant
total =+ price;
remaining =- 1;

// Compliant
total += price;
remaining -= 1;
offset = -1;
```

Only the typo-shaped spacing is reported (space before `=`, none between `=` and the sign,
space after the sign); `x = -1`, `x=-1` and `x = +y` are left alone.

### java/scheduled-pool-without-core-threads

**Scheduled executor without core threads** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: concurrency, executors

Detects scheduled executors configured with a core pool size of 0:
`Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(0)`, `new ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor(0, …)`, and
`setCorePoolSize(0)` on a `ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor`.

**Why it matters.** A `ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor` is a fixed-size pool: its maximum size
has no effect, and it only keeps core threads alive while waiting for delayed tasks. With no
core thread, the pool falls back on a temporary worker that keeps timing out while it waits
for the next due task: on Java 8 this spins a CPU at 100% (a known JDK bug), on later versions
the worker still wakes up every few milliseconds, and the class documentation warns that the
pool may be left without a thread to run tasks once they become due. It is never what the
author wanted from "an idle pool".

**How to fix.** Use at least one core thread (the pool never grows beyond the core size
anyway).

```java
// Noncompliant
ScheduledExecutorService timer = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(0);

// Compliant
ScheduledExecutorService timer = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor();
```

Only the literal `0` is reported, and not a `setCorePoolSize(0)` on a pool that the same method
has already shut down (`pool.shutdown(); pool.setCorePoolSize(0);` is teardown that lets idle
threads exit, not a live pool).

### java/self-assignment

**Variable assigned to itself**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, typo

Detects assignments whose target and value are the same expression: `x = x;`,
`this.x = this.x;`, `a[i] = a[i];`.

**Why it matters.** Such a statement does nothing. It almost always hides a typo: the classic
case is a constructor or setter whose parameter has the same name as the field, where
`value = value;` assigns the parameter to itself and leaves the field untouched.

**How to fix.** Assign what was meant (usually `this.value = value;`) or delete the statement.

```java
// Noncompliant
Point(int x) {
    x = x;              // the field keeps its default value
}

// Compliant
Point(int x) {
    this.x = x;
}
```

`this.x = x` is not reported when `x` is a parameter or local (it assigns that value to the
field); it is reported when no such variable is in scope, so `x` is the field itself — usually a
misspelled parameter (`void setLimit(int limt) { this.limit = limit; }`). Targets with side
effects (`a[i++] = a[i++]`, calls) are not reported.

### java/self-comparing-assertion

**Assertion compares a value with itself**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: tests, suspicious, copy-paste

Detects test assertions whose expected and actual values are the same
expression:

* `assertSame(a, a)` / `assertNotSame(a, a)` (any type);
* `assertEquals(x, x)`, `assertNotEquals(x, x)`, `assertArrayEquals(x, x)` when `x` is a
  primitive, a boxed number, a `String`, an enum or an array — types whose equality is fixed by
  the JDK;
* AssertJ-style `assertThat(x).isEqualTo(x)` / `isSameAs(x)` / `isNotEqualTo(x)` /
  `isNotSameAs(x)`.

**Why it matters.** The assertion cannot fail (or cannot pass), whatever the code under test
does: the test silently checks nothing. It usually comes from copying a line and forgetting to
change one side (`assertEquals(expected.getId(), expected.getId())`-style slips are common).

**How to fix.** Compare the value produced by the code under test with the expected one.

```java
// Noncompliant
assertEquals(expectedTotal, expectedTotal);

// Compliant
assertEquals(expectedTotal, invoice.total());
```

Not reported: arguments that contain calls or `new` (two calls may return different values,
which some tests check deliberately), literals, and `assertEquals(obj, obj)` on other types,
which exercises the reflexivity of a custom `equals`.

### java/separator-used-as-regex

**Separator text passed as a regular expression** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: regex, strings, portability

Detects text meant literally that is passed to a method taking a regular
expression:

* `s.split(".")` and `s.split("|")` on a `String`;
* `File.separator` as the pattern of `split`, `replaceAll`, `replaceFirst`, `matches`, or
  `Pattern.compile`.

**Why it matters.** `String.split` takes a regex. `"."` matches every character, so
`"a.b".split(".")` returns an **empty** array; `"|"` is an empty alternation that matches
between all characters, so the string is cut into single characters. `File.separator` is
`"\"` on Windows — a dangling escape that makes the call throw `PatternSyntaxException`
there, while it works on Linux and macOS.

**How to fix.** Escape the character, or quote the text.

```java
// Noncompliant
String[] parts = version.split(".");
String[] dirs = path.split(File.separator);

// Compliant
String[] parts = version.split("\\.");
String[] dirs = path.split(Pattern.quote(File.separator));
```

Only `String` receivers the resolver proves are checked. `replaceAll(".", "*")` (masking
every character) is deliberate and not reported.

### java/serialization-constructor-missing

**Serializable class that cannot be deserialized** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: serialization

Detects classes that Java serialization can write but not read back:

- a class implementing `Externalizable` without a `public` constructor taking no arguments
  (also when the only constructor is the implicit one of a non-public class);
- a class implementing `Serializable` whose superclass, declared in the same file, is not
  serializable and has no non-private constructor taking no arguments.

**Why it matters.** Deserialization re-creates the object before restoring its state. For an
`Externalizable` it calls the public no-argument constructor, then `readExternal`. For a
`Serializable` class it runs the no-argument constructor of the first non-serializable
superclass. When that constructor is missing or inaccessible, writing works, and every read
fails with `InvalidClassException: no valid constructor`: the problem shows only when the
stored data is needed.

**How to fix.** Add the constructor (`public Foo() {}` for an `Externalizable`, an accessible
no-argument constructor in the non-serializable superclass), or make the superclass
serializable.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Session implements Externalizable {
    Session(String id) { … }                 // no public no-arg constructor
    …
}

// Compliant
public class Session implements Externalizable {
    public Session() { }
    Session(String id) { … }
    …
}
```

Abstract classes are not checked, and the superclass case is reported only when the superclass
is declared in the same file without a superclass or interfaces of its own (it provably isn't
serializable).

### java/serialization-hook-signature

**Serialization hook with an ignored signature** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: serialization

Detects serialization hooks of a `Serializable` class whose declaration makes
Java serialization skip them:

* `writeObject(ObjectOutputStream)`, `readObject(ObjectInputStream)` and `readObjectNoData()`
  that are not `private`, are `static`, or don't return `void`;
* `readResolve()` and `writeReplace()` that are `static` or whose return type is not
  `Object`;
* `writeObject`, `readObject` and `readObjectNoData` declared in a record, where
  serialization never calls them.

**Why it matters.** Serialization finds these methods by reflection, by exact signature. A
hook with the wrong modifiers or return type is not an error — it is silently ignored. Custom
state is then neither written nor restored, validation in `readObject` never runs, and a
singleton's `readResolve` no longer protects it from duplication.

**How to fix.** Use the exact signatures:
`private void writeObject(ObjectOutputStream out) throws IOException`,
`private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException`,
`Object readResolve() throws ObjectStreamException` (any access).

```java
// Noncompliant
public void readObject(ObjectInputStream in) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException { … }
private Config readResolve() { return INSTANCE; }

// Compliant
private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException { … }
private Object readResolve() { return INSTANCE; }
```

Only classes and records the resolver proves `Serializable` are checked; enums (whose
serialization ignores all these hooks) and `Externalizable` classes are skipped.

### java/shift-out-of-range

**Shift distance out of range** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: numbers, bitwise

Detects shifts (`<<`, `>>`, `>>>`, and their compound assignments) by a constant
distance that is negative or not smaller than the width of the shifted value: 32 for `int`
(and `short`, `byte`, `char`, which are promoted to `int`), 64 for `long`.

**Why it matters.** Java uses only the low 5 (or 6) bits of the distance: `x << 32` on an
`int` shifts by 0 and returns `x` unchanged, `1 << 40` is `256`, and `x >> -1` shifts by 31.
The author expected the bits to move out (or a 64-bit result) and gets something else,
silently.

**How to fix.** Shift a `long` when more than 32 bits are needed (`1L << 40`), or correct the
distance.

```java
// Noncompliant
long mask = 1 << 40;
int high = value >>> 32;

// Compliant
long mask = 1L << 40;
long high = longValue >>> 32;
```

Only constant distances are checked, and only when the type of the shifted value is known.

### java/simplifiable-boolean-if-else

**if/else that only differs in a boolean literal**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: readability, redundant

Detects an `if`/`else` whose two branches make the same call, or the same
assignment, and differ only in a `true` / `false` literal: `if (c) button.setEnabled(true);
else button.setEnabled(false);`.

**Why it matters.** The condition already is the boolean being passed. Spelling out both
values doubles the code, hides that the two branches are really one statement, and invites
the branches to drift apart when one of them is edited later.

**How to fix.** Pass (or assign) the condition itself, negated with `!` when the `true` sits in
the `else` branch.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (rows.isEmpty()) {
    exportButton.setEnabled(false);
} else {
    exportButton.setEnabled(true);
}
if (limit > 0) {
    limited = true;
} else {
    limited = false;
}

// Compliant
exportButton.setEnabled(!rows.isEmpty());
limited = limit > 0;
```

Each branch must hold exactly one statement (no comment either). Only calls whose receiver and
other arguments are plain names, field reads, or literals are reported: moving the condition
into the argument list evaluates it after them, which only makes no difference when they have no
side effects. Not reported either: `else if` chains ending in another `if`, compound
assignments, and conditions of type `Boolean` (passing the object would hand a `null` on
instead of failing).

### java/simplifiable-boolean-return

**Boolean return wrapped in an if statement**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: readability, redundant

Detects an `if` statement that returns `true` in one branch and `false` in the
other — either with an `else`, or with the second `return` directly after the `if`.

**Why it matters.** The condition already is the boolean being returned. Wrapping it in an
`if` turns one line into four and makes readers check both branches to understand a simple
expression.

**How to fix.** Return the condition (negated with `!` when the branches are inverted).

```java
// Noncompliant
if (list.isEmpty()) {
    return true;
} else {
    return false;
}

// Compliant
return list.isEmpty();
```

Not reported: the last `if` of a chain of guards that all return the same value
(`if (a != o.a) return false; if (b != o.b) return false; return true;`, typical of
`equals`), where keeping the parallel structure is clearer. Local variable declarations between
the guards (`Point p = (Point) o;`) do not break the chain, and an `if`/`else if` whose
branches all return that value (or hold nothing but such guards) counts as a guard as well.
After a guard returning the
opposite value (`if (x == null) return false; if (x.isEmpty()) return true; return false;`)
the last `if` is reported: `return x.isEmpty();` says the same in one line.

### java/simplifiable-stream

**Stream pipeline with a shorter built-in form**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: streams, idiom

Detects stream pipelines written the long way when the stream API (or the
collection itself) has an operation that says it directly:

* `filter(p).findFirst().isPresent()` or `filter(p).findAny().isPresent()` is `anyMatch(p)`;
  with `isEmpty()` it is `noneMatch(p)`;
* `filter(p).count() > 0` (or `!= 0`, `>= 1`) is `anyMatch(p)`; `filter(p).count() == 0`
  is `noneMatch(p)`;
* `collect(Collectors.counting())` is `count()`;
* `collection.stream().forEach(action)` is `collection.forEach(action)`;
* `forEach(list::add)` (or `forEach(x -> list.add(x))`) into a collection created empty by the
  statement just before is `collect(Collectors.toList())` (`toSet()` for a set).

**Why it matters.** The dedicated operation names the intent — "is there a match?", "how
many?", "gather them" — instead of making the reader reconstruct it from a sequence of steps.
It is also cheaper: `anyMatch` and `noneMatch` stop at the first element that decides the
answer, while `count()` visits every element; `findFirst` must also respect the encounter
order, which parallel streams pay for.

**How to fix.** Use the shorter form.

```java
// Noncompliant
boolean late = orders.stream().filter(Order::isLate).findFirst().isPresent();
if (users.stream().filter(User::isAdmin).count() > 0) { … }
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
users.stream().map(User::name).forEach(names::add);

// Compliant
boolean late = orders.stream().anyMatch(Order::isLate);
if (users.stream().anyMatch(User::isAdmin)) { … }
List<String> names = users.stream().map(User::name).collect(Collectors.toList());
```

Only pipelines the resolver proves to be `java.util.stream` streams (or that start with a
`stream()` call) are considered. Not reported: `parallelStream().forEach(…)` (deliberately
parallel), `count()` compared with anything other than 0 or 1, collections that already hold
elements, are used between their creation and the `forEach`, or are declared with a concrete
type (`ArrayList<String> names`, which a collector's `List` cannot be assigned to), and `collect(toList())` that
could be `toList()`: the latter returns an unmodifiable list, which is only equivalent when
nothing modifies the result.

### java/simplifiable-ternary

**Conditional expression with a boolean literal branch**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: clutter, readability

Detects conditional expressions with one boolean-literal branch and one boolean
branch, which are just `&&` / `||` in disguise:

| Conditional       | Same as      |
|-------------------|--------------|
| `c ? true : x`    | `c \|\| x`   |
| `c ? false : x`   | `!c && x`    |
| `c ? x : true`    | `!c \|\| x`  |
| `c ? x : false`   | `c && x`     |

**Why it matters.** The logical operators say what is meant in fewer symbols; a conditional
with a literal branch makes readers evaluate both paths in their head.

**How to fix.** Rewrite with `&&` / `||` (negating the condition where needed).

```java
// Noncompliant
boolean visible = isAdmin ? true : item.isPublic();

// Compliant
boolean visible = isAdmin || item.isPublic();
```

The other branch must be known to be boolean: a comparison, a logical expression, a
`boolean`/`Boolean` value, or any expression when the context needs a `boolean` (the conditional
initializes or is assigned to a `boolean` variable, is returned from a method declared
`boolean`, or is an operand of `&&`, `||` or `!`), since only a boolean branch compiles there.
`c ? true : false` is reported by `java/boolean-literal-comparison` instead.

### java/sleep-in-synchronized

**Thread.sleep while holding a lock** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading, performance

Detects `Thread.sleep(..)` (and `TimeUnit.X.sleep(..)`) called inside a
`synchronized` block or a `synchronized` method.

**Why it matters.** Sleeping does not release monitors. Every other thread that needs the same
lock — often every caller of the object — is blocked for the whole sleep, turning a pause in
one thread into a stall of the application, and making deadlocks more likely when the sleeper
waits for another thread to make progress.

**How to fix.** Sleep outside the synchronized region, or wait on the monitor with a timeout
(`lock.wait(millis)` releases it while waiting), or use a `ScheduledExecutorService` for
delayed work.

```java
// Noncompliant
synchronized (queue) {
    while (queue.isEmpty()) {
        Thread.sleep(100);
    }
}

// Compliant
synchronized (queue) {
    while (queue.isEmpty()) {
        queue.wait(100);
    }
}
```

Test code (which sometimes holds a lock on purpose to provoke contention) and sleeps inside
lambdas or anonymous classes declared in the synchronized region (they run later, elsewhere)
are not reported.

### java/sleep-in-test

**Thread.sleep in a test**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: tests, flaky

Detects `Thread.sleep(…)` (and `TimeUnit.X.sleep(…)`) in test code.

**Why it matters.** A fixed sleep is a guess about how long something takes. Too short and the
test fails randomly on a slow or busy CI machine; too long and the whole suite gets slower with
every such wait. Either way the test doesn't state what it is actually waiting for.

**How to fix.** Wait for the condition itself: join the thread, wait on a `CountDownLatch` or
`Future` with a timeout, poll with a deadline (for example with Awaitility), or inject a
controllable clock so no real time has to pass.

```java
// Noncompliant
service.startAsync();
Thread.sleep(2000);
assertTrue(service.isRunning());

// Compliant
service.startAsync();
service.awaitRunning(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
assertTrue(service.isRunning());
```

Only test files are checked.

### java/soft-assertions-not-verified

**Soft assertions never verified** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: tests, assertj

Detects a local `SoftAssertions` (or `BDDSoftAssertions`) created with `new`
whose `assertAll()` is never called in the method.

**Why it matters.** Soft assertions do not throw when a check fails: they record the failure
and report all of them together when `assertAll()` is called. Without that call nothing is
ever reported, so every check made through the object passes, whatever the values.

**How to fix.** Call `assertAll()` at the end of the test, or let AssertJ do it: use
`SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(softly -> { … })`, an `AutoCloseableSoftAssertions` in a
try-with-resources statement, or the JUnit 5 `SoftAssertionsExtension`.

```java
// Noncompliant
SoftAssertions softly = new SoftAssertions();
softly.assertThat(user.name()).isEqualTo("Ada");
softly.assertThat(user.age()).isEqualTo(36);

// Compliant
SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(softly -> {
    softly.assertThat(user.name()).isEqualTo("Ada");
    softly.assertThat(user.age()).isEqualTo(36);
});
```

Not reported: objects whose collected failures are read instead
(`softly.assertionErrorsCollected()`, `errorsCollected()`, `wasSuccess()`: the test checks
them itself), objects passed to another method, returned, or stored in a field (the call may
happen elsewhere), and `AutoCloseableSoftAssertions`, which verifies itself when closed.

### java/split-declaration

**Declaration separated from its first assignment**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions, readability
