Detects a local variable declared without a value whose very next statement
assigns it: `String name;` followed by `name = user.getName();`.

**Why it matters.** Splitting the declaration from the first value costs a line and opens a
gap in which the variable exists without a value. Declared together, the variable cannot be
read before it is set, can be `final` (or `var`) at a glance, and the type and the value sit
side by side.

**How to fix.** Give the variable its value in the declaration.

```java
// Noncompliant
String name;
name = user.getName();

// Compliant
String name = user.getName();
```

Only the statement right after the declaration is considered (comments in between do not
matter), and only a plain `=` assignment to the variable itself. Not reported: declarations of
several variables, and variables first assigned inside a `try`, an `if` or a loop, where the
split is needed. The rule is off by default: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

### java/standard-charset-lookup

**Standard charset looked up by name**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: charset, clarity

Detects charsets that `java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets` provides being
looked up by name: `Charset.forName("UTF-8")`, `s.getBytes("UTF-8")`,
`new String(bytes, "UTF-8")`, `new InputStreamReader(in, "UTF-8")`,
`new OutputStreamWriter(out, "UTF-8")`, and — on Java 10 and later, which added the `Charset`
overloads — `URLEncoder.encode(s, "UTF-8")` and `URLDecoder.decode(s, "UTF-8")`.

**Why it matters.** A name is only checked at run time — a typo becomes an exception in
production — and the `String`-based overloads declare the checked
`UnsupportedEncodingException`, which forces pointless `try`/`catch` blocks for charsets every
JVM is required to support. The constants are also slightly faster (no lookup).

**How to fix.** Use the constant: `StandardCharsets.UTF_8`, `US_ASCII`, `ISO_8859_1`,
`UTF_16`, `UTF_16BE`, or `UTF_16LE`, and drop the now-unneeded exception handling.

```java
// Noncompliant
byte[] data = text.getBytes("UTF-8");
Charset latin = Charset.forName("ISO-8859-1");

// Compliant
byte[] data = text.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
Charset latin = StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1;
```

Only string literals naming one of the six standard charsets (or a common alias such as
`"UTF8"`) are reported — for `URLEncoder` / `URLDecoder` also a `static final` constant of this
file holding such a literal; other charsets and names held in variables are left alone.

### java/static-access-through-instance

**Static member accessed through an instance**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: confusing, static

Detects a static method or field reached through an expression of an instance
(`worker.sleep(100)`, `order.COUNTER`) or through the name of a subclass that inherits it
(`MyThread.currentThread()`), when the member is declared in this file or is one of the JDK's
well-known static methods (`Thread.sleep`, `Thread.currentThread`, `Thread.interrupted`,
`String.valueOf`, `String.format`, `Pattern.compile`, the wrapper classes' `parseXxx` and
`valueOf`, …).

**Why it matters.** The call reads as if it acted on that object, but the object is not used
at all — only its declared type, and the expression is not even required to be non-null.
`worker.sleep(100)` pauses the *current* thread, not `worker`; `thread.interrupted()` clears
the flag of the current thread instead of testing `thread`'s. Through a subclass name, the
reader looks for the member in the wrong class.

**How to fix.** Qualify the member with the class that declares it.

```java
// Noncompliant
worker.sleep(100);
if (thread.interrupted()) { … }

// Compliant
Thread.sleep(100);
if (thread.isInterrupted()) { … }
```

Not reported: `this.` and `super.` qualifiers, members of types declared in other files (their
modifiers are unknown), overloads where an instance method of the same name exists with the
same number of parameters, and receivers whose type the resolver does not know.

### java/static-date-format

**Non-thread-safe formatter in a static field**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects `static` fields whose type is `java.text.DateFormat`
(`SimpleDateFormat`), `java.text.NumberFormat` (`DecimalFormat`), `java.text.MessageFormat`, or
`java.util.Calendar`.

**Why it matters.** These classes keep intermediate parsing/formatting state in the instance
and are not thread-safe. A static instance is shared by every thread; concurrent use produces
wrong dates and numbers or random exceptions, typically only under production load.

**How to fix.** Use the immutable, thread-safe `java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter`; or create
the formatter where it is used; or wrap it in a `ThreadLocal`.

```java
// Noncompliant
private static final SimpleDateFormat DAY = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd");

// Compliant
private static final DateTimeFormatter DAY = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd");
private static final ThreadLocal<DateFormat> LEGACY_DAY =
        ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"));
```

Not reported: `private` fields that are only used inside `synchronized` blocks or methods (or
only copied with `clone()`), fields of unknown or other types (e.g. third-party thread-safe
formatters). A `MessageFormat` keeps shared state only in the number, date and choice formats of
its pattern: it is reported when it is created from a literal pattern with a format type
(`{0,number,#.##}`, `{1,date}`); with plain placeholders only (`"Hello {0}"`) formatting creates
what it needs afresh, and a pattern read at run time (a resource bundle) is unknown, so those
are reported only with `report_unknown_message_patterns`.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `report_unknown_message_patterns` | `false` | Also report static `MessageFormat` fields whose pattern is not a string literal (read from a resource bundle, built at run time, or set later). |

### java/static-field-set-in-constructor

**Static field assigned in a constructor** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: suspicious, design

Detects constructors that assign (`=`) a non-final `static` field of their own
class.

**Why it matters.** A static field is shared by all instances, but a constructor runs once per
instance: every new object silently overwrites the value that the others rely on. Code that
reads the field through one instance then sees the state of whichever instance was created
last, and concurrent construction makes the result depend on timing. It usually means the
field was meant to be an instance field (a missing or stray `static`), or that a singleton
is registered from its constructor, which leaks `this` before it is fully built.

**How to fix.** Remove `static` if the value belongs to each instance. If one shared value is
intended, set it once in a static initializer or a static factory method.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Connection {
    private static String url;
    Connection(String url) {
        Connection.url = url;       // the last connection created wins
    }
}

// Compliant
class Connection {
    private final String url;
    Connection(String url) {
        this.url = url;
    }
}
```

Not reported: compound updates such as `count++` or `total += n` (instance counters are
deliberate shared state), writes inside a `synchronized` block, writes explained by a comment
on the same line or the line above (a documented, deliberate choice), classes whose
constructors are all private (the class controls how often they run, as in a singleton), and
test code (test doubles that reset a static flag for each test).

### java/static-init-uses-subclass

**Static initialization uses a subclass**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: concurrency, initialization

Detects a class whose static initialization — a static field initializer or
a `static { }` block — creates an instance of one of its subclasses (`new Sub()`) or calls a
static method of it, when the subclass is declared in the same file and can be used from
elsewhere (it is not `private`).

**Why it matters.** Initializing a class first initializes its superclass. If one thread
starts with the superclass and another with the subclass, each holds the initialization of
one class while waiting for the other: the JVM deadlocks, typically once in a while at
start-up under load. Even on a single thread, starting with the subclass runs the
superclass initializer while the subclass is half initialized, so the new instance sees
default values in the subclass's static fields.

**How to fix.** Move the instance out of the superclass: a holder class
(`class Defaults { static final Base INSTANCE = new Impl(); }`), a static factory method
creating it lazily, or make the subclass `private` so that only the superclass can trigger
its initialization.

```java
// Noncompliant
public abstract class Codec {
    public static final Codec DEFAULT = new Utf8Codec();
}
class Utf8Codec extends Codec { }

// Compliant
public abstract class Codec {
    public static Codec defaultCodec() { return Holder.DEFAULT; }
    private static final class Holder { static final Codec DEFAULT = new Utf8Codec(); }
}
```

Not reported: anonymous subclasses and `private` nested subclasses (only the superclass can
reach them), enum constants with bodies, interfaces, and subclasses declared in other files
(unknown to the file-local analysis).

### java/stream-missing-bulk-method

**Stream overrides only its single-byte method**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: io, performance

Detects a class extending `InputStream`, `FilterInputStream`, `OutputStream` or
`FilterOutputStream` that overrides the single-byte `read()` or `write(int)` but not
`read(byte[], int, int)` or `write(byte[], int, int)`.

**Why it matters.** Almost every caller — buffered streams, readers, `transferTo`, `copy`
utilities — reads and writes whole arrays. `InputStream` and `OutputStream` implement the array
methods by calling the single-byte method once per byte: a virtual call, bounds checks and
often a lock for every byte, which makes such a stream orders of magnitude slower than it needs
to be. For the `Filter` variants it is worse than slow: `FilterInputStream.read(byte[], int,
int)` forwards to the wrapped stream directly, so bulk reads bypass the overridden `read()` and
whatever it does to the bytes; `FilterOutputStream.write(byte[], int, int)` does call
`write(int)`, one byte at a time.

**How to fix.** Override the array method as well, processing the whole range at once.

```java
// Noncompliant
class CountingInputStream extends FilterInputStream {
    @Override
    public int read() throws IOException {
        int b = super.read();
        if (b >= 0) count++;
        return b;
    }
}

// Compliant: also
    @Override
    public int read(byte[] buf, int off, int len) throws IOException {
        int n = super.read(buf, off, len);
        if (n > 0) count += n;
        return n;
    }
```

Not reported: abstract classes (a subclass may add the method), classes of other files in the
hierarchy (their methods are unknown), and test code.

### java/string-builder-char-constructor

**StringBuilder created from a char**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: strings

Detects `new StringBuilder(c)` and `new StringBuffer(c)` where `c` is a `char`
(a character literal or a `char` variable).

**Why it matters.** Neither class has a `char` constructor. The `char` is widened to an `int`
and picked up by the *capacity* constructor, so `new StringBuilder('[')` is an **empty**
builder with room for 91 characters. The text the author meant to start with silently goes
missing.

**How to fix.** Pass a `String`, or append the character.

```java
// Noncompliant
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder('[');

// Compliant
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("[");
StringBuilder sb2 = new StringBuilder().append('[');
```

Only arguments whose type is provably `char` are reported; an `int` capacity is fine.

### java/string-builder-field

**StringBuilder kept in a field**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: design, memory

Detects fields of type `StringBuilder` or `StringBuffer`.

**Why it matters.** A builder is a scratch buffer: it is meant to live while one string is
assembled. Kept in a field it holds on to its (possibly large) internal array for the whole
life of the object, its contents leak from one use to the next unless every path remembers to
reset it, and a shared mutable buffer is unsafe to use from several threads (and even
`StringBuffer`'s synchronization does not make multi-call sequences atomic).

**How to fix.** Create the builder as a local variable where the string is assembled, or keep
the finished `String` (or a list of parts) in the field instead.

```java
// Noncompliant
class ReportWriter {
    private final StringBuilder buffer = new StringBuilder();
    String render(Report r) {
        buffer.append(r.title());
        return buffer.toString();       // grows with every call
    }
}

// Compliant
class ReportWriter {
    String render(Report r) {
        StringBuilder buffer = new StringBuilder();
        buffer.append(r.title());
        return buffer.toString();
    }
}
```

This is a design guideline: classes whose whole purpose is to accumulate text (writers,
code generators) may keep a builder deliberately; suppress the finding there. The rule is
disabled by default.

### java/string-call-with-known-result

**String call with a known result**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: strings, redundant-code

Detects calls on a `String` whose result is fixed by their arguments:

* `replace(x, x)` — the same literal, character or variable on both sides; likewise
  `replaceAll` / `replaceFirst` with the same plain text (no regex or `$` syntax) twice;
* `substring(0)` and `s.substring(0, s.length())`, `concat("")`, `repeat(1)` — the string
  itself;
* `startsWith("")`, `endsWith("")`, `contains("")` — always `true`.

**Why it matters.** Such a call does nothing, so it usually stands for a call with the
wrong arguments: `path.replace("\\", "\\")` meant `replace("\\", "/")`, an escape sequence
lost a backslash, or a prefix constant that is empty by mistake makes a check always pass.
When it really is a no-op, it is noise the reader has to verify.

**How to fix.** Pass the intended arguments, or remove the call.

```java
// Noncompliant
String unix = path.replace("\\", "\\");
if (name.startsWith("")) { ... }

// Compliant
String unix = path.replace("\\", "/");
if (name.startsWith(prefix)) { ... }
```

Only receivers the resolver proves to be `String` are reported, and only when the result is
used (a discarded call is left to `java/ignored-return-value`). `toString()` on a `String`
is covered by `java/redundant-tostring`; arguments that are method calls (which could
return different values) are never compared.

### java/string-concat-in-loop

**String concatenation in a loop**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: performance, strings

Detects `s += …` and `s = s + …` inside a loop body when `s` is a `String`
declared outside that loop.

**Why it matters.** Strings are immutable: every concatenation copies the whole accumulated
text into a new object. Growing a string over *n* iterations therefore costs O(n²) time and
produces a lot of garbage, which becomes noticeable on large inputs (building SQL, CSV,
reports, log lines).

**How to fix.** Accumulate in a `StringBuilder` (or `StringJoiner` / `String.join` /
`Collectors.joining` when there is a separator) and convert once after the loop.

```java
// Noncompliant
String csv = "";
for (String field : fields) {
    csv += field + ",";
}

// Compliant
StringBuilder csv = new StringBuilder();
for (String field : fields) {
    csv.append(field).append(',');
}
String result = csv.toString();
```

Each variable is reported once per loop. Not reported: variables declared inside the loop
body and the variable of an enhanced `for` (they don't accumulate across iterations), a concatenation immediately followed by `break`, `return`, or `throw` (it runs at
most once), a concatenation guarded by a counter test (`if (n == 0) { s = s + x; }` with
`n++` in the loop: it runs on one pass at most), assignments in the loop header, and targets
whose type is unknown.

### java/string-reference-equality

**Strings compared with == or !=**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: strings, equality

Detects `==` and `!=` between two expressions whose static type is `String`, and
between a string literal and any expression that is not known to have another type.

**Why it matters.** For objects, `==` compares references, not contents. Two strings with the
same characters are often distinct objects (anything built at run time, read from input, or
returned by a library), so the comparison can be `false` even when the text is equal. Code that
"works" with literals in tests then fails in production.

**How to fix.** Compare contents with `equals()` (or `Objects.equals(a, b)` when either side may
be `null`, or `equalsIgnoreCase()`).

```java
// Noncompliant
if (status == "ACTIVE") { ... }

// Compliant
if ("ACTIVE".equals(status)) { ... }
if (Objects.equals(a, b)) { ... }
```

Comparisons with `null`, with the result of `intern()`, and with a variable initialized with
`new String(..)` are not reported: such a sentinel (`static final String NOT_FOUND = new
String("?")`) is created as a distinct object precisely so that `==` can tell it apart from
every other string, and `equals` would change the behaviour.

### java/substring-then-search

**Search on a substring instead of an offset** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: performance, strings

Detects a `String` search applied to the result of `substring(k)`:
`s.substring(k).startsWith(p)` and `s.substring(k).indexOf(x)`.

**Why it matters.** `substring` copies the characters from `k` to the end into a new string,
only to search it once and drop it. `String` has overloads that search from an offset without
copying anything: `s.startsWith(p, k)` and `s.indexOf(x, k)`. In a loop over a long text the
copies turn a linear scan into a quadratic one and produce garbage for the collector.

**How to fix.** Search the original string from the offset. `indexOf(x, k)` returns a
position in the original string: subtract `k` if the position within the substring was
needed, and keep testing for `-1` before subtracting.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (line.substring(pos).startsWith("--")) { … }
int end = line.substring(pos).indexOf(';');

// Compliant
if (line.startsWith("--", pos)) { … }
int at = line.indexOf(';', pos);
int end = at < 0 ? -1 : at - pos;
```

Only `substring` with one argument on an expression the resolver proves to be a `String` is
considered. Not reported: `substring(begin, end)` (the searches have no end bound before
Java 21), `lastIndexOf` (its offset overload searches backwards from the offset, which is
not the same), `contains`, `endsWith` and `equals`, which have no offset overload.

### java/suspicious-octal-escape

**Octal escape followed by a digit** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious, strings

Detects octal escapes in string literals that are directly followed by a
digit the escape does not include, such as `"\128"` or `"\477"`.

**Why it matters.** An octal escape takes at most three octal digits, and at most two when the
first is `4`–`7`. `"\128"` is therefore `\12` (a line feed) followed by the character `8`, and
`"\477"` is `'` followed by `7`. Whoever wrote the literal most likely meant one character
with a larger code, or a decimal number — either way the string is not what it looks like.

**How to fix.** Use a Unicode escape (`\u0080`) for the character you mean, split the literal
so the digit is clearly separate (`"\12" + "8"`), or write the digit without an escape.

```java
// Noncompliant
String sep = "\128";

// Compliant
String sep = "\n8";
String high = "\u0080";
```

Not reported: complete octal escapes such as `"\0"`, `"\12"`, or `"\177"` followed by a
non-digit, escaped backslashes (`"\\12"`, a regex back-reference), character literals, and
text blocks.

### java/swapped-arguments

**Arguments swapped with respect to parameter names** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious, typo

Detects calls where two arguments are variables named exactly like the
*other's* parameter: `resize(height, width)` for `void resize(int width, int height)`. Only
methods and constructors declared in the same file are checked, since their parameter names
are known.

**Why it matters.** When both parameters have the same type, the compiler cannot notice the
exchange. Names are the only clue, and here they say that each value goes to the parameter
meant for the other one: the width becomes the height, the source becomes the target, the
start becomes the end.

**How to fix.** Pass the arguments in the order of the parameters, or rename the variables if
the order is deliberate.

```java
// Noncompliant
void copy(Path source, Path target) { … }
copy(target, source);

// Compliant
copy(source, target);
```

Not reported: calls inside methods whose name suggests a deliberate exchange (`reverse`,
`swap`, `transpose`, `flip`, `invert`, `mirror`, `rotate`, `opposite`, …), recursive calls of a
method from within itself (symmetric delegation such as `compare(b, a)`),
overloaded methods with several declarations of the same arity, names of one or two letters
(`a`, `b`, `x`), calls made in both orders in the same method (a symmetric check), and
classes that inherit
from types declared elsewhere (an inherited overload could be the one called).

### java/switch-fallthrough

**switch case falls through**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: switch, suspicious

Detects a non-empty group of statements under classic `case X:` labels that
can run on into the next label because it doesn't end with `break`, `return`, `throw`,
`continue`, or `yield`.

**Why it matters.** Falling through is occasionally intended but far more often a forgotten
`break`: the next case's code then runs too, producing wrong results that tests covering each
case separately may not catch.

**How to fix.** End the case with `break` (or `return`/`throw`). If falling through is
intended, say so with a comment such as `// falls through` just before the next label.

```java
// Noncompliant
switch (level) {
    case WARN:
        warnings++;
    case ERROR:            // WARN also counts as an error
        errors++;
        break;
}

// Compliant
switch (level) {
    case WARN:
        warnings++;
        break;
    case ERROR:
        errors++;
        break;
}
```

Not reported: several labels sharing one group of statements (`case A: case B: …`), the last
group, arrow-form switches (they never fall through), groups whose ending the rule can't be sure
about (a nested `switch`, a loop, a labeled statement, a call to a helper such as `fail(..)` or
`System.exit(..)`), a case that falls only into an empty trailing group (`default:` with
no statements), and fall-throughs documented by a comment containing "fall" (`// falls
through`, `/* FALLTHROUGH */`).

### java/synchronized-on-get-class

**Synchronizing on getClass()**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects `synchronized (getClass())` (or `this.getClass()`) in a class that can
be subclassed.

**Why it matters.** `getClass()` returns the runtime class of the object. In a subclass
instance it is the subclass, so code that means to guard state shared by the whole class
hierarchy (usually static state of the declaring class) locks a different monitor for every
subclass, and instances of different subclasses run the "exclusive" section concurrently.

**How to fix.** Lock the declaring class literally, or a dedicated static lock.

```java
// Noncompliant
synchronized (getClass()) {
    instances++;
}

// Compliant
synchronized (Registry.class) {
    instances++;
}
```

Final classes, enums, records and anonymous classes (which cannot be subclassed) are not
reported.

### java/synchronized-on-reassigned-field

**Synchronized block replaces its own lock** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects a `synchronized (field)` block that assigns a new object to that same
field.

**Why it matters.** A `synchronized` block locks the object the field refers to when the
block starts. Once the block replaces the field's value, the next thread locks the *new*
object and enters immediately, even though the first thread is still inside the block holding
the old one. The mutual exclusion the block was written for is gone precisely when the guarded
state changes.

**How to fix.** Lock a dedicated `final` object and guard the mutable reference with it.

```java
// Noncompliant
synchronized (listeners) {
    listeners = new ArrayList<>(listeners);
    listeners.add(l);
}

// Compliant
private final Object listenersLock = new Object();
synchronized (listenersLock) {
    listeners = new ArrayList<>(listeners);
    listeners.add(l);
}
```

Only fields (plain names resolving to a field, or `this.field`) are checked. Assignments of
`null` and assignments inside lambdas or nested classes declared in the block are not
reported.

### java/synchronized-on-value

**Synchronizing on a string or boxed value**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects `synchronized` blocks whose lock is a string literal, or a
variable/field of type `String` or of a boxed primitive (`Integer`, `Boolean`, `Long`, …).

**Why it matters.** Such values have no private identity. String literals and constants are
interned and shared across the whole JVM; small boxed values come from shared caches
(`Integer.valueOf`, `Boolean.TRUE`). Unrelated code that locks "its own" `"LOCK"` or `0`
contends with, or deadlocks against, yours. Conversely, two equal strings built at run time
are different objects and don't exclude each other at all.

**How to fix.** Lock on a dedicated private object.

```java
// Noncompliant
private static final String LOCK = "LOCK";
synchronized (LOCK) { … }

// Compliant
private static final Object LOCK = new Object();
synchronized (LOCK) { … }
```

Variables and fields of the JDK's value-based classes (`Optional`, `LocalDate`, `Instant`, `Duration`
and the other `java.time` values) are reported too: equal instances may be the same shared
object, and the JDK warns against locking them.

Only literals, variables, and fields are checked (not method results such as `key.intern()`).
A variable initialized with `new String(…)` / `new Integer(…)` is a unique object and is not
reported.

### java/system-exit

**JVM terminated outside main**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: design, error-handling

Detects calls to `System.exit(…)`, `Runtime.getRuntime().exit(…)`, and
`Runtime.getRuntime().halt(…)` outside a `main` method.

**Why it matters.** Terminating the JVM from library or application code takes the decision
away from the caller: it kills application servers, build tools and test runners that host
the code, skips `finally` blocks of the calling threads (and, with `halt`, shutdown hooks),
and makes the code impossible to unit test.

**How to fix.** Throw an exception or return a status, and let the program's entry point
(`main`) decide whether to exit.

```java
// Noncompliant
void loadConfig(Path p) {
    if (!Files.exists(p)) {
        System.exit(2);
    }
}

// Compliant
void loadConfig(Path p) {
    if (!Files.exists(p)) {
        throw new ConfigException("missing " + p);
    }
}
```

Calls anywhere inside a `static main` method (including lambdas and anonymous classes there)
are not reported.

### java/system-out-print

**Printing to System.out or System.err**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: logging

Detects `print`, `println`, `printf`, `format`, `write`, and `append` calls on
`System.out` or `System.err` outside test files.

**Why it matters.** Console output bypasses the logging configuration: it has no level,
timestamp, or source, cannot be filtered or routed, is often lost in containers and
application servers, and is written synchronously, which can slow down hot paths.

**How to fix.** Use the application's logger. Command-line tools that are meant to talk to a
terminal can suppress the rule where console output is the intended user interface.

```java
// Noncompliant
System.out.println("Loaded " + n + " records");

// Compliant
log.info("Loaded {} records", n);
```

Not reported: test code — test files, JUnit 3 test classes kept under a main source root (a
class extending `TestCase` or a `…TestCase` base class) and `@Test` methods — and files
declaring a `static main` method — command-line programs, whose console output is their user
interface. `System` must resolve to `java.lang.System` (a
class of the same name declared in the file is not confused with it).

### java/test-assertion-in-production

**Test assertion in production code** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: tests, dependencies

Detects production code (not a test file) that calls the assertions of a test
library: JUnit's `Assert`/`Assertions`, AssertJ, Hamcrest's `assertThat`, TestNG, Truth.

**Why it matters.** Test libraries are usually test-scoped dependencies: in the packaged
application the class may be missing and the call fails with `NoClassDefFoundError`. Even
when present, their failures are `AssertionError`s, which ordinary `catch (Exception e)`
handlers do not catch, so an input check in production code can bring down a request thread
or a batch job instead of producing a proper error.

**How to fix.** Use a production check: `Objects.requireNonNull`, an explicit `if` that throws
`IllegalArgumentException` / `IllegalStateException`, or the validation utilities of the
framework in use.

```java
// Noncompliant
import static org.junit.Assert.assertNotNull;
void register(User user) {
    assertNotNull(user);
}

// Compliant
void register(User user) {
    Objects.requireNonNull(user, "user");
}
```

Only files of a `main` source set (`…/src/main/…`) are checked: other source sets
(`src/it`, `src/functionalTest`, …) hold tests. Test-support code is not reported either:
files whose path or package mentions `test`, `mock`, `fixture`, `example` or `sample`, files
under a `resources` folder (code templates), and classes whose name contains `Test`,
`Assert` or `Matcher`. Only the public assertion classes of the libraries count (JUnit's
`Assert`/`Assertions`/`TestCase`, AssertJ's `Assertions` family and `Fail`, Hamcrest's
`MatcherAssert`, TestNG's `Assert`/`AssertJUnit`, Truth): a library's internal helpers named
`assert…` are not test assertions, and the libraries' own sources (files in their packages)
are not checked.

### java/test-catch-only-fails

**Test catch block only calls fail()**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: tests, junit

Detects `catch` blocks in test code whose only statement is a `fail(..)` call
of a test library (JUnit, AssertJ, TestNG).

**Why it matters.** A test fails anyway when an exception escapes it, and the report then
shows the exception with its full stack trace. Catching it just to call `fail()` replaces
that with a message (often `e.getMessage()`, sometimes nothing), so the place where the
error happened is lost, and the extra `try`/`catch` makes the test longer and hides what it
actually verifies.

**How to fix.** Let the exception propagate: declare it in the test method's `throws`
clause. To state explicitly that a call must not throw, JUnit 5 has `assertDoesNotThrow`.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Test
void parses() {
    try {
        parser.parse(input);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        fail("unexpected: " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

// Compliant
@Test
void parses() throws IOException {
    parser.parse(input);
}
```

Only test files are checked. Calls that pass the caught exception on as the cause
(`fail(message, e)`) keep its stack trace and are not reported. Catches of `Throwable` or of
an `Error` (`AssertionError`,
`StackOverflowError`, …), which usually add context to a failure on purpose, are not
reported, nor are catches inside lambdas, anonymous classes and overriding methods, where a checked
exception may not be rethrown, nor in methods used as a method reference in the file
(`addTest("dir", this::dirTest)`: the functional interface, usually declared elsewhere, may not
declare the exception either) and `private` helpers called only from such methods.

### java/test-class-naming

**Test class name without a test prefix or suffix**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, naming, tests

Detects top-level test classes, classes with JUnit or TestNG test methods,
whose name neither starts with `Test` nor ends with `Test`, `Tests`, `TestCase` or `IT`.

**Why it matters.** A test class named after the class it tests plus `Test` (`InvoiceParser`
→ `InvoiceParserTest`) is found at once from either side and sorts next to its subject. The
name also matters to the build: by default, Maven's test plugins only run the classes whose
names match their include patterns — `Test*`, `*Test`, `*Tests` and `*TestCase` for unit
tests, `*IT` for integration tests — so a test class named `InvoiceParserChecks` may silently
never run.

**How to fix.** Rename the class (and its file) to match, ideally the name of the class under
test followed by `Test`.

```java
// Noncompliant
class InvoiceParsing {
    @Test
    void readsTotals() { … }
}

// Compliant
class InvoiceParserTest {
    @Test
    void readsTotals() { … }
}
```

Recognized test methods carry the `@Test`, `@ParameterizedTest`, `@RepeatedTest`,
`@TestFactory` or `@TestTemplate` annotation of JUnit 4, JUnit 5 or TestNG (resolved through
the imports); a TestNG `@Test` on the class also counts. Not reported: shared base classes,
whose tests their subclasses run under their own names (abstract classes, and classes named
`…TestBase`, `…TestSupport` or `Abstract…` — `Abstract` as a whole first word — even when they
are not declared abstract); nested classes (JUnit 5 `@Nested` groups); and whether the name
matches the class under test, which needs the rest of the project. The parameter `suffixes`
sets the accepted endings and `prefixes` the accepted beginnings; set `prefixes` to an empty
string to accept endings only, for a team that does not use the `TestInvoiceParser` style.
The rule is off by default: it is part of the `conventions` profile.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `suffixes` | `"Test,Tests,TestCase,IT"` | Comma-separated name endings accepted for test classes. |
| `prefixes` | `"Test"` | Comma-separated name beginnings also accepted (empty: endings only). |

### java/test-could-be-parameterized

**Tests differing only in literals could be one parameterized test**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: tests, duplication

Detects JUnit 5 `@Test` methods of one class whose bodies are the same token
for token except for literal values (numbers, strings, characters, booleans, `null`), when at
least three of them (`min_tests`) share the shape.

**Why it matters.** Copies of one test that differ in their inputs and expected values are a
table written as code: a change to the scenario must be repeated in every copy, the copies
drift apart, and the reader has to diff them to find the cases. A parameterized test states
the scenario once and the cases as data, and every case is still reported on its own.

**How to fix.** Write one `@ParameterizedTest` with the varying literals as parameters, fed by
`@ValueSource`, `@CsvSource` or `@MethodSource`.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Test void parsesOne()   { assertEquals(1, Numbers.parse("one")); }
@Test void parsesTwo()   { assertEquals(2, Numbers.parse("two")); }
@Test void parsesThree() { assertEquals(3, Numbers.parse("three")); }

// Compliant
@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({"1, one", "2, two", "3, three"})
void parses(int expected, String text) { assertEquals(expected, Numbers.parse(text)); }
```

A literal only matches a literal of the same kind (`1` and `1L` differ, as they may select
different overloads). Not reported: tests whose parameters, `throws` clauses or annotations
other than `@Test` and `@DisplayName` differ (`@Disabled`, `@Tag`, `@Timeout`, …), identical
copies (see `java/identical-methods`), JUnit 4 and TestNG tests (their parameterization works
per class), and methods that are already parameterized.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `min_tests` | `3` | Fewest tests differing only in literals that are reported as a group. |

### java/test-lifecycle-method-not-run

**JUnit set-up or tear-down method that does not run** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: tests, junit

Detects JUnit set-up and tear-down methods that JUnit will not run as intended:

- a per-test hook (`@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach`, JUnit 4 `@Before`/`@After`) declared `static`;
- a per-class hook (JUnit 4 `@BeforeClass`/`@AfterClass`; JUnit 5 `@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll`
  outside a `@TestInstance` class) that is not `static`;
- a hook that is `private` or returns a value, or a JUnit 4 hook that is not `public`;
- a hook of one JUnit generation in a class whose tests all belong to the other (a JUnit 4
  `@Before` next to JUnit 5 `@Test` methods): the engine running the tests does not know the
  hook.

**Why it matters.** Depending on the JUnit version, such a hook either makes the whole test
class fail with an initialization error or is silently skipped, so the tests run without the
set-up they rely on (or leave behind what the tear-down should have cleaned). Mixed JUnit 4 and
JUnit 5 annotations are the classic leftover of a half-finished migration: the hook compiles,
looks right, and never runs.

**How to fix.** Declare per-class hooks `static void` and per-test hooks non-static `void`,
not `private` (`public` for JUnit 4), and use the lifecycle annotations of the JUnit
generation the class's tests use.

```java
// Noncompliant
import org.junit.Before;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class ParserTest {
    @Before                       // JUnit 4 hook, JUnit 5 tests: never runs
    void setUp() { parser = new Parser(); }

    @Test
    void parsesEmptyInput() { … }
}

// Compliant
import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeEach;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class ParserTest {
    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() { parser = new Parser(); }

    @Test
    void parsesEmptyInput() { … }
}
```

Only annotations that resolve to JUnit through the imports count. A non-static JUnit 5
`@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll` is not reported when the class or an enclosing class carries
`@TestInstance`, when the class extends another class (which may carry it), or in interfaces;
hooks marked `@Override` are left alone, and so are non-public `setUp()`/`tearDown()` hooks
of a class that extends another class (it may be a JUnit 3 `TestCase`, whose mechanism calls
the protected override itself). A project that switches every test class to the
per-class lifecycle in `junit-platform.properties` should turn the rule off.

### java/test-method-not-run

**Test method that JUnit will not run**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: tests, junit

Detects JUnit test methods (`@Test`, and JUnit 5 `@ParameterizedTest` /
`@RepeatedTest`) that are `private`, `static`, or return a value.

**Why it matters.** JUnit only executes non-private, non-static methods returning `void`.
JUnit 5 silently skips a test method that breaks these rules, so the test *looks* present
and green but never runs; JUnit 4 rejects the whole class at run time. Either way the
behaviour the test was written to protect is unverified.

**How to fix.** Make the method an instance method returning `void` that is not `private`
(JUnit 4 additionally needs `public`). Move any shared logic that returns a value into a
separate helper method.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Test
private void parsesDates() { … }

@Test
int computesTotal() { return assertTotal(); }

// Compliant
@Test
void parsesDates() { … }
```

Only annotations that resolve to JUnit 4 or JUnit 5 (through imports or a qualified name)
are considered; `@TestFactory` methods legitimately return values and are not checked.

### java/test-without-assertion

**Test without assertion**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: tests

Detects `@Test` methods (JUnit 4, JUnit 5, TestNG) that contain no assertion
and no interaction verification.

**Why it matters.** A test without an assertion passes as long as nothing throws. It adds to
the coverage numbers while checking almost nothing, so regressions in the results go unnoticed
and the suite gives false confidence.

**How to fix.** Assert on the outcome (`assertEquals`, AssertJ `assertThat(…)`, Hamcrest
`assertThat(…, is(…))`), verify the expected interactions (Mockito `verify(…)`), or state the
expected exception (`assertThrows`, `@Test(expected = …)`). If the test really only checks that
no exception is thrown, say so with `assertDoesNotThrow(…)`.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Test
void parsesHeader() {
    parser.parse("id;name");
}

// Compliant
@Test
void parsesHeader() {
    assertEquals(List.of("id", "name"), parser.parse("id;name").columns());
}
```

A call counts as an assertion when its name starts with `assert`, `verify`, `expect`, `fail`,
`should`, or `then` (except Mockito stubbing such as `thenReturn`), or contains
`Assert`/`Verify`/`Expect` (`andExpect`, `softly.assertAll`); `assert` and `throw` statements
count too. Calls to helper methods declared in the same file are followed, and so are lambdas
stored in fields of the file and passed to a call (`run(CHECK_ENTRIES)` with
`static final Check CHECK_ENTRIES = f -> assertTrue(..)`); unqualified calls that may reach
an inherited or statically imported helper are assumed to assert, and so are calls on a
tester object — a chain starting at a class or variable whose type is named `…Tester`,
`…Verifier`, `…Assert`, `…Asserts` or `…Assertions` (`Type4Tester.create("1 2 add").pop(3)`),
whose methods check what they are given. Disabled tests
and tests with `expected`/`expectedExceptions` are not reported. Only test files are checked.

### java/this-escape-in-constructor

**this escapes from a constructor**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: concurrency, initialization

Detects constructors that let `this` escape before construction is over:
registering it with another object (`source.addListener(this)`, `registry.register(this)`,
`bus.subscribe(this)`) or starting a thread (`thread.start()`).

**Why it matters.** Once another object or thread holds the new instance, it can call it at
any time, including before the rest of the constructor (and the constructors of any
subclass) has run. The callback then sees fields that are still `null` or `0`, and on other
threads the Java memory model does not even guarantee that the fields already assigned are
visible, `final` ones included, because the object was published before its constructor
finished.

**How to fix.** Finish construction first, then publish: register the listener or start the
thread from a factory method or an explicit `start()` / `init()` method called after `new`.

```java
// Noncompliant
class PriceView implements PriceListener {
    PriceView(PriceFeed feed) {
        feed.addListener(this);
        this.format = new DecimalFormat("0.00");   // not yet set when the first update arrives
    }
}

// Compliant
class PriceView implements PriceListener {
    static PriceView create(PriceFeed feed) {
        PriceView view = new PriceView();
        feed.addListener(view);
        return view;
    }
}
```

Off by default: the risk depends on threads and subclasses a single file does not show. Not
reported: the escape as the very last statement of a constructor of a `final` class (nothing
is left to initialize), registrations with objects the instance creates itself (its own child
components, created with `new` in a field initializer or in the constructor), code inside
lambdas or anonymous classes of the constructor, and constructors (or classes) marked
`@SuppressWarnings("this-escape")`, the name javac's lint uses for this warning.

### java/thread-passed-as-runnable

**Thread passed where a Runnable is expected** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: concurrency, thread

Detects a `Thread` object (a `new Thread(..)`, a variable declared as `Thread` or
a subclass of it) passed where only a `Runnable` is needed: to a `Thread` constructor, to
`Executor.execute`, `ExecutorService.submit`, `ScheduledExecutorService.schedule…` or
`CompletableFuture.runAsync`.

**Why it matters.** The receiver only calls the object's `run()` method on a thread of its
own. The `Thread` object itself is never started: its name, priority, daemon flag,
uncaught-exception handler and thread-local state are silently ignored, and `join()`,
`interrupt()` or `isAlive()` on it do nothing useful. Readers (and the author) usually believe
those settings apply.

**How to fix.** Pass a `Runnable` (a lambda or the task object) instead, and configure the
thread through the executor's `ThreadFactory`; or start the thread yourself.

```java
// Noncompliant
Thread worker = new Thread(this::poll, "poller");
worker.setDaemon(true);
executor.execute(worker);        // runs poll(), not as "poller", not as a daemon

// Compliant
executor.execute(this::poll);
```

Only arguments whose type is provably `Thread` or a subclass are reported; executors are
recognized by their declared JDK types.

### java/thread-run-direct

**Thread.run() called directly**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: concurrency

Detects calls to `run()` on an expression whose type is `java.lang.Thread` (or
a subclass).

**Why it matters.** `run()` is an ordinary method: calling it executes the thread's task
synchronously in the *current* thread. No new thread is started, so the caller blocks and any
intended concurrency silently disappears.

**How to fix.** Call `start()`, which creates the thread and invokes `run()` on it. If the work
really should run inline, call the `Runnable` directly rather than wrapping it in a `Thread`.

```java
// Noncompliant
Thread worker = new Thread(task);
worker.run();

// Compliant
Thread worker = new Thread(task);
worker.start();
```

Only calls on a receiver whose type is provably a `Thread` are reported; `super.run()` and
unqualified `run()` calls inside a `Thread` subclass are not.

### java/thread-subclass-without-run

**Thread subclass without run()** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: concurrency

Detects a class extending `java.lang.Thread` directly — named or anonymous —
that does not override `run()` and never passes a `Runnable` to the `Thread` constructor.

**Why it matters.** `Thread.run()` only runs the `Runnable` given at construction. Without
one and without an override, starting the thread does nothing: the work the class was meant
to do in the background silently never happens. The usual causes are a misspelled or
mis-declared `run` (`Run()`, `run(String)`), or work placed in the constructor.

**How to fix.** Override `public void run()` with the thread's work, or better, implement
`Runnable` and hand it to a `Thread` or an executor.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Poller extends Thread {
    public void Run() { poll(); }
}

// Compliant
class Poller extends Thread {
    @Override
    public void run() { poll(); }
}
```

To stay certain that no subclass provides `run()`, a named class is only reported when it is
`final`, or when it is `private`, local to a method, or instantiated directly in the same
file, and no class of the file (named or anonymous) extends it. Abstract classes and classes
overriding `start()` are skipped, as are constructors passing anything but a name or a
thread group to `super(..)`.

### java/throws-generic-exception

**Method throws a generic exception**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: error-handling, api-design

Detects methods and constructors that declare `throws Exception` or
`throws Throwable`.

**Why it matters.** A generic `throws` clause tells callers nothing about what can go wrong,
and forces every one of them to catch (or re-declare) `Exception`, which in turn swallows
unrelated runtime exceptions. The real failure modes of the method disappear from its
signature.

**How to fix.** Declare the specific checked exceptions the method throws, or wrap them in a
meaningful domain exception.

```java
// Noncompliant
public Report load(Path file) throws Exception { … }

// Compliant
public Report load(Path file) throws IOException, ReportFormatException { … }
```

Not reported: `main`, methods annotated `@Override` (the signature is dictated by the
supertype), methods of anonymous classes, well-known callbacks whose supertype declares the
generic exception (`call()`, `close()`, `finalize()`, `invoke(proxy, method, args)`), test
lifecycle methods, and test code.

### java/todo-comment

**TODO comments should be resolved**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: todo

Flags comments containing a `TODO` marker.

A TODO records work that was knowingly left unfinished. Left in place, it silently becomes permanent and the missing behaviour may surprise users.

**How to fix:** do the work, or move it to the issue tracker and delete the comment.

```text
// Noncompliant
// TODO handle the empty list
```

### java/too-many-assertions

**Test method with too many assertions**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: tests, size

Detects test methods (`@Test`, `@ParameterizedTest`, `@RepeatedTest`, and JUnit 3
`test…` methods) that contain more assertions than `max` (25 by default). An assertion is a
call whose name starts with `assert` (`assertEquals`, `assertThat`, `assertThrows`, soft
assertions…; a fluent chain counts once) or a Java `assert` statement.

**Why it matters.** A test with dozens of assertions checks many behaviors at once. When it
fails, it stops at the first broken expectation and hides the state of all the others; its
name cannot say what it verifies; and every change to one of the behaviors touches the same
long method. Such tests usually grew by appending cases.

**How to fix.** Split the method into tests that each check one behavior, or turn repeated
checks into a parameterized test or a table of cases.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Test
void parser() {
    assertEquals(1, parse("1"));
    assertEquals(2, parse("2"));
    // … 40 more
}

// Compliant
@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({"1, 1", "2, 2"})
void parsesNumbers(String text, int expected) {
    assertEquals(expected, parse(text));
}
```

The count is static: an assertion inside a loop counts once. Only test code and files that
import JUnit's or TestNG's `@Test` are looked at. Assertion calls inside helper methods are not
counted, and neither are verifications of mocks (`verify`).

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max` | `25` | Most assertions allowed in one test method. |

### java/too-many-fields

**Too many fields**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~60 min · Tags: design, size

Detects classes, enums, and records that declare more than `max` (default 20)
fields that are not `static final`. Each variable of a multi-variable declaration
(`int a, b;`) counts.

**Why it matters.** Many fields mean much state to keep consistent. Such classes usually
mix several concepts, are hard to construct and test, and every method potentially depends on
every field.

**How to fix.** Group related fields into small value classes or records (an `Address`
instead of `street`, `city`, `zip`, …) and move behaviour that uses only one group along with
it.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Customer {
    String street; String city; String zip; String country;
    String phone; String mobile; String email; /* … 20 more … */
}

// Compliant
class Customer {
    Address address;
    ContactInfo contact;
}
```

Constants (`static final` fields) are not counted.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max` | `20` | Largest number of non-constant fields (fields that are not `static final`) a class, enum, or record may declare. |

### java/too-many-methods

**Too many methods**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~60 min · Tags: design, size

Detects classes, enums, and records that declare more than `max` (default 35)
methods. Constructors, methods of nested types, and methods of anonymous classes are not
counted.

**Why it matters.** A type with that many methods usually has more than one responsibility.
It is hard to understand as a whole, changes for many unrelated reasons, and tends to keep
growing because it is the obvious place to add "one more" method.

**How to fix.** Identify groups of methods that work on the same subset of state or serve
the same purpose and move them into separate, focused classes (collaborators, helpers,
strategies).

```java
// Noncompliant: one class handles parsing, validation, persistence and reporting
class OrderManager { /* 60 methods */ }

// Compliant
class OrderParser { … }
class OrderValidator { … }
class OrderRepository { … }
```

Not counted: methods annotated `@Override`, whose number is dictated by the implemented
interfaces and superclasses (a JDBC wrapper must implement all of `java.sql.Statement`). Not
reported: interfaces and test files (a test class naturally has one method per test case).

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max` | `35` | Largest number of methods (constructors and `@Override` methods excluded) a class, enum, or record may declare. |

### java/too-many-parameters

**Functions should not have too many parameters**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: brain-overload

Flags functions that declare more than `max` parameters (default 7).

Long parameter lists are hard to call correctly (arguments of the same type are easily swapped) and often signal that the function does too much or that several values belong together.

**How to fix:** group related values into a parameter object, or split the function.

```text
// Noncompliant
createUser(first, last, email, phone, street, city, zip, country) { ... }

// Compliant
createUser(name, contact, address) { ... }
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max` | `7` | Most parameters allowed for one function |

### java/tostring-or-clone-returns-null

**toString() or clone() returns null** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: null-safety, api-misuse

Detects `return null;` in an overriding `toString()` or `clone()`.

**Why it matters.** Callers rely on these methods never returning `null`: string
concatenation, loggers, `String.valueOf`, debuggers and collection `toString()` call
`toString()` freely, and code that clones an object uses the copy immediately. A `null` from
either one surfaces as a `NullPointerException` far from its cause, or as the text `null` in
logs and user-facing messages.

**How to fix.** Return a meaningful string (possibly empty) from `toString()`; from `clone()`
return a copy, or throw `CloneNotSupportedException` / `AssertionError` when cloning is
impossible.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Override
public String toString() {
    if (name == null) {
        return null;
    }
    return name;
}

// Compliant
@Override
public String toString() {
    return name == null ? "" : name;
}
```

Only a literal `return null;` (directly, or as a branch of a conditional expression) in a
zero-parameter `toString()` or `clone()` is reported; lambdas and inner classes in the method
are skipped.

### java/type-parameter-naming

**Type parameter naming**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: naming, convention

Detects type parameters whose name is not a single uppercase letter,
optionally followed by one digit (`T`, `E`, `K`, `V`, `R`, `T2`).

**Why it matters.** The one-letter convention is what makes type variables stand out from
class names in a signature: in `Result<Entity> load(Class<Entity> type)` the reader has to
check whether `Entity` is a real class or a placeholder, while `<E> Result<E> load(Class<E>
type)` is unambiguous. Mixed conventions also make generic code harder to scan.

**How to fix.** Rename the parameter to a meaningful single letter (`E` for elements, `K`/`V`
for keys and values, `T` for a general type, `R` for a result) and describe it in the Javadoc
`@param <T>` tag when more detail is useful.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Cache<KeyType, ValueType> { ... }
<Item> List<Item> copy(List<Item> items) { ... }

// Compliant
class Cache<K, V> { ... }
<E> List<E> copy(List<E> items) { ... }
```

### java/unclear-operator-precedence

**Operators of different precedence mixed without parentheses**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: clarity, operators

Detects an operand that is itself an operation of a different precedence
level, written without parentheses, for the operator pairs that are commonly misread:

* `&&` inside `||` (`a && b || c`);
* arithmetic inside a shift (`x << n + 1`, `a + b >> 1`);
* one bitwise operator inside another (`a & b | c`, `a ^ b & c`);
* a comparison inside a bitwise operator (`flag & x == y`).

**Why it matters.** Everyone knows that `*` binds more tightly than `+`, but few readers are
sure whether `<<` binds more tightly than `+` (it does not: `1 << n + 1` shifts by `n + 1`),
whether `&` binds more tightly than `|`, or how `&&` and `||` group. Code that depends on these
rules is read wrongly, and a wrong reading is "fixed" into a bug. Parentheses cost nothing and
state the intended grouping.

**How to fix.** Add parentheses around the inner operation, after checking that the grouping
is the intended one.

```java
// Noncompliant
if (admin && active || override) { … }
int mask = 1 << bit + 1;

// Compliant
if ((admin && active) || override) { … }
int mask = 1 << (bit + 1);
```

The rule is off by default: mixing `&&` and `||` without parentheses is common in existing
code. Not reported: chains of one operator (`a || b || c`), arithmetic mixed with arithmetic
(`a + b * c`), comparisons inside `&&` / `||`, and shifts inside bitwise operators
(`hi << 8 | lo`).

### java/unguarded-log-argument

**Debug log argument computed without a level check** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: logging, performance

Detects debug- and trace-level logging calls (`debug`, `trace`; `fine`,
`finer`, `finest` and `log(Level.FINE, …)` for `java.util.logging`) with an argument that does
real work — a conversion such as `toString()` or `toJson()`, a call that formats, renders, or
computes something, an object creation, a string concatenation — outside an
`isDebugEnabled()` / `isTraceEnabled()` / `isLoggable(..)` check.

**Why it matters.** Java evaluates every argument before the logger decides to discard the
message. Debug and trace output is normally off in production, so each such call serializes,
formats, copies, or allocates for nothing — and does it on every pass through the code.

**How to fix.** Pass the value itself and let the logger's `{}` placeholder call `toString()`
only when needed, pass a supplier (`() -> state.toJson()`) to an API that accepts one, or wrap
the call in a level check.

```java
// Noncompliant
log.debug("Request {} took {}", request.toJson(), Duration.ofMillis(elapsed));

// Compliant
if (log.isDebugEnabled()) {
    log.debug("Request {} took {}", request.toJson(), Duration.ofMillis(elapsed));
}
log.debug("Request {} took {} ms", request, elapsed);
```

Not reported: arguments that are variables, fields, literals, constants, lambdas, method
references, zero-argument reads (`getName()`, `size()`, a record accessor such as `id()`),
lookups with simple arguments (`map.get(key)`, `getProperty(NAME)`), `String.valueOf(..)` of
a primitive value, or `toString()` on a value of a known enum type (a JDK enum, or one
declared in the file that does not define its own `toString`), whose cost is negligible;
calls whose *message* is a concatenation or `String.format(..)` (reported by
`java/log-message-concatenation`); calls in a method that tests the level before them or under
a condition naming a debug/trace flag; calls in a `private` method that is only called from
such guarded places in the file (`if (log.isDebugEnabled()) { logDetails(store); }`); test
files; and loggers the file does not identify (the receiver's declared type must be a known
logging API, or a conventional logger name in a file importing one).

Spring's `LogAccessor` is covered too. It has no placeholders and no concatenation rule knows
it, so for it a message built by concatenation or `String.format(..)` is reported as well; the
fix is its `Supplier` overload (`log.debug(() -> "Loaded " + rows)`).

### java/unnecessary-fully-qualified-name

**Unnecessary fully qualified name**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: clutter, imports

Detects fully qualified type names (`java.util.List`, `java.lang.String`,
`com.acme.model.Order`) where the simple name already refers to the same type — because it is
imported, lives in `java.lang`, or belongs to the file's own package.

**Why it matters.** The package prefix adds nothing but length. It makes readers wonder
whether a *different* `List` is meant, and it often survives from an automated refactoring or
a copy-paste.

**How to fix.** Use the simple name.

```java
// Noncompliant
import java.util.List;

class Report {
    java.util.List<String> lines = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
    java.lang.String title;
}

// Compliant
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

class Report {
    List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    String title;
}
```

Also detects a class name in front of a static member that the file already imports
with a single static import from that same class: with `import static
org.apache.commons.lang3.StringUtils.isBlank;` in place, `StringUtils.isBlank(name)` can be
`isBlank(name)`. Mixing both spellings of the same call in one file is noise.

Covers type names, annotation names, and qualified static calls or constants
(`java.util.Collections.emptyList()`). For package prefixes (for `java.util.Map.Entry`,
whether `java.util.` can go), the finding is reported only when the simple name provably
resolves to the same type at that position through a single-type import, the file's own
package, or `java.lang` — a clash with another import or with a type of this file keeps the
qualified name. On-demand (`*`) imports don't count (a type of the same package in another
file would win), and `java.lang` types are left alone in files that have any, since they
could make the simple name ambiguous. For class qualifiers, the member must be imported by
exactly one single static import, from the class the qualifier names; the qualifier is kept
when the bare name could mean something else: a method or variable of the same name declared
anywhere in the file, a method every class inherits (`toString`, `equals`, …), members of an
enclosing class that extends or implements another type (it may inherit a member of that
name; `static_imports_under_supertypes` reports them anyway), or a call with explicit type
arguments (`Util.<T>cast(x)` has no unqualified form). Qualifiers naming the class a member belongs to without a static import (`Math.max`,
`Order.DEFAULT` inside `Order`) are a common readable style and are not reported.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `static_imports_under_supertypes` | `false` | Also report class-qualified static members inside classes that extend or implement a type declared elsewhere (such a supertype could declare a member of the same name, which the bare name would then mean). |

### java/unnecessary-return

**Unnecessary return**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: clutter, redundant

Detects a `return;` that is the last statement executed by a `void` method,
a constructor, or a block lambda — directly at the end of the body, or at the end of an
`if`/`else` branch, a `try` block, or a `catch` block that itself ends the body — and, in the
same way, a `continue;` that is the last statement executed by a loop body.

**Why it matters.** Control leaves the method (or goes on with the next iteration) there
anyway. The extra statement is noise,
and it can make readers look for code after it that they might be skipping.

**How to fix.** Remove the `return;` (or `continue;`).

```java
// Noncompliant
void reset() {
    counter = 0;
    return;
}

for (Item item : items) {
    if (item.isStale()) {
        evict(item);
        continue;
    }
}

// Compliant
void reset() {
    counter = 0;
}

for (Item item : items) {
    if (item.isStale()) {
        evict(item);
    }
}
```

A `return;` that skips later statements, or that ends a loop body or a `switch` case, is
not reported; neither is a `continue` that skips later statements, ends a `switch` case
(removing it would fall through), or names a label.

### java/unreachable-code

**Unreachable code**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: unused, control-flow

Detects statements that follow a `return`, `throw`, `break`, `continue`, or
`yield` in the same block and therefore can never run.

**Why it matters.** Code that never runs is misleading: whoever wrote it expected it to have an
effect (cleanup, logging, a state change), so either the jump is misplaced or the code is dead.
The Java compiler rejects most of these, so the rule mainly catches code that is being edited
before it is compiled.

**How to fix.** Move the jump after the statements that must run, or delete the dead code.

```java
// Noncompliant
return result;
cache.clear();          // never runs

// Compliant
cache.clear();
return result;
```

Only the first unreachable statement of each block is reported. Stray `;` are left to
`empty-statement`.

### java/unretained-annotation-lookup

**Reflective lookup of an annotation that is not retained** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: reflection, annotations

Detects reflective annotation lookups — `isAnnotationPresent`,
`getAnnotation`, `getDeclaredAnnotation`, `getAnnotationsByType`,
`getDeclaredAnnotationsByType` — for an annotation that is not retained at run time:
`Override` and `SuppressWarnings` (source-only), or an annotation type declared in the same
file without `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)`.

**Why it matters.** An annotation's retention decides whether it exists at run time. Source
annotations are discarded by the compiler, and the default retention (`CLASS`) keeps them in
the class file but hides them from reflection. The lookup therefore always answers `false` /
`null`, so the feature built on it — a plug-in scan, a validation, a marker — silently never
triggers.

**How to fix.** Add `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)` to your annotation type; for
source-only JDK annotations, find another way to express the information.

```java
// Noncompliant
@interface Audited { }
boolean audited = method.isAnnotationPresent(Audited.class);

// Compliant
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@interface Audited { }
```

Annotation types declared in other files are unknown and not reported.

### java/unsynchronized-accessor

**Getter/setter pair with inconsistent synchronization** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects a getter and a setter of the same field where one is declared
`synchronized` and the other is not: `synchronized void setLimit(int v) { limit = v; }` next
to `int getLimit() { return limit; }`.

**Why it matters.** Making one accessor `synchronized` shows that the field is shared between
threads. But the lock only protects code that takes it: without it, the other accessor may
read a stale value that never reflects the last write (the Java memory model gives no
visibility guarantee without a common lock or `volatile`), and a `long` or `double` may even
be read half-written. The half-applied synchronization gives a false sense of safety.

**How to fix.** Make both accessors `synchronized`, or drop the locks and declare the field
`volatile` when a single read or write is all that is needed.

```java
// Noncompliant
public synchronized void setLimit(int limit) { this.limit = limit; }
public int getLimit() { return limit; }

// Compliant
public synchronized void setLimit(int limit) { this.limit = limit; }
public synchronized int getLimit() { return limit; }
```

Only one-statement accessors named `getX`/`isX` and `setX` of a non-`volatile`, non-`final`
field declared in the same class are considered, both static or both instance methods.
Classes with Lombok annotations are skipped.

### java/untyped-to-array-cast

**Untyped toArray() result cast to a specific array type** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: collections, api-misuse

Detects the result of a no-argument `toArray()` on a collection or stream cast
to a more specific array type: `(String[]) names.toArray()`.

**Why it matters.** `Collection.toArray()` and `Stream.toArray()` create an array whose runtime
type is `Object[]`, whatever the element type. An `Object[]` is never a `String[]`, so the
cast throws `ClassCastException` every time it runs (unless the collection is empty and the
code path is never taken in tests).

**How to fix.** Ask for a typed array.

```java
// Noncompliant
String[] names = (String[]) nameList.toArray();

// Compliant
String[] names = nameList.toArray(new String[0]);
String[] same = nameList.stream().toArray(String[]::new);
```

Only receivers the resolver proves to be a `Collection` or a `Stream` are reported; casts to
`Object[]` and to arrays of a type variable (`(T[])`, whose erasure is `Object[]`) are not.

### java/unused-import

**Unused or redundant import**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: imports, clutter

Detects imports that serve no purpose:

* single-type imports whose name is never used in the file (Javadoc references such as
  `{@link Foo}`, `@see Foo`, and `@throws FooException` count as uses);
* the same import written twice;
* imports of `java.lang` classes, which are always visible;
* imports of classes from the file's own package.

**Why it matters.** Dead imports are noise: they suggest dependencies that don't exist, cause
merge conflicts, and hide the imports that matter.

**How to fix.** Delete the import (most IDEs can "organize imports" automatically).

```java
// Noncompliant
import java.util.List;      // never used
import java.lang.String;    // implicit

// Compliant
import java.util.Map;       // used below
```

Wildcard imports are never reported as unused.

### java/unused-local-variable

**Unused local variable**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: dead-code, unused

Detects local variables whose value is never read. Assigning to a variable
(`x = …`, `x += …`, `x++` as a statement) does not count as reading it.

**Why it matters.** An unused local is noise that readers have to understand and then discard.
It often hides a real mistake: a result that was computed but forgotten, a variable that was
meant to be passed on, or leftovers of a refactoring.

**How to fix.** Delete the variable. If its initializer has a needed side effect (a call),
keep the call as a plain statement.

```java
// Noncompliant
int total = computeTotal(items);
String unusedLabel = format(total);   // never read
return total;

// Compliant
int total = computeTotal(items);
return total;
```

Not reported: the unnamed variable `_`, names that announce the intent (`ignored…`,
`unused…`, `dummy…`), annotated declarations (for example `@SuppressWarnings("unused")`),
try-with-resources resources, catch parameters, pattern variables, and enhanced-`for`
variables. A read of any same-named variable inside the local's scope (for example a field of
a local class) counts as a use.

### java/unused-private-class

**Unused private nested type**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: dead-code, unused

Detects `private` nested classes, interfaces, enums, records, and annotation
types that are not referenced anywhere outside their own declaration.

**Why it matters.** A private nested type is only visible inside its top-level class. If
nothing there mentions it, it is dead code that readers still have to understand and that
keeps its own dependencies alive.

**How to fix.** Delete the type, or use it where it was meant to be used.

```java
// Noncompliant
public class Parser {
    private static class Token { }          // never used
    public Node parse(String s) { … }
}

// Compliant
public class Parser {
    public Node parse(String s) { … }
}
```

Uses are matched by simple name and deliberately generously: the type counts as used when its
name appears as a whole word anywhere else in the file — as a type, in a qualified name, in a
string literal (reflection such as `"Outer$Inner"`), or even in a comment. References from
inside the type itself (its constructors, factory methods) do not count. Annotated types are
not reported.

### java/unused-private-field

**Unused private field**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: dead-code

Detects `private` fields that are never read anywhere in the file: either not
referenced at all, or only assigned (`this.cache = build();`, `count++;`) and never read.

**Why it matters.** A private field can only be used from its own compilation unit, so if
nothing in the file mentions it, it is dead code: it costs memory, misleads readers into
thinking it matters, and often signals an unfinished refactoring or a bug (a value computed and
stored but never used).

**How to fix.** Remove the field (and whatever computes its value), or use it.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Service {
    private final Clock clock = Clock.systemUTC();   // never read
}

// Compliant
class Service {
    private final Clock clock = Clock.systemUTC();
    Instant now() { return clock.instant(); }
}
```

Not reported: `serialVersionUID` / `serialPersistentFields`, annotated fields (injection,
serialization, persistence frameworks read them reflectively — annotations that only document
the field, such as `@Nullable`, `@Deprecated` or `@GuardedBy`, don't count), fields of
Lombok-annotated classes or with Lombok accessors, and fields whose name appears as a string
literal (reflection). A field that is assigned but never read is not reported in a class that
is annotated, declares `Serializable`/`Externalizable`, or has a field with such an
annotation (a persistence or serialization framework may read its fields). Any identifier
with the field's name counts as a read, so a local variable of the same name that is read
keeps the field quiet.

### java/unused-private-method

**Unused private method**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: dead-code, unused

Detects `private` methods that are never called or referenced from anywhere
else in the file.

**Why it matters.** A private method can only be used inside its own compilation unit. If
nothing there calls it, it is dead code: it has to be read, maintained and compiled for
nothing, and it often signals an unfinished refactoring or a call that was lost by mistake.

**How to fix.** Delete the method, or call it where it was meant to be called.

```java
// Noncompliant
class Report {
    public String render() { return header(); }
    private String header() { return "#"; }
    private String footer() { return "--"; }   // never called
}

// Compliant
class Report {
    public String render() { return header() + footer(); }
    private String header() { return "#"; }
    private String footer() { return "--"; }
}
```

Matching is by name and deliberately generous: the method counts as used when its name
appears as a whole word anywhere else in the file — a call on any receiver (overloads
included), a method reference (`this::name`, `Type::name`), a string literal (reflection, JUnit
`@MethodSource`), or even a comment. Occurrences inside the method itself (recursion) do not
