count. Not reported: annotated methods (framework callbacks, `@SuppressWarnings("unused")`)
and the serialization hooks `writeObject`, `readObject`, `readObjectNoData`, `writeReplace`,
and `readResolve`.

### java/unused-private-method-parameter

**Unused parameter of a private method**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: dead-code, unused

Detects parameters of `private` methods that the method body never uses.

**Why it matters.** A private method is only called from its own file, so its signature is
entirely under local control. An unused parameter makes every caller compute and pass a value
for nothing, suggests a dependency that doesn't exist, and often reveals a bug: the value was
meant to be used (a wrong variable was used instead).

**How to fix.** Remove the parameter and the corresponding argument at every call site — or
use it, if it was forgotten.

```java
// Noncompliant
private String label(Order order, Locale locale) {
    return "#" + order.id();              // locale is never used
}

// Compliant
private String label(Order order) {
    return "#" + order.id();
}
```

A parameter counts as used when its name appears anywhere in the code of the body
(conservative), but not inside a string literal or a comment (`"line.separator"` does not use
`line`).
Not reported: `_` and names starting with `unused` or `ignored`, annotated methods and
parameters (framework callbacks, `@SuppressWarnings("unused")`), methods with an empty body,
the serialization hooks (`readObject`, `writeObject`, …), and methods that are referenced as
a method reference (`this::name`) or by name in a string (reflection), where the signature
must stay as it is.

### java/unused-type-parameter

**Unused method type parameter**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: generics, unused

Detects a type parameter of a generic method (`<T> void f(..)`) that appears
nowhere else in the method: not in the return type, the parameters, the `throws` clause, the
bounds of other type parameters, or the body.

**Why it matters.** A method type parameter exists to connect types — an argument to the
result, two arguments to each other. One that connects nothing only makes the signature
harder to read and suggests a relationship that does not exist; callers can even pass an
explicit type argument (`util.<String>clear()`) that has no effect. It is often the leftover
of a refactoring.

**How to fix.** Remove the type parameter.

```java
// Noncompliant
static <T> void clear(List<?> items) { items.clear(); }

// Compliant
static void clear(List<?> items) { items.clear(); }
```

Not reported: methods that may override or implement another method (they must repeat the
parent's type parameters): methods with `@Override`, and non-private instance methods of
classes that extend or implement anything, of anonymous classes and of enum constants;
abstract and interface methods without a body; class-level type parameters (phantom type
parameters are a deliberate technique). A mention anywhere in the method, even in a comment,
counts as a use.

### java/url-in-hash-collection

**URL in a hash-based collection or compared with equals**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: performance, network, equality

Detects `java.net.URL` used as the key type of a `Map` or the element type of a
`Set`, and direct calls to `URL.equals(..)` or `URL.hashCode()`.

**Why it matters.** `URL.equals` and `URL.hashCode` resolve the host name to an IP address.
Every lookup in a `HashMap<URL, …>` or `HashSet<URL>` may block on DNS, results change with
network conditions (two different virtual hosts on one IP are "equal"; offline, equal URLs
may not be), and the hash code of a key can differ between insertion and lookup.

**How to fix.** Use `java.net.URI` for identity and comparison (its `equals` is purely
textual), converting with `url.toURI()` / `uri.toURL()` at the boundaries, or key the
collection by `url.toExternalForm()`.

```java
// Noncompliant
Map<URL, Response> cache = new HashMap<>();

// Compliant
Map<URI, Response> cache = new HashMap<>();
```

Sorted maps and sets are not reported (`URL` is not `Comparable`, so they need a comparator
that never calls `equals`).

### java/useless-catch

**Catch block that only rethrows**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: error-handling, redundant

Detects `catch` clauses whose only statement rethrows the caught exception
unchanged: `catch (IOException e) { throw e; }`.

**Why it matters.** Such a handler does nothing the runtime wouldn't do anyway; it only adds
noise and suggests handling that doesn't exist.

**How to fix.** Remove the `catch` clause (and the `try` if nothing else is left), or actually
handle the exception: add context, translate it, clean up.

```java
// Noncompliant
try {
    store.save(order);
} catch (SQLException e) {
    throw e;
}

// Compliant
store.save(order);
```

Only the **last** `catch` clause of a `try` is checked: a rethrowing clause followed by other
clauses keeps its exception away from the later, broader handlers and is therefore
meaningful.

### java/useless-override

**Override that only calls super**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: redundant, inheritance

Detects an `@Override` method whose whole body is `super.sameMethod(..)` (or
`return super.sameMethod(..)`) called with its own parameters, in the same order.

**Why it matters.** Such a method does exactly what the inherited one does: it adds lines to
read and keep in sync (a new parameter in the parent must be threaded through), and it
misleads readers into looking for a difference that is not there. It is often the leftover of
an override whose extra behavior was removed, or generated by an IDE and never filled in.

**How to fix.** Remove the method.

```java
// Noncompliant
@Override
public void start(Context context) {
    super.start(context);
}

// Compliant: no override at all, or one that adds behavior
@Override
public void start(Context context) {
    super.start(context);
    registerListeners();
}
```

Not reported: overrides that change something besides the body — another annotation
(`@Transactional`, `@Deprecated`, …), annotated parameters, `final` or `synchronized`, or a
visibility wider than the parent's. Since a `public` override of a `protected` method is a
deliberate way to expose it, `public` overrides are only reported when the parent is known to
be public: `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`, and parents declared in the same file. Also not
reported: methods with a comment above them or in their body (other than an IDE stub marker),
which explains why they exist; `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` in annotated classes (they
may exist to stop Lombok or a similar generator); and methods without `@Override` (a
same-named method with other parameter types is an overload that narrows what is accepted).

### java/utility-class-constructor

**Utility class without a private constructor**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: design

Detects utility classes — classes whose members are all `static`, with at
least one static method — that declare no constructor and therefore get an implicit public
one.

**Why it matters.** Instantiating a utility class makes no sense, yet the implicit public
constructor allows `new StringHelper()` and suggests to readers (and to code completion) that
instances are meaningful. It also allows subclassing, which cannot add anything useful.

**How to fix.** Add a `private` constructor (optionally throwing), and consider making the
class `final`.

```java
// Noncompliant
public class Strings {
    public static boolean isBlank(String s) { return s == null || s.isBlank(); }
}

// Compliant
public final class Strings {
    private Strings() { }
    public static boolean isBlank(String s) { return s == null || s.isBlank(); }
}
```

Not reported: classes that declare any constructor, abstract classes, classes that extend
another class or implement interfaces, annotated classes (frameworks may instantiate them;
Lombok's `@UtilityClass` generates the constructor), classes declaring `main`, `premain` or
`agentmain` (application and agent entry points), classes that this file instantiates
(`new Model()`, `Model::new`: whatever their members, they are used as objects), private
nested classes, and classes with instance members or non-static nested classes. Annotations that say nothing about instances do not exempt a class:
`@Deprecated`, `@SuppressWarnings`, API-status and tooling markers (`@API`, `@Beta`,
`@IgnoreJRERequirement`, `@SuppressFBWarnings`), nullness defaults, and Lombok's logger
annotations (`@Slf4j`, `@Log4j2`, …).

### java/value-reference-equality

**Boxed or value objects compared with == or !=**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: equality, boxing

Detects `==` and `!=` between two expressions whose static types are both boxed
numbers or characters (`Integer`, `Long`, `Short`, `Byte`, `Character`, `Double`, `Float`), or
both the same JDK value type that defines equality by content (`BigDecimal`, `BigInteger`,
`LocalDate`, `LocalTime`, `LocalDateTime`, `ZonedDateTime`, `OffsetDateTime`, `Instant`,
`Duration`, `Period`, `UUID`, `Optional`, `OptionalInt`, `OptionalLong`, `OptionalDouble`).

**Why it matters.** On objects, `==` compares references. Boxed values are only shared for a
small cache range (`Integer` from -128 to 127, for example), so `a == b` holds in tests with
small numbers and fails in production with larger ones. Value objects such as `BigDecimal` or
`LocalDate` are created fresh by nearly every operation, so two equal values are almost never
the same object.

**How to fix.** Compare with `equals()` (or `Objects.equals(a, b)` when either side may be
`null`), unbox explicitly (`a.intValue() == b.intValue()`), or, for `BigDecimal`, use
`compareTo(..) == 0` when `2.0` and `2.00` should be equal.

```java
// Noncompliant
Integer expected = order.quantity();
if (expected == stock.available()) { ... }   // both Integer

// Compliant
if (expected.equals(stock.available())) { ... }
```

Not reported: comparisons with `null` or with `Optional.empty()` (a shared instance), with
a primitive (Java unboxes and compares values), between different types (one side `Object`,
say — an identity check on purpose), `Boolean` (only two shared instances exist in practice),
enums and `Class` objects (identity is equality for them), `String` (see
`string-reference-equality`), and any operand whose type is unknown.

### java/virtual-thread-platform-setting

**Platform-only setting on a virtual thread** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: concurrency, virtual-threads

Detects settings that only platform threads support, applied to a thread
created as a virtual thread (`Thread.ofVirtual()…unstarted(..)` / `.start(..)`,
`Thread.startVirtualThread(..)`):

* `setDaemon(false)` — virtual threads are always daemon threads; the call throws
  `IllegalArgumentException`;
* `setPriority(..)` — virtual threads always run at normal priority; the call is silently
  ignored.

**Why it matters.** Code moved from platform to virtual threads keeps its old tuning: the
daemon setting now crashes at run time, and a priority meant to favour latency-critical
work does nothing.

**How to fix.** Remove the call. Work that must keep the JVM alive or needs a priority
belongs on a platform thread (`Thread.ofPlatform().daemon(false).priority(..)`).

```java
// Noncompliant
Thread worker = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(task);
worker.setDaemon(false);
worker.start();

// Compliant
Thread worker = Thread.ofPlatform().daemon(false).unstarted(task);
worker.start();
```

Only direct chains and local variables initialized with a virtual thread and never
reassigned are followed; `setDaemon(true)` (a no-op) is not reported.

### java/volatile-mutable-contents

**Volatile array or collection modified in place**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: concurrency

Detects a `volatile` field holding an array or a non-thread-safe JDK
collection (`ArrayList`, `HashMap`, …) whose elements the class modifies in place —
`values[i] = x`, `items.add(x)`, `cache.put(k, v)` — outside any `synchronized` code.

**Why it matters.** `volatile` only applies to the reference: reading the field sees the
latest array or collection object, but writes to its elements or entries get no visibility
or atomicity guarantee. Other threads can see stale elements, and concurrent `add` / `put`
calls corrupt a `HashMap` or `ArrayList`. The keyword gives a false impression that the
contents are safe to share.

**How to fix.** Use a thread-safe structure (`AtomicIntegerArray`, `ConcurrentHashMap`,
`CopyOnWriteArrayList`), guard every access with a lock, or treat the contents as immutable
and publish a new copy through the volatile field on each change.

```java
// Noncompliant
private volatile Map<String, Session> sessions = new HashMap<>();
void open(String id, Session s) { sessions.put(id, s); }

// Compliant
private final Map<String, Session> sessions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
void open(String id, Session s) { sessions.put(id, s); }
```

Not reported: copy-on-write use (the field is only ever replaced by a new object), fields
also assigned something other than a new JDK array or collection (its thread safety is then
unknown), and changes made inside `synchronized` code. Off by default: it needs the whole
class's accesses to be judged.

### java/wait-notify-on-thread

**wait/notify on a Thread object**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects `wait()`, `notify()` and `notifyAll()` called on a `Thread` object
(including unqualified calls inside a `Thread` subclass).

**Why it matters.** The JVM uses the monitor of a `Thread` object itself: `Thread.join()` is
implemented by waiting on it, and the thread notifies all waiters on it when it terminates.
Using the same monitor for your own signaling mixes both protocols — your waiters wake up when
the thread ends, and your notifications can wake up joiners — which leads to spurious
wake-ups and lost signals that are very hard to diagnose. The `Thread` documentation
recommends never doing it.

**How to fix.** Signal through a dedicated lock object, or use `join()`, a `CountDownLatch`,
or a `Future` to wait for the thread.

```java
// Noncompliant
synchronized (worker) {
    worker.wait();
}

// Compliant
worker.join();
```

Only receivers the resolver proves to be a `java.lang.Thread` are reported.

### java/wait-notify-outside-synchronized

**wait/notify outside synchronized code**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects `wait()`, `notify()`, and `notifyAll()` called on the current object
(unqualified or through `this`) outside any `synchronized` block or `synchronized` method.

**Why it matters.** These methods require the caller to own the object's monitor; otherwise
they throw `IllegalMonitorStateException` at run time. Even when a caller happens to hold the
lock, a condition wait that isn't lexically guarded is easy to break during refactoring and
prone to lost wake-ups.

**How to fix.** Call them inside `synchronized (this) { … }` or from a `synchronized` method,
and wait in a loop that re-checks the condition — or use `java.util.concurrent` tools
(`CountDownLatch`, `BlockingQueue`, `Condition`).

```java
// Noncompliant
void awaitReady() throws InterruptedException {
    while (!ready) {
        wait();
    }
}

// Compliant
synchronized void awaitReady() throws InterruptedException {
    while (!ready) {
        wait();
    }
}
```

Calls inside lambdas (whose calling context is unknown) and classes that declare their own
`wait`/`notify` overloads are not reported.

### java/wait-notify-wrong-monitor

**wait/notify on an object whose monitor is not held** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects `wait()`, `notify()` and `notifyAll()` called on an object (`lock.wait()`)
from synchronized code that holds some other monitor: inside `synchronized (other) { … }` or a
`synchronized` method (which holds `this`), with no enclosing `synchronized (lock)`.

**Why it matters.** These methods require the caller to own the monitor *of the object they
are called on*. Holding another lock does not count: unless every caller already holds the
right monitor, the call throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`. The code looks right at a glance
because it is inside a `synchronized` block, just not the one for this object.

**How to fix.** Synchronize on the object you wait on or notify (`synchronized (lock) {
lock.wait(); }`), or call `wait()`/`notify()` on the object you already hold.

```java
// Noncompliant
synchronized void awaitReady() throws InterruptedException {
    while (!ready) {
        readyLock.wait();        // holds `this`, not `readyLock`
    }
}

// Compliant
void awaitReady() throws InterruptedException {
    synchronized (readyLock) {
        while (!ready) {
            readyLock.wait();
        }
    }
}
```

The receiver must be a plain name or a field path (`lock`, `this.lock`, `a.lock`); it is
compared textually with the locks of the enclosing `synchronized` blocks. One alias is
recognized: a local variable initialized with the other expression and never reassigned
(`Buffer b = buffer; synchronized (b) { buffer.wait(); }` holds the right monitor); other
aliases are not, and such calls stay silent only when a matching block is present. Calls in
lambdas or code outside any synchronized context, and methods that check
`Thread.holdsLock(…)` (their callers hold the lock), are not reported; `wait`
calls whose arguments are not proven numeric are skipped (they may be overloads).

### java/wait-with-nested-lock

**wait() while holding another lock** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading, deadlock

Detects `wait()` called inside nested `synchronized` regions that hold two or
more different monitors, e.g. `synchronized (a) { synchronized (b) { b.wait(); } }`, when the
same file notifies that monitor (`b.notify()`) while holding one of the other monitors (`a`).

**Why it matters.** `wait()` releases only the monitor of the object it is called on. Every
other lock stays held for the whole wait. When the thread that calls `notify()` needs one of
those outer locks first, it blocks, and the waiter is never woken: a deadlock that
appears only under a particular interleaving, often in production.

**How to fix.** Wait while holding only the monitor being waited on: restructure so the outer
lock is released before waiting, or use a single lock (or a `java.util.concurrent` lock with
several `Condition`s).

```java
// Noncompliant
synchronized (registry) {
    synchronized (queue) {
        while (queue.isEmpty()) {
            queue.wait();          // `registry` stays locked while waiting
        }
    }
}

// Compliant
synchronized (queue) {
    while (queue.isEmpty()) {
        queue.wait();
    }
}
```

Monitors are compared by their text (`lock` and `this.lock` are the same; a `synchronized`
method holds `this`), so the same object locked twice (reentrantly) is not counted twice. Only
regions of the same method are considered: locks held by callers are not visible. Without a
notifier in the file that needs the outer lock, keeping it while waiting can be deliberate
(holding off new work while in-flight work drains) and is not reported.

### java/wait-without-loop

**wait() outside a loop**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: concurrency, multi-threading

Detects untimed `Object.wait()` calls, and untimed `await()` / `awaitUninterruptibly()`
calls on a `java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition`, that are not inside a loop in the same method.

**Why it matters.** A waiting thread can wake up without the condition it waits for being
true: spurious wake-ups are allowed by the specification, `notifyAll()` wakes threads
waiting for other conditions, and another thread may consume the state change first. Code
that waits once with `if (!ready) wait();` then proceeds on a false assumption.

**How to fix.** Always wait in a loop that re-checks the condition while holding the lock —
or use higher-level tools (`CountDownLatch`, `BlockingQueue`, `CompletableFuture`).

```java
// Noncompliant
synchronized Item take() throws InterruptedException {
    if (items.isEmpty()) {
        wait();
    }
    return items.remove(0);
}

// Compliant
synchronized Item take() throws InterruptedException {
    while (items.isEmpty()) {
        wait();
    }
    return items.remove(0);
}
```

Any enclosing `while`, `do`, or `for` loop of the same method or lambda counts as a guard.
Only the untimed forms are reported: a timed `wait(millis)` or `await(time, unit)` must already handle waking up
without the condition (the timeout) and is often a deliberate bounded wait. `await()` counts
only when the receiver is proven to be a `Condition` (a `CountDownLatch` or a barrier is not
woken spuriously).

### java/week-year-pattern

**Week-based year in a calendar date pattern**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: date-time

Detects a date pattern passed to `new SimpleDateFormat(..)`,
`SimpleDateFormat.applyPattern(..)`, or `DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern(..)` that uses `Y`
(week-based year) together with month (`M`/`L`) or day-of-month (`d`) fields, and no week
field (`w`); and the reverse mix, a week of year (`w`) with the calendar year (`y`, or `u` in
`java.time`) and no month or day field (`yyyy-'W'ww`).

**Why it matters.** `Y` is the year of the *week* a day belongs to, not the calendar year.
They differ for a few days around New Year: with `YYYY-MM-dd`, 30 December 2024 is
formatted as `2025-12-30`. The bug passes every test run during the rest of the year and
then corrupts dates, file names, and reports in late December or early January. The reverse
mix fails on the same days: 30 December 2024 is in week 1 of 2025, so `yyyy-'W'ww` prints
`2024-W01`.

**How to fix.** Use `y` (`yyyy-MM-dd`, or `uuuu-MM-dd` with `java.time`). Keep `Y` only for
ISO week dates, which also use `w` (`YYYY-'W'ww`), and write week-based dates with `Y`.

```java
// Noncompliant
DateTimeFormatter f = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("YYYY-MM-dd");

// Compliant
DateTimeFormatter f = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd");
```

Quoted text in the pattern (`'Year' YYYY`) is ignored; only string literals are checked.

### java/wildcard-import

**Wildcard (on-demand) import**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, imports

Detects on-demand imports, with or without `static`: `import java.util.*;`,
`import static java.lang.Math.*;`.

**Why it matters.** A wildcard import does not say which names a file uses or where they come
from: a reader (or a review tool showing a diff) cannot tell which package `Entry` or `max`
belongs to. It also makes a file fragile: when a new version of a library adds a class with the
same simple name as one from another wildcard-imported package, the file stops compiling with
an ambiguity error, although nothing in it changed. Single-name imports list the dependencies
exactly and are maintained by every IDE.

**How to fix.** Import each type or static member by name.

```java
// Noncompliant
import java.util.*;
import static java.util.Objects.*;

// Compliant
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import static java.util.Objects.requireNonNull;
```

Parameter `allow_static` accepts static on-demand imports, which some teams allow for
assertion and matcher libraries in tests. The rule is off by default: it is part of the
`conventions` profile. Module imports (`import module java.base;`, Java 25) are not reported
yet: the parser does not read that syntax.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `allow_static` | `false` | Accept static on-demand imports (`import static org.junit.Assert.*;`) and report type imports only. |

### java/wildcard-return-type

**Bounded wildcard in a return type or final type as a bound** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: generics, api-design

Detects two ways of using generic bounds that give callers nothing:

* a bounded wildcard in a method's return type (`List<? extends Shape> shapes()`,
  `Map<String, ? super Integer> counts()`) when every `return` of the method gives one
  concrete type, visible in the declaration of the returned variable or field, or in a `new`
  expression;
* a type parameter whose bound is a final class, an enum or a record (`<T extends String>`):
  no other type can satisfy it.

**Why it matters.** Wildcards make a parameter flexible for the caller; in a return type they
do the opposite. Every caller receives a type it cannot write into, cannot pass where the
plain type is expected, and must repeat the wildcard in its own declarations. The method
knows what it returns and can say so. A type parameter bounded by a final type can only ever
be that type: the generic declaration only adds noise and casts.

**How to fix.** Return the concrete type (`List<Shape>`, or an unmodifiable view if the
wildcard was meant to prevent writes); replace the type parameter by its bound.

```java
// Noncompliant
public List<? extends Shape> shapes() { … }
public <T extends String> T first(List<T> items) { … }

// Compliant
public List<Shape> shapes() { … }
public String first(List<String> items) { … }
```

Not reported: methods that return values of several parameterizations, values whose own
declared type has the wildcard, or values whose type is not written down (results of calls,
`var`, diamonds) — the wildcard may then be needed; unbounded wildcards (`List<?>`) and any
wildcard inside `Class<…>` or
`Constructor<…>` (`Class<? extends Annotation>` is the idiomatic way to return a class
object); `? extends Object`; abstract, `default` and other interface methods, whose wildcard
lets implementations override them with a narrower return type; methods with `@Override`, and
non-private instance methods of types that have a supertype, which may be implementing a
signature they do not choose; bounds with several types.

### js/accessor-field-mismatch

**Getters and setters should use the field that matches their name** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags a class getter or setter that reads or writes the field of *another* accessor of the class,
while the class has a field that matches its own name: `get width() { return this._height; }` in
a class with a `_width` field and a `height` accessor.

**Why:** accessors backed by a field are written by copy and paste, and forgetting to rename the
field in the copy is easy. The mistake is silent: the property returns another property's value,
or a setter stores into the wrong field, and the matching field is left stale.

**Fix:** use the field that matches the accessor's name.

```js
class Box {
  _width = 0;
  _height = 0;
  get width() { return this._height; }       // flagged
  set width(value) { this._height = value; } // flagged
  get height() { return this._height; }      // compliant
}
```

Only accessors whose whole body is `return this.x;` (getter) or `this.x = value;` (setter) are
checked, and only when the class declares or assigns a field named like the accessor with a `_`
or `#` prefix or a `_` suffix. An accessor that exposes a differently named field which belongs to
no other accessor (`get tools() { return this._visibleTools; }` next to a raw `_tools`) is a
deliberate design and is not reported; nor are static accessors.

### js/accessor-pairs

**A property with a setter should also have a getter**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, confusing

Flags a property that has a setter but no getter: a `set` accessor in a class or an object
literal without a `get` accessor of the same name (and, in a class, the same `static`-ness), and a
property descriptor given to `Object.defineProperty`, `Reflect.defineProperty` or
`Object.defineProperties` with a `set` function but no `get`.

**Why:** assigning to such a property works, but reading it always gives `undefined`, which is
rarely what the author or the callers expect (`obj.size = 3; obj.size` is `undefined`). A setter
alone on a subclass is a trap of its own: it replaces the whole inherited accessor, so the getter
of the parent class stops working for instances of the subclass.

**Fix:** add the matching getter, or replace the write-only property with a method
(`setSize(n)`) that says it only writes.

```js
class Box {
  set size(n) { this._size = n; }        // flagged: reads give undefined
}

class Box {
  get size() { return this._size; }
  set size(n) { this._size = n; }        // compliant
}
```

Not reported: getters without setters (read-only properties are normal), empty setters (stubs
that ignore writes on purpose), setters with a
decorator (framework inputs such as `@Input() set value(v)`), abstract and ambient declarations,
setters whose name is computed at run time, classes that also declare a field or method of the
same name, and object literals with a spread (which may bring the getter).

### js/adjacent-overload-signatures

**Overload signatures should be adjacent**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: typescript, convention

Flags overloads of the same function or method that are separated by other
declarations.

**Why:** the overload signatures of one function are a single unit: together they describe every
way it can be called. When they are scattered between other members, readers see only part of the
contract and are likely to miss an overload — or to add a duplicate.

**Fix:** move all overloads (and the implementation) of the name next to each other.

Checked lists: top-level and namespace function declarations (also `export function` and
`declare function`), class methods (static and instance methods are separate names), and the
method, call (`(): T`), and construct (`new (): T`) signatures of interfaces and type literals.
Getters and setters are not overloads and are not checked.

```ts
interface Emitter {
  on(event: 'open', cb: () => void): void;
  close(): void;
  on(event: 'data', cb: (d: string) => void): void; // flagged
}

interface Emitter {
  on(event: 'open', cb: () => void): void;
  on(event: 'data', cb: (d: string) => void): void; // compliant
  close(): void;
}
```

### js/array-callback-return

**Array method callbacks should return a value**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags block-bodied callbacks passed to array methods that use the callback's return value
(`map`, `filter`, `find`, `findIndex`, `findLast`, `findLastIndex`, `some`, `every`, `reduce`,
`reduceRight`, `flatMap`, `sort`, `toSorted`, and `Array.from`'s mapper) when the callback never
returns a value.

**Why:** these methods are defined by what the callback returns. A callback that only has side
effects makes `map` produce an array of `undefined`, `filter` and `find` match nothing, `sort`
leave the order unspecified, and `reduce` lose its accumulator. It usually means a `return` was
forgotten when an arrow function was converted to a block body — or that `forEach` was meant.

**Fix:** return the value, or use `forEach` / a `for … of` loop when only the side effects matter.

```js
const names = users.map((u) => {
  u.name.trim();             // flagged: nothing is returned
});

const names = users.map((u) => {
  return u.name.trim();      // compliant
});

users.forEach((u) => { log(u); }); // compliant: forEach ignores return values
```

Async and generator callbacks, callbacks that always throw, and callbacks passed in any position
other than the first are not checked. Empty callbacks (`() => {}`), `map` callbacks that take no
parameter (mapping an event or observable to void), and callbacks whose second parameter is named
`cb`, `callback`, `done`, or `next` (node-style async iterators such as `es.map`) are deliberate
and not reported either.

### js/array-type

**Array types should use one consistent syntax**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions, typescript

Flags array types written in the other of the two equivalent forms, `T[]` and `Array<T>`
(and `readonly T[]` / `ReadonlyArray<T>`). With the default `array-simple` style, a simple
element type (a keyword, a type name without type arguments, `this`, or an array of those) uses
the short form and anything else uses the generic form.

**Why:** both forms mean the same, and mixing them makes the same type look different from one
line to the next. The short form reads best for simple elements, while for unions, functions or
object types the suffix `[]` is easy to misread (`string | number[]` is not
`(string | number)[]`) and the generic form makes the element type explicit.

**Fix:** rewrite the type in the configured form.

```ts
let names: Array<string>;          // flagged: string[]
let ids: (string | number)[];      // flagged: Array<string | number>
let rows: readonly Row[];          // compliant
let handlers: Array<() => void>;   // compliant
```

Not reported: `Array` or `ReadonlyArray` names declared in the file itself, and references with
no type argument or more than one. Only TypeScript files are checked.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `default` | `"array-simple"` | Style for array types: `array` (always `T[]`), `generic` (always `Array<T>`) or `array-simple` (`T[]` when `T` is a simple name or keyword, `Array<T>` otherwise). |
| `readonly` | `""` | Style for read-only array types (`readonly T[]` / `ReadonlyArray<T>`); empty = same as `default`. |

### js/assert-argument-order

**Assertions should take the actual value in the actual slot**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: tests, confusing

Flags equality assertions whose *actual* slot holds a literal while the *expected* slot holds
the computed value: `expect(3).toBe(items.length)`, `assert.equal('ready', job.state)`.

**Why:** the assertion passes or fails the same way when the two are swapped, but its failure
message does not: `expected 7 to be 3` names the computed value as the expectation and the
constant as what the code produced, which sends the reader looking for the bug in the wrong
place.

**Fix:** put the computed value in the actual slot: the argument of `expect(…)`, the first argument
of `assert.equal` and its relatives.

```js
expect(3).toBe(items.length);                // flagged
assert.strictEqual('ready', job.state);      // flagged

expect(items.length).toBe(3);                // compliant
assert.strictEqual(job.state, 'ready');      // compliant
```

Checked: `expect(…)` with `toBe`, `toEqual` and `toStrictEqual`, and `assert.equal`, `strictEqual`,
`deepEqual`, `deepStrictEqual`, `notEqual`, `notStrictEqual`, `notDeepEqual` and
`notDeepStrictEqual` (Node's `assert` and chai's `assert`, which both take the actual value
first). Literals are strings, numbers and templates without placeholders. Not reported: both
sides literal, `true`/`false`/`null`/`undefined` (other matchers fit better), a computed side
named like an expectation (`expected`, `expectedTotal`), and files that are not tests.

### js/assignment-in-operand

**Assignments and increments should not be nested in other expressions**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: confusing, side-effects

Flags increments, decrements and assignments buried inside a larger expression (a call
argument, an operand of another operator, an array or object literal, a template, a ternary
branch) instead of standing as statements of their own.

**Why:** an expression that both computes a value and changes a variable makes the reader track
two things at once, and the order of those effects is easy to misread (`items[i++]` against
`items[++i]`, `f(a = b)` against `f(a === b)`). Such code is also fragile to edit: moving or
duplicating the expression moves or duplicates the side effect.

**Fix:** perform the update in its own statement, before or after the expression.

```js
process(items[index], index++);          // flagged
total = base + (delta = compute());      // flagged

process(items[index], index);            // compliant
index++;
delta = compute();
total = base + delta;
```

Not reported: statements (`i++;`, `a = b, c = d;`), `for` loop headers, arrow functions whose body
is the assignment (`el => (this.ref = el)`, `() => count++`), the value of a `return`, a variable,
field or parameter initializer, an assignment's right side (`n = count++`, `a = b = 0`, left to
`js/no-multi-assign`), operands of `void` (`void (x = y)` discards the value on purpose),
assignments anywhere in the condition of an `if`, `while`, `do` or `for`
(left to `js/no-cond-assign`), and increments or decrements in a loop condition
(`while (n-- > 0)`). An increment or decrement inside an `if` condition (`if (++attempts > max)`)
is reported: whether the test sees the old or the new value is exactly what readers get wrong. By
default `++`/`--` used directly as an array index (`buf[pos++] = b`) are accepted as idiomatic;
set `report_array_index` to report them too. Off by default: short-circuit updates
(`ready && (done = true)`), id counters (`{ id: next++ }`) and reference counts
(`if (--refs === 0)`) are common JavaScript idioms, so the rule suits focused clean-ups.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `report_array_index` | `false` | Also report `++`/`--` used directly as an array index (`buf[pos++] = b`). |

### js/async-in-constructor

**Constructors should not start asynchronous work they cannot wait for** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: async, design

Flags constructors that start asynchronous work which sets up the object's own state, and drop
the promise: a call to an `async` method of the same class, an `async` arrow function called on the
spot, or a `.then(…)` callback, that assigns a field of `this` once the constructor has returned.

**Why:** a constructor cannot wait. The caller receives the object while the work is still
running, so its first method calls see fields that are not set yet, and nothing tells the caller
when the object becomes usable. A failure of the dropped promise is not attached to anything: it
surfaces as an unhandled rejection far from the code that created the object, or is lost.

**Fix:** move the asynchronous part into a static factory (`static async create()`) that awaits it
before handing out the instance, or into an explicit `init()` the caller awaits. If the object must
start the work itself, keep the promise in a field (`this.ready = this.load()`) so callers can wait
for it and failures stay attached.

```js
class Catalog {
  constructor(api) {
    this.api = api;
    this.load();                              // flagged: items arrive later
  }
  async load() { this.items = await this.api.items(); }
  get size() { return this.items.length; }
}

class Catalog {
  static async create(api) {                  // compliant
    const catalog = new Catalog(api);
    await catalog.load();
    return catalog;
  }
  constructor(api) { this.api = api; }
  async load() { this.items = await this.api.items(); }
  get size() { return this.items.length; }
}
```

Only work that leaves the object half initialized is reported: the async method (or the `then`
callback) assigns a field of `this` after its first `await`, the class reads that field elsewhere,
and nothing prepares the object for the field being missing (no initializer, no optional or
`undefined`-typed declaration, no assignment in the constructor, no parameter property): a class
that starts with `ready = false` and checks it has planned for the wait. Background work that does not set up the object's own state (refreshing something
else, reporting telemetry) is left to `js/floating-promise`. Not reported either: promises kept in
a variable or field, chains ending in `.catch(…)` or given a rejection handler, calls marked as
deliberately detached with `void`, and work started in callbacks created by the constructor (event
listeners, timers), which run later.

### js/ban-ts-comment

**TypeScript directive comments should not disable type checking**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: typescript, suppression

Flags TypeScript comment directives that switch type checking off:
`@ts-ignore`, `@ts-nocheck` at the top of a file, and `@ts-expect-error` without an explanation.

**Why:** these directives silence the compiler instead of fixing the problem it reports.
`@ts-ignore` hides *every* error on the next line — including ones introduced later — and keeps
doing so after the original problem is gone. `@ts-nocheck` disables checking for the whole file.
`@ts-expect-error` is safer (it fails once the error disappears), but without a reason nobody can
tell later whether it is still needed.

**Fix:** correct the types. If a suppression is unavoidable, use `@ts-expect-error` followed by a
short explanation (at least `minimum_description_length` characters, default 3).

The directives are recognised the way TypeScript reads them: at the start of a `//` comment, or on
the last line of a `/* */` comment. Mentions elsewhere in a comment are not flagged.

```ts
// @ts-ignore
legacy.call(1);                          // flagged (the comment above)

// @ts-expect-error
legacy.call(1);                          // flagged: no explanation

// @ts-expect-error: the typings of `legacy` miss the numeric overload
legacy.call(1);                          // compliant
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `minimum_description_length` | `3` | Minimum number of characters explaining a `@ts-expect-error` comment. |

### js/bitwise-on-booleans

**Bitwise operators should not be applied to booleans** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious, typo

Flags the bitwise operators `&` and `|` applied to two boolean expressions, such as
`a > 0 & b > 0` or `!done | failed === true`.

**Why:** with two comparisons on either side, `&` and `|` are almost always a typo for `&&` and
`||`. The result is the number `0` or `1` rather than `true`/`false` (so `=== true` checks and
TypeScript's types disagree), both sides are always evaluated, and the precedence differs from the
logical operators, which makes mixed expressions evaluate in a surprising order.

**Fix:** use `&&` or `||`.

```js
if (x > 0 & y > 0) {}          // flagged
if (isOpen | count === 0) {}   // not reported: `isOpen` is not visibly a boolean

if (x > 0 && y > 0) {}         // compliant
const bits = flags & MASK;     // compliant: numbers
```

Only operands that are visibly booleans are considered: comparisons, `!x`, `instanceof`, `in`,
boolean literals, and `&&`/`||` combinations of those. `^` is not reported (it is a common way to
write "exactly one of" for booleans), nor are the compound forms `|=` and `&=`.

### js/block-scoped-var

**Variables declared with var should not be used outside the block that declares them**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: confusing, es2015

Flags a `var` declared inside a block (an `if`, a loop, a `switch`, a plain `{ }`) that is used
outside that block.

**Why:** `var` ignores blocks: the variable belongs to the whole function, and exists (as
`undefined`) before and after the block. Code that reads it outside the block depends on hoisting
— it sees `undefined` when the block did not run, or the value from the last loop iteration —
which readers rarely expect and which breaks as soon as the declaration is changed to `let` or
`const`.

**Fix:** declare the variable before the block, at the level where it is used, preferably with
`let` or `const`.

```js
if (user) {
  var name = user.name;
}
greet(name);                 // flagged: `name` is undefined when there is no user

let name;                    // compliant
if (user) {
  name = user.name;
}
greet(name);
```

A variable declared with `var` in several blocks counts as declared in each of them. Off by default:
this is a style rule for code that still uses `var`.

### js/callback-extra-arguments

**Functions passed to array methods should not receive the index as an argument they misread** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious, callback

Flags a function passed by name to an array method (`map`, `flatMap`, `filter`, `some`,
`every`, `find`, `findIndex`, `findLast`, `findLastIndex`, or the mapping function of
`Array.from`) when the function gives a meaning to the extra arguments the method passes: the
element's index and the array. The functions checked are those whose second parameter changes
their result:

* `parseInt` and `Number.parseInt` take the index as the radix: `['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt)`
  is `[1, NaN, NaN]` (radix 0 means 10, radix 1 is invalid, `'3'` is not a digit in base 2);
* `String.fromCharCode` and `String.fromCodePoint` turn the index and the array into extra
  characters (or throw a `RangeError`);
* `Array.from` takes the index as its mapping function and throws a `TypeError`.

**Why:** the array methods call their callback with three arguments, not one. A function written
to be called with one argument and an optional second one silently uses the index for that
second one. The code looks right, works for the first element, and goes wrong from the second.

**Fix:** pass an arrow function that forwards only the element (and an explicit radix).

```js
const ids = parts.map(parseInt);                   // flagged
const ids = parts.map((part) => parseInt(part, 10)); // compliant

const codes = values.map(Number);                  // compliant: Number takes one argument
```

Functions that take only one argument (`Number`, `parseFloat`, `Boolean`, `String`, `Math.abs`)
are not reported, nor is `forEach` (the result is not used). With the `local_functions` parameter,
the rule also reports functions of the same file whose second parameter is optional
(`function format(value, digits = 2)` passed as `values.map(format)`), unless that parameter is
named like an index (`i`, `index`, `idx`, `key`, …) or the function reads
`arguments`; `forEach` counts there.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `local_functions` | `false` | Also report functions of the same file whose second parameter is optional (has a default value or `?`) and is not named like an index. |

### js/cognitive-complexity

**Cognitive complexity of functions should not be too high**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: brain-overload, complexity

Flags functions whose **cognitive complexity** is above a threshold (default 15).

Cognitive complexity estimates how hard a function is to *read*: every break in linear flow (`if`, loops, `catch`, `switch`, jumps, chains of mixed boolean operators) adds a point, and nesting makes each of those cost more. Functions that score high take longer to understand, are harder to test exhaustively and attract bugs when changed.

**How to fix:** extract well-named helper functions, return early instead of nesting, and replace flag-driven branching with separate functions or polymorphism.

```text
// Noncompliant: nested branches inside loops inside conditions
process(items) {
  if (enabled) {
    for (item of items) {
      if (item.ok) { if (item.big) { ... } else { ... } }
    }
  }
}

// Compliant: guard clause plus a helper
process(items) {
  if (!enabled) return;
  for (item of items) handle(item);
}
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `threshold` | `15` | Highest cognitive complexity allowed for one function |

### js/collapsible-if

**Nested 'if' statements without 'else' should be merged**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: readability

Flags an `if` statement without `else` whose body is nothing but another `if`
without `else`.

**Why:** two nested conditions that both have to hold are one condition. The extra level of
nesting makes the code harder to read and pushes the real work further to the right.

**Fix:** combine the conditions with `&&`. Nothing is reported when either `if` has an `else`
(merging would change which branch runs), or when a comment precedes the inner `if` (it usually
documents the outer condition).

```js
if (user) {
  if (user.isAdmin) {        // flagged
    grant();
  }
}

if (user && user.isAdmin) {  // compliant
  grant();
}
```

### js/commented-out-code

**Commented-out code should be removed**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: unused, clutter

Flags runs of comments that contain source code rather than prose.

Commented-out code distracts readers, rots as the surrounding code changes and is never compiled or tested. Version control already keeps old code.

**How to fix:** delete it. If it documents an alternative, describe the alternative in prose.

```text
// Noncompliant
// int retries = 3;
// connect(host, retries);
connect(host);
```

Documentation comments, license headers and tool directives are ignored.

### js/consistent-return

**A function should either always or never return a value**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: confusing, suspicious

Flags a predicate, a function whose `return` statements give booleans (`true`, `false`, a
comparison, a negation), that also uses a bare `return;`, which gives `undefined`.

**Why:** the function answers a yes/no question on every path but one, where it answers nothing.
`undefined` happens to be falsy, so a plain `if (isValid(x))` still works, but any caller that
compares the answer (`=== false`), stores it, serializes it or counts it gets a third value that
nobody meant to produce. A bare `return` in a predicate is almost always an early exit written
before the function started returning booleans.

**Fix:** return the boolean that the early exit means, usually `return false;`.

```js
function isEditable(doc) {
  if (!doc) {
    return;                          // flagged: undefined instead of false
  }
  return !doc.readOnly && doc.owner === user;
}

function isEditable(doc) {
  if (!doc) {
    return false;                    // compliant
  }
  return !doc.readOnly && doc.owner === user;
}
```

Only predicates are checked: in other functions a bare `return` often means "no result" on
purpose, which the rule cannot tell from a slip. Not reported either: functions that also return
`undefined` explicitly (a deliberate third state), functions passed directly as arguments
(callbacks, whose callers define what a missing value means), getters, setters, constructors,
generators, and TypeScript functions whose declared return type includes `undefined`, `void`,
`any` or `unknown`.

### js/consistent-type-assertions

**Type assertions should use 'as' and should not be applied to object literals**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, typescript

Flags two forms of TypeScript type assertion: the angle-bracket form `<T>value`, and an
assertion applied to an object literal (`{ … } as T`).

**Why:** `<T>value` and `value as T` mean the same, but the angle-bracket form cannot be used
in `.tsx` files (it reads as JSX) and is easy to mistake for a generic call; one form keeps the
code uniform. An assertion on an object literal is worse than an annotation: `as T` tells the
compiler to trust the author, so a missing property or a misspelled one is not reported, while
`const config: T = { … }` checks the literal against `T` and catches both.

**Fix:** write `value as T`; give object literals a type annotation (or use `satisfies T`).

```ts
const el = <HTMLInputElement>event.target;      // flagged
const el = event.target as HTMLInputElement;    // compliant

const options = { retries: 3 } as Options;      // flagged: a typo in a key would go unnoticed
const options: Options = { retries: 3 };        // compliant
const options = { retries: 3 } satisfies Options; // compliant
```

Not reported: `as const` (and `<const>` is reported only as the angle-bracket form), assertions
to `any`, `unknown` or `never`, object-literal assertions in test files (partial test doubles;
the `object_literal_in_tests` parameter turns them on), and an object literal whose assertion
is itself asserted again (that is a double assertion, see `js/double-assertion`). The
`allow_as_argument` parameter accepts object literals asserted directly as a call argument.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `angle_bracket` | `true` | Report the angle-bracket form `<T>value` (use `value as T`). |
| `object_literal` | `true` | Report type assertions on object literals (`{ … } as T`; annotate instead). |
| `object_literal_in_tests` | `false` | Also report object-literal assertions in test files, where partial objects asserted to a full type are the usual way to build test doubles. |
| `allow_as_argument` | `false` | Accept an object-literal assertion passed directly as a call or `new` argument, where no annotation can be written. |

### js/const-enum

**Enums should not be declared 'const'**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, typescript

Flags `const enum` declarations.

**Why:** a `const enum` has no runtime object: the compiler replaces every use with the literal
value, which needs the declaration's source at compile time. Tools that compile one file at a
time (Babel, esbuild, SWC, `isolatedModules`, type stripping in Node) cannot do that across
files, so exported `const enum`s either fail to build or silently produce different code than
`tsc`. Their values also disappear from the emitted JavaScript, which surprises callers that
look the enum up at run time.

**Fix:** use a regular `enum`, or a `const` object with `as const` and a union type of its
values.

```ts
export const enum Direction { Up, Down }     // flagged
export enum Direction { Up, Down }           // compliant
export const Direction = { Up: 0, Down: 1 } as const;   // compliant
```

Not reported: `declare const enum` and enums inside `declare module` / `declare global` (they
describe code that exists elsewhere).

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

### js/constant-length-comparison

**Lengths should not be compared in a way that is always true or always false** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags comparisons of a `.length` with zero or a negative number that can only have one outcome:
`list.length >= 0` (always true), `text.length < 0` (always false), `items.length > -1`.

**Why:** a length is never negative, so these conditions do not test anything. They are almost
always a slip for the real check — `>= 0` written for `> 0` ("is not empty"), or `< 0` copied from
an `indexOf(…) < 0` test — and the guarded code then runs (or is skipped) for empty collections
too.

**Fix:** write the intended test, usually `list.length > 0` or `list.length === 0`.

```js
if (items.length >= 0) render(items);  // flagged: always true
if (name.length < 0) return;           // flagged: always false

if (items.length > 0) render(items);   // compliant
```

Only lengths of values that look like a string or a collection are checked: array and string
literals, results of calls such as `split`, `filter`, or `Object.keys`, and names that are plural
(`items`, `configFiles`) or say what they hold (`list`, `text`, `path`, `args`, …). A record
whose `length` is an ordinary number field (`edit.length`, `range.length`) may well be negative
and is not reported. Neither are optional chains (`list?.length >= 0` is false when `list` is
missing) nor comparisons passed to a call (`assert(buf.length >= 0, 'not array-like')` checks
that a `length` exists at all). The `.size` of a `Map` or `Set` is checked the same way when the
collection is visibly one: a `new Map(…)` / `new Set(…)` expression, or a variable declared in the
file with such a value and never reassigned (`seen.size < 0`).

### js/constructor-super

**Constructors of derived classes should call super()** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: classes, suspicious

Flags the constructor of a derived class (`class A extends B`) that never calls `super()`.

**Why:** in a class that extends another, `this` does not exist until `super()` has run. A
constructor that never calls it throws a `ReferenceError` as soon as the class is instantiated —
even if the constructor itself never touches `this`, because the object has to be returned when the
constructor ends. This typically happens when a class gains an `extends` clause later, or when the
`super()` call is lost in a refactoring.

**Fix:** call `super(…)` (with the arguments the base class expects) before using `this`, or
remove the `extends` clause if the class does not need a base class.

```js
class Admin extends User {
  constructor(name) {           // flagged: never calls super()
    this.name = name;
  }
}

class Admin extends User {
  constructor(name) {
    super(name);                // compliant
    this.role = 'admin';
  }
}
```

Not reported: constructors that return a value of their own (`return Object.create(…)`, which is
allowed without `super()`), classes that extend `null`, and constructor signatures without a body
(TypeScript overloads and declarations). A `super()` call inside an arrow function in the
constructor counts.

Also flagged: a second `super()` call that runs unconditionally after a first one (both are
statements of the constructor body, outside any `if`, loop, `try`, or callback). The object is
already initialized by the first call, so the second throws a `ReferenceError`.

```js
class Admin extends User {
  constructor(name) {
    super(name);
    this.role = 'admin';
    super(name);                // flagged: throws, `this` is already initialized
  }
}
```

### js/curly

**Control statement bodies should be wrapped in braces**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions, braces

Flags `if`, `else`, `for`, `while` and `do` bodies that are a single statement without braces.

**Why:** a braceless body ends after one statement, whatever the indentation says. A second
line added later at the same indentation looks like part of the body but always runs, and a
nested `if` without braces can take the wrong `else`. Always writing the braces removes that
trap and keeps diffs small when a body grows.

**Fix:** wrap the body in `{ … }`.

```js
if (user)
  greet(user);              // flagged
for (const item of items) process(item);   // flagged: loops always take braces

if (user) {
  greet(user);              // compliant
}
if (!user) return;          // compliant: a one-line if without else
```

By default an `if` that has no `else` and fits on one line (condition and statement) may skip
the braces, as the common style guides allow; the `single_line_if` parameter turns that off. An
`else if` chain is not reported for the `else` (the nested `if` is checked itself), but an `if`
in such a chain gets no one-line exemption.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `single_line_if` | `true` | Accept an `if` without `else` written entirely on one line without braces (`if (done) return;`); when false every body needs braces. |

### js/cyclomatic-complexity

**Cyclomatic complexity of functions should not be too high**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: complexity

Flags functions whose **cyclomatic complexity** (the number of independent paths through the function) is above a threshold (default 10). Off by default: cognitive complexity usually reflects readability better.

Many independent paths mean many test cases are needed to cover the function and a higher chance that some combination is wrong.

**How to fix:** split the function by responsibility, use lookup tables instead of long `if`/`else` chains, and move validation into dedicated helpers.

```text
// Noncompliant: one function handling every case
price(order) { if (a) ... else if (b) ... else if (c) ... /* 12 more */ }

// Compliant
price(order) { return RULES[order.kind](order); }
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `threshold` | `10` | Highest cyclomatic complexity allowed for one function |

### js/deep-nesting

**Control flow should not be nested too deeply**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: brain-overload, complexity

Flags functions whose control-flow statements (`if`, loops, `switch`, `try`) are nested more than `max` levels deep (default 4).

Deeply nested code forces readers to keep many conditions in mind at once and hides the main path of the function.

**How to fix:** use guard clauses and early returns, invert conditions, and extract inner blocks into helper functions.

```text
// Noncompliant
if (a) { for (...) { if (b) { while (c) { if (d) { ... } } } } }

// Compliant
if (!a) return;
for (...) processItem(...);
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max` | `4` | Deepest nesting of control-flow statements allowed in one function |

### js/default-case

**'switch' statements should have a 'default' clause**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: convention, conventions

Flags `switch` statements that have no `default` clause.

**Why:** without `default`, a value that matches no case is silently ignored. Writing the clause
(even one that throws or only holds a comment) shows that the other values were considered.

**Fix:** add a `default:` clause. If falling through is intended, a comment saying `no default`
after the last case documents it and silences this rule.

```js
switch (kind) {         // flagged
  case 'a': runA(); break;
  case 'b': runB(); break;
}

switch (kind) {         // compliant
  case 'a': runA(); break;
  default: throw new Error(`Unknown kind ${kind}`);
}

switch (kind) {         // compliant
  case 'a': runA(); break;
  // no default
}
```

### js/default-case-last

**The 'default' clause should be the last clause of a 'switch'** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions

Flags a `default` clause that is not the last clause of its `switch`.

**Why:** readers expect `default` at the end, as the case that handles "everything else". A
`default` in the middle still only runs when no other case matches, but it can fall through into
the cases below it, so the control flow differs from what its position suggests, and a case
added after it is easy to overlook.

**Fix:** move the `default` clause to the end (adding a `break` where it relied on falling
through).

```js
switch (kind) {
  default: handleOther(); break;     // flagged
  case 'a': handleA(); break;
}

switch (kind) {
  case 'a': handleA(); break;
  default: handleOther();            // compliant
}
```

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

### js/default-export

**Modules should use named exports instead of a default export** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: conventions, modules

Flags default exports: `export default …` and `export { name as default }`.

**Why:** a default export has no name of its own, so every importer picks one: the same module
ends up imported as `Button`, `Btn` and `PrimaryButton` in different files, searches for the name
miss some uses, and renaming the export does not update its importers. Named exports keep one
name everywhere, are completed by editors, and make a typo in an import a compile error instead
of a silently different binding.

**Fix:** export the declaration by name and import it with braces.

```js
export default function formatDate(d) { … }        // flagged
import formatDate from './format-date';

export function formatDate(d) { … }                // compliant
import { formatDate } from './format-date';
```

Not reported: files where a framework or tool requires a default export, configured by the
`allow_files` parameter (by default configuration files such as `*.config.*` and `.*rc.*`,
Storybook stories and Cosmos fixtures, Yeoman `generators` and codemod `transforms` folders, the
page, route and layout files and folders of Next.js, Remix, Nuxt, Gatsby and Docusaurus, and
`__mocks__` folders), `export default` objects that define a `fetch`
handler (the module format of worker runtimes), and code inside `declare module`.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `allow_files` | `"*.config.*, *.conf.*, .*rc.*, *.workspace.*, ormconfig.*, *.stories.*, *.story.*, *.fixture.*, .storybook/, generators/, transforms/, pages/, routes/, layouts/, middleware/, plugins/, server/, theme/, __mocks__/, page.*, layout.*, template.*, loading.*, error.*, global-error.*, not-found.*, default.*, opengraph-image.*, twitter-image.*, icon.*, apple-icon.*, sitemap.*, robots.*, manifest.*, root.*, entry.client.*, entry.server.*"` | Comma-separated patterns of files where default exports are accepted: an entry ending in `/` is a folder name anywhere in the path (`pages/`), any other entry is matched against the file name with `*` as a wildcard (`*.config.*`). The defa… |

### js/default-param-last

**Parameters with defaults should come after the required ones**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: api-design, confusing

Flags a parameter with a default value that comes before a parameter without one.

**Why:** a default only applies when the argument is missing or `undefined`, and arguments are
matched by position. A caller that wants the default of an early parameter but has to pass a later
one must write `undefined` explicitly (`connect(undefined, options)`), which is easy to get wrong
and hides what the default was meant to do. Most of the time the defaulted parameter was simply
meant to be optional and belongs at the end.

**Fix:** move the parameters with defaults after the required ones, or group the optional values
in an options object.

```js
function connect(port = 8080, host) { … }        // flagged
connect(undefined, 'db.local');

function connect(host, port = 8080) { … }        // compliant
connect('db.local');
```

Not reported: parameters followed only by optional (`b?: T`), defaulted, rest or decorated
parameters (dependency injection fills decorated parameters, callers do not),
functions passed directly as arguments (their parameter order is set by the caller, as in
`reduce((acc = 0, x) => …)`), and Redux-style reducers (`(state = initial, action) => …`), whose
signature the store dictates.

### js/double-assertion

**Type assertions should not be chained through 'any'**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: conventions, typescript

Flags a type assertion chained through `any` or `{}` to reach another type:
`value as any as T`, `value as {} as T`, `<T><any>value`.

**Why:** TypeScript refuses an assertion between unrelated types; going through `any` forces it
through and silences every check on the way. When such a conversion is really needed (test
doubles, data from an untyped source), `unknown` is the honest intermediate: it says "no type
information here" without switching off checking around it, and it stands out in review. `any`
in the middle additionally lets the value leak as `any` if the outer assertion is later removed.

**Fix:** fix the types so a single assertion (or none) is enough; otherwise go through
`unknown`, ideally after a runtime check.

```ts
const user = payload as any as User;        // flagged
const user = payload as unknown as User;    // compliant (reported only with unknown=true)
const user = parseUser(payload);            // better: validate at runtime
```

With the `unknown` parameter the rule also reports `as unknown as T`, for code bases that want
every double assertion reviewed. Not reported: `as const` as the outer assertion.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `unknown` | `false` | Also report double assertions through `unknown` (`value as unknown as T`). |

### js/duplicated-block

**Blocks of code should not be duplicated**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: duplication

Flags blocks of code that appear, token for token, in more than one place (by default at least 100 tokens spanning at least 10 lines; literal values and whitespace are ignored).

Duplicated code must be changed in several places at once; sooner or later one copy is missed and the copies drift apart.

**How to fix:** extract the shared logic into a function, class or module and call it from each place.

### js/empty-collection-access

**Collections that are never filled should not be read** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags reads of a local array, `Map`, or `Set` that starts empty and is never filled: iterating
it, looking something up, or checking its length.

**Why:** a collection that nothing ever adds to is always empty, so every read of it has a fixed
answer — loops over it never run, lookups always miss, `.length` is always `0`. This is usually a
bug: the code that was supposed to fill it was lost, or it fills a different variable with a
similar name.

**Fix:** fill the collection where intended (often a missing `push`/`set`), read the right
variable, or remove the dead code.

```js
const seen = new Set();
for (const user of users) {
  if (seen.has(user.id)) continue;   // flagged: seen is always empty
  notify(user);
}

const seen = new Set();
for (const user of users) {
  if (seen.has(user.id)) continue;   // compliant
  seen.add(user.id);
  notify(user);
}
```

Only `const`/`let` variables declared inside a function and initialized with `[]` or
`new Map()`/`new Set()`/`new Array()` without arguments are considered, and only when every use
is visible: a collection that is exported, passed to a function, returned, stored elsewhere,
reassigned, or used through an unknown method is not reported. Top-level constants are skipped
(an empty list there is often a placeholder filled in by hand later), and so are literals holding
a comment (usually commented-out entries). Spreading an empty list (`[...defaults, ...extra]`)
is not counted as a read: tests often pass an empty list on purpose.

### js/enum-initializers

**Enum members should not mix implicit and explicit values in a fragile way** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: typescript, enums, pitfall

Flags TypeScript enums that mix members with explicit values and members numbered implicitly
in a way that breaks when the enum changes: implicit members placed before the first explicit one
(`enum State { Idle, Busy, Done = 2 }`), and implicit members whose number coincides with an
explicit value (`enum Level { Low = 1, Medium, High = 2 }`, where `Medium` is also 2).

**Why:** an implicit member takes the number after the member before it. Implicit members in front
of explicit ones are numbered from 0 while the later values are fixed, so adding a member among
them shifts them silently and soon collides with the explicit values; two members with the same
number compare equal and one of them can no longer be told apart (in `switch`, in stored data,
in reverse lookups).

**Fix:** give every member an explicit value, or none at all.

```ts
enum State { Idle, Busy, Done = 2 }              // flagged: Idle and Busy are implicit
enum Level { Low = 1, Medium, High = 2 }         // flagged: Medium is 2 as well

enum State { Idle = 0, Busy = 1, Done = 2 }      // compliant
enum Direction { Up, Down, Left, Right }         // compliant: all implicit
enum Code { A = 100, B, C }                      // compliant: a chosen starting number
enum Order { Refresh = 10, Run, Debug, Collapse = 20, Clear } // compliant: numbered sections
```

Not reported: an explicit value followed by implicit members (a chosen starting number, or one
per section) as long as no implicit number collides with an explicit one. Collisions are only
computed for plain numeric values.

### js/eqeqeq

**Use strict equality operators**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags loose equality operators `==` and `!=`.

**Why:** loose equality converts its operands before comparing, with rules few people remember:
`'' == 0`, `'0' == false`, and `[1] == 1` are all `true`. Strict equality (`===`, `!==`) compares
without conversion, so the result is what the code says.

**Fix:** use `===` / `!==`, converting explicitly (`Number(x)`, `String(x)`) where a conversion is
really wanted.

```js
if (count == '0') {}      // flagged
if (count === 0) {}       // compliant
if (value == null) {}     // compliant: matches null and undefined (parameter `allow_null`)
if (typeof x == 'string') {} // compliant: typeof always yields a string
```

Comparisons where conversion cannot happen are not flagged: `typeof` expressions and two literals of
the same type.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `allow_null` | `true` | Allow `== null` / `!= null`, the idiom for "null or undefined". |

### js/exception-not-thrown

**Errors that are created should be thrown**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: error-handling, suspicious

Flags error objects that are created and immediately discarded: a statement consisting only of
`new Error(…)` or `new SomethingError(…)`.

**Why:** creating an error does nothing by itself. A statement like `new ValidationError('bad
input');` was almost certainly meant to be `throw new ValidationError('bad input');` — as written,
the check it guards silently lets invalid data through.

**Fix:** add the missing `throw` (or `return` the error if the caller is meant to handle it).

```js
if (!user) {
  new Error('user is required');        // flagged: created, never thrown
}

if (!user) {
  throw new Error('user is required');  // compliant
}
const err = new Error('later');         // compliant: the error is kept
```

### js/extra-arguments

**Functions should not be called with more arguments than they declare**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags calls that pass more arguments than the called function declares, when the
function is defined in the same file.

**Why:** JavaScript silently drops arguments that have no parameter, so the extra value never
reaches the function. Usually the call was written against an older or imagined signature, an
argument was put in the wrong call (`format(date, locale)` vs. `format(date), locale`), or the
function lost a parameter in a refactoring and its callers were not updated.

**Fix:** remove the extra argument, or add the missing parameter to the function.

```js
function greet(name) { return `Hello ${name}`; }

greet('Ada', 'Lovelace');   // flagged: 'greet' takes 1 parameter
greet('Ada');               // compliant
```

Only functions whose parameter list is known for sure are checked: function declarations and
`const` function expressions / arrow functions of the same file that are never reassigned or
overloaded, have no rest parameter, and never read `arguments`. Calls with spread arguments are
ignored.

### js/file-too-long

**Files should not have too many lines of code**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~60 min · Tags: brain-overload, size

Flags files with more than `max_lines` lines of code (default 1000; blank and comment-only lines are not counted).

Very large files tend to mix responsibilities, are slow to navigate and review, and cause frequent merge conflicts.

**How to fix:** split the file along its responsibilities into smaller modules or classes.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_lines` | `1000` | Most lines of code allowed in one file |

### js/fixme-comment

**FIXME, XXX and HACK comments should be resolved**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: todo

Flags comments containing `FIXME`, `XXX` or `HACK` markers.

A marker word used as placeholder text is not reported: quoted (`file name "XXX"`), as a member name (`Thread.XXX`), inside inline code or emphasis (`set<em>XXX</em>()`), or in a run of X placeholders (`XXXX XXX XX n`).
