These markers admit that the code is known to be wrong or fragile. Unlike a TODO, the current behaviour itself is suspect.

**How to fix:** correct the code and delete the marker, or track the problem in the issue tracker with enough context to fix it later.

```text
// Noncompliant
total = total * 1.1; // FIXME rounding is wrong for negative amounts
```

### js/floating-promise

**Promises should be awaited, returned, or handled**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: async, promise

Flags promises that are created and then ignored: a statement that calls an `async`
function defined in the same file, or a `.then(onFulfilled)` / `.finally(…)` chain without a
rejection handler, whose result is neither awaited, returned, nor handled.

**Why:** nothing waits for a floating promise. The code after it runs before the work finishes, and
if the promise rejects, the error is not caught by any surrounding `try`/`catch`: it surfaces as an
unhandled rejection (which terminates Node.js processes by default) or is lost entirely.

**Fix:** `await` the promise, `return` it to the caller, attach a `.catch(…)` handler (or a second
argument to `.then`), or — when running it in the background is intended — mark it with `void`.

```js
async function save(doc) { /* … */ }

save(doc);                        // flagged
fetchUser().then(render);         // flagged: rejections are not handled

await save(doc);                  // compliant
void save(doc);                   // compliant: explicitly fire-and-forget
fetchUser().then(render).catch(showError); // compliant
```

Without type information only promises whose origin is visible are checked: calls to `async`
functions declared in the same file (function declarations and never-reassigned variables holding
an `async` function), and `.then` / `.finally` chains. Chains on Cypress's `cy` object are not
promises and are ignored.

### js/for-direction

**For-loop counters should move toward the loop bound**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `for` loops whose counter moves away from the bound in the loop condition, such as
`for (let i = 0; i < n; i--)`.

**Why:** if the counter moves in the wrong direction the condition stays true, so the loop runs
until the counter overflows to `-Infinity`/`Infinity` or never ends; if the condition starts out
false the loop never runs. Either way the `++`/`--` (or `+=`/`-=`) was almost certainly
mistyped.

**Fix:** make the update move the counter toward the bound (`i++` for `<`/`<=`, `i--` for
`>`/`>=`), or fix the comparison.

```js
for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i--) {}      // flagged
for (let i = items.length - 1; i >= 0; i++) {} // flagged
for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {}      // compliant
```

Only updates with a known direction are checked: `++`, `--`, and `+=`/`-=` with a numeric
literal.

### js/for-equality-termination

**For-loop conditions should not test for equality with a bound the counter can skip** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags a `for` loop that stops when its counter becomes *equal* to the bound (`i != n`) while the
counter can jump over the bound: it is also changed inside the loop body, it moves by a step that
provably misses the bound, or it moves by a fraction.

**Why:** `i != n` only ends the loop when `i` lands exactly on `n`. A counter that is sometimes
advanced twice (skipping an escaped character, a pair of items) or that moves by 2 from an odd
distance steps over the bound and the loop runs on — reading past the end of the data, or never
ending. Fractional steps accumulate rounding errors and may never hit the bound at all.

**Fix:** use a relational test (`i < n`, `i > n`), which stops however the bound is crossed.

```js
for (let i = 0; i !== text.length; i++) {
  if (text[i] === '\\') i++;          // flagged: can skip past text.length
}
for (let i = 0; i != 9; i += 2) {}    // flagged: 0, 2, … 8, 10 never equals 9
for (let x = 0; x != 1; x += 0.1) {}  // flagged: rounding never lands on 1

for (let i = 0; i < text.length; i++) {
  if (text[i] === '\\') i++;          // compliant
}
for (let i = 0; i != n; i++) {}       // compliant: a step of 1 cannot skip the bound
```

Steps that are not literals (`i += step`) and loops whose counter is not updated arithmetically
(`node != null; node = node.next`) are not reported.

### js/for-loop-counter-misuse

**A for loop's header should govern its iteration** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: loops, confusing

Flags `for` loops whose header does not govern the loop: the update clause changes none of
the variables the condition tests, or the body assigns a new value to the loop counter.

**Why:** readers take a `for` header as the full description of the iteration: where it starts,
when it stops, how it advances. When the update advances some other variable (`j++` in a loop over
`i`), the condition never changes and the loop only ends through a `break`, or never; this is
almost always a typo. When the body reassigns the counter, the header no longer tells the truth,
and an off-by-one hides easily in the interplay of the two updates.

**Fix:** update the variable the condition tests; when the body has to move the position itself,
use a `while` loop so that all the moves are in one place.

```js
for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; j++) {   // flagged: j++ never changes i
  total += rows[i];
}

for (let i = 0; i < parts.length; i++) {
  if (parts[i] === '--') {
    i = parts.length;                     // flagged: the body moves the counter
  }
}

for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i++) {   // compliant
  total += rows[i];
}
```

Not reported: `++`, `--`, compound assignments (`i += 2`) and their long forms (`i = i + 2`) of the
counter in the body, which skip elements by a fixed step (a common parsing idiom), assignments inside nested functions,
conditions that call functions or use `this`, and conditions whose values the body changes
(writing a tested variable, calling a method on it or passing it to a function).

### js/function-too-long

**Functions should not have too many lines of code**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: brain-overload, size

Flags functions with more than `max_lines` lines of code (default 80; blank and comment-only lines are not counted).

Long functions usually do several things at once. They are harder to name, to understand and to reuse, and changes to them are riskier.

**How to fix:** extract cohesive steps into separate, well-named functions.

```text
// Noncompliant
importFile(path) { /* parse, validate, transform, save, notify — 150 lines */ }

// Compliant
importFile(path) { save(transform(validate(parse(path)))); notify(path); }
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_lines` | `80` | Most lines of code allowed in one function |

### js/getter-return

**Getters should return a value**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags getters (`get name() { … }` in classes and object literals, and `get` functions in
`Object.defineProperty` descriptors) that never return a value.

**Why:** reading the property calls the getter, and a getter without `return <value>` always
yields `undefined`. That is almost never the intent — usually the `return` was forgotten, or the
value was assigned to a variable and then dropped.

**Fix:** return the value. If the getter is meant to fail, make it `throw`.

```js
class Order {
  get total() {
    this.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0); // flagged: result is discarded
  }
}

class Order {
  get total() {
    return this.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0); // compliant
  }
}
```

Getters whose body always throws are not reported: a `throw`, a call of a same-file function that
always throws, or a test library's failing assertion that always throws (`assert.fail(…)`, also as
`t.assert.fail(…)`, `expect.fail(…)`, `should.fail(…)`, `expect.unreachable(…)`; not `t.fail(…)`,
which records a failure and returns). Also not reported: TypeScript accessor declarations without
a body, and getters that use a bare `return;` while declaring a return type that includes
`undefined` or `void`.

### js/identical-operands

**Both operands of an operator should not be the same expression**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, copy-paste

Flags logical operators, `^`, division, and remainder whose two operands are the same expression:
`a.id || a.id`, `isReady && isReady`, `size / size`, `mask ^ mask`.

**Why:** such an expression does not compute anything useful: `x || x` and `x && x` are just `x`,
`x / x` is `1`, `x % x` and `x ^ x` are `0`. Like comparing a value with itself, it is almost always a copy-paste
slip where one side should name something else (`a.id || b.id`).

**Fix:** correct the operand that was meant to differ, or simplify the expression.

```js
const name = user.nickname || user.nickname;   // flagged: probably user.fullName
if (isValid && isValid) {}                     // flagged

const name = user.nickname || user.fullName;   // compliant
```

Only side-effect-free operands (names, `this`, property accesses, and operators over those) are
compared; calls are never assumed to return the same value twice. Comparisons are covered by
`js/no-self-compare`. Not reported because they have legitimate uses: `x - x` (the finiteness test
`x - x === 0`), `x + x`, `x * x`, and `x & x` / `x | x` (a common way to truncate a number to a
32-bit integer, as in `hash = hash & hash`).

### js/ignored-call-result

**Results of string and array methods that return a new value should be used** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious, unused

Flags a statement that calls a string or array method which returns a new value and changes
nothing — `name.trim();`, `list.concat(more);`, `text.replace(/x/g, '');` — so the result is lost.

**Why:** strings are immutable, and methods such as `concat`, `slice`, or `toSorted` leave the
array alone. The statement has no effect: the author almost certainly expected the method to
update the value in place, and the code that follows still sees the old value.

**Fix:** use the result — `name = name.trim();` — or, for arrays, call the in-place method
(`push`, `sort`, `splice`).

```ts
function clean(name: string, list: number[]) {
  name.trim();               // flagged: the trimmed string is thrown away
  list.concat([4]);          // flagged
  name = name.trim();        // compliant
  list.push(4);              // compliant
}
```

Without type information only receivers that are visibly strings or arrays are checked: literals,
`String(…)`, results of other string methods on those, and variables or parameters declared with a
`string` / array type annotation or initialized with a literal and never reassigned. Methods that
take a callback (`map`, `filter`, …) are left alone, since the callback may be the point of the
call (a `replace` with a function as replacement is skipped for the same reason).

### js/immediately-returned-variable

**Values should be returned directly rather than through a temporary variable**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: redundant, readability

Flags a local variable that is declared with a value and then returned or thrown by the very
next statement, and used nowhere else.

**Why:** the variable adds a name and a line without adding information; the reader has to check
that nothing happens to it in between, only to find that nothing does.

**Fix:** return (or throw) the expression directly.

```js
const label = `${prefix}-${name}`;       // flagged
return label;

const error = new Error('closed');       // flagged
throw error;

return `${prefix}-${name}`;              // compliant
throw new Error('closed');               // compliant
```

Not reported: declarations with a type annotation (in TypeScript the annotation states or checks the
type of the value), destructuring, `using` declarations (the value is disposed of when the block
ends), function, arrow and class expressions (the variable gives them their `name`), variables used
anywhere else, and pairs separated by a comment.

### js/in-operator-misuse

**The 'in' operator should not be used on primitives or to search arrays** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags the `in` operator used on a primitive value (`'a' in 'abc'`) or used to look for a value in
an array (`'admin' in ['admin', 'owner']`).

**Why:** `in` tests whether an *object* has a *property* with that name. On a string, number or
boolean it throws a `TypeError` at run time. On an array, it checks the indexes (`'0'`, `'1'`, …)
and `length`, never the elements, so `'admin' in ['admin', 'owner']` is `false`.

**Fix:** use `includes` for membership — `['admin', 'owner'].includes(role)`,
`'abc'.includes('a')` — or a `Set`.

```js
if ('admin' in ['admin', 'owner']) {}      // flagged: always false
if ('x' in 'xyz') {}                       // flagged: throws a TypeError
if (['admin', 'owner'].includes(role)) {}  // compliant
if ('id' in record) {}                     // compliant: property test on an object
if (0 in sparse) {}                        // compliant: index test on an array
```

Arrays count when they are visible: literals, `Object.keys(…)`, `Array.from(…)`, or variables
declared or initialized as arrays. On arrays, only string literals that are not array indexes are
reported; a numeric or unknown key may be a deliberate index test.

### js/incoming-value-overwritten

**Parameters and loop or catch variables should not be overwritten before they are read** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, unused

Flags a parameter, a caught error, or a `for…of` / `for…in` loop variable that is assigned a new
value before its incoming value is ever read: `function scale(size) { size = 10; … }`.

**Why:** the value the caller passed (or the error that was caught, or the current element of the
loop) is thrown away unread. Either the assignment is a mistake — it was meant for another variable,
or it should only apply in some cases — or the parameter is not needed and callers are misled into
passing a value that has no effect.

**Fix:** assign to a new local variable, make the assignment conditional (`size ??= 10`), or remove
the parameter.

```js
function resize(image, width) {
  width = 800;                        // flagged: the width passed in is ignored
  return scale(image, width);
}

function resize(image, width = 800) { // compliant
  return scale(image, width);
}
```

Only plain assignments that are statements of the function, `catch`, or loop body itself, before
any statement that mentions the variable, are reported; an assignment that reads the old value
(`width = width || 800`) is not. Parameters of callbacks (functions passed as arguments, whose
signature the caller decides), of functions that use `arguments`, parameters read in another
parameter's default value, TypeScript parameter properties, names starting with `_`, and variables
used by nested functions are skipped.

### js/index-of-positive-check

**'indexOf' results should not be tested with '> 0'**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `indexOf` results tested with `> 0` (or `0 <`).

**Why:** `indexOf` returns `-1` when the value is missing and `0` when it is the very first
element or character. `> 0` therefore treats a match at the start as "not found" — a classic
off-by-one that only shows up for some inputs.

**Fix:** test for presence with `!== -1` (or `>= 0`), or use `includes`. If a match at position 0
really must be excluded, write it out (`index > 0` on a named variable) so readers see it is
deliberate.

```js
if (tags.indexOf('urgent') > 0) {}      // flagged: misses tags[0]

if (tags.indexOf('urgent') !== -1) {}   // compliant
if (tags.includes('urgent')) {}         // compliant
if (path.indexOf('/', 1) > 0) {}        // compliant: search starts after position 0
```

Not reported: searches for a single punctuation character (`name.indexOf(':') > 0`), which usually
mean "a separator after a non-empty prefix" on purpose, and calls with a start position.

### js/invalid-regexp

**Regular expressions built from literals should be valid**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: regex, suspicious

Flags `new RegExp(…)` and `RegExp(…)` calls whose pattern or flags, given as literals, are not a
valid regular expression.

**Why:** a regular expression literal (`/…/`) is checked when the file is parsed, but a pattern
passed as a string is only compiled when the call runs. An unbalanced bracket, a dangling
quantifier, or an unknown flag then throws a `SyntaxError` at run time — often on a rarely taken
path, long after the code shipped.

**Fix:** correct the pattern or the flags. Remember that backslashes in a string literal need
doubling (`'\\d+'`), or use a regular expression literal when the pattern is constant.

```js
new RegExp('[a-z');           // flagged: unterminated character class
new RegExp('a+', 'gg');       // flagged: duplicated flag
RegExp('(?<name>x)(?<name>y)'); // flagged: duplicated group name

new RegExp('[a-z]+', 'gi');   // compliant
new RegExp(userPattern);      // compliant: not a literal, not checked
```

Only string literals (and template literals without substitutions) are checked, and only when
`RegExp` is the global constructor.

### js/invalid-replacement-reference

**Replacement strings should only refer to existing capture groups** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: regex, suspicious

Flags replacement strings of `replace` / `replaceAll` that refer to a capture group the regular
expression does not have: `$3` when the pattern has two groups, `$1` when it has none, or
`$<name>` when no group has that name.

**Why:** a reference to a missing group is not an error. `$3` is inserted as the literal text
`$3`, and a missing `$<name>` is replaced by nothing, so the output is silently wrong. It usually
means a group was removed from the pattern (or turned into a non-capturing `(?:…)`) without
updating the replacement, or the groups were miscounted.

**Fix:** refer to an existing group, add the missing group to the pattern, or write `$$` for a
literal dollar sign.

```js
date.replace(/(\d+)-(\d+)/, '$2/$3');        // flagged: there is no group 3
text.replace(/(?:a|b)+/g, '[$1]');          // flagged: the group is non-capturing
text.replace(/(?<word>\w+)/, '<$<wrod>>');  // flagged: no group named 'wrod'

date.replace(/(\d+)-(\d+)/, '$2/$1');        // compliant
price.replace(/\d+/, '$$&');                // compliant: `$$` is a dollar sign
```

Only a regular expression literal combined with a string literal (or a template literal without
substitutions) is checked.

### js/invariant-return

**A function should not return the same value on every path** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: suspicious, confusing

Flags a function with several `return` statements that all return the same literal value
(`true`, `0`, `'ok'`, `null`, …) and that cannot end without one of them.

**Why:** separate `return` statements suggest that the function answers differently depending on
the path taken, but here every path gives the same answer, so callers testing the result test
nothing. This usually means an edit was left half done (one branch should return `false`), or the
function no longer needs a result at all.

**Fix:** return the value that each branch really means, or make the function return nothing and
update its callers.

```js
function validate(order) {          // flagged: every path returns true
  if (!order.items.length) {
    showError('empty order');
    return true;
  }
  return true;
}

function validate(order) {          // compliant
  if (!order.items.length) {
    showError('empty order');
    return false;
  }
  return true;
}
```

Only function declarations and functions assigned to a variable are checked, and only when every
use of them in the file is a call whose result is not handed on: methods, callbacks, functions passed
around as values, and functions whose result a caller returns often give a fixed value because the
calling code expects it (`return false` to cancel an event, `return true` to keep a visitor
going). Not reported: functions that can reach their end without a `return`, `return undefined`,
generators, and functions with a single `return`.

### js/invisible-character

**Source code should not contain invisible or bidirectional control characters** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: unicode, confusing, security

Flags characters in the source that a reader cannot see but the engine does:

* bidirectional control characters (U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069, U+200E, U+200F, U+061C)
  anywhere, comments included: they reorder how the text after them is displayed, so code can
  look different from what runs;
* raw zero-width characters (zero-width space and joiners, word joiner, a byte order mark inside
  the file, Hangul fillers) and raw control characters in strings, template literals, regular
  expressions and code (identifiers, the space between tokens);
* no-break spaces (U+00A0, U+202F, U+2007) and soft hyphens in code, and in literals where they
  pass for something else: on their own (a one-character string), at the start or end of the
  literal, or next to an ordinary space.

**Why:** two strings that print the same but differ by an invisible character compare unequal,
and a search for one does not find the other; an identifier holding a zero-width joiner is a
different identifier from the one it looks like; a no-break space between tokens looks like an
ordinary space; a bidirectional override can make a comment seem to end where it does not, or a
string seem to hold what it does not. None of this shows in a code review.

**Fix:** remove the character, or write it as an escape (`'\u{A0}'`), which states the intent.
In JSX text and attribute values, where escapes are not read, use an expression
(`{'\u{200B}'}`) or an HTML entity.

```js
const price = amount + ' EUR';       // flagged if this space is a raw no-break space (U+00A0)
const price = amount + '\u{A0}EUR';  // compliant
```

Not reported: escapes (`'\u{200B}'`), a byte order mark at the start of the file; a no-break
space or soft hyphen between two visible characters of a literal (`64 KB`, French spacing inside
`« »` or before `:`, a hyphenation point inside a long word), which is typography in text meant
for display, and every no-break space or soft hyphen in JSX text and attribute values; zero-width
joiners and non-joiners next to other non-ASCII characters (they join emoji into one picture, such
as a family of three, and shape Persian or Indic words); invisible characters other than
bidirectional controls in comments; and C1 control characters (U+0080 to U+009F), which appear
when a file in a legacy encoding is read as Latin-1: such files are skipped. JavaScript does not
translate `\u` escapes outside literals before parsing (unlike Java), so an escape in a comment
is just text and is not reported.

### js/jsx-key

**Elements rendered in a list should have a 'key' prop**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: react, jsx

Flags JSX elements created in a list without a `key` prop: elements of an array
literal made only of JSX, and elements returned from the callback of `.map()`, `.flatMap()`, or
`Array.from(items, callback)`.

**Why:** React identifies the children of a list by their `key`. Without it, React falls back to
the position in the list, so inserting, removing, or reordering items re-uses the wrong
component instances: state and focus jump to other rows, inputs show stale values, and more DOM
is re-created than necessary. React also logs a warning for every such list.

**Fix:** give the outermost element returned for each item a `key` that is stable and unique among
its siblings — usually an id from the data (`key={user.id}`). A fragment in a list needs the long
form `<Fragment key={…}>`, because `<>…</>` cannot take a key.

Only files that show they use React or Preact are checked — an import from a React-family package
(`react`, `preact`, `react-dom`, `next/…`, `mobx-react-lite`, …), a global `React`, or a JSX
pragma naming React — because other JSX runtimes (Solid, prompt renderers, server-side HTML
templating) have no keys. Not flagged either: elements with a spread attribute (`{...props}` may
provide the key), elements inside `React.Children.toArray(…)` (which assigns keys itself), and
arrays that also contain non-JSX values (typically tuples such as `[value, <Dialog />]` returned
from a hook).

```jsx
<ul>{users.map((user) => <li>{user.name}</li>)}</ul>             // flagged

<ul>{users.map((user) => <li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li>)}</ul> // compliant
```

### js/jsx-no-array-index-key

**Array indexes should not be used as JSX keys**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: react, jsx

Flags JSX `key` props computed only from the index parameter of an array callback
(`items.map((item, i) => <Row key={i} />)`), including `String(i)`, `i.toString()`, `` `${i}` ``,
and `'row-' + i`.

**Why:** React uses `key` to match list children between renders. An index is not tied to the item:
when items are inserted, removed, filtered, or reordered, each index now points at a different item,
so React re-uses the wrong component instances. Local state, focus, and uncontrolled input values
end up on the wrong rows, and more of the list is re-rendered than needed.

**Fix:** use a value that identifies the item itself, such as an id from the data
(`key={item.id}`). An index is acceptable only for static lists that never change order; add a
suppression comment there to document it.

```jsx
todos.map((todo, index) => <Todo key={index} {...todo} />);   // flagged
todos.map((todo) => <Todo key={todo.id} {...todo} />);        // compliant
```

Only React/Preact files are checked. Keys that combine the index with other values
(`` `${row.id}-${i}` ``) and lists built with `Array.from({ length }, …)` are not flagged.

### js/jsx-no-duplicate-props

**JSX elements should not repeat a prop**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: react, jsx, suspicious

Flags a JSX element that sets the same prop more than once
(`<input value={a} value={b} />`).

**Why:** only the last value takes effect; the earlier one is silently discarded. A repeated prop
is almost always a merge or copy-paste mistake, and the code does not do what the first value
suggests.

**Fix:** remove one of the props, or rename it to the prop that was meant. Props are compared
exactly (case-sensitive; `xlink:href` style names included). Values coming from a spread
(`{...props}`) are not considered.

```jsx
<Button type="submit" onClick={save} type="button" />  // flagged

<Button type="submit" onClick={save} />                // compliant
<Button {...defaults} type="button" />                 // compliant: overriding a spread is fine
```

### js/jsx-no-leaked-render

**Numbers should not be used as '&&' conditions in rendered JSX** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: react, suspicious

Flags conditional rendering with `&&` whose condition is a number: `{items.length && <List />}`,
`{count && <Badge />}` where `count` is declared as a number.

**Why:** `a && b` evaluates to `a` when `a` is falsy. For a number that is `0` (or `NaN`), and
unlike `false`, `null` or `undefined`, a number *is* rendered: the page shows a stray "0" where
nothing was meant to appear (in React Native, rendering it outside `<Text>` crashes the app).

**Fix:** make the condition a boolean: `items.length > 0 && …`, `!!count && …`, or use a
conditional expression `count ? <Badge /> : null`.

```jsx
{items.length && <List items={items} />}      // flagged: renders 0 for an empty list
{items.length > 0 && <List items={items} />}  // compliant
{isOpen && <Dialog />}                        // compliant: not a number
```

Operands count as numbers when they visibly are: a `.length` read, a numeric literal, arithmetic
(`a - b`, `a * b`, …), `Number(…)` / `parseInt(…)` / `parseFloat(…)`, or a variable or parameter
declared with the type `number`. Only `&&` expressions rendered as JSX children or returned from a
function are checked, not attribute values, and only in files that use React or Preact (other JSX
renderers, such as prompt builders, may not print numbers).

### js/jsx-no-unstable-key

**JSX keys should not be regenerated on every render** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: react, performance

Flags JSX `key` props computed from a fresh random or time-based value on every render:
`Math.random()`, `Date.now()`, `new Date()`, `crypto.randomUUID()`, and the id generators of the
`uuid`, `nanoid`, `cuid`, and lodash `uniqueId` packages.

**Why:** React matches elements between renders by their key. A key that changes on every render
never matches, so React throws the old element away and mounts a new one each time: local state,
focus, input contents, and scroll positions are lost, effects run again, and the whole subtree is
rebuilt — a real performance cost in lists.

**Fix:** use an id that belongs to the data (`key={item.id}`). If the data has none, create the ids
once, when the data is loaded or created, and store them with it.

```jsx
items.map((item) => <Row key={Math.random()} item={item} />); // flagged
items.map((item) => <Row key={uuid()} item={item} />);        // flagged

items.map((item) => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />);       // compliant
```

Only React/Preact files are checked, and only calls whose result is certainly new each time: the
globals above and functions imported from those packages. Forcing a remount with a random key is
reported too: change the key only when a remount is wanted (for example, from a counter in state).

### js/max-nested-functions

**Functions should not be nested too deeply**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: complexity, readability

Flags a function nested more than `max` (default 4) levels deep, counting the function itself
(with the default, a fifth function inside four enclosing ones): callback pyramids, closures
inside closures inside methods.

**Why:** every level of nesting adds a scope whose variables stay visible below it and an
indentation level the reader has to keep track of. Deep nests make it hard to see which variables
a callback captures, in which order things run, and where errors go. They usually grow one small
callback at a time, which is why a limit helps.

**Fix:** give inner callbacks names and move them out to the module or class level, pass what they
need as parameters, or flatten promise chains with `async`/`await`.

```js
load(id, (err, doc) => {                 // 1
  parse(doc, (err, tree) => {            // 2
    render(tree, (err, html) => {        // 3
      save(html, (err) => {              // 4
        notify(() => done());            // 5: flagged
      });
    });
  });
});

const doc = await load(id);              // compliant
const html = await render(await parse(doc));
await save(html);
await notify();
```

Only the outermost function past the limit is reported, once per nest. Not counted: arrow
functions whose body is a single expression (`x => x.id`), which open no block, functions called
on the spot (module wrappers such as `(function () { … })()`), functions handed to such a
wrapper (UMD module factories: `(function (factory) { … }(function ($) { … }))`), AMD
`define(…)` factories, and in test files the callbacks of `describe`, `it`, `test` and their
hooks.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max` | `4` | Maximum depth of nested functions (the function itself counts as a level). |

### js/misleading-array-mutation

**Results of in-place array methods should not be stored as if they were copies**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `const sorted = list.sort()` (likewise `reverse`, `fill` and `copyWithin`) when `list` is used
again afterwards.

**Why:** these methods change the array in place and return that same array, not a copy.
Storing the result under a new name reads as "a sorted copy, the original stays as it was", but
both names now refer to one reordered array — every later use of the original sees the new
order, which is rarely what the code that follows expects.

**Fix:** sort a copy — `list.toSorted()`, `list.toReversed()`, `[...list].sort()` — or, if the
change in place is intended, drop the second name and keep using the original.

```js
const names = ['b', 'a'];
const sorted = names.sort();          // flagged: `names` is sorted too
render(names, sorted);

const sorted = [...names].sort();     // compliant
const sorted = names.toSorted();      // compliant
```

Only arrays the code visibly creates or declares are checked (array literals, `Array.from`,
`Object.keys`, variables or parameters with an array type), and only when the original array is
read again after the call in a way that depends on its order — `length`, `includes`, `some`,
`every`, or spreading it into an array that is sorted again do not count. `splice` is not reported:
its result is the removed elements, which is exactly what it is used for.

### js/misleading-if-layout

**An if should not be laid out as if it were an else branch** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: confusing, braces

Flags two layouts that make an `if` read differently from how it runs:

- an `if` written on the line of the closing brace of the `if` statement before it
  (`} if (…) {`): it reads like `else if`, but it is a separate statement, tested even when the
  branch above ran;
- an `else` lined up under an outer brace-less `if` while it belongs to an inner one: `else`
  always pairs with the nearest `if`, so the branch runs when the *inner* condition is false,
  not the outer one.

**Why:** both are typical slips. A missing `else` turns a chain of exclusive cases into
independent tests, so a value handled by the first branch falls into the checks of the next ones
too; an `else` indented for the wrong `if` runs in exactly the cases the reader thinks it does
not.

**Fix:** add the missing `else`, or start the second `if` on its own line if the tests really
are independent. For the `else`, put braces around the inner `if`.

```js
if (value instanceof Map) {
  handleMap(value);
} if (Array.isArray(value)) {      // flagged: meant `else if`?
  handleList(value);
}

if (user)
  if (user.admin)
    grant();
else                               // flagged: belongs to `if (user.admin)`
  login();

if (value instanceof Map) {
  handleMap(value);
} else if (Array.isArray(value)) { // compliant
  handleList(value);
}
```

For the first layout, only an `if` whose line starts with the closing brace of an `if` statement
whose last branch is a block is checked (one-line code such as minified bundles is not), and only
when some branch of that statement can run to its end: when every branch returns, throws, breaks
or continues, the second `if` behaves like `else if` anyway. A comment between the brace and the
`if` counts as a deliberate separation. For the second, the
`else` must start its line with exactly the indentation of the outer `if`, which must start its
line too, and the inner `if` must sit at another column.

### js/misleading-indentation

**Statements should not be indented as if a brace-less body guarded them** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious, confusing

Flags a statement that is indented like the body of the brace-less `if`, `else`, `for` or `while`
above it, although it is not part of that body and always runs.

**Why:** without braces, only the first statement after `if (…)` is conditional. A second
statement written at the same indentation reads as if it were guarded too — the classic way a
check or a cleanup ends up running unconditionally (or a new line is added "inside" an `if` that
does not contain it).

**Fix:** add braces if both statements belong to the body, or outdent the statement to the level
of the `if` if it is meant to run every time.

```js
if (!user)
  log('no user');
  return;             // flagged: runs every time

if (!user) {
  log('no user');
  return;             // compliant
}
```

Only a body written on its own line is checked, and the next statement must start its own line
with exactly the same indentation as that body, deeper than the header. Bodies in braces and
statements on the same line are left alone.

### js/mutable-export

**Exported bindings should not be mutable**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: conventions, modules

Flags exported bindings that can be reassigned: `export let` and `export var`, and
`export { name }` of a module-level `let` or `var` that the module assigns again.

**Why:** an ES module export is a live binding. When the exporting module reassigns it, every
importer sees the new value at some later point, which is shared mutable global state in
disguise: the value an importer reads depends on timing and import order, and importers cannot
assign it themselves. Most of the time the binding never changes and should simply be `const`;
when it does change, an explicit getter or setter function makes the change visible.

**Fix:** export a `const`, or keep the mutable variable private and export functions that read
or change it.

```js
export let currentUser = null;            // flagged
export function setUser(user) { currentUser = user; }

let currentUser = null;                   // compliant
export function getUser() { return currentUser; }
export function setUser(user) { currentUser = user; }
```

Not reported: `export { name }` of a `let` that is never assigned after its declaration (it is
constant in practice; `js/prefer-const` reports the `let`), `declare` statements and code inside
`declare module` / `declare global`.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

### js/mutable-public-static-field

**Public static fields should not hold shared mutable containers**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: design, encapsulation

Flags public `static` fields of exported TypeScript classes that are not `readonly` and hold a
mutable container: an array or object literal, or a new `Map`, `Set`, `WeakMap`, `WeakSet`,
`Array` or `Object`.

**Why:** such a field is global mutable state. Any module that imports the class can replace the
container or change its contents at any time, without validation, and every other user of the
class sees the change. Bugs caused by it are hard to trace, and tests influence each other
through it.

**Fix:** make the field `private` (or `#private`) and expose what callers need through methods;
for a constant table, make it `readonly` with a read-only type (`readonly string[]`,
`ReadonlyMap`, `as const`) or freeze it.

```ts
export class Registry {
  static handlers = new Map<string, Handler>();          // flagged
  static defaults = { retries: 3 };                      // flagged
}

export class Registry {
  private static handlers = new Map<string, Handler>();  // compliant
  static readonly DEFAULTS = Object.freeze({ retries: 3 }); // compliant
  static register(name: string, h: Handler) { Registry.handlers.set(name, h); }
}
```

Not reported: `readonly`, `private`, `protected` and `#private` fields, fields with a decorator or
`declare`, fields typed or asserted as read-only (`as const`), fields holding functions or other
values, conventional framework statics (`defaultProps`, `propTypes`, `contextTypes`,
`childContextTypes`, `styles`, `properties`, `observedAttributes`, `$inject`) and the names listed
in the `allow` parameter, classes that the module does not export, plain JavaScript files (which
have no `readonly`), and test files. Library-specific conventions (a chart library's
`defaultOption`, say) are reported by default: other modules can and do replace or change such a
shared default; list them in `allow` where a project accepts the convention.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `allow` | `""` | Comma-separated names of static fields to accept, for conventions a framework reads from the class (e.g. `defaultOption,dependencies`). |

### js/naming-convention

**Names should follow the casing convention of their kind**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, naming

Flags declared names whose casing does not match the convention of their kind: classes,
interfaces, type aliases, enums and type parameters in PascalCase; functions, methods,
variables and parameters in camelCase; `const` declarations may also use UPPER_CASE.

**Why:** in JavaScript and TypeScript the casing of a name tells the reader what it is: a type
or constructor (`UserService`), a value or function (`userService`, `loadUser`), or a fixed
module constant (`MAX_RETRIES`). Mixing conventions (`user_name` next to `userName`, a class
called `parser`) hides that signal and makes names harder to guess and to search for.

**Fix:** rename the declaration (and its uses) to the expected style.

```ts
class user_service {}                 // flagged: PascalCase expected
function load_user(user_id) {}        // flagged twice: camelCase expected
const MAX_RETRIES = 3;                // compliant: module-level constant

class UserService {}                  // compliant
function loadUser(userId) {}          // compliant
```

The styles are loose, as in common linters: camelCase starts with a lower-case letter and has
no underscore (`parseXMLDocument` is fine), PascalCase starts with an upper-case letter and has
no underscore (`URL`, `T`), UPPER_CASE has no lower-case letter; an underscore between two
digits (`draft2020_12`) or before a trailing number (`editor_1`) does not count. Leading and trailing underscores and `$` are accepted
(parameters), and each kind's styles can be configured.
Defaults that keep the rule quiet where the name is not the author's choice or where the
convention itself allows more than one style:

* functions and variables may also be PascalCase (components, constructor functions, classes
  and schemas held in variables), except a variable whose value is a plain string, number or
  boolean literal;
* `const` declarations may be UPPER_CASE whatever their value (the Google guides keep
  UPPER_CASE for module-level constants: set `local_constants` to follow them);
* names that come from elsewhere are not checked: imports and `require(...)` results,
  destructured names, variables exported from a `namespace` (read as members, like enum
  members), declarations documented as `@deprecated` (kept under their old name for
  compatibility), variables initialized from a field of the same name
  (`const user_id = body.user_id`), variables and parameters also used as shorthand properties
  (`{ user_id }`: the name is a key of some data format), object-literal keys, interface and
  type-literal members, quoted or computed keys, class fields (the `properties` parameter turns
  them on), members of classes that extend or implement another type (their names follow the
  base type), decorated members and members marked `override`, function or class expressions
  stored under a property name, anything declared with `declare` or inside `declare module` /
  `declare global`, names wrapped in double underscores (`__dirname`,
  `__webpack_public_path__`) or starting with `UNSAFE_`, top-level names of scripts (files without
  `import` or `export`, whose top-level names are globals other scripts and pages call), and
  files under a vendored, external, generated or test-fixture folder (`skip_dirs`), whose name contains
  `generated`, or that start with an `eslint-disable` comment for all rules (bindings and
  bundles copied from elsewhere);
* enum members are not checked unless `enum_members` lists the accepted styles.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `types` | `"PascalCase"` | Allowed styles for classes, interfaces, type aliases, enums and type parameters (comma-separated: camelCase, PascalCase, UPPER\_CASE, snake\_case; empty = not checked). |
| `functions` | `"camelCase, PascalCase"` | Allowed styles for named functions (PascalCase covers components and constructor functions). |
| `methods` | `"camelCase"` | Allowed styles for class methods. |
| `variables` | `"camelCase, PascalCase"` | Allowed styles for variables other than module-level constants. PascalCase is accepted only when the initial value is not a plain string, number or boolean literal. |
| `constants` | `"camelCase, PascalCase, UPPER_CASE"` | Allowed styles for `const` declarations at module (or namespace) level. PascalCase as for variables. |
| `local_constants` | `"camelCase, PascalCase, UPPER_CASE"` | Allowed styles for `const` declarations inside functions and blocks (the Google guides want camelCase there: remove UPPER\_CASE to follow them). PascalCase as for variables. |
| `pascal_case_values` | `false` | Accept PascalCase also for variables and constants whose initial value is a plain string, number or boolean literal. |
| `parameters` | `"camelCase, PascalCase"` | Allowed styles for function parameters and catch parameters. |
| `enum_members` | `""` | Allowed styles for enum members (empty = not checked: projects differ between PascalCase and UPPER\_CASE, and member names often mirror external identifiers). |
| `properties` | `""` | Allowed styles for class fields and accessors (empty = not checked: field names often mirror external data). |
| `allow` | `""` | Comma-separated names that are never reported. |
| `allow_prefixes` | `"UNSAFE_"` | Comma-separated prefixes; names starting with one are never reported (framework-reserved names such as React's `UNSAFE_` methods). |
| `skip_dirs` | `"vendor, vendors, third_party, third-party, thirdparty, external, generated, __generated__, fixtures, __fixtures__"` | Comma-separated folder names: files under such a folder are not checked (vendored or generated code, mirrors of other packages, sample code used as test input). Files whose name contains `generated` are skipped too. |
| `leading_underscore` | `true` | Accept leading underscores (`_private`, `_unused`); when false they are reported. |
| `trailing_underscore` | `true` | Accept trailing underscores (`default_`); when false they are reported. |
| `dollar` | `true` | Accept `$` in names (`$el`, `value$`); when false they are reported. |

### js/negated-comparison

**Negated equality tests should use the opposite operator**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: readability

Flags a negated equality test that the opposite operator states directly: `!(a === b)` is
`a !== b`, `!(a == b)` is `a != b`, and the reverse.

**Why:** the `!` in front of the parentheses is one more step for the reader, and it is easy to
overlook when scanning a condition. The direct operator states the condition as it is.

**Fix:** drop the `!` and the parentheses and use the opposite operator.

```js
if (!(status === 'done')) { … }     // flagged
if (status !== 'done') { … }        // compliant
```

Ordering comparisons are not reported: `!(a < b)` is not the same as `a >= b` when either side is
`NaN`, `undefined` or a value that does not convert to a number, and the rule cannot see the types.
Off by default: this is a readability preference.

### js/no-alert

**Browser dialogs 'alert', 'confirm', and 'prompt' should not be used**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: user-experience

Flags calls to the browser's blocking dialogs: `alert(…)`, `confirm(…)`, and
`prompt(…)`, also through `window.`, `self.`, or `globalThis.`.

**Why:** these dialogs freeze the page until dismissed, cannot be styled, are blocked or
suppressed in some contexts, and are often leftover debugging output.

**Fix:** use the application's own notification or modal components, or a logger for debugging.
Local functions or variables named `alert`, `confirm`, or `prompt` are not reported.

```js
alert('Saved!');                  // flagged
if (window.confirm('Delete?')) {} // flagged

notifications.info('Saved!');     // compliant
const ok = await dialog.confirm('Delete?'); // compliant
```

### js/no-array-constructor

**Array literals should be used instead of the 'Array' constructor**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: convention

Flags `Array(…)` and `new Array(…)` called with zero arguments or with two or more
arguments.

**Why:** the `Array` constructor is ambiguous: with one numeric argument it creates an empty
array of that length, with several arguments it creates an array of those elements. An array
literal always means "these elements" and is shorter.

**Fix:** use an array literal: `[]`, `[a, b]`. A single argument (`new Array(n)`, a pre-sized
array) and calls with TypeScript type arguments (`new Array<Item>()`) are not reported.

```js
const empty = new Array();      // flagged
const pair = Array(x, y);       // flagged

const empty = [];               // compliant
const pair = [x, y];            // compliant
const slots = new Array(size);  // compliant
```

### js/no-array-delete

**Array elements should not be removed with 'delete'**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `delete array[index]` on a value that is declared as an array.

**Why:** `delete` removes the property but does not shift the following elements or change
`length`. The array is left with a hole: `length` still counts it, `forEach`/`map` skip it, and
indexing it yields `undefined`. Code that meant "remove this element" silently misbehaves.

**Fix:** use `array.splice(index, 1)` to remove the element in place, or `filter` / `toSpliced` to
build a new array. To keep the slot but clear it, assign `undefined` explicitly.

The rule needs evidence that the value is an array: a local variable, parameter, or class property
with an array or tuple type annotation, or one initialized with an array literal / `new Array()` /
`Array.from()` / `Array.of()` and never reassigned.

```ts
const queue: Job[] = load();
delete queue[0];              // flagged

queue.splice(0, 1);           // compliant
const cache: Record<string, Job> = {};
delete cache[key];            // compliant: not an array
```

### js/no-async-promise-executor

**Promise executors should not be async functions**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: async, error-handling

Flags `new Promise(async (resolve, reject) => { … })` — an `async` function passed as the
executor of a promise.

**Why:** the `Promise` constructor ignores the promise returned by the executor. If the async
executor throws (or an awaited call rejects), the error goes nowhere: the new promise never
settles and the rejection is unhandled. It also signals that the wrapper is unnecessary, since an
async function already returns a promise.

**Fix:** remove the `new Promise` wrapper and use the async function directly, or make the
executor synchronous and call `reject` on errors.

```js
const data = new Promise(async (resolve) => {   // flagged
  resolve(await load());
});

const data = (async () => load())();            // compliant
const data = new Promise((resolve, reject) => { // compliant
  load().then(resolve, reject);
});
```

### js/no-case-declarations

**Lexical declarations in 'case' clauses should be wrapped in a block**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: pitfall, switch

Flags `let`, `const`, `class`, and function declarations placed directly in a
`case` or `default` clause, without braces around the clause body.

**Why:** all clauses of a `switch` share one block scope. A declaration in one clause is visible
in every other clause, but it is only initialized when its own clause runs: using the name from
another clause throws a `ReferenceError` (temporal dead zone) or sees a function that was never
meant for that branch, and declaring the same name in two clauses is a syntax error.

**Fix:** wrap the clause body in braces so the declaration gets its own scope.

```js
switch (action.type) {
  case 'add':
    const item = action.item;      // flagged
    list.push(item);
    break;
  case 'remove': {
    const index = action.index;    // compliant: the clause has its own block
    list.splice(index, 1);
    break;
  }
}
```

### js/no-code-after-done

**Assertions should not run after a test's 'done' callback is called** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: tests, suspicious

Flags assertions (and further `done` calls) that run after a callback-style test has called
`done()`: statements after `done()` in the same block, or after an `if (…) done(…)` without
`else` or `return`.

**Why:** calling `done` tells the test runner that the test is over. An assertion that runs
afterwards is no longer part of this test: when it fails, the failure is reported against
another test, turns into an unhandled error, or is lost — the test passes either way. Calling
`done` a second time is an error of its own in most runners.

**Fix:** make `done()` the last thing the test does — move the assertions before it — and
`return` after `done(error)` in error branches.

```js
it('loads', (done) => {
  load((err, data) => {
    if (err) done(err);          // flagged: execution continues below
    done();
    expect(data).toBeDefined(); // flagged: runs after the test ended
  });
});

it('loads', (done) => {
  load((err, data) => {
    if (err) return done(err);
    expect(data).toBeDefined();
    done();                     // compliant
  });
});
```

Only the first parameter of a function passed to `it`, `test`, `specify` or a
`before…`/`after…` hook counts as `done`, and only statements that contain an assertion
(`expect`, `assert`, `should`) or another `done` call are reported — plain clean-up after `done()`
is harmless.

### js/no-compare-neg-zero

**Comparisons with '-0' should use 'Object.is'**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags comparisons with negative zero, such as `x === -0` or `x < -0`.

**Why:** comparison operators treat `-0` and `+0` as the same value, so `x === -0` is also true
for `0`. Code that compares with `-0` almost always means to detect negative zero specifically,
which this comparison cannot do.

**Fix:** use `Object.is(x, -0)` to detect negative zero, or compare with `0` if the sign does not
matter.

```js
if (x === -0) {}          // flagged: also true for 0
if (Object.is(x, -0)) {}  // compliant
if (x === 0) {}           // compliant
```

### js/no-compound-case-label

**Case labels should hold a single value** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: switch, suspicious

Flags a `case` label that tries to list several values with a comma or a logical operator:
`case 'a', 'b':` or `case 'a' || 'b':`.

**Why:** a `case` compares the `switch` value with *one* value, the result of its expression. The
comma operator evaluates to its last operand, so `case 1, 2:` only matches `2`; `'a' || 'b'`
evaluates to `'a'`, so `case 'a' || 'b':` only matches `'a'`. The other values silently fall to
`default`.

**Fix:** write one `case` per value; consecutive labels share the same body.

```js
switch (key) {
  case 'Enter', 'Space':     // flagged: only matches 'Space'
    submit();
    break;
  case 'Up' || 'Down':       // flagged: only matches 'Up'
    move();
    break;
}

switch (key) {
  case 'Enter':
  case 'Space':              // compliant
    submit();
    break;
}
```

A logical operator is only reported when both operands are constants (literals, `UPPER_CASE`
names, or enum-like members such as `Keys.Up`), and never in `switch (true)`, where each `case`
holds a whole condition.

### js/no-cond-assign

**Assignments should not be used as conditions**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags an assignment used directly as the condition of an `if`, `while`, `do … while`,
`for`, or `? :` expression, unless it is wrapped in an extra pair of parentheses.

**Why:** `if (a = b)` looks almost exactly like `if (a == b)`. When a comparison was meant, the
code overwrites `a` and tests the assigned value instead — a bug that is easy to type and hard to
spot.

**Fix:** use `===` if a comparison was meant. If the assignment is intentional (a common idiom
when reading in a loop), wrap it in an extra pair of parentheses, or compare the result
explicitly.

```js
if (user = currentUser) {}                 // flagged
if (user === currentUser) {}               // compliant

while ((match = re.exec(text))) {}         // compliant: extra parentheses mark intent
while ((line = reader.next()) !== null) {} // compliant: explicit comparison
```

In a `for` header a single pair of parentheses is enough, since the header itself uses none.

### js/no-confusing-non-null-assertion

**Non-null assertions should not be placed next to an equals sign**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: typescript, confusing

Flags a non-null assertion written directly before `==`, `===`, or `=`
(`a! == b`, `a?.b! === c`, `a! = b`).

**Why:** the `!` next to the operator looks like part of it, so `a! == b` reads as `a != b` — the
exact opposite of what the code does. The assertion itself also has no effect on a comparison, and
readers of `a! = b` easily miss that this is an assignment.

**Fix:** if you meant "not equal", write `!=` / `!==`. Otherwise remove the `!`, or wrap the
operand in parentheses to make the assertion explicit.

```ts
if (user.id! == otherId) {}     // flagged: looks like `!=`
config.value! = computeValue(); // flagged

if (user.id == otherId) {}      // compliant
if (user.id != otherId) {}      // compliant: the intended "not equal"
(config.value!) = computeValue(); // compliant: the assertion is explicit
```

### js/no-console

**Console calls should be removed**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: logging

Flags calls to `console` methods (`console.log`, `console.debug`, …) outside test files.

**Why:** console output left in application code is usually leftover debugging. It clutters the
output users and operators see, may leak data, and cannot be filtered or routed like proper logging.

**Fix:** remove the call, or use the project's logger. Methods listed in the `allow` parameter (for
example `warn,error`) are accepted. A local variable or parameter named `console` is not the global
console and is not flagged. Calls inside a class that is itself a console-backed logger are not
flagged either: a class whose name ends in `Logger`, `LoggerService`, `Log` or `Console`
(`FormattedConsoleLogger`, `DebugConsole`), or that extends or implements a type named that way
(`extends AbstractLogger`, `implements ILogger`), since writing to the console is its purpose.
Other classes that merely log (`LoggingInterceptor`, `LoggerMiddleware`) are still reported.

```js
console.log('user', user);   // flagged
logger.debug('user', user);  // compliant
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `allow` | `""` | Comma-separated console methods that are allowed, e.g. `warn,error`. |

### js/no-const-assign

**Constants should not be reassigned** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags assignments, compound assignments (`+=`), and increments of a variable declared with
`const`.

**Why:** a `const` binding cannot be changed. Every such write throws a `TypeError` when it runs
(TypeScript rejects it at compile time, but plain JavaScript only fails at run time — often on a
rarely taken path).

**Fix:** declare the variable with `let` if it really must change, or assign the new value to a
different variable.

```js
const total = 0;
for (const item of items) {
  total += item.price;       // flagged: throws TypeError
}

let total = 0;               // compliant
for (const item of items) {
  total += item.price;
}
```

Changing the *contents* of a constant object or array (`list.push(x)`, `config.debug = true`) is
fine and not reported: only the binding itself is constant.

### js/no-constant-condition

**Conditions should not be constant**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `if` statements and `? :` expressions whose condition is a constant — a literal, an
object or function literal, `typeof x`, `void x`, `undefined`, or an operator applied only to such
values.

**Why:** a constant condition always takes the same branch, so the other branch is dead code.
This is usually left-over debugging (`if (false)`), a typo, or a mistaken test such as
`if (x || {})` or `if (typeof x)`, which are always true.

**Fix:** use the intended condition, or remove the dead branch and the test.

```js
if (false) { debugMode(); }      // flagged
if ([]) { handle(); }            // flagged: an array is always truthy
const v = 0 ? a : b;             // flagged
if (config.debug) { debugMode(); } // compliant
```

Loop conditions such as `while (true)` are idiomatic infinite loops and are only checked when the
`check_loops` parameter is enabled.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `check_loops` | `false` | Also check loop conditions (`while (true)`, `do … while (1)`). |

### js/no-debugger

**Debugger statements should be removed**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `debugger` statements.

**Why:** a `debugger` statement pauses execution whenever developer tools are open. It is a
debugging aid that should never reach shared code: in production it can freeze a user's page, and in
tests it can hang a run.

**Fix:** delete the statement. Use breakpoints in your editor or browser instead.

```js
function total(items) {
  debugger; // flagged
  return items.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
```

### js/no-delete-var

**delete should not be applied to variables** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `delete` applied to a plain variable name: `delete cache;`.

**Why:** `delete` removes *properties* from objects. On a variable declared with `var`, `let`,
`const`, or as a parameter it does nothing and evaluates to `false`; in strict mode and in ES
modules it is a syntax error. The author usually wanted to clear the variable or remove a property
of the object it holds.

**Fix:** assign `undefined` or `null` to release the value, or delete the property that was meant
(`delete cache[key]`).

```js
let session = load();
delete session;            // flagged: has no effect

session = null;            // compliant
delete registry[name];     // compliant: removes a property
```

Names that are declared nowhere in the file are not reported: they may be properties of the
global object (created by an assignment in another script), which `delete` does remove.

### js/no-dupe-class-members

**Class members should not be declared twice**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags class members (methods, fields, accessors) declared more than once with the same
name in the same class body.

**Why:** the later declaration silently replaces the earlier one, so one implementation is dead
code. This usually comes from a merge or copy-paste, and the surviving version may not be the one
the author expected.

**Fix:** remove or rename one of the members.

```js
class Cart {
  total() { return this.items.length; }
  total() { return sum(this.items); }   // flagged: replaces the first `total`

  get size() { return this._size; }
  set size(v) { this._size = v; }      // compliant: getter/setter pair
}
```

Static and instance members are separate namespaces. TypeScript overload signatures, abstract
members, and `declare` fields are not counted, and computed keys are compared only when they are
literals.

### js/no-dupe-disjunctions

**Regular expression alternatives should not be repeated or hidden by earlier ones** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: regex, suspicious

Flags an alternative of a regular expression that can never be the one that matches: it repeats
an earlier alternative of the same group (`/(png|jpg|png)/`), or, at the top level of the
pattern, an earlier alternative already matches its beginning (`/\r|\r\n/`).

**Why:** alternatives are tried from left to right, and the first one that matches wins. A copy
of an earlier alternative is dead weight — usually a typo for the alternative that was meant
(`jpeg`?). At the top level, where nothing follows the alternatives, a shorter alternative that is
a prefix of a later one always wins, so the longer one is never used: `/\r|\r\n/` splits Windows
line ends into two breaks (and an empty line between them), and `/Mon|Monday/` replaces only
`Mon`.

**Fix:** remove the duplicate or correct it; put longer alternatives before their prefixes
(`/\r\n|\r/`).

```js
/\.(png|jpg|png)$/     // flagged: 'png' twice
text.split(/\r|\r\n/)  // flagged: '\r\n' is never matched
/\.(png|jpe?g)$/       // compliant
text.split(/\r\n|\r/)  // compliant
```

Only regular expression literals are checked. Inside a group, a shorter alternative does not hide
a longer one (backtracking can still choose it when what follows the group fails), so that case is
not reported; the top-level case is only reported when the literal is passed directly to `split`,
`replace`, `replaceAll`, `match` or `matchAll`, or `exec` is called on it — a literal stored for
later may be spliced into a bigger pattern, and `test` or `search` give the same answer either way.

### js/no-dupe-else-if

**Conditions in an if-else-if chain should not be duplicated**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `else if` conditions that can never be true because an earlier condition of the same
`if … else if` chain already covers them.

**Why:** a branch of the chain only runs when every earlier condition was false. If an earlier
condition is the same test (or a weaker one, like `a` before `a && b`, or `a || b` before `b`), the
later branch is dead code — usually a copy-paste error where the condition was not updated.

**Fix:** correct the duplicated condition, or merge the branches.

```js
if (kind === 'a') {
  handleA();
} else if (kind === 'b') {
  handleB();
} else if (kind === 'a') {   // flagged: already handled above
  handleC();
}
```

Only conditions without side effects are compared (no calls, assignments, or `await`), and a
condition with side effects in between ends the comparison, so a chain that deliberately
re-evaluates state is not reported.

### js/no-dupe-keys

**Object literal keys should be unique**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags object literals that define the same key more than once.

**Why:** the last definition silently wins, so an earlier value is lost. This is almost always a
copy-paste mistake or a merge error. Keys are compared by their runtime name: `a`, `'a'`, and
`['a']` are the same key, and so are `1`, `1.0`, `0x1`, and `'1'`.

**Fix:** remove one of the definitions or rename the key.

```js
const config = {
  timeout: 1000,
  retries: 3,
  timeout: 5000,          // flagged: overrides the first `timeout`
};

const point = {
  get x() { return this._x; },
  set x(v) { this._x = v; }, // compliant: a getter/setter pair
};
```

Spread elements and computed keys that are not literals are ignored.

### js/no-duplicate-case

**Switch case labels should be unique**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `case` labels of a `switch` that repeat an earlier label of the same `switch`.

**Why:** `switch` runs the first matching `case`, so a repeated label can never be reached. The
duplicate is usually a copy-paste slip where the new value was not filled in, which means the
value that was meant is not handled at all.

**Fix:** change the duplicated label to the intended value, or merge the two cases.

```js
switch (action.type) {
  case 'add':
    return add(state, action);
  case 'remove':
    return remove(state, action);
  case 'add':                 // flagged: unreachable
    return reset(state);
}
```

Labels are compared by value for literals (`'a'` and `` `a` `` are the same) and by structure for
other side-effect-free expressions; labels that call functions are not compared.

### js/no-duplicate-enum-values

**Enum members should have distinct values**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: typescript, suspicious

Flags enum members initialized with the same literal value as an earlier member
of the same enum.

**Why:** enum members are meant to be distinguishable. When two members share a value, comparisons
and `switch` statements cannot tell them apart, and a reverse lookup (`Color[1]`) returns only the
last name. This is nearly always a copy-paste mistake.

**Fix:** give the member its own value. If a second name for the same value is really wanted, make
the intent explicit by referring to the first member (`Gray = Color.Grey`).

Only explicit string and number literal initializers are compared (`'a'`, `1`, `-1`, `0x1`); members
without an initializer or with computed initializers are ignored. Numeric values are not compared
in `const enum`s or in enums whose name contains `Const` (`Constants`, `LayoutConsts`): those are
typically bags of named numbers — sizes, bit masks, character codes — where equal values are
intended.

```ts
enum Status {
  Active = 1,
  Disabled = 2,
  Deleted = 2,        // flagged: same value as Disabled
}

enum Color {
  Grey = 'grey',
  Gray = Grey,        // compliant: an explicit alias
}
```

### js/no-duplicate-imports

**Imports from the same module should be merged**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: imports, redundant

Flags a second `import` declaration from the same module when the two could be written as one.

**Why:** the module is loaded once either way, but two declarations split the names taken from it
in two places. Readers have to look twice to see what the file uses from the module, edits add a
third line instead of extending the first, and merge conflicts on import lists get harder to
resolve.

**Fix:** move the names into the first declaration.

```ts
import { readFile } from 'fs';
import { writeFile } from 'fs';          // flagged

import { readFile, writeFile } from 'fs'; // compliant
```

Only declarations that fit in one are reported: a default import combines with named imports or
with a namespace import, but a namespace import cannot share a declaration with named imports, and
two default or two namespace imports cannot be merged. TypeScript `import type` declarations are
compared only with each other (a type-only default and type-only named imports cannot share one
either). Side-effect imports (`import './polyfill'`), imports with different attributes
(`with { type: 'json' }`), and imports inside different `declare module` blocks are left alone.

### js/no-duplicate-string

**String literals should not be duplicated**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: duplication

Flags a string literal that appears several times in the same file (by default:
at least 10 characters long, 3 or more times).

**Why:** a repeated literal — an error message, a setting name, an event name — has to be kept
in sync by hand. Changing one copy and forgetting another is a classic source of bugs, and the
repetition hides the fact that all these places mean the same thing.

**Fix:** define the value once as a named constant (or enum member) and use it everywhere.

Not counted: module specifiers (`import`/`export … from`, `require(…)`, `import(…)`),
directives such as `'use strict'`, property and member names (`{ 'a-b': 1 }`, `obj['key']`),
TypeScript literal types (`type Mode = 'light-theme'`), JSX attribute values, and declarations
in `declare` blocks. Test files are not checked.

```js
log('Connection refused by server');
retry('Connection refused by server');
throw new Error('Connection refused by server');   // flagged (reported at the first one)

const REFUSED = 'Connection refused by server';     // compliant
log(REFUSED);
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `min_length` | `10` | Minimum length (in characters) of a string literal to be considered. |
| `threshold` | `3` | Number of occurrences from which a literal is reported. |

### js/no-duplicated-branches

**Branches should not have identical bodies**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: duplication, suspicious

Flags branches of an `if` / `else if` chain, and cases of a `switch`, whose bodies are
identical to an earlier branch.

**Why:** two conditions leading to exactly the same code are either a copy-paste slip (one branch
was meant to be edited after pasting) or needless repetition that hides the fact that the
conditions share an outcome.

**Fix:** if the duplication is intended, merge the branches: combine the conditions with `||`, or
stack the `case` labels. Otherwise, correct the branch that was meant to differ.

```js
if (kind === 'a') {           // compliant: first occurrence
  prepare();
  render(item);
} else if (kind === 'b') {    // flagged: same body as the first branch
  prepare();
  render(item);
}

switch (kind) {
  case 'a':
  case 'b':                   // compliant: labels stacked
    prepare();
    render(item);
    break;
}
```

Only non-trivial bodies are compared: at least two statements (a closing `break` does not count),
or one statement spread over several lines. A `case` that falls through into the next one is never
compared.

### js/no-else-return

**'else' should not follow an 'if' block that returns**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: readability

Flags an `else` block that follows an `if` whose branch always ends with `return`.

**Why:** when the `if` branch returns, the code after it only runs in the other case anyway. The
`else` adds a level of nesting and makes the function's main path harder to follow.

**Fix:** remove the `else` and move its statements after the `if`. In an `if … else if … else`
chain, the final `else` is reported only when *every* branch before it returns, so removing it
cannot change behavior. `else if` itself is never reported.

```js
function sign(n) {
  if (n < 0) {
    return -1;
  } else {            // flagged
    return 1;
  }
}

function sign(n) {    // compliant
  if (n < 0) {
    return -1;
  }
  return 1;
}
```

### js/no-empty

**Blocks should not be empty**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags empty block statements: empty `if`/`else` branches, loop bodies, `try`, `catch`,
and `finally` blocks, stand-alone `{}` blocks, and `switch` statements without cases.

**Why:** an empty block usually means unfinished code, or an error that is silently swallowed (an
empty `catch`). When doing nothing *is* intended, readers cannot tell without a note.

**Fix:** add the missing code, remove the block, or put a comment inside explaining why nothing needs
to happen. A block containing a comment is not flagged. Empty function bodies are not covered by
this rule.

```js
try {
  save();
} catch (e) {}            // flagged

try {
  save();
} catch (e) {
  // Best effort: the cache is rebuilt on next start.
}                         // compliant
```

### js/no-empty-alternative

**Regular expressions should not contain stray empty alternatives** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: regex, suspicious

Flags an empty alternative in a regular expression that makes it match where it should not: a
stray `|` at the start or end of the whole pattern (`/foo|/`), or a doubled `||` between two
alternatives (`/(png||jpg)/`).

**Why:** an empty alternative matches the empty string. At the top level of the pattern it matches
at every position of every input, so `test()` is always `true` and `replace()` inserts its
replacement between all characters. Inside a group, `||` between two alternatives silently makes
the whole group optional. Both are almost always a typo — a leftover separator or a doubled pipe.
