**Fix:** remove the extra `|`; if the group really is optional, say so with `?`
(`(png|jpg)?`).

```js
/error|warning|/.test(line)    // flagged: always true
/\.(png||jpg)$/                // flagged: the extension is optional
/error|warning/.test(line)     // compliant
/\.(png|jpg)?$/                // compliant
```

An empty first or last alternative inside a group (`(|s)`, `(s|)`) is a common, deliberate way of
writing "optional" and is not reported. Only regular expression literals are checked.

### js/no-empty-character-class

**Regular expressions should not contain empty character classes** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: regex, suspicious

Flags an empty character class `[]` in a regular expression literal.

**Why:** `[]` is valid syntax but matches no character at all, so any regular expression that
requires it can never match: `/^a[]b/.test(s)` is always `false`. It usually comes from an
unescaped `]` (`/[]a]/` was meant to match `]` or `a`) or from a class whose contents were deleted.

**Fix:** put the intended characters in the class, escape a literal bracket (`/[\]a]/`), or use
`[^]` / `[\s\S]` if "any character" was meant.

```js
const tag = /<[]+>/;       // flagged: can never match
const tag = /<[^>]+>/;     // compliant
const any = /[^]/;         // compliant: the negated empty class matches any character
```

### js/no-empty-function

**Functions should not be empty**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags functions, methods, and arrow functions with an empty body `{}` that contains
no comment.

**Why:** an empty body may be unfinished work, or a deliberate no-op; the reader cannot tell
which. A short comment removes the doubt and documents why doing nothing is correct.

**Fix:** implement the function, or put a comment inside the body explaining why it is empty.
Not reported: constructors (see `js/no-useless-constructor`; TypeScript constructors with
parameter properties and `private`/`protected` constructors are meaningful), TypeScript overload
signatures and abstract methods (they have no body), arrow functions used as a parameter's
default value, functions whose name says they do nothing (`noop`), members of null objects,
mocks, and stubs (classes or objects named `Null…`, `Noop…`, `Mock…`, `Fake…`, `Stub…`,
`Dummy…`), and test files.

```js
function onError() {}           // flagged
const handlers = {
  close() {},                   // flagged
};

function onError() {
  // Errors are reported by the caller.
}                               // compliant
const noop = () => {};          // compliant: the name documents it
```

### js/no-empty-interface

**Interfaces should not be empty**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: typescript, redundant

Flags interfaces that declare no members and extend at most one other type.

**Why:** an empty interface `interface Empty {}` accepts almost any value (it is the same as `{}`),
which is rarely what the author meant. An empty interface that only extends a single type,
`interface Props extends BaseProps {}`, is just another name for that type and adds a declaration
readers must look up.

**Fix:** remove the interface and use the existing type, or write a type alias
(`type Props = BaseProps`). If members are coming later, add them now or leave the interface out
until they exist.

Not flagged: interfaces that extend two or more types (they combine them), interfaces merged with
another declaration of the same name (class/interface merging is a deliberate pattern), interfaces
inside `declare module` / `declare global` blocks (module augmentation), and interfaces whose body
contains a comment explaining why they are empty.

```ts
interface Options {}                         // flagged
interface ButtonProps extends BaseProps {}   // flagged

type ButtonProps = BaseProps;                // compliant
interface Both extends First, Second {}      // compliant: combines two types
```

The same goes for the empty object type `{}` written as the type of a variable, parameter,
property, or return value, or as a type alias: `{}` does not mean "an empty object" but "any value
except `null` and `undefined`" — strings and numbers included. Use `object` for "some object",
`unknown` for "anything", or `Record<string, never>` for "an object with no properties". `{}` is
not reported where it is a deliberate tool: in constraints and intersections (`T extends {}`,
`T & {}`, meaning "not nullish"), directly as a type argument or type-parameter default, and inside
conditional or mapped types. As a member of a union inside a type argument (`Ref<Task | {}>`) it
is reported: the union then accepts any value that is not null or undefined, which defeats the
other members.

```ts
function save(options: {}) {}                // flagged
type Props = {};                             // flagged
function save(options: Record<string, never>) {} // compliant
type NonNullish<T> = T & {};                 // compliant
```

### js/no-empty-pattern

**Destructuring patterns should not be empty**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags destructuring patterns that bind nothing: `const {} = obj`, `const [] = list`,
`function f({}) {}`, or a nested `{ a: {} }`.

**Why:** an empty pattern declares no variables, so it has no effect beyond checking that the
value is not `null`/`undefined`. It usually comes from a typo — `{ a: {} }` where a default value
`{ a = {} }` was meant — or from a refactoring that removed the last binding.

**Fix:** name the values you need, use a default value (`{ a = {} }`), or remove the pattern.

```js
const { settings: {} } = config;   // flagged: binds nothing
const { settings = {} } = config;  // compliant: default value
function render({ title }) {}      // compliant
```

An empty object pattern as the first parameter of a function that takes more parameters, or of a
callback passed to `test(…)`, `it(…)` or their hooks (`test.beforeAll(async ({}, testInfo) => …)`),
is not reported: test runners such as Playwright read the fixtures a test needs from that first
parameter and require it to be a destructuring pattern even when it names none.

### js/no-eval

**Strings should not be evaluated as code**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: security

Flags code that compiles strings at run time: `eval(…)`, `Function(…)` /
`new Function(…)`, and `setTimeout` / `setInterval` called with a string instead of a function
(also through `window.`, `self.`, or `globalThis.`).

**Why:** evaluating strings as code opens the door to code injection when any part of the string
comes from outside, defeats static analysis, minification, and Content Security Policies, and is
slow.

**Fix:** use a function (`setTimeout(() => tick(), 100)`), a lookup object instead of building
names dynamically, or `JSON.parse` for data. Local functions named `eval` or `Function` are not
reported; `setTimeout` is only reported when its first argument is visibly a string.

```js
eval('run' + step + '()');              // flagged
const add = new Function('a', 'b', 'return a + b');   // flagged
setTimeout('refresh()', 1000);          // flagged

steps[step]();                          // compliant
setTimeout(refresh, 1000);              // compliant
```

### js/no-ex-assign

**Catch clause parameters should not be reassigned**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: error-handling

Flags assignments to the parameter of a `catch` clause (`catch (e) { e = … }`).

**Why:** after the assignment, the caught exception is gone: later code in the handler — logging,
rethrowing, cleanup decisions — works with the replacement instead, and the original stack trace
and message are lost. Readers also expect the catch parameter to be the thrown value.

**Fix:** store the derived value in a new variable.

```js
try { run(); } catch (err) {
  err = new Error('run failed');           // flagged: original error lost
  throw err;
}

try { run(); } catch (err) {
  throw new Error('run failed', { cause: err }); // compliant
}
```

### js/no-exclusive-tests

**Focused tests should not be committed**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: tests, suspicious

Flags focused tests in test files: `.only` on `describe`, `it`, `test`, `context`,
`suite`, or `specify` (including `test.only.each`), and the Jasmine shortcuts `fdescribe` and `fit`.

**Why:** focusing a test is a debugging aid. When it is committed, the runner quietly executes only
the focused tests and skips everything else in the file (or the whole run), so the suite keeps
passing while most of it no longer runs. Failures go unnoticed until someone removes the marker.

**Fix:** remove `.only` (or rename `fit` / `fdescribe` back to `it` / `describe`) before committing.

```js
describe.only('cart', () => {});   // flagged
it.only('adds an item', () => {});  // flagged
fit('removes an item', () => {});   // flagged

describe('cart', () => {});         // compliant
it('adds an item', () => {});       // compliant
```

Only files recognised as tests are checked, and only when the test function is the global one or
is imported (from Jest, Vitest, Mocha, Playwright, …).

### js/no-explicit-any

**Avoid the any type**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: typescript

Flags explicit `any` in TypeScript type positions.

Off by default; turn it on if your team forbids `any`. Many TypeScript code bases allow it on
purpose (in tests, at untyped library boundaries, while migrating from JavaScript), and there it
would be most of a first scan's findings. `mote migrate --from eslint` and `mote init
--from eslint` turn it on when the ESLint configuration enables
`@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any`, directly or through typescript-eslint's `recommended`,
`strict` or `all` configurations.

**Why:** `any` switches the type checker off for everything the value touches: property accesses,
calls, and assignments are all accepted, and the lack of checking spreads to whatever the value flows
into. Bugs the compiler would have caught reach runtime.

**Fix:** use the real type, a generic type parameter, or `unknown` (which forces a check before use).

```ts
function parse(input: any) {}        // flagged
const data = JSON.parse(text) as any; // flagged

function parse(input: string) {}     // compliant
function first<T>(items: T[]): T {}  // compliant
function handle(value: unknown) {}   // compliant
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ignore_rest_args` | `false` | Allow `any` in the type of a rest parameter (`...args: any[]`). |

### js/no-extend-native

**Built-in prototypes should not be extended**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: pitfall, globals

Flags code that adds or replaces properties on the prototypes of built-in objects:
`Array.prototype.last = …`, `Object.defineProperty(String.prototype, 'x', …)`,
`Object.assign(Date.prototype, {…})`.

**Why:** a built-in prototype is shared by every script in the process or page, so the change
leaks into code that did not ask for it: libraries iterating with `for…in` suddenly see the new
property, two packages adding the same name overwrite each other, and when the language later
gains a method of that name (as happened with `Array.prototype.flatten`, renamed `flat` because of
this) the old definition breaks code relying on the standard one.

**Fix:** write a plain helper function (`last(array)`), or a subclass, instead of patching the
built-in.

```js
Array.prototype.last = function () {          // flagged
  return this[this.length - 1];
};

export function last(array) {                 // compliant
  return array[array.length - 1];
}

if (!Array.prototype.at) {                    // compliant: a guarded polyfill
  Array.prototype.at = function (i) { /* … */ };
}
```

Only the global ECMAScript constructors are checked (`Object`, `Array`, `String`, `Number`,
`Function`, `Promise`, `Map`, `Date`, `RegExp`, the error types, typed arrays, …); a local
variable of the same name is not a built-in. Not reported: polyfills guarded by a test that
mentions the property (`if (!Array.prototype.at)`, `if (!('at' in Array.prototype))`,
`X.prototype.at = X.prototype.at || …`, `X.prototype.at ??= …`), and putting back a property saved
earlier from the same place, as test cleanup does (`Object.defineProperty(Array.prototype, 'at',
saved)` where `saved` only ever holds `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Array.prototype, 'at')`, or
`Array.prototype.at = originalAt` where `originalAt` only ever holds `Array.prototype.at`); the
temporary override itself is still reported.

### js/no-extra-boolean-cast

**Redundant boolean conversions should be removed**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: redundant

Flags `!!x` and `Boolean(x)` where the result is used in a place that already
converts its value to a boolean: the condition of `if`, `while`, `do … while`, `for`, or `?:`,
the operand of `!`, and the argument of `Boolean(…)`.

**Why:** those contexts test truthiness anyway, so the conversion is noise that makes the
condition longer and suggests the author was unsure how it works.

**Fix:** remove the double negation or the `Boolean` call. Keep them where a real boolean value
is needed, such as a return value, an assignment, or a property.

```js
if (!!user) {}              // flagged
while (Boolean(next)) {}    // flagged

if (user) {}                // compliant
const hasUser = !!user;     // compliant: stores a boolean
```

### js/no-extra-non-null-assertion

**Non-null assertions should not be doubled or combined with optional chaining**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: typescript, suspicious

Flags non-null assertions that are redundant or contradict the code around them:
a doubled assertion (`value!!`) and an assertion immediately followed by optional chaining
(`value!?.name`, `callback!?.()`).

**Why:** a second `!` adds nothing, and `!` followed by `?.` says two opposite things at once — "this
is never nullish" and "this may be nullish". Usually one of them is a typo or a leftover from an
edit, and a reader cannot tell which behaviour was intended.

**Fix:** keep a single `!`, or — when the value really can be missing — drop the `!` and keep the
optional chaining.

```ts
const size = cache!!.size;      // flagged
const name = user!?.name;       // flagged
onDone!?.();                    // flagged

const size = cache!.size;       // compliant
const name = user?.name;        // compliant
```

### js/no-extraneous-class

**Classes should not be used as namespaces for static members**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: conventions, classes

Flags classes that only hold static members and are used as a namespace.

**Why:** a class whose members are all `static` is never meant to be instantiated: it only groups
functions and constants under a name, which is what a module already does. The class adds a
constructor nobody should call, `this` inside its methods refers to the class (and breaks when a
method is passed around as a callback), and bundlers cannot drop the members that are not used.

**Fix:** turn the static members into exported functions and constants of the module; callers
can still group them with `import * as name from '…'`.

```ts
export class StringUtils {                    // flagged
  static capitalize(s: string) { return s[0].toUpperCase() + s.slice(1); }
  static readonly SEPARATOR = '-';
}

export function capitalize(s: string) { return s[0].toUpperCase() + s.slice(1); }
export const SEPARATOR = '-';                 // compliant
```

A constructor that is private, protected or empty does not count as an instance member (it is
the usual way to block instantiation). Not reported: classes that extend or implement another
type, decorated classes and classes with decorated members (frameworks register and
instantiate them), abstract classes (meant to be extended), empty classes (often used as tokens
or markers), classes merged with an interface or namespace of the same name, classes the same
file uses other than by reading a member (passed as a value such as `imports: [LoggerModule]`,
extended, instantiated or used as a type), and `declare` classes.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

### js/no-fallthrough

**Switch cases should not fall through unintentionally**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `switch` cases that run into the next case because they do not end with `break`,
`return`, `throw`, or `continue`.

**Why:** falling through is legal but rarely intended; a forgotten `break` makes the next case's
code run too, which is a classic source of subtle bugs. When falling through *is* intended, readers
need to be told.

**Fix:** end the case with `break` (or `return`/`throw`), or — if the fall-through is deliberate —
put a comment such as `// falls through` right before the next case.

```js
switch (level) {
  case 'debug':
    enableTracing();
  case 'info':               // flagged: 'debug' falls into 'info'
    enableLogging();
    break;
  case 'warn':
    notify();
    // falls through
  case 'error':              // compliant: documented
    alert();
}
```

Empty cases that share a body (`case 'a': case 'b': …`) are fine, and so are comments such as
`// fall through`, `/* fallthrough */`, `// no break`, or `// intentionally …` between the two cases.
Cases ending in an infinite loop, a nested `switch`, `process.exit()`, `assert(false)`, or a call
whose name says it never returns (`fail…`, `throw…`, `assertNever…`, `unreachable…`) are not
reported. The finding is reported on the case that is fallen into.

### js/no-for-in-array

**Arrays should not be iterated with 'for…in'** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `for (… in …)` loops over an array: an array literal, `Object.keys(…)` /
`Object.values(…)` / `Object.entries(…)`, `Array.from(…)`, or a variable declared or initialized as
an array.

**Why:** `for…in` walks the *property names* of an object, as strings. Over an array it yields
`'0'`, `'1'`, … instead of the elements — `for (const key in Object.keys(obj))` gives the indexes
of the key list, not the keys — plus any enumerable property added to the array or to
`Array.prototype`, and skips the holes of sparse arrays. Index arithmetic on the string keys
(`key + 1`) concatenates instead of adding.

**Fix:** use `for…of` for the elements (`for (const key of Object.keys(obj))`), `forEach`, or a
counting loop for the indexes.

```js
for (const key in Object.keys(options)) {}  // flagged: '0', '1', …
for (const i in [1, 2, 3]) {}               // flagged
for (const key of Object.keys(options)) {}  // compliant
for (const key in options) {}               // compliant: an object
```

Arrays are only recognized when that is visible in the file: without type information, a `for…in`
over a parameter or a call result is not reported. A loop whose key is only used to index the same
array (`for (const i in list) use(list[i])`) works despite the string keys and is not reported
either.

### js/no-func-assign

**Function declarations should not be reassigned**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags assignments to the name of a function declaration (`function f() {}` … `f = …`),
including the name of a named function expression inside its own body.

**Why:** overwriting a declared function replaces it for every caller, which is rarely intended
and very hard to follow; usually the assignment was meant for a different variable. Assigning to
the name of a named function expression from inside it silently does nothing in sloppy mode and
throws in strict mode.

**Fix:** assign to a separate variable. If the function really needs to be swappable, declare it
with `let` (`let handler = function () {}`) so the intent is explicit.

```js
function handler() {}
handler = () => {};         // flagged

let handler = function () {};
handler = () => {};         // compliant: an ordinary variable
```

### js/no-global-assign

**Built-in globals should not be reassigned** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags assignments to built-in globals of the language: `undefined = 0`, `NaN = …`,
`Object = …`, `Promise = MyPromise`, `JSON = …`, and the other standard objects and functions
(also `window` and `document` in browsers).

**Why:** `undefined`, `NaN`, `Infinity`, `window`, and `document` cannot be changed: the assignment
is silently ignored in sloppy code and throws in strict code. Replacing a standard object such as
`Object`, `Array`, or `Promise` changes it for every script and library on the page, which breaks
code far away from the assignment. It is usually a missing declaration (`let Map = …` was meant)
or a typo.

**Fix:** declare a local variable with another name (or with `let`/`const` if a local was meant).

```js
Promise = CustomPromise;          // flagged: replaces Promise everywhere
undefined = null;                 // flagged: has no effect, or throws

const TaskPromise = CustomPromise; // compliant
```

Not reported: names declared in the file (they are not the globals), and polyfills that assign only
when the built-in is missing (`if (typeof Promise === 'undefined') Promise = …`, `Map = Map || …`).

### js/no-identical-functions

**Functions should not have identical implementations**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: duplication

Flags a function, method, or arrow function whose body is identical to the body of
another function in the same file. Bodies are compared structurally, so formatting, comments,
quote style, and optional semicolons or parentheses do not matter. Only bodies whose statements
span at least 3 lines (`min_lines`) are considered, and two closures only count as identical when
their names refer to the same variables (callbacks capturing different loop variables are not
interchangeable). Bodies that consist of a single `throw` ("not supported" stubs) and test files
are not checked.

**Why:** duplicated logic has to be fixed and changed in several places; sooner or later the
copies drift apart and one of them keeps the bug.

**Fix:** keep one implementation and call it from the other place, or extract the shared body
into a helper that both use.

```js
function totalPrice(items) {
  let sum = 0;
  for (const i of items) sum += i.price * i.qty;
  return sum;
}
function orderValue(items) {        // flagged: same body as totalPrice
  let sum = 0;
  for (const i of items) sum += i.price * i.qty;
  return sum;
}

const orderValue = totalPrice;      // compliant
```

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `min_lines` | `3` | Minimum number of lines spanned by a body's statements. |

### js/no-import-assign

**Imported bindings should not be reassigned** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: modules, suspicious

Flags writes to an imported binding (`import { count } from './a'; count = 1;`) and to a
property of a namespace import (`import * as utils from './u'; utils.helper = …;`).

**Why:** ES module imports are live, read-only views of the exporting module's bindings, and a
namespace object is sealed. Assigning to either throws a `TypeError` in a real ES module runtime.
Code that seems to work today usually does so only because a bundler or test runner turned the
module into CommonJS — it breaks as soon as it runs as native ESM.

**Fix:** copy the value into a local variable and change that, or have the exporting module
provide a function that updates its own state. To replace a module's functions in tests, use the
test framework's module mocking instead of assigning to the namespace object.

```js
import { retries } from './config.js';
retries = 5;                     // flagged: throws TypeError

import * as fs from 'node:fs';
fs.readFile = fakeReadFile;      // flagged: namespace objects are read-only

import { retries } from './config.js';
let attempts = retries;          // compliant
attempts = 5;
```

Writes to properties of a *named* or default import (`config.debug = true`) are allowed: they
change the imported object, not the binding. Namespace property writes in test files are not
reported, because many test setups compile modules to CommonJS on purpose to allow monkey-patching.

### js/no-inferrable-types

**Types that are inferred from a literal initializer should not be written out**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: typescript, redundant, conventions

Flags explicit primitive type annotations on variables, parameters with a default
value, and class properties whose initializer is a literal of exactly that type
(`let count: number = 0`).

**Why:** TypeScript infers `number` from `0`, `string` from `'x'`, `boolean` from `true`, and so on.
Writing the type as well only repeats what the initializer already says, adds noise to every
declaration, and must be kept in sync by hand.

**Fix:** remove the annotation and let the type be inferred.

Covered pairs: `string` with a string or template literal; `number` with a numeric literal (also
`-1`, `Infinity`, `NaN`); `boolean` with `true`, `false`, or `!expr`; `bigint` with a bigint
literal; `symbol` with `Symbol()`; `RegExp` with a regular-expression literal. `readonly` and
optional class properties are not flagged (there the annotation changes the inferred type), nor are
`null`/`undefined` annotations (without strict null checks they would widen to `any`).

```ts
let retries: number = 3;                 // flagged
function greet(name: string = 'world') {} // flagged
class Timer { private running: boolean = false; } // flagged

let retries = 3;                         // compliant
let mode: 'fast' | 'slow' = 'fast';      // compliant: a narrower type than inferred
class Timer { readonly limit: number = 5; } // compliant: would infer the literal type 5
```

### js/no-infinite-loop

**Loops with a constant true condition should have a reachable exit** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags a `while (true)`, `do … while (true)` or `for (;;)` loop that contains no way out: no
`break` or `continue` that leaves it, no `return`, no `throw`, and no call to `process.exit`.

**Why:** a loop whose condition is always true only ends through a statement inside it. When there
is none, the loop spins forever and — JavaScript being single-threaded — freezes the page or the
server with it. The usual cause is a forgotten `break`, a `continue` written where a `break` was
meant, or an exit condition that was refactored away.

**Fix:** add the missing exit (`break`, `return`, `throw`), or write the real stop condition in the
loop header.

```js
while (true) {                  // flagged: nothing leaves the loop
  const job = queue.shift();
  if (!job) continue;
  run(job);
}

while (true) {                  // compliant
  const job = queue.shift();
  if (!job) break;
  run(job);
}
```

Deliberate endless loops are left alone: loops in generators (they pause at each `yield`), loops
that `await` (polling or worker loops that yield to the event loop), and loops inside a
`try … catch` of the same function (they end by an exception thrown from a call). Unlike
`js/no-constant-condition` with `check_loops`, which reports every constant loop condition, this
rule only reports loops that cannot end.

### js/no-labels

**Labeled statements should not be used**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: confusing, control-flow

Flags labeled statements (`outer: for (…)`), on loops and on any other statement.

**Why:** labels exist for `break label` and `continue label` jumps across several levels of
nesting. The reader has to find the label to know where execution continues, and the nesting that
made the jump necessary is a readability problem of its own. A label on a block or an `if`, where
`break label` acts as a local `goto`, is rarer still and surprises most readers.

**Fix:** move the nested loops into a function and `return` from it, or use array methods that
stop early (`some`, `find`), or restructure the condition.

```js
search:                                  // flagged
for (const row of rows) {
  for (const cell of row) {
    if (cell.matches(query)) {
      found = cell;
      break search;
    }
  }
}

found = findFirstMatch(rows, query);     // compliant: the inner loops `return cell`
```

Not reported: `name: Identifier;` in JavaScript files, which is a type annotation written in the
wrong language rather than a label.

### js/no-lone-blocks

**Nested blocks should not be redundant**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: redundant

Flags stand-alone `{ … }` blocks nested directly in another block, a function
body, or the top level, when they do not declare anything scoped to the block.

**Why:** since `var` and plain statements ignore block boundaries, such a block does not create
any scope; it only adds indentation and suggests a structure (a missing `if`, a lost loop) that is
not there.

**Fix:** remove the braces, or turn the block into a function if it groups a distinct step.
Blocks that declare `let`, `const`, `class`, functions, or TypeScript types are compliant (the
block limits their scope), as are labeled blocks, the single block of a `case` clause, and
blocks directly preceded by a comment (a named section of a long function). Empty
blocks are left to `js/no-empty`.

```js
function run() {
  prepare();
  {                  // flagged
    execute();
  }
  {                  // compliant: limits the scope of `tmp`
    const tmp = load();
    use(tmp);
  }
}
```

### js/no-lonely-if

**An 'if' should not be the only statement of an 'else' block**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: readability

Flags an `else` block whose only statement is an `if` statement.

**Why:** `else { if (…) … }` adds a level of braces and indentation for nothing; `else if` says
the same thing and keeps the chain flat and easy to scan.

**Fix:** merge the block into an `else if`.

```js
if (a) {
  run();
} else {
  if (b) {          // flagged
    stop();
  }
}

if (a) {            // compliant
  run();
} else if (b) {
  stop();
}
```

### js/no-loop-func

**Functions scheduled from a loop should not capture a variable shared by all iterations** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: closure, async

Flags a function created inside a loop and scheduled to run later — a timer, a promise
callback, an event handler, a function stored in an array or a property — that reads a loop
variable shared by all iterations: a `var` declared in the loop, or an outer variable that the
loop keeps updating.

**Why:** a `var` (or a variable declared outside the loop) is one binding for the whole loop, not
one per iteration. Functions that run after the loop has moved on all see its *final* value: every
handler reports the last index, every timer processes the last item.

**Fix:** declare the loop variable with `let` or `const` in the loop head or body (each iteration
then gets its own binding), or pass the current value to the callback explicitly.

```js
for (var i = 0; i < buttons.length; i++) {
  buttons[i].addEventListener('click', () => select(i)); // flagged: every button selects the last index
}

for (let i = 0; i < buttons.length; i++) {
  buttons[i].addEventListener('click', () => select(i)); // compliant: one `i` per iteration
}
```

Only functions whose call is visibly deferred are checked: passed to `setTimeout`, `setInterval`,
`setImmediate`, `requestAnimationFrame`, `requestIdleCallback`, `queueMicrotask`, or
`process.nextTick`, to `.then` / `.catch` / `.finally`, to `.addEventListener` / `.on` / `.once` /
`.one` / `.subscribe`, to `.push` / `.unshift`, assigned to a property (`el.onclick = …`), or given
as an `on…` JSX prop. Callbacks that run at once (`forEach`, `map`, `new Promise(…)`) are not
reported, and neither are functions whose scheduling is awaited, yielded, or returned, or that are
followed by a statement ending the loop (`break`, `return`, `throw`). Loop variables declared with
`let` or `const` are safe.

### js/no-loss-of-precision

**Number literals should not lose precision**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags number literals whose written value cannot be stored exactly as a JavaScript number
(a 64-bit float), so the program silently uses a different value.

**Why:** numbers have about 15–17 significant decimal digits and exact integers only up to
2^53. `9007199254740993` becomes `9007199254740992`, `1.0000000000000001` becomes `1`, and `1e400`
becomes `Infinity`. The source then claims a value the program never sees — typically an ID,
a timestamp, or a constant copied from another language.

**Fix:** use a `BigInt` (`9007199254740993n`) or a string for large identifiers, or write the
value with the precision a number can actually hold.

```js
const id = 9007199254740993;     // flagged: stored as 9007199254740992
const id = 9007199254740993n;    // compliant: BigInt
const ratio = 0.1;               // compliant: 0.1 reads back as 0.1
```

A literal is accepted when rounding the stored number to the digits that were written gives back
exactly those digits. A fraction written with 17 or more significant digits — a constant copied
from a table with more precision than any double holds (`0.0640568928626056260850430826`) — is
accepted too, since storing the nearest double (still 15–17 digits) is the expected outcome,
unless rounding visibly changes the value: it collapses to a short number (`1.0000000000000001`
becomes `1`) or changes magnitude (`9.99999999999999999999` becomes `10`). Integers beyond 2^53
are always reported.

### js/no-magic-numbers

**Numbers should be named constants**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: readability, conventions

Flags numeric literals ("magic numbers") used directly in expressions, conditions and calls
instead of through a named constant.

**Why:** a bare `86400` or `0.075` says nothing about what it means, and when the same value
appears in several places, changing it means finding every copy, and not changing an unrelated
literal that happens to have the same value.

**Fix:** give the value a name: a module-level `const`, a `static readonly` field, or an enum
member.

```js
if (retries > 5) { setTimeout(poll, 86400000); }     // flagged: 5 and 86400000

const MAX_RETRIES = 5;
const ONE_DAY_MS = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
if (retries > MAX_RETRIES) { setTimeout(poll, ONE_DAY_MS); }   // compliant
```

Not reported: the numbers listed in `ignore` (default `-1, 0, 1, 2`); a literal that is the whole
value given to a name (a variable, a class field, an object property, an assignment target, a
default parameter, a JSX attribute, or the state created by a one-argument call such as
`ref(10)` or `useState(5)`); entries of array literals that are themselves named, turned into a
`Map` or `Set` that is named, or iterated by `for … of` (data tables); any literal in the
initializer of a module-level `const`, a `static` or `readonly` class field, or an enum member;
array indexes; literals in types and decorators; the radix of `parseInt(s, 16)` and
`n.toString(16)`; and test files. Off by default: the rule is useful for focused clean-ups but
noisy on most code bases.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ignore` | `"-1,0,1,2"` | Comma-separated numbers that are never reported (compared by value, so `1` also accepts `1.0` and `0x1`). |

### js/no-misleading-character-class

**Character classes should not contain characters made of several code points** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: regex, suspicious

Flags a character class (`[…]`) that lists a character made of several code points as if it
were one: an emoji or other character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane without the `u` flag,
a letter followed by a combining accent, an emoji with a skin-tone modifier or variation selector,
a flag (two regional indicators), or an emoji sequence joined with zero-width joiners.

**Why:** a character class matches exactly one code point (one UTF-16 unit without the `u`
flag). Listing a multi-part character spreads its parts over the class: `/^[👍]$/` without `u`
matches half of the emoji and never the whole, `[é]` written as `e` + accent also matches a bare
accent, and `[🇫🇷]` matches either half of any flag.

**Fix:** add the `u` (or `v`) flag for characters outside the BMP; for sequences, use an
alternation instead of a class (`(?:👍🏽|👍)`), or with the `v` flag `[\q{👍🏽}]`.

```js
/^[👍]$/.test(s)        // flagged: two code units without the u flag
/[é]/                   // flagged when written as e + U+0301 (combining acute)
/^[👍]$/u.test(s)       // compliant
/^(?:👍🏽|👍)$/u         // compliant
```

Ranges (such as the common `[\u0300-\u036f]` for stripping accents) and marks listed without a
base character are not reported. Only regular expression literals are checked.

### js/no-misused-new

**Constructors should be declared correctly**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: typescript, suspicious

Flags constructor declarations in the wrong place: a `constructor` method in an
interface, a construct signature `new (): I` in an interface `I` that returns the interface itself,
and a bodiless class method named `new` that returns the class.

**Why:** these look like constructors but are not. `constructor()` in an interface declares an
ordinary method that happens to be called "constructor". `new (): I` inside `interface I` says that
instances of `I` can themselves be called with `new` to produce another `I` — almost never true. A
class method `new(): C` is a normal method named `new`, not the class constructor. The type checker
accepts all three, so the mistake only shows up when the declared shape does not match reality.

**Fix:** declare constructors in classes with `constructor(...)`. To describe a constructor
function, put the construct signature on a separate type describing the class itself
(`interface WidgetConstructor { new (): Widget }`).

```ts
interface Widget {
  new (): Widget;          // flagged
  constructor(): void;     // flagged
}

interface WidgetConstructor {
  new (): Widget;          // compliant: constructs a different type
}
class Widget {
  constructor() {}         // compliant
}
```

### js/no-misused-promises

**Promises should not be used as conditions, spread, or given to callbacks that ignore them** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: async, promise

Flags promises used where a plain value is expected: a call of an `async` function tested as a
condition, spread into an array or object, or an `async` callback given to an array method that
expects a plain answer (`filter`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `findIndex`, `sort`) or ignores what
the callback returns (`forEach`).

**Why:** a promise is an object, so it is always truthy: `if (isAllowed(user))` is true even when
`isAllowed` resolves to `false`, and `list.filter(async (x) => check(x))` keeps every element.
Spreading a promise copies nothing (`{ ...load() }`) or throws (`[...load()]`). `forEach` does not
wait for an `async` callback: the code after the loop runs before the callbacks finish, and their
rejections are not handled.

**Fix:** `await` the promise first (`if (await isAllowed(user))`), resolve the values before
filtering (`const flags = await Promise.all(list.map(check))`), and replace
`forEach(async …)` with a `for…of` loop that awaits, or with `await Promise.all(list.map(async …))`.

```js
async function isAllowed(user) { /* … */ }

if (isAllowed(user)) grant();                    // flagged: always true
items.forEach(async (item) => await save(item)); // flagged: nothing waits for the saves

if (await isAllowed(user)) grant();              // compliant
for (const item of items) await save(item);      // compliant
```

Without type information only visible promises are checked: calls of `async` functions declared
in the same file (and never reassigned), and `async` function literals passed as callbacks.

### js/no-mixed-enums

**Enums should not mix string and number members**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: typescript, confusing

Flags enums that mix string members with numeric members.

**Why:** numeric and string enum members behave differently at runtime: numeric members get a
reverse mapping (`Kind[0] === 'A'`) and accept arbitrary numbers where the enum type is expected,
string members do neither. Code iterating over the enum (`Object.values(Kind)`) or validating input
must then deal with both kinds, which is an easy source of bugs. A mixed enum is usually an
accident, such as a member added later with the wrong kind of value.

**Fix:** make all members strings or all members numbers. If both are needed, split the enum.

Members without an initializer count as numbers. When any initializer is not a plain literal (a
reference or a computed expression) the enum is not checked, because its kind cannot be known
without type information. `const enum`s and `declare enum`s are not checked either: they leave no
enum object at runtime, and are often used as a bag of related compile-time constants.

```ts
enum Level {
  Low = 0,
  High = 'high',     // flagged: string member in a numeric enum
}

enum Level {
  Low = 'low',
  High = 'high',     // compliant
}
```

### js/no-multi-assign

**Assignments should not be chained**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: readability

Flags chained assignments such as `a = b = c` and `const a = b = c`.

**Why:** a chain hides an assignment in the middle of an expression. It is easy to misread
which variables are declared (in `const a = b = 0`, only `a` is; `b` is assigned — possibly
creating a global), and all targets silently share the same object.

**Fix:** write one assignment per statement. Each chain is reported once, at its second
assignment.

```js
a = b = 0;          // flagged
const x = y = [];   // flagged

a = 0;              // compliant
b = 0;
```

### js/no-multi-str

**String literals should not be continued with a backslash line break** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions

Flags string literals continued on the next line with a backslash at the end of the line.

**Why:** a backslash before a line break removes the line break from the string, but nothing
else: the next line's indentation becomes part of the text, and a single space after the
backslash turns the continuation into a syntax error that is invisible in most editors. The
string's real content is hard to see.

**Fix:** join the pieces with `+`, use a template literal (whose line breaks are kept), or
build the text with `join`.

```js
const message = 'The file could not \
  be saved';                                   // flagged: the text contains the spaces
const message = 'The file could not ' +
  'be saved';                                  // compliant
const message = `The file could not
be saved`;                                     // compliant: the line break is part of the text
```

Not reported: template literals, and string attributes in JSX, where a backslash is an ordinary
character.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

### js/no-namespace

**ES modules should be used instead of namespaces**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: typescript, modules, conventions

Flags TypeScript `namespace` (and legacy `module Name`) declarations.

**Why:** namespaces are TypeScript's pre-ES-module way of organising code. ES modules already give
every file its own scope and explicit imports/exports, which bundlers, tree shaking, and other tools
understand. Namespaces compile to extra runtime objects, cannot be tree-shaken, and are not
supported by tools that strip types without a full compiler (such as Babel or `isolatedModules`
builds in some configurations).

**Fix:** move the contents to their own module and `import` / `export` them.

Not flagged: `declare module 'name' { … }` (typing an external module), `declare global { … }`,
and `declare namespace` / anything inside an ambient declaration, which only describe code that
exists elsewhere.

```ts
export namespace Geometry {             // flagged
  export function area(r: number) { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}

// geometry.ts
export function area(r: number) { return Math.PI * r * r; } // compliant

declare module 'untyped-lib' {           // compliant
  export function run(): void;
}
```

### js/no-nested-component-definition

**Components should not be defined inside other components**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: react, performance

Flags React components defined inside the body of another component: a capitalized
function that returns JSX, declared directly in a component and then rendered as `<Inner />` or
passed on as a component.

**Why:** each render of the outer component creates a brand-new `Inner` function. React compares
component types by identity, so it sees a different component every time: it unmounts the old
subtree and mounts a new one on every render. All state inside `Inner` (and its children) is reset,
inputs lose focus, effects re-run, and the whole subtree is rebuilt from scratch.

**Fix:** move the inner component to the top level of the module and pass it the values it needs as
props. If it only exists to share markup, call it as a plain function (`{renderRow(item)}`) or
inline the JSX.

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  function Row({ item }) { return <li>{item.name}</li>; }  // flagged
  return <ul>{items.map((item) => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />)}</ul>;
}

function Row({ item }) { return <li>{item.name}</li>; }    // compliant: module level
function List({ items }) {
  return <ul>{items.map((item) => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />)}</ul>;
}
```

Only React/Preact files are checked. Inner functions that are only ever called directly
(`{Header()}`) are not flagged, because React never sees them as components, and neither are
components created inside hooks such as `useMemo` or `useCallback`.

### js/no-nested-ternary

**Ternary operators should not be nested**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: readability

Flags a conditional (ternary) expression used directly as the condition or a
branch of another conditional expression.

**Why:** chained `?:` operators force the reader to track several conditions and their pairing
at once; precedence and indentation make it easy to misread which value belongs to which case.

**Fix:** use `if`/`else` statements, a `switch`, a lookup table, or extract the inner choice into
a well-named variable or function. Each group of nested ternaries is reported once, at the first
nested one.

```js
const label = n === 0 ? 'none' : n === 1 ? 'one' : 'many';   // flagged

function labelFor(n) {                                     // compliant
  if (n === 0) return 'none';
  return n === 1 ? 'one' : 'many';
}
```

### js/no-new-native-nonconstructor

**Symbol and BigInt should not be used with new** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `new Symbol(…)` and `new BigInt(…)`.

**Why:** `Symbol` and `BigInt` are functions that create primitive values, but they are not
constructors: using them with `new` throws a `TypeError`. The habit comes from `new String(…)` and
`new Number(…)`, which do work (and create wrapper objects nobody wants).

**Fix:** call them without `new`.

```js
const id = new Symbol('id');     // flagged: throws TypeError
const big = new BigInt(10);      // flagged

const id = Symbol('id');         // compliant
const big = BigInt(10);          // compliant
```

Only the globals are checked: a local class or import named `Symbol` is not reported.

### js/no-new-wrappers

**Primitive wrapper objects should not be created with 'new'**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `new String(…)`, `new Number(…)`, and `new Boolean(…)`.

**Why:** these create wrapper *objects*, not primitive values. They behave surprisingly:
`new Boolean(false)` is truthy, `new String('a') === 'a'` is `false`, and `typeof` reports
`'object'`. There is practically never a reason to want one.

**Fix:** use the literal, or call the function without `new` to convert a value:
`String(x)`, `Number(x)`, `Boolean(x)`. A local class or variable with one of these names is not
reported.

```js
const flag = new Boolean(false);   // flagged: truthy object
const count = new Number(input);   // flagged

const flag = false;                // compliant
const count = Number(input);       // compliant
```

### js/no-non-null-assertion

**Non-null assertions should not be used**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: typescript, conventions

Flags the TypeScript non-null assertion operator (`value!`).

**Why:** `!` tells the compiler "trust me, this is never `null` or `undefined`" without any check at
runtime. When the assumption is wrong — often after a later refactoring — the code fails far away
from the real cause with `Cannot read properties of undefined`. The assertion also hides the case
from readers, who cannot see why the value is guaranteed to exist.

**Fix:** handle the missing case explicitly: narrow with a check (`if (!value) { … }`), use optional
chaining (`value?.name`) or a default (`value ?? fallback`), or fix the declared type so that it is
not nullable in the first place.

Test files are not checked: there, a wrong assumption makes the test fail on the spot, which is
exactly what an assertion in a test is for.

```ts
const name = user!.name;                 // flagged

if (!user) {
  throw new Error('no current user');
}
const name = user.name;                  // compliant: narrowed by the check
const label = user?.name ?? 'anonymous'; // compliant
```

### js/no-obj-calls

**Built-in namespace objects should not be called** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags the built-in namespace objects `Math`, `JSON`, `Reflect`, `Atomics`, and `Intl` called as
functions (`Math()`) or constructors (`new JSON()`).

**Why:** these globals are plain objects that group related functions; they are neither functions
nor constructors. Calling them throws a `TypeError`. The code usually meant one of their members,
such as `Math.max(…)` or `JSON.parse(…)`.

**Fix:** call the intended member function.

```js
const biggest = Math(a, b);        // flagged: throws TypeError
const copy = new JSON(text);       // flagged

const biggest = Math.max(a, b);    // compliant
const copy = JSON.parse(text);     // compliant
```

Only the globals are checked: a local variable or import named `Math` or `Intl` is not reported.

### js/no-object-constructor

**Empty objects should be created with a literal, not the 'Object' constructor** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions

Flags `new Object()` and `Object()` called without arguments.

**Why:** both create an empty plain object, exactly like the literal `{}`, but longer and less
familiar; a reader may wonder whether a local `Object` or some special behavior is involved. The
literal form is also the one that can be written with its properties directly
(`{ id, name }`).

**Fix:** use an object literal.

```js
const cache = new Object();   // flagged
const cache = {};             // compliant
```

Not reported: calls with an argument (`Object(value)` converts a value to an object, which is a
different operation) and a local function or class named `Object`.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

### js/no-param-reassign

**Function parameters should not be reassigned**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: confusing

Flags assignments to a function parameter: `param = …`, `param += …`, `param++`,
destructuring assignments, and `for (param of …)`.

**Why:** after a reassignment, the parameter no longer holds what the caller passed, so readers
(and debuggers) looking at the name can be misled. In non-strict code, reassigning a parameter
also changes `arguments[i]`.

**Fix:** copy the value into a local variable and work with that, or use a default parameter
value. Changing a property of the object a parameter points to (`options.x = 1`) is not
reported.

```js
function greet(name) {
  name = name || 'guest';          // flagged
  return `Hello ${name}`;
}

function greet(name = 'guest') {   // compliant
  return `Hello ${name}`;
}
```

### js/no-prototype-builtins

**Object.prototype methods should not be called directly on objects**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious, objects

Flags calls of `hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf`, and `propertyIsEnumerable` made
directly on an object: `obj.hasOwnProperty('id')`.

**Why:** these methods come from `Object.prototype`, so calling them through the object assumes
the object inherits them unchanged. Objects created with `Object.create(null)` have no prototype
(the call throws `TypeError: obj.hasOwnProperty is not a function`), and any object parsed from
JSON or built from user input can carry an own property named `hasOwnProperty` that shadows the
built-in — a crash at best, a security hole at worst.

**Fix:** use `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` (ES2022), or call the prototype method explicitly with
`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, key)`.

```js
if (config.hasOwnProperty('port')) {}                    // flagged
if (Object.hasOwn(config, 'port')) {}                    // compliant
if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(config, 'port')) {} // compliant
```

### js/no-redeclare

**Functions should not be redeclared**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, pitfall

Flags a function declared twice in the same scope, and a function and a `var` with a
value sharing one name.

**Why:** function and `var` declarations may legally repeat, but they all bind the *same*
variable. A second `function save() {}` silently replaces the first one for every caller, even
those written above it (declarations are hoisted), and `var save = …` in the same scope as
`function save` overwrites the function once that line runs. Such repeats are usually a merge or
copy-paste accident.

**Fix:** rename one of the declarations, or delete the stale one.

```js
function format(value) { return value.trim(); }
function format(value) { return value.toUpperCase(); } // flagged: replaces the first

var render = createRenderer();
function render() {}                                   // flagged: overwritten by the var

function format(value) { return value.trim(); }        // compliant
function formatUpper(value) { return value.toUpperCase(); }
```

Not flagged: TypeScript overloads and declaration merging (interfaces, namespaces, enums, classes),
`declare` statements, parameters redeclared with `var`, `var name;` without a value (it changes
nothing), and `var` declared twice — that only reuses one variable, which is untidy rather than
wrong.

### js/no-redundant-boolean

**Boolean literals should not be used redundantly**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: redundant

Flags boolean literals that add nothing: a ternary that picks between `true` and
`false` (`c ? true : false`), an `if` that returns `true` in one branch and `false` in the other
(with an `else`, or with the second `return` right after the `if`), and a comparison of a boolean
value with `true` or `false` (`(a > b) === true`).

**Why:** the literal restates what the expression already is and makes the reader stop to check
for a trick.

**Fix:** use the condition directly (`!!c` or `Boolean(c)` when it is not already a boolean) or
negate it (`c ? false : true` is `!c`, `x === false` is `!x`); return the condition instead of
`if (c) { return true; } return false;`.

Comparisons are only reported when the other operand is certainly a boolean: a comparison, a
negation, `instanceof`/`in`, a `Boolean(…)`/`Array.isArray(…)` call, a combination of those with
`&&`/`||`, or a variable or parameter declared as `boolean` or initialized from such an
expression. `flag === true` where `flag` may also be `undefined` is a real check and is left
alone, and so is a variable that is also compared with the other boolean, `null`, or `undefined`
(a tri-state value, whatever its declared type).

The last `if` of a chain of guards that all return the same literal is not reported
(`if (a.x !== b.x) return false; if (a.y !== b.y) return false; return true;`, typical of equality
checks), where keeping the parallel structure is clearer; declarations between the guards and
`else if` guards count as part of the chain. After a guard returning the opposite literal the last
`if` is reported.

```ts
const visible = count > 0 ? true : false;   // flagged
if (isReady(x) && (a > b) === true) {}      // flagged
function isEmpty(list) {
  if (list.length === 0) {                  // flagged
    return true;
  }
  return false;
}

const visible = count > 0;                  // compliant
if (options.enabled === true) {}            // compliant: the type is unknown
function isEmpty(list) {
  return list.length === 0;                 // compliant
}
```

### js/no-redundant-type-constituents

**Union and intersection types should not contain redundant members**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: typescript, types, redundant

Flags members of TypeScript union (`A | B`) and intersection (`A & B`) types that add nothing:
the same member written twice, `any` or `unknown` in a union (they swallow every other member),
`never` in a union (it contributes no values), `any` or `unknown` in an intersection, and a literal
type next to its own base type (`'auto' | string`, `0 | number`, `true | boolean`).

**Why:** the type reads as if it listed distinct alternatives, but the compiler reduces it to
something simpler, so the listed alternatives are documentation that is not enforced. `'auto' |
string` looks like it singles out `'auto'`, yet it accepts every string; `User | any` turns off
type checking for every use while suggesting that values are users.

**Fix:** remove the absorbed member, or change the type to say what was meant (`'auto' | 'none'`,
`User | undefined`).

```ts
type Width = 'auto' | string;          // flagged: 'auto' is already a string
type Input = Config | any;             // flagged: any absorbs Config
type Id = string | number | string;    // flagged: string repeated

type Width = 'auto' | 'fill' | number; // compliant
type Input = Config | undefined;       // compliant
```

Only members written in the type itself are compared: type aliases, interfaces and types from
other files are out of reach. Not reported: the autocompletion idiom `'auto' | (string & {})`,
and `never` in an intersection (the compiler already reduces the whole type to `never`, which is
usually the point of writing it).

### js/no-require-imports

**ES imports should be used instead of require()**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: typescript, modules

Flags CommonJS `require()` calls and `import x = require('x')` in TypeScript
files.

**Why:** in TypeScript, `require()` returns `any` unless the result is annotated by hand, so
everything taken from the module escapes type checking. Mixing `require` with ES `import`s also
makes the module format of a file unclear and defeats tools that rely on static imports (tree
shaking, bundlers, `isolatedModules`).

**Fix:** use an ES `import` statement, or a dynamic `import()` for modules loaded on demand.

Not flagged: a local function or parameter named `require` (AMD loaders, `createRequire`), and
`.cts` files, which are CommonJS by definition.

```ts
const fs = require('fs');              // flagged
import path = require('path');         // flagged

import * as fs from 'fs';              // compliant
const lazy = await import('./heavy');  // compliant
```

### js/no-return-assign

**Assignments should not be made in 'return' statements**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: confusing

Flags assignments inside a `return` statement or in the expression body of an arrow
function, unless the assignment is wrapped in its own parentheses.

**Why:** `return a = b` reads very much like `return a === b`; the reader cannot tell whether a
comparison was intended. Returning and assigning in one step also hides a side effect.

**Fix:** assign first, then return the variable. If returning the assigned value is intended,
wrap the assignment in parentheses to make that explicit: `return (this.cache = compute())`.

```js
function reset() {
  return count = 0;                // flagged
}
items.forEach(i => total += i);    // flagged

function reset() {
  count = 0;                       // compliant
  return count;
}
items.forEach(i => (total += i));  // compliant: explicit
```

### js/no-self-assign

**Variables and properties should not be assigned to themselves**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags assignments whose target and value are the same: `x = x`, `[a, b] = [a, b]`,
`({ a } = { a })`, and property self-assignments such as `this.name = this.name` when they are
evidently a typo.

**Why:** assigning a variable to itself does nothing. It is nearly always an incomplete edit — the
right-hand side was meant to be a parameter, another variable, or a freshly computed value — so the
intended update silently never happens. A destructuring "swap" written with both sides in the same
order is the same mistake.

**Fix:** assign the value that was meant (often a parameter or a differently named variable), or
delete the statement.

```js
function setName(name) {
  this.name = this.name;   // flagged: should be `this.name = name`
}

[first, second] = [first, second]; // flagged: not a swap
[first, second] = [second, first]; // compliant
```

Assigning a property to itself can deliberately re-run a setter (`picker.items = picker.items`,
`canvas.width = canvas.width`, `location.href = location.href`), so a standalone property
self-assignment is only reported when there is evidence of a typo: a variable or parameter with
the property's name is in scope, or the object is `this` in a class that has no base class and no
setter or decorated field with that name.

### js/no-self-compare

**Values should not be compared with themselves**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags comparisons whose two operands are the same side-effect-free expression, such as
`x === x`, `a.length < a.length`, or `item.id !== item.id`.

**Why:** such a comparison always gives the same answer (the only exception is `NaN`, which is
not equal to itself). It is almost always a typo where one side should name a different variable
— `a.id === b.id` written as `a.id === a.id`.

**Fix:** compare against the intended value. To test for `NaN`, use `Number.isNaN(x)`, which says
what it means.

```js
if (user.id === user.id) {}        // flagged
if (user.id === other.id) {}       // compliant
if (x !== x) {}                    // flagged: use Number.isNaN(x)
```

### js/no-self-import

**A module should not import itself** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: modules, suspicious

Flags an `import` or `export … from` whose relative path points back at the file itself:
`import { helper } from './utils'` inside `utils.ts`.

**Why:** a module importing itself never gets anything it does not already have. At best the
import is dead weight; at worst the imported bindings are read before the module has finished
initializing and are `undefined` (or throw in the temporal dead zone). It is usually a wrong path —
the import was copied from a sibling file, or the file was renamed.

**Fix:** remove the import and use the local declarations directly, or correct the path to the
module that was meant.

```js
// file: src/format.js
import { pad } from './format';     // flagged: imports itself
import { pad } from './strings';    // compliant
```

Only relative specifiers (`./…`, `../…`) are checked, with or without a JavaScript/TypeScript
extension; `./dir` and `./dir/index` resolve to `dir/index.*`.

### js/no-self-state-update

**State setters should not be called with the current state value**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: react, suspicious

Flags a React state setter called with the state variable it belongs to:
`setItems(items)` for `const [items, setItems] = useState(…)`.

**Why:** React compares the new state with the current one and skips the update when they are the
same value (`Object.is`). So the call either does nothing, or — the usual story — it follows an
in-place change (`items.push(x); setItems(items);`) that React never sees: the component does not
re-render and the screen shows stale data. Called from an older closure, it can also quietly
reset the state to an outdated value.

**Fix:** pass a new value — `setItems([...items, x])`, `setUser({ ...user, name })` — or the
updater form `setItems((prev) => [...prev, x])`; remove the call if it has no purpose.

```jsx
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
items.push(item);
setItems(items);                      // flagged: same array, no re-render
setItems([...items, item]);           // compliant
```

Only setters from `useState` imported from React (or Preact) are checked, and only when the
argument is the state variable itself (not a shadowing parameter of the same name).

### js/no-set-state-in-render

**State setters should not be called unconditionally during render** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: react

Flags a React state setter called unconditionally while a component renders: a statement
`setCount(…)` directly in the body of the component that declared `[count, setCount] =
useState(…)` (or a `useReducer` dispatch), or `this.setState(…)` directly in a class component's
`render()` method.

**Why:** setting state schedules another render. When the call runs on every render, each render
triggers the next one: React stops with a "Too many re-renders" error (function components) or
loops until the stack overflows (class components).

**Fix:** set state in an event handler or an effect, or compute the value during render instead of
storing it. To adjust state when a prop changes, guard the call with a condition that becomes
false after the update.

```jsx
function Counter({ start }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  setCount(start);                          // flagged: renders forever
  return <span>{count}</span>;
}

function Counter({ start }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(start); // compliant: initial state
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}
```

Only calls that certainly run on every render are reported: a statement directly in the component
body (not inside `if`, loops, `&&`, callbacks, or effects), with a setter that the same component
got from `useState` / `useReducer` imported from React or Preact (or called as `React.useState`).

### js/no-shadow-restricted-names

**Built-in global names should not be redeclared**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, confusing

Flags variables, parameters, functions, classes, catch parameters, and imports named
`undefined`, `NaN`, `Infinity`, `eval`, or `arguments`.

**Why:** every reader (and many tools) assumes these names mean the built-in values and functions.
A local binding with one of these names silently changes what the name means in its scope:
`undefined` can suddenly hold a value, `NaN` checks compare against something else, and `eval` or
`arguments` no longer do what they normally do. In strict mode code most of these bindings are
syntax errors.

**Fix:** rename the binding.

```js
function parse(input, undefined) {}  // flagged
const NaN = computeFallback();       // flagged
try { run(); } catch (eval) {}       // flagged

function parse(input, fallback) {}   // compliant
```

Not flagged: `var undefined;` without an initializer that is never assigned (it still holds
`undefined`), the classic `(function (undefined) { … })()` guard whose `undefined` parameter
never receives an argument, and TypeScript `declare` / ambient declarations.

Bindings named after words reserved in strict mode (`implements`, `interface`, `let`, `package`,
`private`, `protected`, `public`, `static`, `yield`) are flagged too: they only parse in sloppy
scripts, so the code breaks as soon as it becomes a module, a class body, or gains
`'use strict'`.

```js
var interface = load();              // flagged: a syntax error in strict code
```

### js/no-sparse-arrays

**Array literals should not contain holes**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags array literals with holes — consecutive commas such as `[1, , 3]` or a leading
comma `[, a]`.

**Why:** a hole is not `undefined`: it is a missing element that many array methods (`forEach`,
`map`, `filter`, spreading into function arguments) treat differently. Holes are also easy to miss
when reading, so a double comma is usually a typo — an element was deleted or never written.

**Fix:** remove the extra comma, or write `undefined` explicitly if an empty slot is wanted.

```js
const colors = ['red', , 'blue'];          // flagged
const colors = ['red', 'blue'];            // compliant
const slots = ['red', undefined, 'blue'];  // compliant: explicit
```

A trailing comma (`[1, 2,]`) is not a hole, and holes in destructuring patterns
(`const [, second] = pair`) are fine.

### js/no-template-curly-in-string

**Template placeholders should not appear in ordinary strings**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags ordinary `'…'` or `"…"` strings that contain a template placeholder such as `${name}`
where `name` is a variable in scope (or `this`).

**Why:** placeholders are only substituted inside backtick template literals. In a quoted string
`${name}` is printed literally, so the message shows `Hello ${name}` instead of the user's name —
a mistake that is easy to make when switching quote styles.

**Fix:** use backticks for the string.

```js
const name = user.name;
const greeting = 'Hello ${name}!';   // flagged
const greeting = `Hello ${name}!`;   // compliant
const pattern = '${workspaceFolder}/out'; // compliant: no such variable, a placeholder syntax
```

Many strings are deliberately written in another placeholder syntax (snippets, configuration
variables such as `${1:label}`, `${env:HOME}`, or `${workspaceFolder}`). To stay precise, a string
is only reported when every placeholder in it is a plain JavaScript expression whose first name is
`this` or a variable in scope, when it has text besides the placeholders (`'${fileName}'` alone
is a token), and when it contains no backtick (code samples). Test and suite titles
(`describe('GET /users/${id}', …)`) are labels and are not reported, nor is a placeholder that
names a variable holding an object, function or class (`${field}` for `const field = new
Field(…)`): substituting it would print `[object Object]`, so the string uses another placeholder
syntax that happens to share the name.

### js/no-this-alias

**'this' should not be assigned to a variable**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: style

Flags `this` being stored in a variable (`const self = this`, `that = this`).

**Why:** copying `this` into a variable was the pre-ES2015 way to reach the outer `this` from a
nested `function` callback. Arrow functions keep the surrounding `this`, so the alias is no longer
needed; it adds a second name for the same object and makes readers check which one each callback
uses.

**Fix:** turn the nested callbacks into arrow functions and use `this` directly. Destructuring
(`const { items } = this`) is fine and not flagged.

Not flagged either, because an arrow function cannot replace the alias there: variables used inside
a class body (`new class extends Base { run() { that.go(); } }`), an object-literal method, getter,
or setter, a generator function, or a `function` that also needs its own `this` or `arguments`
(`el.onclick = function () { that.log(this.id); }`). Nor are variables read by code written before
they receive `this` (a callback created before `super()` returns), or variables assigned again
later: such a variable is a cursor that merely starts at `this`
(`let node = this; while (node) { node = node.parent; }`).

```js
const self = this;                       // flagged
button.onclick = function () { self.save(); };

button.onclick = () => this.save();      // compliant
const { items, total } = this;           // compliant: destructuring
```

### js/no-this-before-super

**'this' should not be used before super() in a derived constructor** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: classes, suspicious

Flags `this` or `super.member` used in the constructor of a derived class before `super()` has
been called.

**Why:** in a class that extends another, the instance is created by the base class constructor.
Until `super()` returns, `this` is uninitialized and any access to it — reading a field, calling a
method, even passing `this` as an argument to `super(…)` itself — throws a `ReferenceError`.

**Fix:** move the `super(…)` call before the first use of `this`. Values that must be computed
first can go into local variables or into the arguments of `super(…)`.

```js
class Button extends Widget {
  constructor(label) {
    this.label = label;        // flagged: runs before super()
    super(label);
  }
}

class Button extends Widget {
  constructor(label) {
    super(label);
    this.label = label;        // compliant
  }
}
```

Only uses that come before the first `super()` call in the source text are reported, and only in
the constructor itself: an arrow function created before `super()` may use `this` when it is called
later, and a nested `function` or class has its own `this`.

### js/no-throw-literal

**Only 'Error' objects should be thrown**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: error-handling

Flags `throw` statements whose value is certainly not an `Error`: a string, number,
boolean, `null`, `undefined`, template literal, object or array literal, arithmetic or string
concatenation, or a function.

**Why:** only `Error` objects carry a stack trace, and code that handles exceptions usually
expects `error.message` and `error.stack`. A thrown string or plain object makes failures much
harder to diagnose and breaks such handlers.

**Fix:** throw an `Error` (or a subclass): `throw new Error('…')`. Values whose type cannot be
seen from the source (variables, calls, `new X()`) are not reported.

```js
throw 'Invalid state';                   // flagged
throw { code: 42 };                      // flagged
throw `Missing ${name}`;                 // flagged

throw new Error('Invalid state');        // compliant
throw error;                             // compliant: may be an Error
```

### js/no-unassigned-vars

**Variables that are read should be assigned**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, unused

Flags `let` and `var` variables that are declared without a value, never assigned
anywhere, and yet read.

**Why:** such a variable is always `undefined`, so every read of it yields the same useless value.
Usually an assignment was forgotten or went to another variable by mistake; sometimes the variable
is simply left over and its reads are dead code.

**Fix:** assign the intended value, or remove the variable and use `undefined` (or the right
variable) directly.

```js
let timeout;
setTimeout(run, timeout);    // flagged at the declaration: always undefined

let timeout = 1000;          // compliant
setTimeout(run, timeout);
```

Not flagged: variables assigned anywhere in the file (including in callbacks or destructuring),
`for…in` / `for…of` heads, exported, `declare`d, and ambient variables, variables typed as only
