`undefined` / `null` / `void` (deliberately empty), and top-level variables of
classic scripts (another script may assign them).

### js/no-undeclared-assignment

**Variables should be declared before they are assigned**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious, globals

Flags assignments to a name that is declared nowhere: not in the file, not as a known
browser or Node.js global, and not in a `/* global … */` comment.

**Why:** assigning to an undeclared name does not create a local variable. In sloppy-mode scripts it
silently creates (or overwrites) a property of the global object, shared by every script on the page
and every call of the function — a classic source of state leaking between calls and of clashes
with other code. In strict mode and in ES modules the same statement throws a `ReferenceError` at
runtime. Almost always, a `let`, `const`, or `var` was forgotten.

**Fix:** declare the variable where it is first assigned. If a global really is intended, write it
explicitly as `globalThis.name = …` (or `window.name`) and declare it with a `/* global name */`
comment where it is read.

```js
function total(items) {
  sum = 0;                    // flagged: 'sum' is never declared
  for (const item of items) sum += item.price;
  return sum;
}

function total(items) {
  let sum = 0;                // compliant
  for (const item of items) sum += item.price;
  return sum;
}
```

To stay precise, a name is only reported when everything the file does with it happens inside one
function and starts with the assignment (a variable used like a local), when it is not a known
global (`window`, `location`, `module`, `exports`, `on…` handlers, …), and when the file does not
test it with `typeof`, list it in a `/* global */` comment, or `declare` it. TypeScript files are
not checked: the compiler already rejects assignments to names that no declaration file declares.
Files using `with` or direct `eval` are skipped.

### js/no-unexpected-multiline

**A line should not start with '(', '[' or a template that continues the previous line** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags a line that starts with `(`, `[` or a template literal and is therefore glued to the
expression on the line above: a call, an index, or a tagged template instead of a new statement.

**Why:** JavaScript only inserts a semicolon at a line break when the next line cannot continue
the current statement. A line starting with `(`, `[` or `` ` `` always can, so the two lines run
as one expression: the previous value is called with the parenthesized text as arguments, indexed
with the bracketed list, or used as a template tag. The result is a `TypeError` ("… is not a
function") or, worse, a silently wrong value — and the layout makes it look like two statements.

**Fix:** end the previous statement with a semicolon, or start the new line with one
(`;[a, b] = [b, a]`). If the continuation is intended, keep it on the same line.

```js
const total = a + b
(items || []).forEach(add)        // flagged: calls `b(...)`

const parts = line.split(',')
[first, second] = parts           // flagged: indexes `split(...)`

const total = a + b;
(items || []).forEach(add);       // compliant
```

A continuation line indented deeper than the line it continues is taken as deliberate layout
(`makeHandler(options)` followed by an indented `(listener)` line) and is not reported, nor are
optional calls and indexes (`?.(`, `?.[`) and a function expression called on the next line (an
IIFE laid out that way on purpose).

### js/no-unknown-property

**JSX attributes on DOM elements should use React's prop names** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: react, suspicious

Flags HTML-style attribute names on built-in elements in React JSX: `class`, `for`, lowercase event
handlers such as `onclick`, and lowercase or dashed spellings such as `tabindex`, `maxlength` or
`stroke-width`, where React expects `className`, `htmlFor`, `onClick`, `tabIndex`, `maxLength`,
`strokeWidth`.

**Why:** React maps its own camel-cased prop names to the DOM. An event handler under the HTML
name (`onclick={handle}`) is never attached — the click silently does nothing. The other HTML
spellings are passed through with a warning in the console, work differently from the React name
in places (`class` is not reflected in `className`, `for` in `htmlFor`), and break type checking.

**Fix:** use the React name.

```jsx
<label class="field" for="name">Name</label>     // flagged twice
<button onclick={save}>Save</button>            // flagged: never called
<input tabindex="1" maxlength={20} />           // flagged twice
<label className="field" htmlFor="name">Name</label>
<button onClick={save}>Save</button>            // compliant
```

Only files that import React (or `react-dom`, `next`) and no other JSX library are checked
(Preact, Solid, Vue, Qwik and others accept the HTML names). Components (`<Button class=…>`),
custom elements (`<my-widget class=…>`), `data-*` and `aria-*` attributes, and names outside a
fixed table of known misspellings are not reported.

### js/no-unnecessary-type-constraint

**Type parameters should not be constrained to 'any' or 'unknown'**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: typescript, redundant

Flags type parameters constrained to `any` or `unknown` (`<T extends unknown>`).

**Why:** every type already satisfies `unknown` and `any`, so the constraint restricts nothing. It
only makes the signature longer and suggests to readers that some restriction applies.

**Fix:** remove the `extends` clause: `<T>`.

In `.tsx` files an arrow function's `<T extends unknown>` is a common way to stop the parser from
reading `<T>` as a JSX tag; that form is not flagged (the shorter alternative is `<T,>`).

```ts
function first<T extends unknown>(items: T[]): T {}   // flagged
function first<T>(items: T[]): T {}                   // compliant
function byId<T extends { id: string }>(items: T[]) {} // compliant: a real constraint
```

### js/no-unreachable

**Unreachable code should be removed**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, unused

Flags statements that can never run because they follow a `return`, `throw`, `break`, or
`continue` in the same block (directly, or after an `if`/`else` or `try` whose every path leaves).

**Why:** unreachable code is dead weight at best. More often it is a bug: a debugging `return`
left in place, or a statement accidentally placed after the exit it was meant to precede, so the
code the author expected to run never does.

**Fix:** remove the dead statements, or move them before the exit.

```js
function save(record) {
  return store.put(record);
  audit(record);            // flagged: never runs
}

function load() {
  return read();
  function read() {}        // compliant: function declarations are hoisted
}
```

Hoisted declarations (functions, `var` without initializer), TypeScript type declarations, and a
redundant plain `break;` (as in `return x; break;` at the end of a `switch` case) are not
reported. Loops, `switch` statements, and labeled blocks are conservatively assumed to complete
normally.

### js/no-unreachable-loop

**Loops should be able to run more than one iteration** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, loops

Flags `for`, `while`, and `do … while` loops whose body always leaves the loop during the first
iteration, through `return`, `throw`, or `break`.

**Why:** such a loop runs its body at most once, so it is not a loop at all. Usually an exit that
should be conditional is not: the `return` meant for "found it" sits outside the `if`, or a
`break` was added for debugging and left in place. Every element after the first is silently
ignored.

**Fix:** move the exit into the condition it belongs to, or replace the loop with an `if` if a
single pass is really intended.

```js
for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
  if (items[i].id === id) {
    found = items[i];
  }
  break;                       // flagged loop: only items[0] is ever checked
}

for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
  if (items[i].id === id) {
    found = items[i];
    break;                     // compliant
  }
}
```

A `continue` anywhere in the body means another iteration is possible, so such loops are not
reported. `for…of` and `for…in` loops are not reported either: returning from the first iteration
is a common way to take the first element of an iterable or to test whether an object has any
key. `do { … } while (false)` blocks are not loops by intent and are skipped too, and so is an exit
with a comment right before it or on its line, which marks it as deliberate (`break; // only the
first case while debugging`).

### js/no-unsafe-finally

**Control flow should not leave a 'finally' block**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~10 min · Tags: error-handling

Flags `return`, `throw`, `break`, and `continue` statements that leave a `finally` block.

**Why:** a `finally` block runs after the `try` or `catch` has already decided how to finish —
returning a value or propagating an exception. Leaving `finally` with a jump throws that decision
away: an exception from the `try` is silently swallowed, or the returned value is replaced. The
code then behaves as if the error never happened.

**Fix:** keep `finally` to cleanup only; move the `return`/`throw` into the `try` or `catch`.

```js
function read() {
  try {
    return parse();
  } finally {
    return null;          // flagged: discards parse()'s result and any exception
  }
}

function cleanup(items) {
  try {
    process(items);
  } finally {
    for (const item of items) {
      if (item.done) break; // compliant: the break stays inside the finally block
      item.close();
    }
  }
}
```

Jumps that stay inside the `finally` block (a `break` of a loop inside it, a `throw` caught by a
`try` inside it) and code in nested functions are not reported.

### js/no-unsafe-function-type

**The 'Function' type should not be used**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: typescript, types

Flags the built-in `Function` type used in TypeScript type positions.

**Why:** `Function` accepts any function-like value — including classes — and calling a value of
that type is unchecked: any number of arguments of any type is accepted and the result is `any`.
It is `any` for functions: mistakes in how the callback is called or what it returns reach
runtime unnoticed.

**Fix:** write the actual signature, e.g. `(event: Event) => void`, or `(...args: never[]) =>
unknown` for "any function I will not call". Generic helpers can take a type parameter
constrained to a function type.

```ts
function onChange(listener: Function) {}            // flagged
function onChange(listener: (value: string) => void) {} // compliant
```

A local type or class that happens to be named `Function` is not reported.

### js/no-unsafe-negation

**Negation should not be applied to the left operand of 'in' or 'instanceof'**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `!` applied to the left operand of `in` or `instanceof` without parentheses, as in
`!key in obj` or `!value instanceof Date`.

**Why:** `!` binds tighter than `in` and `instanceof`, so `!key in obj` means `(!key) in obj` —
it checks whether `"true"` or `"false"` is a key of `obj`. The author almost certainly meant
`!(key in obj)`, and the condition silently gives the wrong answer.

**Fix:** put the negation around the whole test: `!(key in obj)`. If negating the left operand
really is intended, add parentheses to say so: `(!key) in obj`.

```js
if (!key in cache) {}               // flagged
if (!(key in cache)) {}             // compliant
if (!(value instanceof Date)) {}    // compliant
```

### js/no-unsafe-optional-chaining

**Optional chains should not be used where undefined throws**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: null-handling, suspicious

Flags an optional chain (`a?.b`) whose result is used where `undefined` throws: spread into an
array or argument list, destructured, iterated with `for…of`, called or constructed after
parentheses, used as the right side of `in` / `instanceof`, or extended by a class.

**Why:** `?.` exists because the value may be missing; when it is, the whole chain evaluates to
`undefined`. Using that result where a value is mandatory throws a `TypeError` —
`[...list?.items]` or `const { id } = user?.profile` fail exactly in the case the `?.` was written
for. Parentheses end the short-circuit, so `(obj?.method)()` calls `undefined` instead of skipping
the call.

**Fix:** provide a fallback (`[...(list?.items ?? [])]`, `const { id } = user?.profile ?? {}`), keep
the call inside the chain (`obj?.method()`), or drop the `?.` if the value can never be missing.

```js
const all = [...group?.members];          // flagged: TypeError when group is missing
const { name } = config?.user;            // flagged
for (const item of order?.items) {}       // flagged
(api?.refresh)();                          // flagged: calls undefined

const all = [...(group?.members ?? [])];  // compliant
const { name } = config?.user ?? {};      // compliant
api?.refresh();                           // compliant
const copy = { ...config?.user };         // compliant: spreading undefined into an object is fine
```

Not reported: chains whose optional part can never be nullish (`(list || [])?.map(…)`), results
passed through `??` or `||` to a fallback, results asserted with a TypeScript `!` or a type
assertion (`(a?.b as Item).name`), chains in the arguments of an optional call on the same object
(`a?.f([...a?.b])` only runs when `a` exists), chains already tested by an enclosing condition
(`if (a?.b) { for (const x of a?.b) … }`, `a?.b && [...a?.b]`) or whose object that condition
already reads without `?.` (`if (a.kind === 1) { … a?.b … }`), and elements that passed a
`.filter()` testing the same chain (`list.filter((e) => e?.b).map((e) => [...e?.b])`).

### js/no-unused-expressions

**Expressions should not be evaluated only to be discarded**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, unused

Flags expression statements that compute a value and throw it away without any possible
effect: `a === b;`, `x;`, `total + tax;`, `'text';` outside the directive prologue, `[a, b];`.

**Why:** such a statement changes nothing, so it is almost always a mistake — a missing
assignment (`total = total + tax`), a missing `return`, or `==` typed for `=`.

**Fix:** assign or return the value, or delete the statement. To evaluate something only for its
side effects, write `void expr`.

```js
count + 1;                     // flagged: the result is discarded
isReady === true;              // flagged: a comparison with no effect
count += 1;                    // compliant
ready && start();              // compliant: short-circuit call
isValid ? accept() : reject(); // compliant
void promise;                  // compliant: explicitly discarded
```

Only statements that cannot have any effect are reported: nothing in them calls code (calls,
`new`, tagged templates, spreads, class definitions), writes (assignments, `++`/`--`, `delete`),
or suspends (`await`, `yield`). A statement that is just a property read (`el.offsetHeight;`,
`expect(x).to.be.true;`) is accepted because getters are sometimes read for their effect, and so
are JSX elements, directives (`'use strict'`), a file consisting of a single function, object, or
array expression (a snippet evaluated by a tool), and TypeScript type tests written as
`value satisfies Type;`.

Setting the `allow_short_circuit` parameter to `false` also reports short-circuit statements such
as `ready && start();` and `cache || load();`, for codebases that prefer an explicit `if`.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `allow_short_circuit` | `true` | Accept short-circuit statements such as `ready && start()`; set to false to report them too. |

### js/no-unused-private-class-members

**Private class members should be used** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: unused, dead-code

Flags private class members that nothing uses: `#name` fields, methods and accessors,
and TypeScript `private` fields, methods and accessors.

**Why:** a private member can only be reached from inside its class, so when the class never uses
it, no other code can either. It is dead code: it costs readers time, keeps imports and
dependencies alive, and a field that is written but never read suggests that some logic was lost in
an edit.

**Fix:** delete the member (and whatever only exists to feed it), or use it where it was meant to
be used.

```ts
class Cache {
  #hits = 0;                           // flagged: assigned below but never read
  #evict() { /* … */ }                 // flagged: never called
  private legacyKey = 'v1';            // flagged: never used
  store(key: string) { this.#hits = 1; }
}

class Cache {
  #hits = 0;
  get hits() { return this.#hits; }    // compliant: read
}
```

A `#name` field counts as used only when it is read: assigning it alone keeps it flagged, since
`#name` fields are invisible to serialization and reflection. A TypeScript `private` member counts
as used when it is accessed at all, or when its name appears anywhere in the file as a property
access, a string, or a destructured key (other instances, `this['name']`, test hooks). Not
reported: decorated members (framework hooks), constructor parameter properties (dependency
injection declares dependencies with them, and a dependency may be requested only to be created),
fields initialized by a function called on the spot (a substitute for a static block), TypeScript
`private` members of classes decorated as components or directives (templates may use them),
TypeScript `private` members of classes that access `this` with computed keys, `declare` fields,
constructors, ambient declarations, and brand fields that are never assigned: a field such as
`private __brand: void` or `#brand!: never` exists only to make the class nominally distinct for
the type checker (TypeScript treats classes with private members as compatible only with their
own subclasses) and is never meant to be read. A `_`/`$`-prefixed name ending in `brand` counts
as a brand; a plain `brand` only when it is declared with a type and no value.

Known limitation: TypeScript's `private` is checked at compile time only, and bracket access
(`module['preload']()`) is allowed to bypass it, including from other files (typically a test or a
sibling class of the same package). The rule reads one file at a time and cannot see such a use:
suppress the finding on that member, or make the member public (`/** @internal */`) if other
files are meant to call it.

### js/no-unused-vars

**Unused declarations should be removed**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: unused

Flags variables, functions, classes, imports, types, enums, and parameters that are
declared but never used.

**Why:** unused declarations are noise: readers must work out that they do nothing, and they often
point at a bug — a value computed and then forgotten, or a typo that made the real code use another
name. Unused imports also slow builds and can keep dead modules in a bundle.

**Fix:** remove the declaration. If it must stay (e.g. a positional callback parameter), prefix its
name with `_`.

```ts
import { readFile, writeFile } from 'fs'; // flagged: writeFile

function load(path: string, options: object) { // flagged: options
  const unused = 42;                           // flagged
  let result;                                  // flagged: assigned but never read
  result = readFile(path);
}

items.map((item, index) => index);             // compliant: `item` precedes a used parameter
const { id, ...rest } = user;                  // compliant: `id` is excluded from `rest`
```

What counts as a use: any read, any type reference (`x: Foo`, `typeof x`), JSX usage (`<Foo />`),
a mention in JSDoc (`{@link Foo}`, `@param {Foo}`), and export. Updating a variable from its own
value in a statement (`count++;`, `total += n;`) is not a use: a variable that is only ever
updated that way is never read, so it is reported like one that is only assigned. Not reported: names starting with
`_`, exported declarations, `declare` / ambient declarations, merged or overloaded declarations,
catch parameters, `using` declarations, decorated classes, the `React` import in files with JSX,
and top-level declarations of non-module scripts (they are globals). With the `caught_errors`
parameter on, unused catch parameters are reported too (`catch {` needs no binding since ES2019).

Parameters are reported only where the author controls the signature — function declarations,
constructors, methods of classes that neither extend nor implement anything (and are not
`override`), and functions assigned to a variable without a type annotation — and only when no
later parameter is used. Callbacks, object-literal members, setters, parameter properties,
decorated, destructured, and rest parameters are never reported, nor are the parameters of an
empty method (a hook whose signature is there for subclasses to override).

Type parameters of functions and methods are reported when nothing mentions them
(`function first<T>(list: string[])`): a caller can pass a type argument that changes nothing.
Only signatures that nothing outside can depend on are checked: functions and arrow functions
that are not exported, overloaded, merged, or ambient, and `private` / `#` methods and fields
that are not overloaded or decorated. Public methods (a subclass or an interface may share the
signature) and type parameters of classes, interfaces, and type aliases (an unused one can
deliberately tag a type) are left alone.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `caught_errors` | `false` | Also report unused catch-clause bindings (`catch (e)` where `e` is never used; `catch {` needs no binding). |

### js/no-use-before-define

**Variables should not be used before their declaration** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, scope

Flags a `let`, `const`, or `class` binding that is used before its declaration has run, in the
same function: `print(total); const total = 1;` or `const size = size + 1;`.

**Why:** unlike `var` and function declarations, these bindings exist from the start of their scope
but stay uninitialized (the "temporal dead zone") until the declaration executes. Any read or write
before that — even `typeof total` — throws a `ReferenceError`. It typically happens when statements
are reordered, or when a helper is moved below the code that uses it.

**Fix:** move the declaration above its first use, or move the use below it.

```js
render(config);                 // flagged: ReferenceError
const config = loadConfig();

const config = loadConfig();    // compliant
render(config);

function show() {
  return formatter.format(1);   // compliant: runs later, when show() is called
}
const formatter = new Intl.NumberFormat();
```

Only uses that certainly run first are reported: a use inside a function, arrow function, or class
body is skipped, because it runs only when called — possibly after the declaration. Type-only uses
in TypeScript and `export { name }` lists are not uses. `var` and function declarations are hoisted
and never reported.

### js/no-useless-assignment

**Values assigned to variables should be read**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: unused, suspicious

Flags values stored in a local variable that can never be read: the variable is
assigned again before anything reads it, or the function ends (or returns) first.

**Why:** a dead store is wasted work at best. More often it is a mistake: the wrong variable was
assigned, a read was forgotten, or an initial value is misleading because every path replaces it.

**Fix:** remove the useless assignment (or initializer), or use the value where it was meant to be
used.

```js
function label(user) {
  let text = 'unknown';        // flagged: overwritten on the next line
  text = user.name;
  if (!text) {
    text = 'anonymous';
    return 'nobody';           // the value 'anonymous' is never read
  }
  return text;
}

function label(user) {
  let text = user.name;        // compliant
  if (!text) text = 'anonymous';
  return text;
}
```

The analysis is deliberately conservative. Only local variables and parameters of the enclosing
function are considered, and a store is reported only when the code between it and the
overwrite (or the exit) runs straight through: no `break`/`continue`, no enclosing loop between the
store and the end of the function when the variable could be read on the next iteration, and no
enclosing `try`. An `if`/`else` whose every branch assigns the variable (or returns) before
reading it counts as an overwrite, and so does a `switch` with a `default` clause in which every
clause (following fall-through) assigns it or returns before a `break`, and a plain nested block
`{ … }` that assigns it before reading it. Increment and compound-assignment statements
(`count++;`, `total += x;`) are stores too: their new value is flagged when nothing reads it. A
`var` declared several times in the same function is one variable, and a repeated
`var x = value;` overwrites it like an assignment. Variables used by nested functions or classes
are never reported, and neither are variables that are never read at all, including variables
that are only ever incremented or updated from their own value (see `js/no-unused-vars`).

```js
function next(ids) {
  let index = 0;
  while (ids[index]) index++;
  register(ids[index]);
  index++;                     // flagged: the new value is never read
}
```

### js/no-useless-catch

**A catch clause should do more than rethrow the caught error** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: exceptions, redundant

Flags a `catch` clause whose only statement throws the caught value again, unchanged:
`catch (e) { throw e; }`.

**Why:** the error would have propagated to the caller anyway. The handler does nothing, yet it
looks like error handling, so readers go looking for a purpose it does not have, and the extra
nesting hides the code that matters.

**Fix:** remove the `catch` clause; drop the whole `try` when it has no `finally` either. If the
error does need handling, add it: context in a wrapping error (`new Error('…', { cause: e })`),
cleanup, a fallback value.

```js
try {                          // flagged: the catch only rethrows
  await store.save(order);
} catch (err) {
  throw err;
}

await store.save(order);       // compliant

try {                          // compliant: the error gets context
  await store.save(order);
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error(`saving order ${order.id} failed`, { cause: err });
}
```

Not reported: handlers that do anything else before rethrowing (logging, cleanup), that throw a
different value or a wrapper, and destructured catch parameters.

### js/no-useless-concat

**String literals should not be concatenated on the same line**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: redundant

Flags `+` between two string (or template) literals on the same line.

**Why:** joining two literals produces a constant the author could simply have written as one
literal; the split makes the text harder to read and to search for.

**Fix:** merge the literals into one. Concatenations that span lines (a long text wrapped over
several lines) are not reported.

```js
const greeting = 'Hello, ' + 'world';   // flagged
const greeting = 'Hello, world';        // compliant
const long = 'first part of a long sentence ' +
  'continued on the next line';         // compliant
```

### js/no-useless-constructor

**Useless constructors should be removed**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: redundant

Flags class constructors that do exactly what the implicit default constructor
would do: an empty constructor in a class without `extends`, or a constructor in a derived class
that only passes its parameters, unchanged and in order, to `super(…)`.

**Why:** the constructor is dead weight: more code to read that changes nothing.

**Fix:** remove it. Not reported: `private` and `protected` constructors (they restrict who can
create instances), constructors with TypeScript parameter properties (`constructor(private
x: number) {}`) or decorated parameters, constructors containing a comment, overloaded
constructors, and TypeScript constructors whose typed parameters narrow the inherited signature.

```js
class Shape {
  constructor() {}                    // flagged
}
class Circle extends Shape {
  constructor(...args) {
    super(...args);                   // flagged: the default does the same
  }
}

class Square extends Shape {
  constructor(size) {
    super(size, size);                // compliant: adapts the arguments
  }
}
```

### js/no-useless-empty-export

**Empty 'export {}' should be removed when the file is already a module**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: redundant, modules

Flags `export {}` in a file that already imports or exports something else.

**Why:** an empty `export {}` has exactly one purpose: turning a file without any `import` or
`export` into an ES module (so its declarations stay private to the file). As soon as the file has
another `import` or `export`, it is a module anyway and the empty export is dead code that makes
readers wonder what it is for.

**Fix:** delete the `export {}`.

Type-only imports and exports (`import type`, `export type`) do not count as "something else": they
are removed from the compiled output, so the empty export may still be what keeps the emitted file a
module.

```ts
import { run } from './run';
export {};                     // flagged

// globals.ts — nothing else is imported or exported
declare global { interface Window { app: App } }
export {};                     // compliant: makes this file a module
```

### js/no-useless-escape

**Unnecessary escape characters should be removed**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: redundant, regex

Flags backslashes that do not change the meaning of the next character in strings, template
literals, and regular expression literals: `'\:'`, `` `\"` ``, `/\#/`, `/[\.]/`.

**Why:** an unnecessary escape adds noise and suggests that the character is special when it is
not. It is also often a sign of a misunderstanding — for example `'\d'` in a string is just `d`
(the author probably meant `'\\d'` for a regular expression), and `/\e/` matches the letter `e`
rather than an escape character.

**Fix:** remove the backslash, or double it if a literal backslash was intended.

```js
const time = '12\:30';          // flagged
const quote = "it\'s";          // flagged: no need to escape ' inside "…"
const price = /\$\d+\,\d{2}/;   // flagged: the comma needs no escape
const dots = /[\.\*]/;          // flagged (twice): no need inside a character class

const time = '12:30';           // compliant
const quote = 'it\'s';          // compliant: the delimiter must be escaped
const price = /\$\d+,\d{2}/;    // compliant: `$` and `\d` need the backslash
```

Not checked: tagged templates (the tag sees the raw text, as with `String.raw`), JSX attribute
strings (backslashes are not escapes there), and regular expressions with the `u` or `v` flag
(where an unnecessary escape is already a syntax error, or required by the syntax). Inside
character classes, `\-`, `\^`, `\[`, `\]`, `\/`, and `\\` are never reported.

### js/no-useless-rename

**Values should not be renamed to the same name**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: redundant

Flags renames to the same name: `{ a: a }` in destructuring,
`import { a as a }`, and `export { a as a }`.

**Why:** the rename does nothing but makes the reader compare both names to find out.

**Fix:** use the short form: `{ a }`, `import { a }`, `export { a }`.

```js
const { id: id, name } = user;       // flagged
import { readFile as readFile } from 'fs';   // flagged

const { id, name } = user;           // compliant
import { readFile as read } from 'fs';       // compliant: a real rename
```

### js/no-useless-return

**A bare 'return' should not end a function, nor 'continue' a loop body**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: redundant

Flags a bare `return;` that is the last statement of a function body, and a `continue;`
that is the last statement of a loop body.

**Why:** a function returns when it reaches its end anyway, and a loop goes on with its next
iteration when its body ends, so the statement does nothing. It makes readers wonder whether
something was meant to be returned, or whether code after it was lost.

**Fix:** remove the `return;` or `continue;`. A `return;` that ends a function early (inside an
`if`, a loop, or followed by other code) is not reported, nor is a final `return;` in a function
that returns a value on other paths, where it documents the `undefined` result, or a `return;`
that is the whole body (an explicit "do nothing"). Likewise a `continue;` inside an `if` of the
loop, a labeled `continue outer;` (which leaves an inner loop), and a loop body made only of
`continue;` are not reported.

```js
function save(item) {
  store.put(item);
  return;             // flagged
}

for (const item of items) {
  store.put(item);
  continue;           // flagged
}

function save(item) {
  if (!item) {
    return;           // compliant: early exit
  }
  store.put(item);
}
```

### js/no-var

**Use let or const instead of var**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: es2015, style

Flags `var` declarations.

**Why:** `var` is function-scoped and hoisted, so a variable declared inside a block leaks out of it,
can be used before its declaration line (as `undefined`), and is shared by every closure created in a
loop. `let` and `const` are block-scoped and fail loudly when used too early.

**Fix:** use `const` for bindings that are never reassigned and `let` for the others. Check that no
code relied on the variable being visible outside its block.

```js
var count = 0;          // flagged
for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) {} // flagged

const limit = 10;       // compliant
let total = 0;          // compliant
```

Ambient declarations (`declare var`, `declare global { var … }`) are not flagged: TypeScript
requires `var` there.

### js/no-wrapper-object-types

**Primitive types should be used instead of wrapper object types**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: typescript

Flags the built-in wrapper object types `String`, `Number`, `Boolean`, `BigInt`,
`Symbol`, and `Object` used as types.

**Why:** `String`, `Number`, … describe the *wrapper objects* created by `new String('x')`, not the
primitive values code actually passes around. They accept primitives (so mistakes go unnoticed) but
a value typed `Number` cannot be used in arithmetic, and wrapper objects compare by identity
(`new String('a') !== 'a'`). `Object` accepts every value except `null`/`undefined`, primitives
included, which is rarely the intent.

**Fix:** use the primitive types `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `bigint`, `symbol`; use `object`
for "any non-primitive" or `unknown` for "any value".

Only the global names are flagged: a locally declared or imported type with the same name is left
alone.

```ts
function greet(name: String): Boolean {}   // flagged twice
let options: Object = {};                  // flagged

function greet(name: string): boolean {}   // compliant
let options: object = {};                  // compliant
```

### js/not-callable

**Values that are not functions should not be called** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags calls and `new` expressions that always throw a `TypeError` because the callee is not a
function or not a constructor: a literal called like a function (`'text'()`, `[a, b]()`,
`null()`), a class declared in the same file called without `new`, and `new` applied to an arrow
function, an `async` function, or a generator declared in the same file.

**Why:** these calls can never work, so the code path that contains them is broken. They usually
come from a missing semicolon — a line starting with `(` or `[` continues the literal on the line
above (`'use strict'` followed by `(function () { … })()` calls the string) — or from a refactoring
that turned a function into a class or an arrow function.

**Fix:** add the missing semicolon, call the class with `new`, or turn the arrow function into a
regular function or a class.

```js
const message = 'hello'
(function () { run(); })();       // flagged: calls the string 'hello'

class Point { constructor(x) { this.x = x; } }
const p = Point(1);               // flagged: classes need `new`

const make = (x) => ({ x });
const q = new make(1);            // flagged: arrow functions are not constructors
```

Only callees whose nature is certain are checked: literals, and classes or functions declared in
the same file whose binding is never reassigned.

### js/one-var

**Each declaration statement should declare one variable**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: conventions, declarations

Flags `var`, `let` and `const` statements that declare more than one variable.

**Why:** one name per statement is easier to read, to annotate with a type or a comment, to
change from `let` to `const`, and to move or delete in a diff. In a combined statement a `;`
typed instead of a `,` silently turns the remaining names into assignments to undeclared
variables (`var a = 1; b = 2`), and long lists hide which names are initialized.

**Fix:** write one declaration per variable.

```js
let width = 0, height = 0;    // flagged

let width = 0;                // compliant
let height = 0;
```

Not reported: the head of a `for` loop (`for (let i = 0, n = list.length; i < n; i++)`), where
several counters belong together, and `declare` statements.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

### js/overwritten-before-read

**Values should not be overwritten before they are read**

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, copy-paste

Flags a property or map entry that is written and then, a statement or two later,
written again before anything could read it: `obj.a = 1; obj.a = 2;` or
`map.set('k', a); map.set('k', b);`.

**Why:** the first value is lost. This is nearly always a copy-paste mistake: the second statement
was meant to target another property or key, or the first one is left over from an edit.

**Fix:** change the target of one of the writes, or delete the first one.

```js
style.width = w;
style.width = h;              // flagged on the first line: `style.height` was meant

headers.set('Accept', json);
headers.set('Accept', text);  // flagged on the first line

style.width = w;              // compliant
style.height = h;
```

Only straight-line code is considered: the writes must be in consecutive statements (other
assignments to different properties of the same object may sit between them), and the second value
must be simple — no calls, `new`, `await`, or assignments, and no mention of the object — so that
nothing can observe the first value in between. Not reported: writes to `this` in classes that
declare setters, a property first set to a constant (`el.hidden = true; el.hidden = false;` is a
common way to poke a setter or reset state), writes next to an explanatory comment,
and test files, which often assign twice on purpose to exercise setters.

### js/prefer-array-some

**Use some() instead of find() to test whether an element matches**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: array, confusing

Flags `list.find(…)` (or `findLast`) whose result is only used as a condition:
`if (users.find((u) => u.admin))`, `!items.find(…)`, `Boolean(list.find(…))`, or a local
`const found = list.find(…)` that is only ever tested (`if (!found) throw …`).

**Why:** `find` returns the matching element, not whether there is one. Used as a condition, the
answer is wrong whenever the match itself is falsy — `0`, `''`, `false`, `null` — and readers
have to work out that only the existence of a match matters. `some` returns `true` or `false` and
says exactly that.

**Fix:** use `some` with the same callback.

```js
if (users.find((u) => u.admin)) grant();    // flagged
if (users.some((u) => u.admin)) grant();    // compliant

const found = users.find((u) => u.admin);   // flagged: only tested below
if (!found) throw new Error('no admin');

const admin = users.find((u) => u.admin);   // compliant: the element is used
if (admin) grant(admin);
```

Only calls whose first argument is a function literal are checked (a `find(selector)` of a DOM or
query library is something else), and only where the result decides a branch: the test of `if`,
loops, and `? :`, the operand of `!`, `Boolean(…)`, and `&&` / `||` operands in those positions.
Comparisons such as `list.find(…) !== undefined` are left alone. A local is checked only when it
is a `const` or `let` declared inside a function, never reassigned, and used at least once, with
every use in one of those positions.

### js/prefer-arrow-callback

**Callbacks should be arrow functions when they do not need their own 'this'**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, es2015

Flags anonymous `function` expressions passed as callbacks when an arrow function would
behave the same: the function does not use `this`, `arguments`, `super` or `new.target`, and is
not a generator. A `function` expression bound with `.bind(this)` is flagged too.

**Why:** an arrow function is shorter, and it says at a glance that the callback has no `this`
of its own: it cannot be called with a surprising receiver, and code later added to it that
uses `this` sees the enclosing one, which is almost always what was meant. `function () { … }
.bind(this)` is the older spelling of exactly that.

**Fix:** write the callback as an arrow function.

```js
items.forEach(function (item) { total += item.price; });   // flagged
items.forEach((item) => { total += item.price; });          // compliant

button.addEventListener('click', function () {
  this.classList.toggle('active');                          // compliant: uses its own `this`
});
```

Not reported: functions that mention `this`, `arguments`, `super` or `new.target` anywhere in
their text (even in a nested function: the rule stays on the safe side), generators, functions
with a TypeScript `this` parameter, named function expressions (unless `allow_named_functions`
is false and the name is not used inside), and functions passed to AngularJS-style
`controller`, `service` and `provider` registrations, which are instantiated with `new`.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `allow_named_functions` | `true` | Accept named function expressions as callbacks (the name shows up in stack traces, which an arrow function passed as an argument would lose). |

### js/prefer-as-const

**'as const' should be used instead of repeating a literal type**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: typescript, redundant

Flags a literal type that merely repeats the literal value next to it:
`let mode: 'dark' = 'dark'`, `'dark' as 'dark'`, `<'dark'>'dark'`, and class properties declared
the same way.

**Why:** the value is written twice, and the two copies must be kept in sync by hand — change one
and the code no longer compiles, or worse, a later edit updates only one of them. `as const` states
the intent ("keep the literal type") once.

**Fix:** write `'dark' as const` (or drop the annotation on a `const`, which already infers the
literal type).

```ts
let mode: 'dark' = 'dark';          // flagged
const size = 3 as 3;                // flagged
let strict: true = true;            // flagged (string, number, and boolean literals)

let mode = 'dark' as const;         // compliant
let mode: 'dark' | 'light' = 'dark'; // compliant: a wider type on purpose
```

### js/prefer-const

**Variables that are never reassigned should be declared with 'const'**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: convention

Flags `let` declarations whose variables are never assigned again after being
initialized, and `let x;` declarations whose only assignment follows in the same block.

**Why:** `const` tells the reader up front that the binding keeps its value for its whole scope,
so they don't have to scan the rest of the function for reassignments. It also lets tools catch
accidental reassignment.

**Fix:** declare the variable with `const`. A declaration is only reported when *every* variable
it declares is never reassigned (so `let i = 0, n = a.length` in a loop where `i` changes is left
alone), and every declarator has an initializer (or it is the head of a `for…of` / `for…in` loop).
Mutating the object a variable points to (`list.push(x)`, `obj.a = 1`) is not a reassignment.

A variable declared without a value (`let user;`) is reported at its assignment when that
assignment is the only one, is a plain statement in the same block as the declaration, and nothing
uses the variable before it: declare it there with `const` instead.

```js
let total = price * qty;       // flagged: never reassigned
for (let item of items) {}     // flagged

let user;
user = await load(id);         // flagged: declare it here with `const`

const total = price * qty;     // compliant
let count = 0;                 // compliant: reassigned below
count++;
```

With the `destructuring` parameter set to `any`, a declaration whose variables are only partly
reassigned (`let { a, b } = obj; b = 1;`) is reported too, naming the variables that could be
`const` (the declaration has to be split). Top-level `let` in non-module scripts is not reported:
another script can assign it.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `destructuring` | `"all"` | `all`: report a declaration only when none of its variables is reassigned. `any`: also report the never-reassigned variables of a declaration whose other variables are reassigned (the declaration must then be split). |

### js/prefer-for-of

**Index loops that only read the current element should be 'for…of' loops**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: conventions, es2015

Flags index loops (`for (let i = 0; i < list.length; i++)`) whose counter is only used to
read the current element (`list[i]`).

**Why:** when the index itself is never needed, the counter, the bound and the subscript are
three places to get wrong (`<=` for `<`, the wrong array in the subscript, a counter changed in
the body) for no benefit. `for…of` says directly that each element is visited once, in order.

**Fix:** loop over the elements.

```js
for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {      // flagged
  total += items[i].price;
}

for (const item of items) {                   // compliant
  total += item.price;
}

for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {      // compliant: the index is used
  console.log(i, items[i]);
}
```

Only loops of exactly this shape are reported: the counter starts at 0, is compared with `<`
to the `length` of a variable or a property path, goes up by one, and every use of it in the body
is a read of that same `list[i]`. Not reported when the element is assigned, incremented or
deleted (`list[i] = …`), called as a method (`list[i]()`, which would lose `list` as `this`),
or when the counter is used anywhere else, including after the loop. Note that for strings,
`for…of` visits code points rather than UTF-16 units.

Off by default: part of the opt-in `conventions` set.

### js/prefer-number-isnan

**The global 'isNaN' and 'isFinite' should not be used on values that may not be numbers**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, numbers

Flags calls to the global `isNaN()` and `isFinite()` whose argument may not be a number.

**Why:** both functions convert their argument to a number before testing it, and the conversion
has surprising results: `isNaN('')`, `isNaN(' ')` and `isNaN(null)` are `false` (they convert to
`0`), `isFinite('')` and `isFinite(null)` are `true`, and `isNaN('12px')` is `true` while
`parseFloat('12px')` is `12`. Code that uses them to check whether user input "is a number"
therefore accepts empty and blank strings. `Number.isNaN()` and `Number.isFinite()` never
convert: they answer for numbers only.

**Fix:** convert explicitly first and test the result (`Number.isNaN(parseFloat(text))`, or a
regular expression for the accepted format), or call `Number.isNaN(x)` / `Number.isFinite(x)` when
`x` is already a number. For a date, test `Number.isNaN(date.getTime())`.

```js
if (!isNaN(input.value)) { save(input.value); }       // flagged: '' passes
if (isFinite(event.key)) { digit(event.key); }        // flagged: ' ' passes

const n = Number.parseFloat(input.value);
if (!Number.isNaN(n)) { save(n); }                    // compliant
```

Not reported: arguments that are certainly numbers, where the global functions give the same
answer (`isNaN(parseInt(s, 10))`, `isNaN(a / b)`, `isNaN(date.getTime())`, a `number` variable, a
variable whose last assignment before the call stores such a value, the result of a helper named
like `parseLocalizedInt` or `toNumber`), dates (which convert to their time value), and calls
guarded by `typeof x === 'number'`, `x instanceof Date` or a regular expression that checks the
text first (`/^\d+$/.test(x) && isFinite(x)`). In TypeScript, whose declarations only accept numbers,
a call is reported only when the argument is visibly something else: a string, or a value cast to
`any`, `unknown` or `string` to get past the type check.

### js/prefer-readonly

**Private members that are never reassigned should be readonly**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~1 min · Tags: typescript, immutability, conventions

Flags private class members (TypeScript `private` fields, parameter properties, and `#name`
fields) that are never assigned after construction and could be declared `readonly`.

**Why:** `readonly` tells readers that a member keeps the value it got at construction, and lets
the compiler reject a later assignment that would break that assumption. A private member is only
visible inside its class, so whether it is ever reassigned can be decided from the class alone.

**Fix:** add `readonly` to the declaration.

```ts
class Cache {
  private store = new Map<string, number>();     // flagged: never reassigned
  constructor(private http: HttpClient) {}       // flagged
  private hits = 0;                              // compliant: incremented in get()
  get(key: string) { this.hits++; return this.store.get(key); }
}

class Cache {
  private readonly store = new Map<string, number>(); // compliant
  constructor(private readonly http: HttpClient) {}
}
```

Assignments in the constructor itself count as initialization; an assignment anywhere else —
another method, a callback or arrow function created in the constructor, a static block, or a
write through another instance of the class — makes the member mutable. Not reported: static
members, decorated members and parameters (frameworks may assign them), accessors, and classes
that write to `this` through computed keys or `Object.assign(this, …)`. Off by default: the rule
states a style of declaring immutability rather than finding a defect.

### js/prefer-rest-params

**Rest parameters should be used instead of 'arguments'**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: es2015, convention

Flags uses of the implicit `arguments` object inside functions.

**Why:** `arguments` is not a real array (no `map`, `slice`, or `forEach` without borrowing them
from `Array.prototype`), it hides from the signature which values the function accepts, and in
sloppy mode it is linked to the named parameters, so assigning one silently changes the other.
Arrow functions do not even have their own `arguments`.

**Fix:** declare a rest parameter, `function log(...parts)`, which is a real array and shows up in
the signature.

```js
function sum() {
  return Array.prototype.reduce.call(arguments, (a, b) => a + b, 0); // flagged
}

function sum(...values) {                                               // compliant
  return values.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
```

`arguments.length` and `arguments.callee` on their own are not reported.

### js/prefer-spread

**Spread syntax should be used instead of '.apply()'**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: es2015, convention

Flags `Function.prototype.apply` calls that only exist to pass an array as the
argument list: `fn.apply(null, args)`, `obj.method.apply(obj, args)`.

**Why:** since ES2015 the spread operator does the same thing directly, `fn(...args)`, without
repeating the receiver and without the `null`/`undefined` placeholder that readers must decode.

**Fix:** call the function with spread arguments.

```js
Math.max.apply(Math, values);          // flagged
logger.warn.apply(logger, parts);      // flagged
fn.apply(undefined, args);             // flagged
handlers[name].apply(handlers, args);  // flagged
makeHandler().apply(null, args);       // flagged

Math.max(...values);                   // compliant
logger.warn(...parts);                 // compliant
handler.apply(context, args);          // compliant: a different `this` is the point
```

Only calls whose `this` argument is exactly what a plain call would use are reported: the object
the method is read from (by name or by a computed key), or `null`/`undefined` for a plain function
or a function returned by a call.

### js/prefer-template

**Template literals should be used instead of string concatenation**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: no · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: convention, conventions

Flags string concatenation with `+` that mixes string literals with other values.

**Why:** a template literal shows the resulting text in one piece, with the values in place, and
avoids the easy mistakes of concatenation: missing spaces, forgotten `+`, and accidental numeric
addition (`'total: ' + a + b`).

**Fix:** write a template literal: `` `Hello ${name}!` ``. Each concatenation chain is reported
once. Concatenations of literals only are left to `js/no-useless-concat`.

```js
const msg = 'Hello ' + name + '!';     // flagged
const msg = `Hello ${name}!`;          // compliant
const sum = a + b;                     // compliant: no string literal
```

### js/prefer-type-predicate

**Type-testing functions should be declared as type predicates** (incubating)

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: typescript, types

Flags TypeScript functions declared to return `boolean` whose whole body is a `typeof` or
`instanceof` test of their parameter: `function isDate(v: unknown): boolean { return v instanceof
Date; }`.

**Why:** such a function is a type guard in all but name. Declared as returning `boolean`, it tells
the compiler nothing, so callers that test it still have to cast (`if (isDate(v)) (v as
Date).getTime()`). Declared as a type predicate (`v is Date`), it narrows the argument wherever it
is called. Without the `: boolean` annotation, TypeScript infers the predicate by itself; the
annotation is what turns it off.

**Fix:** declare the return type as a predicate on the parameter, or remove the annotation.

```ts
function isDate(v: unknown): boolean {              // flagged
  return v instanceof Date;
}

function isDate(v: unknown): v is Date {            // compliant
  return v instanceof Date;
}
```

Only a single `return` (or an arrow's expression body) testing a parameter is reported, with
`typeof` against `'string'`, `'number'`, `'boolean'`, `'bigint'`, `'symbol'`, `'undefined'` or
`'function'`, or with `instanceof`. Not reported: negated tests (`!==`, `!(x instanceof Y)`), which
narrow in the other branch, `typeof … === 'object'` (true for `null` too), combinations with `&&`
or `||`, destructured parameters, signatures without a body, and methods other than private ones
(a public or overriding method usually implements a boolean contract, such as `matches(other)`,
that callers reach through the base type, where a predicate narrows nothing).

### js/preserve-caught-error

**Errors thrown from a catch block should keep the caught error as their cause**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: error-handling

Flags a new built-in error (`Error`, `TypeError`, …) thrown from a `catch` block that does not
keep the caught error as its `cause`.

**Why:** the caught error carries the real cause — its message, its stack trace, and often a
chain of earlier causes. Throwing a fresh error that ignores it discards all of that, so the logs
only show the generic wrapper and the original failure is lost. Copying the caught error's
message into the new one (`new Error('failed: ' + err.message)`) keeps the words but still loses
the stack trace that says where the failure happened, and the cause chain behind it.

**Fix:** pass the caught error as the `cause` option (supported by all current engines and
Node.js 16.9+; TypeScript needs the `es2022` library). Error reporters and `console` print the
whole chain.

```js
try {
  config = JSON.parse(text);
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error('invalid configuration');                  // flagged: `err` is lost
}

try {
  config = JSON.parse(text);
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error(`invalid configuration: ${err.message}`);  // flagged: the stack is lost
}

try {
  config = JSON.parse(text);
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error('invalid configuration', { cause: err }); // compliant
}
```

Only `throw new …` directly in the `catch` block (not inside a nested function) is checked, and
only for the built-in error constructors, which all accept the `cause` option. An options object
counts when its `cause` mentions the caught error or names a variable declared in the `catch`
block; an options argument that is not an object literal (or that spreads another object) is
trusted. Not reported: a `catch` without a parameter, an `AggregateError` whose list of errors
mentions the caught error, and a new error whose message quotes the caught error's `stack`. With
the `quoted_message` parameter off, a new error that mentions the caught error anywhere in its
arguments is accepted, as it was before.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `quoted_message` | `true` | Also report a new error that only quotes the caught error (`new Error('failed: ' + err.message)`) without passing it as `cause`. |

### js/reduce-without-initial-value

**'reduce' on a possibly empty array should have an initial value** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious

Flags `reduce(fn)` and `reduceRight(fn)` without an initial value on an array that can plainly be
empty: the result of `filter(…)`, of `Object.keys/values/entries(…)`, or an empty literal.

**Why:** without an initial value, `reduce` starts from the first element — and throws
`TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value` when there is none. A filter that
matches nothing, or an object without keys, is a normal situation, so the code works in tests and
fails on the first empty input in production.

**Fix:** pass the initial value as the second argument (`0` for a sum, `''` for a join, `{}` for
an object being built), or check for an empty array first.

```js
const total = items.filter(isPaid).reduce((sum, x) => sum + x.amount);     // flagged
const total = items.filter(isPaid).reduce((sum, x) => sum + x.amount, 0);  // compliant
```

Receivers whose emptiness cannot be seen from the call (variables, parameters, other calls) are
not reported.

### js/redundant-nested-condition

**Nested conditions should not repeat a test the enclosing if already decided** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: suspicious, redundant

Flags an `if` nested directly in another `if` that tests a condition the outer one already decided:
the same condition again inside the `then` branch (always true), its negation there (always false),
or the same condition inside the `else` branch (always false). A part of an outer `a && b`
tested again in the `then` branch counts too.

**Why:** the inner test cannot change the outcome, so either it is dead weight, or — more often —
it was meant to test something else (a copy-paste slip, a variable renamed in one place only), and
the intended check is missing.

**Fix:** test the intended condition, or remove the redundant `if`.

```js
if (user.isAdmin) {
  if (user.isAdmin) grant();       // flagged: always true here
}
if (isOpen) {
  close();
} else {
  if (isOpen) retry();             // flagged: always false here
}

if (user.isAdmin) {
  if (user.isActive) grant();      // compliant
}
```

Only conditions without side effects (names, property reads, literals, comparisons, `!`, `&&`,
`||`) are compared, and only when nothing between the two tests can change them: the inner `if` is
the first statement of the branch, or follows statements that contain no calls, assignments, or
`await`.

### js/redundant-regex-syntax

**Regular expressions should not contain redundant syntax**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: regex, redundant, readability

Flags parts of regular expression literals that say nothing or say it the long way:
quantifiers of exactly one (`a{1}`, `a{1,1}`), long forms of the short quantifiers (`{0,}` for `*`,
`{1,}` for `+`, `{0,1}` for `?`), character classes holding a member twice or a member another
member already covers (`[aa]`, `[a-zx]`, `[\d0-9]`, `[\w_]`), classes of a single letter, digit or
underscore (`[a]`, `[_]`), empty non-capturing groups (`(?:)`, `a(?:|)b`), alternations whose
branches are all single characters (`a|b|c`, `\s|,`), group names that nothing reads, and runs of
literal spaces (`/a   b/`).

**Why:** a regular expression is read symbol by symbol. Redundant parts make the reader wonder
what they add, and a class with a repeated or covered member often means that the author meant a
different member (`[a-zA-z]` for `[a-zA-Z]`). An empty non-capturing group matches only the
empty string and does nothing: it is usually a leftover of an edit, or content that was never
filled in. An alternation of single characters makes the reader check every branch for a longer
one, where a class states in one step that one character is matched. A group name that nothing
reads suggests code that looks the group up, and there is none. A run of spaces cannot be counted
at a glance.

**Fix:** drop the redundant part (or fill in the empty group), use the short form, or state the
count (`/a {3}b/`).

```js
const id = /[0-9]{1}[a-z_a]+/;      // flagged: {1}, and 'a' is inside a-z
const id = /[0-9][a-z_]+/;          // compliant

const time = /\d{1,}:\d{0,1}/;      // flagged: {1,} is +, {0,1} is ?
const time = /\d+:\d?/;             // compliant

const list = /\s*(,|;)\s*/;         // flagged: one of two characters
const list = /\s*([,;])\s*/;        // compliant

line.split(/(?<sep>[,;])/);         // flagged: nothing reads the name 'sep'
line.split(/([,;])/);               // compliant
```

Only literals (`/…/`) are checked. Not reported: escapes (see `js/no-useless-escape`), a
single-character class used to quote a special character (`[.]`, `[*]`) or a space (`[ ]`),
members that only coincide under the `i` flag, classes using set operations (`v` flag), and
classes holding a word without any `|` (`[\spunctuation]`, usually a placeholder that code replaces
in the pattern's source), empty capturing groups (`()`, `(?<name>)`: they still take a group
number, which code may rely on to pad the numbering, and with the `d` flag they record a
position), a pattern that is nothing but an empty group (`/(?:)/`, the usual way to write an
empty regular expression), an empty non-capturing group followed by a digit (`\1(?:)0`, which
keeps a back-reference from swallowing the digit), alternations with a repeated branch (see
`js/no-dupe-disjunctions`) or with a branch that is `.`, a property escape (`\p{L}`) or longer
than one character, and named groups of a literal whose matches code may read: group names are
checked only for a literal passed straight to `test`, `search`, `split`, or `replace` /
`replaceAll` with a replacement string that has no `$<`, and a `\k<name>` in the pattern counts
as a use.

### js/regex-control-character

**Regular expressions should not contain raw control characters** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: regex, suspicious

Flags a regular expression literal that contains a raw, invisible control character (U+0000 to
U+001F other than tab) typed directly into the pattern.

**Why:** the character is invisible in editors and reviews, so the pattern does not read as what it
matches; it usually got there by accident (pasted from a terminal or a binary file), and tools that
normalize or strip control characters change the pattern without anyone noticing.

**Fix:** write the character as an escape (`\x1b`, `\u0000`, `\cA`), which also documents the
intent, or remove it if it is not meant to be there.

```js
const ansi = /␛\[[0-9;]*m/g;     // flagged when ␛ is the raw ESC character
const ansi = /\x1b\[[0-9;]*m/g;  // compliant
```

Escapes for control characters are not reported: matching them on purpose (terminal colors,
binary protocols) is legitimate. A raw tab is not reported either.

### js/regex-lazy-quantifier-at-end

**Lazy quantifiers should not end a searched regular expression** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: regex, suspicious

Flags a lazy quantifier (`*?`, `+?`, `??`, `{n,m}?`) at the very end of a regular expression
literal that is searched for in a string: the pattern of `replace`, `replaceAll`, `split`,
`match`, `matchAll` or `search`, or a literal whose `exec` or `test` is called directly
(`/<!--.*?/.test(html)`).

**Why:** a lazy quantifier repeats as few times as it can, and takes one more repetition only when
the rest of the pattern fails to match without it. At the end of the pattern nothing follows, so
nothing ever asks for more: `.*?` matches the empty string, `\w+?` exactly one character, `{2,5}?`
exactly two. The pattern reads as if it captured "the rest", but it never does. Usually the part
that should end the match (`-->`, a closing quote, `$`) was forgotten.

**Fix:** write what ends the match after the quantifier, or make the quantifier greedy if the
longest run was meant.

```js
html.replace(/<!--.*?/g, '');        // flagged: removes only "<!--"
html.replace(/<!--.*?-->/g, '');     // compliant

const [, key] = /key=(\w+?)/.exec(line);   // flagged: captures one character
const [, key] = /key=(\w+)/.exec(line);    // compliant
```

Not reported: a lazy quantifier followed by an anchor or assertion (`.*?$`, `\w+?\b`, a
lookahead), which makes it extend; a fixed count (`{2}?`); lazy quantifiers inside lookarounds or
inside a repeated group; and regular expressions stored in a variable or built with `new RegExp`,
whose use is not visible where they are written.

### js/regex-too-complex

**Regular expressions should not be too complex**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~20 min · Tags: regex, complexity, readability

Flags regular expression literals whose structure scores above `max` (default 20).

**Why:** a regular expression packs a whole matcher into one line with no names and no comments.
Past a certain size nobody can check by reading whether it accepts what it should, changes become
guesswork, and nested repetitions are where catastrophic backtracking hides.

**Fix:** split the pattern into named parts (`const date = /…/.source`), check the simple parts with
string methods, or use a small parser for structured input; at the least, document the parts.

The score adds, for each element, one point plus one per level of group nesting it sits in:
each alternative after the first (`|`; a list of plain words such as `(get|put|post)` counts as a
single alternative), each repetition of a group with variable length (`(…)*`, `(…)?`), and each
lookaround; repetitions of a single character, class or escape (`\s+`, `[0-9]*`), character
classes and back-references add one point each. Fixed repetitions (`\d{4}`), plain characters, escapes and anchors are free.

```js
// flagged
const semver = /^(0|[1-9]\d*)\.(0|[1-9]\d*)\.(0|[1-9]\d*)(?:-((?:0|[1-9]\d*|\d*[a-zA-Z-][0-9a-zA-Z-]*)(?:\.(?:0|[1-9]\d*|\d*[a-zA-Z-][0-9a-zA-Z-]*))*))?(?:\+([0-9a-zA-Z-]+(?:\.[0-9a-zA-Z-]+)*))?$/;

// compliant: the parts are named
const num = /0|[1-9]\d*/.source;
const ident = /[0-9a-zA-Z-]+/.source;
const semver = new RegExp(
  `^(${num})\\.(${num})\\.(${num})(?:-(${ident}(?:\\.${ident})*))?(?:\\+(${ident}(?:\\.${ident})*))?$`,
);
```

Only literals (`/…/`) are checked.

**Parameters**

| Name | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max` | `20` | Maximum complexity score of a regular expression literal. |

### js/require-yield

**Generator functions should yield** (incubating)

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: generators, suspicious

Flags generator functions (`function*`) whose body never uses `yield`.

**Why:** calling a generator does not run its body; it returns an iterator, and the body only runs
as the iterator is consumed. A generator without `yield` produces no values: loops over it do
nothing, and its code runs lazily — or never, if nobody iterates. Usually the `*` is left over from
a refactoring or the `yield` was forgotten (for example `return item` written instead of
`yield item` inside a loop).

**Fix:** add the missing `yield`, or remove the `*` and make it a plain function.

```js
function* ids(items) {       // flagged: nothing is ever yielded
  for (const item of items) {
    return item.id;
  }
}

function* ids(items) {       // compliant
  for (const item of items) {
    yield item.id;
  }
}
```

Not reported: generators with an empty body or a body that is a single `return` or `throw` (a
placeholder or an empty sequence), and generators that are class or object methods or property
values: those usually implement a protocol — an interface, a base class, `[Symbol.iterator]` —
where yielding nothing is a legitimate answer.

### js/reversed-compound-operator

**Compound assignment operators should not be reversed** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: suspicious, typo

Flags assignments written as `x =+ y`, `x =- y`, or `x =! y`: the characters of a compound
operator (`+=`, `-=`, `!=`) typed in the wrong order.

**Why:** `x =+ y` is valid code, but it means `x = +y` — the value of `y` replaces `x` instead of
being added to it. Likewise `x =- 1` sets `x` to `-1`, and `x =! y` stores the negation of `y`
where a comparison was probably meant. The code runs without error and computes the wrong value.

**Fix:** swap the characters (`x += y`), or, if the unary operator is intended, write it next to
its operand with a space after the `=` (`x = -1`).

```js
total =+ item.price;    // flagged: sets total to the price
count =- 1;             // flagged: sets count to -1

total += item.price;    // compliant
count = -1;             // compliant: spacing shows the intent
```

Only the typo layout is reported: the unary operator directly after `=` and followed by a space.

### js/rules-of-hooks

**React hooks should be called unconditionally at the top level** (incubating)

Severity: **HIGH** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~15 min · Tags: react, hooks

Flags React hooks (`useState`, `useEffect`, any `useXxx(…)`) that are not called
unconditionally at the top level of a function component or custom hook: calls inside an `if`, a
ternary, after `&&`/`||`/`??`, inside a `switch` case, a loop, or a `catch` block; calls placed after
an early `return`; and calls made from a nested function (a callback, an event handler, a helper
defined inside the component).

**Why:** React tells hooks apart only by the order in which they are called during a render. If a
hook is skipped on one render and not on the next — or called a different number of times — every
later hook reads the state of a different one. The result is corrupted state or a
"Rendered fewer hooks than expected" crash, often only in rare code paths.

**Fix:** call hooks at the top level of the component or custom hook, before any early return, and
move the condition *inside* the hook (`useEffect(() => { if (enabled) … })`). Logic that needs a hook
in a callback should read the hook's value in the component and pass it down.

Components are recognised by a capitalised name (also when wrapped in `memo`, `forwardRef`, or
another call assigned to a capitalised name) and custom hooks by a `use` + capital name (also when
wrapped in a call assigned to such a name, including a function memoized with `useCallback`:
`const useValue = useCallback((key) => { … }, [])` is a custom hook whose hooks run in the render
of whoever calls it, not in the render that defines it). Hook calls
in functions that are neither (class methods, plain helpers, test callbacks) are not reported. Only
files that show they use React or Preact (an import from a React-family package, a global
`React`, or a JSX pragma naming React) are checked, since `useXxx` is a common name elsewhere.

```jsx
function Profile({ user }) {
  if (!user) return null;
  const [tab, setTab] = useState('info');   // flagged: after an early return
  if (user.admin) {
    useAudit(user);                          // flagged: conditional
  }
}

function Profile({ user }) {
  const [tab, setTab] = useState('info');   // compliant
  useAudit(user, { enabled: user?.admin });  // compliant: condition moved into the hook
  if (!user) return null;
}
```

### js/self-comparing-assertion

**Assertions should not compare a value with itself**

Severity: **MEDIUM** · Quality: reliability · Kind: bug · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~5 min · Tags: tests, suspicious, copy-paste

Flags test assertions that compare a value with itself: `expect(total).toBe(total)`,
`assert.equal(result, result)`, `expect(a.id).to.equal(a.id)`.

**Why:** such an assertion always passes (or, negated, always fails), whatever the code under test
does. It is nearly always a copy-paste slip — the expected value was meant to be a literal, another
variable, or the result of a different call — and it hides a missing check.

**Fix:** compare against the value the test means to verify.

```js
expect(cart.total).toBe(cart.total);     // flagged: always passes
assert.strictEqual(user.name, user.name); // flagged

expect(cart.total).toBe(30);             // compliant
assert.strictEqual(user.name, 'Ada');    // compliant
```

Only side-effect-free expressions (names, property accesses) are compared; two calls such as
`expect(make()).toEqual(make())` may legitimately return equal values and are not reported. Nor
are assertions in a test whose title says it checks stability (`it('returns the same id on
subsequent calls', …)`): reading a getter twice is then the point of the test.

### js/skipped-test-without-reason

**Skipped tests should say why they are skipped**

Severity: **LOW** · Quality: maintainability · Kind: code-smell · Enabled by default: yes · Remediation: ~2 min · Tags: tests

Flags skipped tests and suites (`it.skip`, `test.skip`, `describe.skip`, `xit`, `xdescribe`, …)
with no comment saying why.

**Why:** a skipped test silently stops protecting the code. Without a reason nobody knows whether
it is flaky, waiting for a fix, or obsolete, so it tends to stay skipped for good, and the next
person to touch it cannot tell whether turning it back on is safe.

**Fix:** say why on the line of the skip or just above it (ideally with an issue reference), or
delete the test if it is no longer relevant.

```js
it.skip('imports a large file', async () => { … });   // flagged

// Flaky on Windows CI, see #1234
it.skip('imports a large file', async () => { … });   // compliant
```

A comment on the same line, on the line directly above, or at the top of the test's body counts
as the reason, and so does a title that states one (`'TODO …'`, `'flaky: …'`, an issue number or link). Not reported:
skips decided at run time (`test.skip(condition, 'reason')`, `this.skip()`, `it.skipIf(…)`),
`todo` tests, skipped tests inside a suite that is itself skipped (the suite is reported), and
files that are not tests. Only the test globals and imported test functions are
checked.

### js/sort-without-comparator

**Numeric arrays should be sorted with a compare function**
